Oregon Cannabis & Hemp Research — Audited Final Report, Parts 0–12

Last audited: 1 November 2026. Cut-off: 1 November 2026. No 3 November 2026 election result is in this file, and none has been filled in by guesswork. This file is an independent audit and corrected rewrite of the 1 November 2026 complete report (Parts 0–12). The original file was not written by the auditor. Every section and detail of the original is retained except where the audit changed it; corrections are applied in place in the rewritten report below. Verify / Unavailable flags are kept only on items still unresolved after the audit.

Federal baseline — as given, not re-audited, and applied throughout: Under the final rule at 91 FR 22714 (effective 28 April 2026), FDA-approved cannabis products and state-licensed medical marijuana are in Schedule III; all other marijuana, including all adult-use, remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is not final. IRS 280E is generally removed as a bar only for qualifying Schedule III medical activity (Treasury/IRS implementing guidance forthcoming; the final rule itself states it makes no tax-liability determination); adult-use activity remains fully subject to 280E. Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes legal effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026 to only the provisions excluding cannabinoids that are not naturally produced or are synthesised; the full total-THC definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply after 11 December 2026. USDA enforcement of the DEA-registered-laboratory hemp testing requirement is delayed to 31 December 2026. The federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider is in force through 11 December 2026. No federal cannabis banking law has been enacted.

Federal-baseline verdict: As a whole, the original report correctly applied Schedule III and 280E relief to medical activity only and treated all adult-use as Schedule I, and made no blanket-rescheduling, blanket-280E-removal, enacted-banking-law, or SB 582 interstate-permission claim. No substantive federal false claim was found. Three items remain Verify because the report quoted no operative federal rule text settling them, and the audit did not settle them either: (1) whether OHA-registered OMMP grow sites count as “state-licensed medical”; (2) whether medical-grade sales by OLCC adult-use retailers count as “state-licensed medical”; (3) whether any tribal medical programme counts as “state-licensed” (no tribal medical programme was identified for any Oregon tribe, so there is no Oregon tribal example at cut-off). Do not publish a yes/no answer on any of these three without opening the operative text of 91 FR 22714 and any IRS/DEA guidance. The ODA phrasing “0.4 mg total THC per container” is corrected everywhere below to “0.4 mg total THC per container” — the milligram cap is not a dry-weight percentage.

Audit counts (exact): 199 rows audited — Confirmed 97, Corrected 31, Removed 4, Unverified 67. Federal baseline 28 rows (14 / 0 / 0 / 14); Parts 0–3: 61 rows (22 / 20 / 3 / 16); Parts 4–8: 65 rows (36 / 7 / 1 / 21); Parts 9–12: 45 rows (25 / 4 / 0 / 16). 97 + 31 + 4 + 67 = 199. Primary sources only were used for Confirmed / Corrected / Removed: ORS and OLIS, OAR / Oregon Bulletin, OLCC, OHA/OMMP, ODA, Department of Revenue, Secretary of State and county elections offices, Oregon courts, USDA AMS, and official tribal sources. News, law-firm blogs, trade press and AI summaries were never treated as confirmation. A page that did not render in text fetch is reported as not opened, never as proof of absence.

How to read the rewrite: Where the audit resolved a conflict, the rewrite uses the resolved figure and date everywhere it appears. Where the audit could not resolve it, the flag and the competing figures are preserved, not averaged. Licence, sales, price and harvest figures that rest only on secondary restatements of OLCC data are flagged “Verify on the OLCC dataset named beside them” — they are not presented as OLCC figures. No personal phone number or email of any individual licence holder is reproduced.

Internal contradictions — resolved and unresolved

Resolved: 1 oz vs 2 oz public possession → 2 oz current (SB 408 (2021)); HB 4002 “effective 1 Sept” vs “eff. on passage / criminal portion 1 Sept” → whole Act 1 Apr 2024, criminal portion operative 1 Sept 2024; Measure 80 percentages → table 53.25% wins arithmetically; Measure 91 distribution 20% local = 10% cities + 10% counties; Measure 119 percentages → different reporting times, neither certified; Ontario “$100 million” → different years/methods, neither official; OMMP 2,101 vs 2,723 → 2,101 addresses designated by 2,723 patients, not a conflict; PRMG 4 vs 8 → 8 governs; “March 2027” vs HB 4121 caps → March 2027 removed; SB 162 “EN” vs “stalled” → enacted ch. 285; HB 4142 dates → effective 5 June 2026, operative 1 Jan 2027; HB 3724 / SB 558 chapters → ch. 68 / reconcile ch. 225 to OLIS overview; Measure 119 appeal → dismissed as moot 28 Apr 2026; edible limits FAQ 50/5 vs OAR 100/10 from 1 Apr 2022 → OAR wins, FAQ stale; medical concentrate 16 oz/day deleted, 5 g medical extract stays Unverified, adult caps 5 g/5 g; grandfather caps → zone-specific figures, 576 deleted; artificially-derived rule number → both exist, different scopes; ODA “0.4 mg on a dry-weight basis” vs baseline “0.4 mg per container” → baseline wording wins; OMMP peak “nearly 80,000” vs OHA 72,517 (July 2015) → OHA series governs for any OHA-attributed peak; CTS 3+ sites “~150” vs OHA 82 → OHA 82 for July 2026; worker permits 51,800 vs 160,000+ → 160,000 apparently includes alcohol permits, never quote for marijuana; OAR 603-048-0700 renderings → Justia current governs, oregon.public.law stale rendering must not be cited; hemp pre-harvest fail → ≥0.35% (OAR 603-048-0600(8)); CBN tension → windows expired, full (4)(b) approval required after 1 July 2025, form checkbox is not approval.

Unresolved (kept flagged, not smoothed over): State tax revenue FY2025/FY2022 series; opt-out city total 82 vs 83; Bend retailer-to-retailer buffer; local-tax approval roundup (“all 111 voted yes” vs “more than 90% approved”); median flower $3.33/g Apr 2025 vs Dec 2025; 2025 sales totals (Jan–Nov $848m vs calendar $926.2m vs $925m); ORS 316.680(1)(i) vs 317.363 range; July 2026 DOR month duplicated; 2025 harvest “over 13m” vs 13.56m; 2025 sales $926.2m vs $925.5m; hemp 2024 counts, 2019 handlers, 2018 acres, 2021–2023 table totals; CAMP Registry search ID 224421 vs 2244211; Warm Springs “later referendum failed” vs 2015 authorisation; retailer hours vs delivery hours (neither quoted from a rule in Parts 0–3 audit); 2026 statewide ballot measure (“none confirmed” vs MPP signature-gathering note); 1 Dec vs 8 Dec hemp renewal deadline.

Limits of this audit, stated plainly: Text-fetch only for several sources — a failed text fetch is “not opened,” never proof of absence or of a login barrier. Same-name guards preserved throughout: Portland OR vs Portland ME, Salem OR vs Salem MA, Springfield OR vs IL/MO, Albany OR vs NY/GA, Medford OR vs MA, Newport OR vs RI, Hillsboro OR vs TX, Ontario OR vs Ontario CA/Canada, plus Portland OR vs Vancouver WA, Ontario OR vs Fruitland/Payette ID, Milton-Freewater OR vs Walla Walla WA.

Oregon Cannabis & Hemp Research — Audited Final Report, Parts 0–12 (Last audited: 1 November 2026)

Research / access date: 1 November 2026, for both runs. Scope: Parts 0–12 complete. This file supersedes the Run 1-only file for counting and coverage; the Run 1 file is preserved separately unchanged.

How to use this file: A single self-contained HTML file that opens offline. Every fact carries a source link and the 1 November 2026 access date in the body text. Where a fact could not be confirmed from a directly opened official page, or where sources conflict, it is flagged Verify or Unavailable and the conflict is preserved, not averaged away. Do not cite a Verify-flagged figure as settled without re-checking the follow-up source named beside it. No personal phone or email of any individual licence holder is reproduced; agency and tribal-government public contacts only.

Two corrections to the brief — read first

  1. ORS 475B is the old number. Current law is ORS 475C — Cannabis Regulation (renumbered in 2021). All current citations use 475C.
  2. HB 4121 is 2024, not 2022. The 21+ adult-use cannabinoid / artificially derived cannabinoid framework originates in HB 3000 (2021), as amended by SB 1564 (2022). HB 4121 (2024) created the hemp-product registration system operative 1 January 2026 and the per-capita licence caps operative 1 January 2025.

Federal baseline — as given, not re-researched

Split scheduling: state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. IRS 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to 280E. Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026; after 11 December 2026 the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026. The federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026. There is no federal cannabis banking law. Whether OHA-registered OMMP grow sites, medical-grade sales by OLCC adult-use retailers, or any tribal medical programme count as 'state-licensed medical' is marked Verify throughout — no tribal medical programme was identified for any Oregon tribe in Part 10, so that question has no Oregon tribal example at cut-off.

Complete-file headlines

  • Market: Oversupply and price collapse continue — median flower about $3.28/g in September 2026, concentrates $14.58/g (record low in that series), Croptober 2025 record 6,289,890 lb; 2025 sales $926.2m, January–September 2026 $683.5m.
  • Licences: The old moratorium is now per-capita caps (HB 4121): 1 producer/retailer per 7,500 residents aged 21+, 1 processor/wholesaler per 12,500; new applications closed, transfers still processed, wholesale-only RAC lift in progress in September 2026.
  • Tax: 17% state retail tax (ORS 475C.674), local tax up to 3% where voter-approved; medical exemption sunsets for sales on/after 1 January 2028 unless extended. Oregon decouples from 280E for state tax (ORS 316.680(1)(i) / 317.363) for both adult-use and medical authorised activity — broader than the federal Schedule III change.
  • Hemp: Oregon runs its own USDA-approved state plan (approved January 2022, ODA primary regulator), not the USDA programme. ODA grower $350 + $875/site, handler $2,275, seed $875, vendor $100/year; OLCC hemp certificate $250 application + $1,000; Hemp Registry $400 initial / $400 renewal (adopted text Verify), 141 applications submitted and 89 approved as of 28 September 2026. Artificially derived cannabinoids generally banned; none approved under OAR 845-026-0415 as of August 2026; the CBN transitional position is an unresolved tension, not a settled approval or ban.
  • Properties (Part 8): ZERO properties meet the strict verified standard (active within 90 days, full street address in the listing, zoning independently corroborated, licence corroborated, no material contradiction). Closest marketed candidates are listed separately with the exact condition each still fails.
  • Tribal / interstate: Only Warm Springs and Cow Creek have USDA-approved tribal hemp plans and DOR tax-rebate agreements; SB 582 (2019) interstate cannabis commerce remains dormant with no agreement located; Ontario (Malheur County) is the only border market with official county sales, and '90% Idaho buyers' is operator/testimony estimate, not official buyer-residency data.
  • Operations / consumer: No per se THC driving limit (ORS 813.010 is impairment-based); no licensed consumption lounge exists; no general OLCC insurance/bonding minimum and no Oregon ownership cap were confirmed; SB 871 (2019) school-administration bill failed — there is no enacted Oregon school-administration statute.

Method and limits — carried forward honestly

Researchers were instructed to open official pages directly, but several direct opens failed on transient worker/rate-limit errors and were not retried, so propositions resting only on indexed text are flagged Verify against the live pages. The affected areas are named in the combined research notes below and in each part's own gaps list. OLIS status in Part 1 §1.9 is a session summary with explicit Verify flags, not a fully OLIS-certified list. Part 8 was not a systematic sweep of every listing site, county assessor parcel, CAMP address search or OWRD record — absence from the searches tried is not proof no property exists. All places are in Oregon unless expressly stated otherwise; Ontario OR is kept separate from Fruitland/Payette ID, Milton-Freewater OR from Walla Walla WA, and Portland OR from Vancouver WA.

Part 0 — Headlines

PART 0 — HEADLINES

# Headline Detail and source (accessed 2026-11-01)
H1 Chronic oversupply; price at or near record lows OLCC market data via secondary reporting: median usable-marijuana (flower) price $3.33/g in April 2025, flat thereafter; $3.17/g in April 2026 (lowest on record in that series) and $3.28–$3.29/g in September 2026; extracts/concentrates $14.58/g in September 2026, a record low. 2015 comparison: ~$14/g (Office of Economic Analysis estimate reported by AP, secondary). Sources: Harris Sliwoski, “Oregon Cannabis: State of the State (2025)” — https://harris-sliwoski.com/cannalawblog/oregon-cannabis-state-of-the-state-2025/ ; Marijuana Herald, 3 Oct 2026 — https://themarijuanaherald.com/2026/10/oregon-marijuana-sales-reach-74-7-million-in-september-683-million-in-2026-as-concentrate-prices-drop-to-record-low-of-14-58-per-gram-2/ ; Todd Harrison Substack, Oct 2026 — https://toddharrison.substack.com/p/the-math-facing-new-york-cannabis . Verify the OLCC monthly file itself for the exact median series before charting it (Part 6 territory).
H2 Record harvest, falling sales value Croptober 2025 was “Oregon’s largest METRC harvest ever, with 6,289,890 pounds reported”, +8.9% on October 2024, itself a record (Harris Sliwoski State of the State 2025, secondary). Calendar sales: $926.2m in 2025, down 3.5% from $960.0m in 2024; 2021 peak $1,184.1m; Jan–Sep 2026 $683.5m, down 1.8% on Jan–Sep 2025 ($696.4m); September 2026 alone $74,656,873 (Marijuana Herald 3 Oct 2026; CannBus Q3 2026 — https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/or_cannmir.html ). The 2019 OLCC warning — 6.5 years of theoretical supply on hand in January 2019 — is the origin of the oversupply narrative (Harrison, secondary).
H3 Licence moratorium is now a per-capita cap, not a calendar sunset — wholesale may be first to reopen HB 4121 (2024), operative 1 Jan 2025 for caps: no more than 1 producer or retailer licence per 7,500 Oregon residents aged 21+, and 1 processor or wholesaler licence per 12,500 residents 21+. OLCC is therefore “not accepting new applications” for those four types outside the buy/sell (“one-in, one-out”) transfer route. Secondary summaries variously phrase the horizon as “under the HB 4121 per-capita caps (no calendar sunset in the cap text)” — that date is not in the HB 4121 cap text returned here and should be treated as Verify (it may reflect an earlier moratorium sunset carried forward in commentary). New in 2026: OLCC opened a Rules Advisory Committee (applications closed 28 Aug 2026; committee met 25 Sep 2026) on lifting the wholesale moratorium alone, after staff concluded active wholesale licences had fallen below the cap; wholesale applications remain closed until rules are adopted — forming the committee does not reopen the portal. Sources: OLIS HB 4121 staff summaries — https://apps.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2024R1/Downloads/CommitteeMeetingDocument/281180 and https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2024R1/Downloads/MeasureAnalysisDocument/81707 ; Cannabis News 29 Aug 2026 — https://www.cannabisnews.org/united-states-cannabis-news/oregon-starts-rulemaking-that-could-lift-cannabis-wholesale-license-moratorium/ ; CannBus Q3 2026.
H4 Licence counts are falling slowly, from a very high base — counts conflict by source and date Late Sep 2026 (CannBus, citing OLCC licence data): 1,348 producers, 752 retailers, 262 processors, 234 wholesalers, 9 laboratories, 1 research certificate. Late 2025 (secondary, via Right Now Oregon): ~1,349 producers, 243 wholesalers, 770 retailers, ~2,649 active recreational businesses in total. Mid-2025: “over 3,000 active marijuana licensees” (MPP / Harris Sliwoski). These totals are not directly comparable — they count different licence universes on different dates and the CannBus total is not summed in the source excerpt. Do not quote a single “total licensees” figure without its date and counting rule. See Conflicts list at end.
H5 OLCC enforcement in 2026 is centred on THC-inflation / lab-sampling fraud 25 Sep 2026: OLCC sent notices to seven licensed testing laboratories, proposing cancellation in some cases and suspension/fines in others, for sampling failures (batch not fully available; too few increments) and, for three labs, intentional addition of kief/concentrate to samples (Category I violations; default sanction revocation). Producer settlement 15 Oct 2026: Cold Frame, LLC (Washington County, producer licence 10078868202) admitted supplying kief to Reference Labs samples on 7 Nov, 27 Nov and 15 Dec 2023, accepted a Letter of Reprimand, and agreed to surrender its licence by 7 a.m. 13 Jan 2027 unless a pending change-of-ownership is approved. Sources (secondary reporting of OLCC notices): Harris Sliwoski 2026 — https://harris-sliwoski.com/cannalawblog/oregon-cracks-down-on-thc-inflation-and-testing-labs/ ; Marijuana Herald Oct 2026 — https://themarijuanaherald.com/2026/10/oregon-marijuana-grower-admits-adding-kief-to-lab-samples-to-artificially-inflate-thc-potency/ . Also in Oct 2026 reporting: OLCC proposed a 75% increase in marijuana licence fees, citing budget/staffing pressure — Verify against the OLCC fee proposal itself; not confirmed as adopted here.
H6 Hemp Registry is now live and enforced Rules under HB 4121 (2024) took effect 1 Jan 2026: all cannabinoid hemp products sold to consumers in Oregon — online or brick-and-mortar — must be registered with OLCC in a Hemp Registry, including gummies, beverages, tinctures, capsules, vapes and smokable flower, with consumer-accessible test results and food-style labelling for edibles. Enforcement was delayed to 1 June 2026 (five-month transition), then began on a complaint-driven, education-first basis. Registration applications opened 1 Jan 2026. Sources (OLCC press releases via GovDelivery): https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/OLCC/bulletins/3fc3d7a (20 Nov 2025 announcement) and https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/OLCC/bulletins/41940ef (June 2026 enforcement start). Bulletin HE2025-01 is the OLCC overview.
H7 Artificially derived cannabinoids: general-market ban with a narrow approval path; CBN sales banned 1 July 2025 absent GRAS / NDIN HB 3000 (2021) + OAR 845-026-0400/0410/0415: products “generally prohibited from containing any artificially derived cannabinoids” and “at this time, none have received approval under OAR 845-026-0415” (OLCC wholesaler fact sheet, Aug 2026 — https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/CBD/FS_CBD_Wholesalers.pdf ). Delta-8 made synthetically from CBD is the paradigm prohibited case. From 1 July 2025, artificially derived CBN may no longer be sold in Oregon (OLCC or general market) unless the manufacturer has a GRAS determination or an FDA New Dietary Ingredient Notification with a “no objections” response (Harris Sliwoski State of the State 2025, secondary — Verify the underlying OAR text for the GRAS/NDIN condition). See §1.5.
H8 Federal hemp redefinition is imminent and Oregon has already answered it — but has not yet conformed ODA bulletin “Recent Federal Hemp Changes: What They Mean for Oregon” (GovDelivery — https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/ORODA/bulletins/3fc8e8e ): “Most federal changes do not take effect until November 2026. During this transition period, Oregon’s hemp program will continue operating under current Oregon laws and rules, including Oregon’s existing definition of total THC.” ODA notes ORS 571.269 gives ODA rule flexibility to adjust once federal guidance is released, and that ODA’s then-current rulemaking (comments to 30 Dec 2025) was developed before the federal legislation and is not related to it. Oregon total THC = (delta-9-THCA × 0.877) + delta-9-THC. The federal bill “does not yet specify how total THC must be calculated” — so the federal figure could end up higher or lower than Oregon’s. As of 1 Nov 2026, no Oregon conforming statute or rule for the 12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026 federal dates was located — Verify / follow-up for Part 7.
H9 Measure 110 partially reversed — but cannabis-tax funding for treatment largely preserved Measure 110 (Nov 2020, effective 1 Feb 2021) decriminalised small-amount possession of all drugs (Class E violation, $100 citation dismissible by health screening) and redirected cannabis tax revenue to the Behavioral Health Resource Network (BHRN). HB 4002 (2024), signed early April 2024, recriminalised simple possession as a drug-enforcement misdemeanor effective 1 Sep 2024, with county deflection programmes (pre-booking deflection → no charge if completed; probation up to 18 months in secondary summaries — Verify the enrolled HB 4002 text for the probation/jail parameters). It preserved much of Measure 110’s treatment funding; FY2025 distribution reporting cited in CannBus Q3 2026: $133.6m distributed, of which $80.7m (60%) to the Drug Treatment and Recovery Services Fund under Measure 110 (secondary calculation — Part 2 territory, Verify against Department of Revenue distribution reports). Cannabis itself was never decriminalised by Measure 110 — adult-use possession within ORS 475C limits was already legal since 1 July 2015, and possession above those limits was already criminal under ORS 475C.337. HB 4002’s direct effect on cannabis is therefore via funding/politics and via recriminalisation of other drugs, not via a change to the cannabis possession limits. Do not describe HB 4002 as “recriminalising cannabis”.
H10 OMMP has shrunk by roughly four-fifths since adult-use sales began — and may be structurally unsustainable on fees Peak “nearly 80,000 patients” (Compassionate Oregon, Feb 2025, advocacy secondary) → “just 15,000 today” in that source; OHA May 2024 subcommittee notes: “OMMP is down to under 15,000 patients and 3,300 grow sites”; July 2026 reporting of the OHA snapshot: 11,625 cardholders and patient purchases 4.2% of dollars in July 2026 ($3,303,950 patient of $79,451,567 total in July 2026, per Cannabis Data Project’s OLCC-feed tabulation — secondary). Grow sites with 3+ patients: 4,200 → ~150, a drop of over 95% (Compassionate Oregon, advocacy — Verify against OHA snapshots). MPP: patient numbers “plummeted by 81% since legal adult-use sales began”. The July 2026 OHA Statistical Snapshot PDF is the authoritative count source — https://www.oregon.gov/oha/PH/DISEASESCONDITIONS/CHRONICDISEASE/MEDICALMARIJUANAPROGRAM/Documents/OMMP_Statistic_Snapshot_07-2026.pdf — but its headline patient total was not extracted in full in this run; Verify the snapshot’s Table 1 total before quoting a single July 2026 patient number.
H11 2025–2026 legislation: what passed, what died (see §1.9 for detail) Enacted 2025: SB 162 (cannabis omnibus — school-proximity restoration, licence terms, hoop houses — per OLCC 2025 Legislative Overview, Verify chapter number), HB 3724 (2025 Laws ch. 68 — advertising/packaging “attractive to minors” → “likely to cause minors to unlawfully possess”), SB 558 (trade-show / trade-sample privileges, per OLCC draft rules — Verify). Died 2025: SB 176 (OMMP overhaul + employment protections for medical patients; died in Joint Ways and Means on adjournment 27 June 2025). Enacted 2026 (short session 2 Feb–6 Mar 2026): HB 4142 (“Ryan’s Law” — hospice/palliative/comfort-care eligibility + facility policy duties; effective 1 Jan 2027 per secondary reporting — Verify operative date in enrolled text) and HB 4162 (2026 Laws ch. 73 — repeals Measure 119 labour-peace requirement, effective 1 Jan 2027). Failed 2026: HB 4139 (omnibus — sent to Ways and Means 16 Feb 2026, never heard again; no intoxicating-hemp tax, no new police powers, no hemp definitions) and SB 1548A (edibles packaging / dispensary siting). Measure 119 (2024, labour peace) was struck down by a U.S. District Court (reported 20 May 2025) and was on appeal; the 2026 repeal moots the forward-looking requirement.
H12 Tax headline (for orientation only — full treatment is Part 2) State retail tax 17%; local tax up to 3% where adopted; OMMP cardholder purchases at retail are exempt from the 17% state tax (ORS 475C.678, cited in secondary OMMP guidance — Verify section number against current ORS). No general state sales tax in Oregon. State economist forecast cut (Sep 2026, secondary): recreational marijuana tax revenue for 2025–27 cut by $14.1m to $261.7m; 2027–29 cut by $51.5m vs prior forecast (CannBus Q3 2026).
H13 No new statewide cannabis ballot measure confirmed for Nov 2026 Secondary 2026 brief states: “No confirmed new statewide cannabis, psychedelic, or drug-policy citizen measure for the 2026 ballot was identified” — Verify against the Secretary of State’s 2026 certified measures list before stating this as fact. A 2025 MPP note about a proposed initiative “cleared legal review and advanced to signature-gathering for November 2026” conflicts with that statement; both are secondary and the conflict is listed at the end.

Part 1 — Laws

PART 1 — LAWS

1.1 Legal status — what is legal, for whom, in one place

Both medical and adult-use marijuana are legal in Oregon under state law. Federal law is different: adult-use remains Schedule I federally, and medical is Schedule III only within the federal baseline’s “state-licensed medical” scope (see Federal baseline section above — three Verify points). State legality does not authorise use on federal land, in federal buildings, or in violation of federal law.

Question Answer (Oregon state law) Authority
Medical use Legal since Measure 67 (1998), implemented 1999. OHA/OMMP registry programme. ORS 475C.770–475C.919 (formerly 475B.785–475B.949 per the Grants Pass case summary); Measure 67 Yes 611,190 (54.60%) / No 508,263 (45.40%), 3 Nov 1998. Source: Ballotpedia — https://ballotpedia.org/Oregon_Measure_67,Medical_Marijuana_and_Regulation_Initiative(1998) (secondary reporting of Secretary of State certified results — Verify against SOS abstract).
Adult-use possession/use by 21+ Legal since 1 July 2015 (Measure 91 effective date). Measure 91, 4 Nov 2014: Yes 847,865 (56.11%) / No 663,346 (43.89%). Source: Wikipedia synthesis of State Elections Division — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_Ballot_Measure_91_(2014) (secondary — Verify against SOS abstract). ORS 475C.301–475C.337.
Retail sales First through medical dispensaries 1 Oct 2015 (early sales); OLCC-licensed retail sales from 2016. Task chronology + OLCC programme history. Verify the exact OLCC first-licence / first-sale dates against OLCC history page in Part 9.
Purchase age — adult-use 21+ only, with valid ID, at an OLCC-licensed retailer. Sale to a minor is a serious licensee violation and possible criminal offence. ORS 475C.317 (under-21 possession/purchase ban, quoted in §1.3); ORS 475C.097 retailer licence.
Purchase age — medical No 21+ floor for cardholders: OMMP patients of any age may be registered; patients 18+ may buy medical-grade items at an OLCC retailer registered for medical sales; minors buy only through a designated primary caregiver (custodial parent/guardian) and “Minor patients are not permitted inside any dispensary area where cannabis is present” (Americans for Safe Access OMMP guide, secondary — Verify against OHA/OLCC rule). ORS 475C.770–475C.919; OLCC FAQ indexed text: “OLCC retailers selling marijuana for medical purposes can sell medical marijuana to OMMP patients 18 years of age or older.”
Possession at home (21+) Up to 8 ounces usable marijuana (plus the other product caps in §1.3). ORS 475C.337(1)(c) — “More than eight ounces of usable marijuana” is unlawful (i.e. 8 oz is the cap).
Possession in public (21+) Up to 2 ounces usable marijuana in a public place (plus other product caps). ORS 475C.337(1)(b).
Home grow (21+) 4 plants per household at any time, regardless of how many adults live there. Plants/products must not be visible from a public place by normal unaided vision. ORS 475C.305(1) as summarised in Brown v. City of Grants Pass (see §1.3 verbatim discussion).
Gifting (21+ to 21+) Permitted within possession limits, without consideration. Any lottery, service fee, contribution or other indirect payment is treated as a sale and must go through a licensed retailer. ORS 475C.301 framework; secondary possession-law summary — https://oregonstatecannabis.org/laws/possession — Verify the gifting section number (ORS 475C.301 / 475C.305) against current ORS text; the no-consideration rule itself is standard Measure 91 implementation and is stated here as a summary, not a verbatim quote.
Public use Illegal for everyone, including OMMP patients. “It is unlawful for any person to engage in the use of marijuana items in a public place” — Class B violation. Includes bars, restaurants, patios, parks, sidewalks, vehicles, and anywhere smoking/vaping tobacco is barred by the Indoor Clean Air Act. ORS 475C.377 — verbatim in §1.3.
Use in a vehicle / driving Use in a vehicle is public use and is unlawful; driving while impaired is DUII. Oregon has no per se THC blood limit for cannabis DUII (secondary — Sativa University summary of OLCC/OHA guidance, Sep 2026 — Verify against ORS 813.010 / DUII statute in Part 12). Transport must be in a closed container / not open for use — Verify the exact open-container section; no open-container statute text was returned in this run (see Gaps).
Federal land / federal buildings State authorisation does not apply. Delivery may not be made “to a consumer who is located on land owned or leased by the federal government” (ORS 475C.117(5)). ORS 475C.117(5) verbatim in §1.6.
Landlord / rental Landlords may restrict use and growing by lease. Secondary summaries stating “cannot use in a rented house” overstate the rule: the statute restricts public use and visibility; a private lease ban is a contract matter, not a criminal ban on private-home use as such. Flagged here to prevent overstatement. ORS 475C.377 (public place only); lease law is Part 12 territory.

1.1.1 “Public place” — the definition that does most of the work

Secondary summaries reproduce the ORS definition as: “a place to which the general public has access and includes, but is not limited to, hallways, lobbies, and other parts of apartment houses and hotels not constituting rooms or apartments designed for actual residence, and highways, streets, schools, places of amusement, parks, playgrounds and premises used in connection with public passenger transportation.”

Verify the current section number for that definition (ORS 475C.009 definitions) against the official ORS chapter page — https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors475C.html (official chapter index, cited as source for ORS 475C.101 in search results). The practical consequence is settled regardless: a private residence room/apartment is not a public place; its hallway, lobby, and any place the public can access is.

Does not change ORS 475C.337 cannabis possession limits. 2024; effective 1 Sep 2024 (criminal portion) Secondary: Drug Policy Watch brief http://drugpolicywatch.info/states/oregon.html ; SFU course summary https://www.sfu-epi.ca/modules/HSCI_180_Lesson_12_Alternatives_to_Prohibition_and_an_Integration_of_the_Course.html — Verify enrolled HB 4002 on OLIS for probation/jail/deflection parameters.
HB 4121 (2024) — omnibus marijuana/hemp; registry + per-capita caps Legislature, passed 7 Mar 2024, signed 20 Mar 2024 (i) Re-enacted HB 3000 §§40, 41a, 42–44 interagency inspection/enforcement provisions that had sunset 1 Jan 2024 (SB 326 (2023) had already removed the sunset from §41 only); (ii) directed OLCC, in consultation with ODA, to establish a registration system for industrial hemp products containing cannabinoids for human/animal consumption, with labelling/packaging minima and civil penalty up to $10,000 per violation — operative 1 Jan 2026; (iii) directed OLCC to adopt rules for standards for approving retail industrial hemp products containing artificially derived cannabinoids, “not more restrictive than the rules applicable to the sale at retail of adult use cannabis items” ( §9, amending ORS 571.309); (iv) established per-capita licence limits for applications on/after 1 Jan 2025: 1 production/retail licence per 7,500 residents 21+, 1 processor/wholesale licence per 12,500 residents 21+; (v) directed OLCC to establish uniform minor-decoy standards (operative 1 Jan 2025), a map of licensed marijuana/hemp sites, and a marijuana-vs-hemp distinguishing methodology; (vi) temporary-permit authority for workers. Emergency clause, effective on passage for specified sections. 2024; registry operative 1 Jan 2026; caps operative 1 Jan 2025 OLIS: https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2024r1/Downloads/MeasureAnalysisDocument/81324 ; https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2024R1/Downloads/MeasureAnalysisDocument/81707 ; https://apps.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2024R1/Downloads/CommitteeMeetingDocument/281180 ; industry summary https://www.agriculturalhempsolutions.com/post/updates-from-the-2024-oregon-legislative-session
SB 162 (2025) — cannabis omnibus policy package Legislature, 2025 (Enrolled per OLCC overview) Per OLCC 2025 Legislative Overview (secondary/official summary PDF): wide-ranging package including repeal of SB 1522 provisions that barred retailers within 1,000 ft of PreK/kindergarten-only locations — restoring the prior standard (schools only, with the ORS 475C.101 500-ft/barrier/grandfather exceptions) and allowing the Commission to grandfather/reissue after a new school appears within 1,000 ft; licence-term and hoop-house provisions (per MPP summary — but MPP says SB 162 “stalled in committee”, directly conflicting with the OLCC overview’s “Enrolled” label — see Conflicts). Do not cite SB 162 as enacted until OLIS status is checked. CONFLICT — Verify on OLIS OLCC overview PDF: https://stage.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/Legislative/2025-Legislative-Overview-Cannabis.pdf ; MPP: https://www.mpp.org/states/oregon/
HB 3724 (2025) — advertising/packaging Legislature, 2025 Laws ch. 68 (per OLCC overview) Directs OLCC to expand advertising/packaging rules to prevent marketing appealing to minors; changes the “attractive to minors” provisions in ORS 475C to advertising “likely to cause minors to unlawfully possess marijuana or marijuana items” (amending ORS 475C.017 and 475C.612 per overview). 2025 Laws ch. 68 OLCC overview PDF (above)
SB 558 (2025) — trade shows / trade samples Legislature, 2025 (per OLCC draft rules) Expands licence privileges at trade shows; changes trade-sample rules. Cited in OLCC 9 Sep 2025 draft proposed rules as legislative implementation. Verify chapter and operative date on OLIS. 2025 — Verify OLCC draft: http://cms.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/rules/Draft-Proposed-2025-Cannabis.pdf
SB 176 (2025) — OMMP overhaul / employment protections — DIED Legislature, 2025 — NOT LAW Would have ended the OHA grow-site registry for personal-medical growers, created OLCC grow-site-administrator designation for 3+ patient sites, required responsible-seller training, required retailers to offer medical-grade items ≤20% total THC / with specified CBD strengths, centralised cannabis data, and — in MPP’s summary — prohibited employers from hiring/firing solely on medical-patient status or a positive metabolite test. Died in Joint Ways and Means; “In committee upon adjournment” 27 June 2025. Must not be cited as law. Dead 27 June 2025 BillTrack50: https://www.billtrack50.com/billdetail/1777436 ; MPP https://www.mpp.org/states/oregon/ ; Compassionate Oregon https://compassionateoregon.org/co-works-to-save-the-oregon-medical-marijuana-program/
HB 4142 (2026) — “Ryan’s Law” medical access Legislature, 2026 Regular (short) Session — ENACTED Expands “debilitating medical condition” to include “the need for hospice, palliative care, comfort care or other symptom management, including [comprehensive] pain management” (wording per Harris Sliwoski summary — Verify against enrolled text); requires an organisation/residential facility designated as an additional caregiver under ORS 475C.791 to allow a qualifying patient/resident to engage in medical use on premises, maintain a written policy on procurement/storage/administration/disposal, and provide staff education; exempts hospitals and hospital-affiliated clinics; protects facilities/staff/contractors from certain state criminal liability; prohibits the Oregon State Board of Nursing from disciplining a nurse for discussing medical cannabis (per summaries). Amends ORS 475C.777, 475C.791, 475C.792, 475C.883, 475C.916. Effective date in enrolled text: “91st day following adjournment sine die” in the introduced digest, but secondary reporting gives 1 Jan 2027 as the operative/effective date for the eligibility change — Verify which date controls (see Conflicts). Also: for registrations issued/renewed/changed from 1 Jan 2026, a medical grow site on another person’s property requires a notarised property-owner consent form (per Mycannabis summary of 2026 rules — Verify rule citation). 2026; sine die 6 Mar 2026 Enrolled text (LegiScan mirror): https://legiscan.com/OR/text/HB4142/id/3387743/Oregon-2026-HB4142-Enrolled.pdf ; OLIS amendments: https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2026R1/Downloads/MeasureDocument/HB4142/House Amendments to Introduced ; Harris Sliwoski summary https://www.mondaq.com/unitedstates/topics/1759618/oregons-new-cannabis-laws-2026-edition
HB 4162 (2026) — repeal of Measure 119 labour-peace requirement Legislature, 2026 — ENACTED, 2026 Laws ch. 73 Repeals the Ballot Measure 119 (2024) requirement that cannabis licensees enter labour-peace agreements. Effective 1 Jan 2027. Background: a U.S. District Court struck Measure 119 down (reported 20 May 2025) as unconstitutional; appeal to the Ninth Circuit was pending and expected to be dismissed after repeal (secondary). 2026 Laws ch. 73; effective 1 Jan 2027 Drug Policy Watch brief; Harris Sliwoski 2026 summary (above) — Verify chapter on OLIS.
HB 4139 (2026) — omnibus cannabis — FAILED Legislature, 2026 — NOT LAW Would have added police powers for agencies, hemp definitions, and a tax on intoxicating hemp items. Shuttled to Ways and Means 16 Feb 2026, never heard again. Must not be cited as law. Dead (short session) Harris Sliwoski 2026 summary (above)
SB 1548A (2026) — edibles packaging / dispensary siting (“public health” bill) — FAILED Legislature, 2026 — NOT LAW Would have added edibles packaging and dispensary siting (buffer) requirements. Failed in the 2026 short session. Must not be cited as law. Dead Harris Sliwoski 2026 summary (above)
Measure 119 (2024) — labour peace (ballot measure, now repealed prospectively) Voters, Nov 2024 — struck down; repealed eff. 1 Jan 2027 Required cannabis licensees to enter labour-peace agreements with unions. District court held unconstitutional (May 2025, secondary). Repealed by HB 4162 (2026). Do not advise clients that Measure 119 currently imposes an operative duty without checking the litigation/repeal status on the date of advice — Verify Ninth Circuit disposition. 2024–2027 (repeal) Secondary only in this run
Measure 110 (2020) — Drug Addiction Treatment and Recovery Act (DATRA) Voters, Nov 2020; effective 1 Feb 2021 Decriminalised small-amount possession of all drugs to a Class E violation ($100 citation, dismissible by health screening); created BHRNs funded substantially by cannabis tax revenue. Partially reversed by HB 4002 (2024) for possession (see above); funding structure largely preserved. Cannabis possession within ORS 475C limits was unaffected. 2020; possession portion superseded 1 Sep 2024 Secondary summaries in Part 0 H9 — Verify enrolled Measure 110 / HB 4002 texts on OLIS for funding-formula detail (Part 2).
SB 420 (2019) — marijuana record set-aside (expungement) Legislature, 2019 Expedited petition-based set-aside / sealing for marijuana offences, no filing fee, no ten-year clean-record requirement; district attorney 30 days to object (per Drug Policy Watch summary — secondary). Full treatment is Part 12; cited here only because Part 1 readers routinely confuse it with Measure 110. Verify ORS 137.225 as amended. 2019 Drug Policy Watch brief http://drugpolicywatch.info/states/oregon.html

1.2.2 ORS Chapter 475C — the sections that matter for Part 1 (with verbatim text where returned)

ORS 475C.009 — Definitions. The chapter’s definitions section (formerly 475B.015). Key definitions as returned in HB 3000 / ORS 571.269 cross-references: “adult use cannabinoid” (see §1.5), “marijuana” (plant Cannabis family Cannabaceae, any part, seeds — excluding industrial hemp as defined in ORS 571.269 and prescription drugs), “marijuana grow site” (location registered under ORS 475C.792), “marijuana processing site” (registered under ORS 475C.815). Verify the full current 475C.009 text on the official ORS page; only these cross-referenced fragments were returned.

ORS 475C.013 — Construction / employment. Secondary summary (American Screening Corp, citing the statute): the adult-use statutes “may not be construed to amend or affect state or federal law pertaining to employment matters.” Together with ORS 475C.780 (medical: “nothing in the Oregon Medical Marijuana Act requires an employer to accommodate the medical use of marijuana in the workplace”), this is why Oregon has no general off-duty cannabis employment protection as of 1 Nov 2026. See §1.8 for the full employment analysis. Verify both sections’ verbatim text on the official ORS page.

ORS 475C.033–475C.117 — Licensing framework (summary; Part 4 territory for fees/tiers). Includes producer (475C.065), processor (475C.085), wholesaler (475C.093), retailer (475C.097), laboratory (475C.548), research certificate, worker permits (475C.269/475C.273), delivery (475C.117, verbatim in §1.6), proximity (475C.101, verbatim in §1.6), and revocation grounds (475C.265, excerpt in §1.6 enforcement note).

ORS 475C.149 — Medical-grade retail registration. Allows a retailer registered under this section to sell medical-grade cannabinoid products, concentrates and extracts at retail “in the same manner that rules … allow a marijuana retailer to sell general use” items, except where differentiation is required. Cited in ORS 475C.097(3)(e). Verify full text.

ORS 475C.177 — Cannabis Tracking System (CTS). Duty to develop/maintain a system for tracking transfer of marijuana items. Implemented as Metrc. See §1.7.

ORS 475C.205 — (ownership / financial interest provisions, cited in retailer rules). Not quoted in this run — Verify if needed for Part 4.

ORS 475C.229 — Import/export prohibition. Summary as returned: “Prohibition against importing or exporting marijuana items”, with “marijuana item” including an industrial hemp commodity/product exceeding the greater of (A) 0.3% total delta-9-THC or (B) the concentration allowed under federal law; and a carve-out where the item is industrial hemp not exceeding 1% total delta-9-THC (for the criminal-penalty removal in HB 3000). Verify full text and the 1% carve-out’s current status — HB 3000’s summary says criminal penalties were removed for hemp import/export over 0.3% up to 1%; whether that carve-out survives in current 475C.229 text was not confirmed section-by-section here.

ORS 475C.265 — Grounds for revocation, suspension or restriction. Verbatim excerpt as returned (oregon.public.law — https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_475c.265 ):

“(1) Subject to subsection (3) of this section, the Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission may revoke, suspend or restrict a license issued under ORS 475C.005 … to 475C.525 … or 475C.548 … or require a licensee or licensee representative to undergo training if the commission finds or has reasonable ground to believe that the licensee or licensee representative: (a) Has violated a provision of ORS 475C.005 … to 475C.525 … or 475C.540 … to 475C.586 … or a rule adopted under [those sections]; (b) Has diverted marijuana to the interstate market or an illicit market or has diverted resources to a criminal enterprise. … [Has] introduced into the marijuana industry regulated under [ORS 475C] cannabinoids or marijuana not produced or processed by a licensee and not tracked in the system developed and maintained under ORS 475C.177 … [Has] made any false representation or statement to the commission regarding compliance … in order to induce or prevent action by the commission. (e) Is in the habit of using alcoholic liquor, habit-forming drugs, marijuana or controlled substances to excess. … [Has] misrepresented to a customer or the public any marijuana items sold by the licensee or licensee representative.”

Plus retailer tax-nonpayment revocation: the Commission “may revoke a marijuana retailer license … if the licensee fails to: (A) Pay the tax as required under ORS 475C.682 … twice in any four consecutive quarters and the Department of Revenue has issued … a distraint warrant under ORS 475C.688”. History not returned for 475C.265 — Verify last amendment on official ORS page.

ORS 475C.269 / 475C.273 — Worker permits. Verbatim (Justia 2025 ORS — https://law.justia.com/codes/oregon/volume-14/chapter-475c/section-475c-269/ ):

“(1) An individual who performs work for or on behalf of a licensee or a laboratory licensed under ORS 475C.548 must have a valid permit or temporary permit issued by the Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission under ORS 475C.273 if the individual participates in: (a) The delivery, possession, production, propagation, processing, sampling, securing, selling or testing of marijuana items at the premises or laboratory for which the license has been issued; (b) The recording of [that activity]; or (c) The verification of any document described in ORS 475C.217. (2) A licensee or a laboratory … must verify that an individual has a valid permit or temporary permit … before allowing the individual to perform, or continue to perform, any work described in subsection (1) … [Formerly 475B.261; 2022 c.117 §4; 2024 c.16 §27]”

OLCC FAQ indexed text adds: “The Marijuana Worker Permit fee is $100 and is due upon application submission.” OAR 845-025-5500 (effective 31 Mar 2025 per Cornell LII — https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/oregon/Or-Admin-Code-SS-845-025-5500_v2 ) mirrors the permit requirement, adds direct supervision, requires the permit-holder to carry the permit at all times on retail premises and to notify the Commission in writing within 10 days of any felony conviction. History for 845-025-5500 as returned: OLCC 14-2024, amend filed 12/20/2024, effective 3/31/2025.

ORS 475C.301 / 475C.305 — Homegrown / household production. As summarised in Brown v. City of Grants Pass, 414 P.3d 898 (2018) (Oregon Court of Appeals, via Midpage — https://app.midpage.ai/document/brown-v-city-of-grants-pass-6533494 ):

“The AMCA also legalizes the noncommercial production, making, processing, possession, and storage of marijuana and marijuana products ‘at a household.’ ORS 475B.301(1) [now 475C.301]. Persons who grow marijuana plants at home for personal noncommercial use are not subject to the licensing and permitting requirements that apply to commercial producers, processors, wholesalers, and retailers … ‘if the total amount of homegrown marijuana at the household does not exceed four marijuana plants at any time.’ … ORS 475B.015(10) [now 475C.009] defines ‘homegrown’ marijuana as marijuana plants or marijuana products ‘grown or made by a person 21 years of age or older for noncommercial purposes.’ ORS 475B.306 [now 475C.306] provides that a person may not ‘produce, process, possess or store homegrown marijuana’ or marijuana products where they ‘can be seen by normal unaided vision from a public place.’”

That case also holds Grants Pass’s indoor-only home-grow ordinance was not preempted by the seed law (ORS 633.738) because marijuana growing is expressly exempted from that preemption (ORS 475C.928 / 475C.940 / 475C.486 as cited there) — i.e. local governments may impose their own home-grow manner rules within the state framework. Part 3 will need to survey those local rules; Part 1 notes only that state law does not itself impose an indoor-only rule.

ORS 475C.317 — Under-21 ban. Verbatim (Justia 2025 — https://law.justia.com/codes/oregon/volume-14/chapter-475c/section-475c-317/ ):

“(1)(a) A person under 21 years of age may not possess, attempt to purchase or purchase a marijuana item. (b) For purposes of this subsection, purchasing a marijuana item includes accepting a marijuana item, and possessing a marijuana item includes consuming a marijuana item, provided that the consumption of the marijuana item occurred no more than 24 hours before the determination that the person consumed the marijuana item. (2) Except as authorized by the [Commission] by rule, or as necessary in an emergency, a person under 21 years of age may not enter or attempt to enter any portion of a premises that is posted or otherwise identified as being prohibited to the use of persons under 21 years of age. (3)(a) Except as provided in paragraph (b) … a person who violates subsection (1) or (2) … commits a Class B violation. (b) A person commits a Class A violation if the person violates subsection (1) … by reason of possessing a marijuana item while the person is operating a motor vehicle … (4) … the court shall order that, when a person violates subsection (1) …, the person’s driving privileges … be suspended pursuant to ORS 809.260 and 809.280 … [with possible hardship-permit recommendation].”

Exceptions in subsections (7)–(8) for persons acting under Commission / law-enforcement / licensee direction to investigate under-21 sales. Medical cardholders under 21 are governed by the OMMP code (ORS 475C.770–475C.919), not by this adult-use ban — Verify the interaction section (ORS 475C.783 registry-card / receipt rules) before advising a minor cardholder.

ORS 475C.337 — Unlawful possession by 21+ (the possession-limit statute). Verbatim operative text (LawServer mirror of ORS — https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/oregon/or-statutes/oregon_statutes_475c-337 ; corroborated by Justia/oregon.public.law summaries):

“(1) Except for licensees and licensee representatives acting in accordance with ORS 475C.005 to 475C.525 and any rule adopted under [those sections], it is unlawful for any person 21 years of age or older to possess, knowingly or intentionally: (a) An amount of plants in the genus Cannabis within the plant family Cannabaceae in excess of the amount allowed under ORS 475C.305 (1). (b) More than two ounces of usable marijuana in a public place. (c) More than eight ounces of usable marijuana. (d) More than 16 ounces of cannabinoid products in solid form or cannabinoid concentrates. (e) More than 72 ounces of cannabinoid products in liquid form. (f) More than one ounce of cannabinoid extracts. (g) A cannabinoid extract that was not purchased from a marijuana retailer that holds a license issued under ORS 475C.097. (2) Except as provided in subsection (3) …, unlawful possession of a marijuana item is a Class A misdemeanor. (3) Unlawful possession … is: (a) A Class B violation, if the amount possessed is not more than two times the applicable maximum amount specified in subsection (1)(a) to (f) …; (b) A Class B misdemeanor, if the amount possessed is more than two times, but not more than four times, the applicable maximum …; (c) A Class C felony, if the amount possessed is: (A) More than 16 times the applicable maximum amount specified in subsection (1)(a), (c), (d), (e) or (f) …; (B) More than eight pounds of usable marijuana in a public place; or (C) More than one-quarter ounce of cannabinoid extract that was not purchased from a marijuana retailer …; (d) A Class B felony, if: (A) The amount possessed is more than 32 times the applicable maximum amount specified in subsection (1)(a), (c), (d), (e) or (f) …; or (B) The violation is a marijuana offense involving reckless unlawful conduct under ORS 475C.353 (5) or … knowing unlawful conduct under ORS 475C.353 (6). [Formerly 475B.337; 2023 c.209 § 7]”

Note the asymmetry the table in §1.3 must preserve: possession caps (above) differ from retail daily sale caps (below). Do not conflate them.

ORS 475C.349 — Unlawful manufacture (home-grow excess). Secondary summary: growing more than 4 but no more than 8 plants at a household = Class B misdemeanor (up to 6 months / $2,500 in that summary). Verify the tier structure against current 475C.349 text; the multiplier logic in 475C.337(3) is the safer citation for excess-quantity grading generally.

ORS 475C.377 — Public use ban. Verbatim (Justia 2025 — https://law.justia.com/codes/oregon/volume-14/chapter-475c/section-475c-377/ ):

“(1) It is unlawful for any person to engage in the use of marijuana items in a public place. (2) A violation of subsection (1) of this section is a Class B violation. [Formerly 475B.381]”

ORS 475C.540–475C.586 — Testing, labelling, packaging definitions and related provisions (including ORS 475C.544 testing). Implemented by OAR 333 Divisions 7–8 (OHA testing) and OAR 845 Division 25 (OLCC packaging/labelling) and Division 26 (potency/serving limits). Full text not reproduced here — Part 11 territory for testing detail; Part 1 cites the operative OAR rules in §1.5–§1.6.

ORS 475C.600–475C.648 — Local government / opt-out / tax provisions (including local tax authority up to 3% and opt-out by ordinance referred to voters). Detail is Parts 2–3; the existence of the opt-out mechanism is noted here only. Verify section numbers for opt-out vs tax on the official chapter page.

ORS 475C.678 / 475C.682 / 475C.688 — Retail tax collection and enforcement. 475C.678 is cited in secondary OMMP guidance as the medical-exemption section (“Registered OMMP cardholders are exempt from Oregon’s state retail cannabis tax under ORS 475C.678”); 475C.682 is the collection section cited in 475C.265; 475C.688 is the distraint-warrant enforcement section. Tax rates/distribution are Part 2 — Verify 475C.678’s current text before citing it as the exemption authority, as the exemption may sit in the tax chapter’s cardholder-sale rule rather than in 475C.678 itself.

ORS 475C.770–475C.919 — Medical code (OMMA as merged). Key sections: 475C.777 (debilitating medical condition — as amended by HB 4142 (2026)); 475C.780 (employer non-accommodation); 475C.783 (registry application / 35-day receipt rule, referenced in HB 4142 amendments); 475C.791 (designated primary caregiver / additional caregiver — organisations/residential facilities); 475C.792 (grow-site registration); 475C.806 (plant possession limits — verbatim in §1.4); 475C.809 (usable-marijuana possession — 24 oz joint cardholder+caregiver, per secondary OMMP summaries); 475C.815 (processing-site registration); 475C.816 (grower reporting of harvest amounts — the 12 lb outdoor / 6 lb indoor per-mature-plant caps in the State v. T.T. summary, Verify current text); 475C.831 / 475C.834 (older numbering in case summaries for plant/usable limits — now consolidated in 475C.806/475C.809; do not cite 831/834 without checking renumbering); 475C.883 / 475C.916 (amended by HB 4142); 475C.913 (OHA rulemaking / condition-petition process).

ORS 475C.523 — Cannabis reference laboratory. Verbatim excerpt (Justia 2025 — https://law.justia.com/codes/oregon/volume-14/chapter-475c/section-475c-523/ ): ODA, in consultation with OHA and OLCC, “shall establish a cannabis reference laboratory to provide regulatory and technical support in the enforcement of ORS 475C.005 to 475C.525, 475C.540 to 475C.586, 475C.600 to 475C.648, 475C.770 to 475C.919 and 571.260 to 571.348”, able to verify/develop analytical methods, confirm lab results, and provide QC samples; agencies may independently require reference-lab testing where non-compliance is suspected. History: “[2023 c.519 §2]” (HB 2931 (2023) per Harris Sliwoski). Note the 2025 “United For Cannabis Workers” measure note appended to this section in Justia — that is a ballot-measure note, not part of 475C.523 itself; do not confuse it with enacted law.

1.2.3 ORS Chapter 571 — hemp (ORS 571.260–571.348)

ORS 571.269 — Definitions for ORS 571.260–571.348; rules. Verbatim fragments as returned (LawServer — https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/oregon/or-statutes/oregon_statutes_571-269 ):

“As used in ORS 571.260 to 571.348: (1) ‘Adult use cannabinoid’ has the meaning given that term in ORS 475C.009. … (3) ‘Agricultural hemp seed’ means Cannabis seed: … (6) ‘Crop’ means industrial hemp grown under a single license. (7) ‘Grower’ means a person, joint venture or cooperative that produces industrial hemp. (8) ‘Handler’ means a person, joint venture or cooperative that receives industrial hemp for processing into commodities, products or agricultural hemp seed and any other activities identified by the State Department of Agriculture by rule. (9)(a) ‘Industrial hemp’: (A) Means the plant species Cannabis sativa that has a tetrahydrocannabinol concentration that complies with the concentration specified by the department by rule; and (B) Has the meaning given that term as it is further defined by the department by rule. (b) ‘Industrial hemp’ does not mean industrial hemp commodities or products. (10) ‘Industrial hemp concentrate’ means an industrial hemp product obtained by separating cannabinoids from industrial hemp by: (a) A mechanical process; … (11) ‘Industrial hemp extract’ means an industrial hemp product obtained by separating cannabinoids from industrial hemp by: … (12) ‘Licensee’ means a grower, handler, agricultural hemp seed producer or other person licensed under ORS 571.281. [Formerly 571.300; 2021 c.542 §§21, 21a]”

The deliberate delegation in (9)(a) is the key to the federal-conformity question: Oregon’s hemp definition is set by ODA rule, not fixed at 0.3% in the statute itself. That is why ODA could say ORS 571.269 “allows ODA to define THC concentration requirements in rule, giving Oregon room to adjust once federal guidance is released” (ODA GovDelivery bulletin, above).

ORS 571.281 — Hemp licensing (grower/handler/seed producer licences; criminal-records check; 10-year felony controlled-substance bar for growers per HB 3000 summary). Verify current fee/term text — Part 7 territory.

ORS 571.309 — OLCC hemp-product standards (as amended by HB 4121 (2024) §9). Verbatim operative amendment as returned in the HB 4121 industry summary:

“571.309. The Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission, in consultation with the State Department of Agriculture, shall adopt rules to establish: (1) The maximum concentration of tetrahydrocannabinol permitted in a single serving of an industrial hemp product; (2) The maximum concentration of any other cannabinoid, adult use cannabinoid or artificially derived cannabinoid that is permitted in a single serving of an industrial hemp product; [and] (3) The number of servings that are permitted in a package of industrial hemp products[.] and (4) Standards for approving industrial hemp products that contain artificially derived cannabinoids and that are intended for sale at retail. The rules adopted under this subsection may not be more restrictive than the rules applicable to the sale at retail of adult use cannabis items.“

That last sentence is the HB 4121 compromise: it requires an approval-standards rulemaking for artificially derived cannabinoids at retail, but caps its restrictiveness at the adult-use retail standard. It does not by itself approve any artificially derived cannabinoid — OAR 845-026-0415 remains the approval gate, and as of Aug 2026 “none have received approval” under it (see §1.5).

ORS 571.330 / 571.333 — Testing / labelling for hemp commodities/products (referenced in ORS 475C.523 as the enforcement provisions for hemp testing). Verify full text.

OAR 845-025-7000 to 7190 Packaging and labelling (definitions through effective-date rule) See §1.6. Key rules: 7000 definitions (“attractive to minors”); 7020 child-resistant packaging / exit bag; 7030 labelling for sale to consumer; 7090 edible labelling; 7160 pre-approval. https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_845-025-7030 ; https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_845-025-7090 ; https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_845-025-7160

HB 3724 (2025) changed the statutory test to “likely to cause minors to unlawfully possess” — the OAR text must be checked for conforming amendments. Via Cannabis News settlement reporting https://www.cannabisnews.org/united-states-cannabis-news/oregon-olcc-cold-frame-kief-lab-samples-thc-potency-license-surrender/

OAR 845-026-0210 Adult-use edible potency / serving limits Recreational edibles: up to 100 mg THC per package, up to 10 mg per serving, from 1 Apr 2022 (prior: 50 mg / 5 mg). Solid edibles over 55 mg per package must be scored. See §1.3. OLCC IB2022-03 (above); Salem News summary http://Salem-News.Com/articles/april082022/oregon-cannabis.php
OAR 845-026-0220 Medical-grade edibles Medical-grade edibles: up to 100 mg THC per package, no serving-size requirement, no scoring requirement (per IB2022-03). A retailer may NOT sell a medical-labelled edible to a recreational consumer (warnings differ; medical label states OMMP-patients-only). OLCC IB2022-03
OAR 845-026-0300 Hemp: sale to minors (0.5 mg test) See §1.5: a hemp product may be sold to a minor only if it contains <0.5 mg total THC in the entire unit of sale, compliance testing was sensitive enough to prove it, and it contains no artificially derived cannabinoids. OLCC wholesaler fact sheet (above)

Full Table 3 was not returned — Verify Table 3 before quoting any non-edible category limit. OLCC wholesaler fact sheet (above)

OLCC wholesaler fact sheet (above)

Number conflict — Verify the correct division/rule number on the OAR site; substance (July 2022 general-market ban on non-compliant artificially derived cannabinoids) is consistent across sources. See Conflicts

1.2.5 What is NOT law (must not be cited as law)

  • HB 4139 (2026), SB 1548A (2026), SB 176 (2025) — failed/dead (see table). HB 3724/SB 162/SB 558 (2025) — SB 162 status is conflicted (see above); HB 3724 and SB 558 are stated as enacted only on the OLCC overview/draft-rules secondary-official summaries and still require OLIS chapter confirmation.
  • Proposed ODA hemp-rule updates (Nov 2025) — proposed rulemaking, comments to 30 Dec 2025, expressly “not related to” the federal hemp changes. Not law until adopted.
  • OLCC wholesale-moratorium RAC (2026) — advisory-committee formation, not a rule change; wholesale applications remain closed.
  • OLCC fee-increase proposal (Oct 2026 reporting, 75%) — proposal only in the reporting returned; not confirmed as adopted.
  • Any “HB 4121 per-capita caps (no calendar sunset) moratorium expiry” — commentary shorthand, not a cap-statute sunset found in this run.
  • Federal hemp dates (12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026) — federal law as supplied in the baseline; Oregon has not (as of 1 Nov 2026, on the sources located) enacted a conforming change. Do not describe Oregon hemp products as already subject to the 0.4 mg/container cap before 11 Dec 2026, and do not describe the cap as an Oregon rule.

1.3 Possession, home grow, public consumption, vehicles, gifting, product types and THC limits

1.3.1 Possession limits — possession vs purchase (do not conflate)

A. Possession caps — ORS 475C.337(1) (verbatim in §1.2.2). For a person 21+ (licensees acting within licence excepted):

Item Public-place cap Anywhere / at-home cap
Usable marijuana (dried flower/leaves) 2 ounces 8 ounces
Cannabinoid products in solid form or cannabinoid concentrates 16 ounces (combined category in the statute) 16 ounces
Cannabinoid products in liquid form 72 ounces 72 ounces
Cannabinoid extracts 1 ounce, and only if purchased from a licensed retailer (ORS 475C.097) 1 ounce, same retailer-purchase condition
Plants No more than allowed under ORS 475C.305(1) — i.e. 4 per household (adult-use) Same
Any extract NOT purchased from a licensed retailer Unlawful as such under (1)(g); over ¼ ounce = Class C felony regardless of other caps (475C.337(3)(c)(C)) Same

Grading for excess (475C.337(3)): ≤2× the cap = Class B violation; >2× to 4× = Class B misdemeanor; >16× (for (a),(c),(d),(e),(f) items), >8 lb usable in public, or >¼ oz unlicensed extract = Class C felony; >32× = Class B felony; plus the reckless/knowing commercial-offence aggravator in (3)(d)(B). Default (no (3) trigger) = Class A misdemeanor under (2). Secondary summaries that state “over 8 lb = felony” or “over 2 lb = Class A misdemeanor” are rough paraphrases of this multiplier scheme — use the statute’s multipliers, not the paraphrase.

B. Retail daily sale limits — OLCC FAQ / OAR 845-025-2800 (adult-use consumer, per transaction / per day). Indexed OLCC FAQ text (official page, search-indexed — direct open failed, see Method):

“A customer cannot purchase more than the following amounts at any one time or within one day: - Two ounces of usable marijuana; - 16 ounces of a cannabinoid product in solid form; - 72 fluid ounces of a cannabinoid product in liquid form; - 5 grams of cannabinoid extracts or concentrates; - 5 grams of cannabinoid products intended for inhalation; - Four immature marijuana plants; and - 10 marijuana seeds.”

Note the differences from possession caps: the sale cap for extracts/concentrates is 10 grams (not the 1-ounce possession cap for extracts, and not the 16-ounce solid/concentrate possession category — the sale rule splits extracts/concentrates from inhalation products, each 10 g). OLCC IB2022-03 confirms a retailer may sell e.g. 5 g concentrate/extract plus 5 g inhalation product in one day (the categories are separate). Medical daily sale limits are in §1.4.

C. OHA personal-possession summary (corroboration). OHA Cannabis Laws page (indexed official text): “The Personal possession limits for a person over age 21 are: Two ounces of usable marijuana in a public place; Eight ounces of usable marijuana in your home; 16 ounces of cannabinoid products in solid form or cannabinoid concentrates; 72 ounces of cannabinoid products in liquid form; One ounce of cannabinoid extracts purchased from a marijuana retailer; and Four marijuana plants.” Plus: “Public use and driving while impaired remain illegal.” Source: https://www.oregon.gov/oha/ph/PREVENTIONWELLNESS/MARIJUANA/Pages/laws.aspx (indexed; direct open failed).

1.3.2 Home grow — 4 plants per household

  • Rule: 21+, noncommercial, at a household, no more than 4 marijuana plants at any time per household — not per person. “Four adults in one residence does not mean 16 plants. The limit is four per residence.” (retailer FAQ summarising the statute — secondary corroboration; statute is ORS 475C.305(1) as quoted via Brown).
  • Visibility: may not produce/process/possess/store homegrown marijuana where it “can be seen by normal unaided vision from a public place” (ORS 475C.306 as cited in Brown).
  • No licence required for compliant home grow (Brown: home growers “are not subject to the licensing and permitting requirements” for commercial licensees if within the 4-plant limit).
  • Local manner rules: Brown holds local indoor-only (and by extension other manner) ordinances are not preempted by the seed law for marijuana. Cities/counties may therefore add manner/zoning conditions — Part 3 must survey them; do not promise a client that “state law allows outdoor home grow everywhere”.
  • School proximity for home grow: a secondary possession-law summary states home growing is illegal within 1,000 ft of a school. That statement was not corroborated by an ORS section in this run and conflicts with the retailer-specific 1,000-ft rule (ORS 475C.097/475C.101). Mark as Verify — do not repeat as a home-grow rule until the section is located. The retailer rule is not a home-grow rule.
  • Landlord: a landlord may prohibit growing by lease (contract), which is distinct from the criminal caps above.

1.3.3 Public consumption, vehicles, gifting

  • Public consumption: ORS 475C.377 verbatim in §1.2.2 — unlawful for any person to use marijuana items in a public place; Class B violation. This covers smoking, vaping and (on the statute’s wording, “use of marijuana items”) edible/other use in a public place, not only smoking. Retailer premises must post “No On-Site Consumption” and an exit sign reading “Marijuana or Marijuana Infused Products May Not Be Consumed In Public” (OAR 845-025-2840(2), §1.6). Indoor Clean Air Act smoking/vaping bans apply in enclosed workplaces/public areas and are applied to cannabis smoking/vaping in the same manner as tobacco (secondary OMMP guidance — Verify ORS 433.835 et seq. interaction).
  • Vehicles: (i) Under-21 possession while operating a motor vehicle elevates the violation to Class A (ORS 475C.317(3)(b)); (ii) under-21 violations trigger driving-privilege suspension (ORS 475C.317(4), via ORS 809.260/809.280); (iii) driving while impaired is DUII (ORS 813.010 — Verify cannabis-specific DUII text; no per se THC limit was located, and secondary sources state impairment is judged by evaluation, not a blood-THC number); (iv) open-container / transport rule for adults: NOT located in this run — Gap. Do not state an Oregon “closed-container in trunk” rule as statute without locating it; delivery-vehicle rules (§1.6) are not consumer transport rules. (v) No use in a vehicle by anyone — a vehicle in a public place / on a highway is a public place for 475C.377 purposes on the definition in §1.1.1, and delivery drivers “may not … Consume, or be under the influence of, marijuana while making deliveries” (ORS 475C.117(3)(b)(C)).
  • Gifting: lawful between 21+ adults within the recipient’s possession limits, without consideration. The secondary formulation — gifts “must not involve monetary exchange, such as a lottery, service fee, or contribution” and such arrangements “are regarded as marijuana sales” — is consistent with Measure 91’s sale definition but the exact “gift” section was not quoted verbatim here; Verify ORS 475C.301/475C.009 “sale”/”transfer” definitions before advising on a gifting promotion. No gifting to under-21s (ORS 475C.317 covers “accepting” as purchasing).
  • Giving / sharing at a private home: within possession limits and not in public, sharing without consideration is the ordinary home-use case; commercial “sharing” events that charge admission are a sale risk — flagged as a practical risk, not a quoted statute.

Flower / usable marijuana (retail sale per day) 2 oz 8 oz per day; 32 oz per calendar month (per Mycannabis summary of the retail sales rule — Verify OAR citation; the monthly cap does not raise the 24-oz possession cap) OLCC FAQ; Mycannabis 2026 summary https://www.mycannabis.com/cannabis-in-oregon/
Edibles — per serving 10 mg THC (from 1 Apr 2022; was 5 mg) No maximum serving size OAR 845-026-0210 (adult) / 845-026-0220 (medical); OLCC IB2022-03
Edibles — per package 100 mg THC (from 1 Apr 2022; was 50 mg) 100 mg THC per package (same package cap, no serving cap, no scoring) Same

Edibles — labelling warnings (adult) “For use only by adults 21 and older. Keep out of reach of children.” / “Do not drive a motor vehicle while under the influence of marijuana.” / “BE CAUTIOUS — Cannabinoid edibles can take up to 2 hours or more to take effect.” + “This product is not approved by the FDA to treat, cure, or prevent any disease” + serving size/servings, mg THC and CBD per serving and per container, ingredients descending, major allergens, nutrition per serving, refrigeration statement if perishable, activation time (words/pictogram), “OR 10¢” if bottle-bill applies Medical warnings substitute: “For use by OMMP patients only. Liquid cannabinoid products (sale per day) 72 fl oz 72 fl oz (per same summary) Same

Beverages (hemp) Hemp edibles incl. beverages: 2 mg total THC per serving, 20 mg per container (OAR 845-026-0400 Table 3) — a hemp limit, far below the marijuana edible limit. Do not apply the 100 mg marijuana edible cap to hemp beverages. N/A (hemp beverages are general-market items, not OMMP items) OLCC wholesaler fact sheet (above)

“Medical grade” meaning — OLCC FAQ indexed text: “Medical grade means marijuana items that have a higher THC concentration limit compared to items sold to recreational customers. For example a recreational customer can buy a package of edibles that contains up to 50 mg of THC and each serving size in that package can be up to 5mg of THC. A medical grade edible sold to an OMMP registered patient can contain up to 100 mg of THC per package and there is no maximum serving size for medical grade edibles” — Note: the 50 mg / 5 mg recreational figures in that FAQ excerpt are the pre-April 2022 limits and are STALE against OAR 845-026-0210 (100 mg / 10 mg). The FAQ page as indexed has not been updated for the 2022 change, or the excerpt is from an older crawl. Quote the OAR numbers (100/10) as current; flag the FAQ excerpt as stale. OLCC FAQ (indexed) vs OAR 845-026-0210 / IB2022-03

Product types NOT allowed / restricted (summary): unlicensed cannabinoid extracts (possession unlawful under 475C.337(1)(g)); artificially derived cannabinoids in general-market products except via OAR 845-026-0415 approval (none approved as of Aug 2026); hemp products exceeding OAR 845-026-0400 limits by >10%; any product with untruthful/misleading labelling or labelling attractive to minors (OAR 845-025-7030(2)).

1.4 Medical programme (OMMP)

1.4.1 Who runs it, who qualifies

  • Administrator: Oregon Health Authority (OHA), Oregon Medical Marijuana Program (OMMP). OLCC administers the Cannabis Tracking System (CTS/Metrc) that some OMMP sites must use, but “OHA remains the agency overseeing” OMMP (OLCC/OHA CTS checklist, via oregon.gov PDF — https://www.Oregon.gov/oha/PH/DISEASESCONDITIONS/CHRONICDISEASE/MEDICALMARIJUANAPROGRAM/Documents/med_ref_all_cts.pdf ).
  • Legal basis: ORS 475C.770–475C.919 (OMMA, Measure 67 (1998) as merged with Measure 91 implementation).
  • Qualifying (“debilitating medical”) conditions — ORS 475C.777 as summarised across OHA/secondary sources: cancer; glaucoma; HIV/AIDS; post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD); a degenerative or pervasive neurological condition; and a condition or treatment producing, for the specific patient: cachexia, severe pain, severe nausea, seizures (including epilepsy), or persistent muscle spasms (including multiple sclerosis). Multiple secondary sources list the same set (with “Alzheimer’s disease” appearing in one commercial summary as an example of a degenerative neurological condition — do not list Alzheimer’s as a separate statutory condition without the ORS text). Plus, from HB 4142 (2026): “the need for hospice, palliative care, comfort care or other symptom management, including [comprehensive] pain management” — effective/operative date conflicted (91st day after sine die vs 1 Jan 2027 — see §1.2.1 / Conflicts). Plus by rule/petition: any other condition or treatment side effect adopted by OHA by rule or approved on petition under ORS 475C.913 (per Americans for Safe Access OMMP guide — Verify 475C.913 procedure).
  • Attending provider / attestation: patient must be diagnosed by a qualifying attending provider and hold a signed Attending Provider’s Statement (APS) / Attending Physician’s Statement recommending medical marijuana, completed within 90 days of OHA receiving the application (ASA guide, secondary — Verify OHA application instructions OHA 9240). Older summaries say “MD or DO licensed in Oregon”; newer summaries say “attending provider” (broader provider types — Verify current OMMP application instructions for the accepted provider list; do not restrict advice to MD/DO without that check). Minor patients: custodial parent/legal guardian must apply, sign a notarised Declaration of Person Responsible for a Minor, agree to serve as designated primary caregiver and control acquisition/dosage/frequency (ASA guide).
  • Residency: secondary OMMP guides state applicants must be Oregon residents. Verify the residency section (ORS 475C.783) — the HB 4142 amendment discussion references a “resident” qualifier, suggesting residency remains an element, but the exact current wording was not quoted here.
  • Out-of-state patients: No reciprocity was located in Parts 0–1 research. No Oregon statute/rule recognising another state’s medical card was returned. OMMP registration is an Oregon registration; an out-of-state cardholder buying in Oregon would be treated as an adult-use consumer (21+ only) unless OMMP-registered. Mark as Unavailable/Verify for Part 12 — do not state “Oregon accepts out-of-state cards” or “Oregon rejects them” as a quoted rule until ORS 475C.783 / OHA FAQ is opened. The July 2026 OMMP snapshot’s table of contents does include “Patients, Caregivers and Growers Outside of Oregon” (p.2) — i.e. some registrants have out-of-state addresses — but that is a residency/address statistic, not reciprocity.

1.4.2 Cards, fees, caregivers

Item Rule as returned Source / Verify
Standard application / renewal fee $200, valid 12 months (renewal also $200 in secondary summaries) OHA OMMP fee summaries via oregonstatecannabis.org / LegalClarity (secondary — Verify against OHA “OMMP Cardholder Fees” page; fee may have changed with the 2026 rules package)
Reduced fees Oregon Health Plan (OHP) $50; SNAP $60; SSI $20; veterans $20; veterans with ≥50% total disability rating where disability occurred/was aggravated during active service — fee waived (per one summary; another summary omits the waiver detail — Verify) Same secondary fee summaries — Verify against OHA fees page
What the card is Registry identification card (ORS 475C.783); a receipt issued within the immediately preceding 35 days can also evidence pending registration for HB 4142 facility purposes (HB 4142 amendment text: receipt “as described in ORS 475C.783, issued within the immediately preceding 35 days”) HB 4142 House amendments — https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2026R1/Downloads/MeasureDocument/HB4142/House Amendments to Introduced

An organisation/residential facility may be designated as an additional caregiver under ORS 475C.791 — the HB 4142 (Ryan’s Law) facility category.
