1.4.3 Grow sites, plant limits, processing sites

Per-patient / per-cardholder plant possession — ORS 475C.806(1)(a) (LawServer — https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/oregon/or-statutes/oregon_statutes_475c-806 ):

“(1)(a) A registry identification cardholder and the designated primary caregiver of the registry identification cardholder may jointly possess: (A) Six or fewer mature marijuana plants; and (B) Twelve or fewer immature marijuana plants.”

Designated grower limits — ORS 475C.806(2): a person may be designated to produce by no more than 8 registry identification cardholders; for each cardholder the grower may produce no more than (A) 6 mature plants, (B) 12 immature plants 24 inches or more in height, and (C) the OHA-by-rule amount of immature plants under 24 inches in height. OHA FAQ summaries give that under-24-inch figure as 36 (6 mature + 12 immature ≥24” + 36 immature <24” per patient at a grow site) — Verify the OHA rule number for “36” before quoting it as statute; the statute itself delegates the <24” number to OHA rule.

Address (grow-site) caps — ORS 475C.806(1)(b) and (3):

  • Patient/caregiver’s own production address (not a designated-grower site): up to 6 mature per cardholder, up to 12 mature total; up to 12 immature per cardholder, up to 24 immature total at the address; such an address generally may not also be used for ORS 475C.305 home-grow plants (with a co-resident non-cardholder exception — see (1)(b)(C) fragment in the return).
  • Designated-grower site within city limits in a residential zone: no more than 12 mature, 24 immature (≥24”), plus the OHA-rule <24” amount at the address (475C.806(3)(a)).
  • Outside city limits (and, per secondary summaries, non-residential zones within a city): higher address caps — secondary summaries give 48 mature / 96 immature (≥24”); grandfathered pre-1 Jan 2015 sites: 96 mature / 192 immature (≥24”) / 576 immature (<24”) in one secondary summary. Verify 475C.806(4)–(5) (grandfathering) text — the grandfather figures are secondary-only here.
  • Grow-site registration: under ORS 475C.792 (OHA registration system). HB 4142 (2026) amends 475C.792, including (per enrolled excerpts) a requirement for a person producing at an address other than their own to submit an application — and, per 2026-rule summaries, a notarised property-owner consent form for grow sites on another person’s property for registrations issued/renewed/changed from 1 Jan 2026. Verify the consent-form rule citation (OHA form / OAR) before advising on it.
  • Usable-marijuana harvest caps for designated growers: State v. T.T. summary of ORS 475C.809 (formerly 475B.834) (older numbering): a designated grower “may possess the amount of usable marijuana that the grower harvests from mature marijuana plants, not to exceed 12 pounds of usable marijuana per mature plant in outdoor grow sites and six pounds for indoor grow sites, provided that the amount does not exceed the amount reported to [OHA] under ORS 475C.816.” Verify current section number and whether the 12 lb / 6 lb figures survive in current 475C.809/475C.816 text.
  • Processing sites: registered under ORS 475C.815. As of July 2026, secondary reporting of the OHA snapshot states there are currently no medical-only processing sites (and no medical-only dispensaries) left in Oregon — every processing/sale channel is OLCC-licensed. Verify against the July 2026 snapshot itself; if true, “OMMP processing site” is a registration category with (near-)zero active sites, and OMMP patients’ processed products come from OLCC processors’ medical-grade lines.
  • Grow-site tracking: see §1.7 (CTS for 3+ patient sites; OMMOS monthly reporting for ≤2 patient sites with triggers; exemption for self-grow at own residence with ≤2 patients and no transfers).

1.4.4 Purchase limits, tax exemption, and how the programme has shrunk

  • Purchase limits at retail (medical): flower 8 oz per day, 32 oz per calendar month (secondary summary of retail sales rule — Verify OAR); solid 16 oz, liquid 72 oz, extract 5 g, immature plants 4 (per OHA FAQ summary via LegalClarity — Verify, see §1.3.4 warning on the concentrate figure). The monthly flower cap does not increase the 24-oz possession cap — a patient cannot lawfully possess 32 oz at once on the basis of the monthly purchase allowance.
  • Tax exemption: OMMP cardholder purchases at retail are exempt from the 17% state retail tax (ORS 475C.678 as cited in secondary guidance — Verify section; Part 2 will confirm the exemption mechanism and whether local 3% tax also exempts cardholders — do not assume the local tax is also exempt without Part 2).
  • Shrinkage (see also Part 0 H10): peak ~80,000 patients (pre-adult-use-sales era, advocacy figure) → under 15,000 by May 2024 (OHA subcommittee notes) → 11,625 cardholders in July 2026 reporting (Cannabis Data Project tabulation of OLCC/OHA data — secondary). Patient share of retail dollars fell from $109.3m (2020) to $40.4m (2025) on CannBus’s OLCC-data calculation (2020: $1,111.0m total; 2021 peak total $1,184.1m; 2025 total $926.2m). Grow sites with 3+ patients fell 4,200 → ~150 (>95% drop, advocacy figure — Verify). Drivers routinely cited (secondary, not OHA findings): adult-use availability without a $200 card + provider visit, higher medical-grade product availability at adult-use retailers, fee burden, and grow-site compliance/reporting burden. Causal claims are secondary inference — OHA has not, in the material returned, published a causal study of the decline.
  • Programme-sustainability risk: Compassionate Oregon (Feb 2025, advocacy): fee-funded programme faces a “significant funding shortfall, jeopardizing its ability to cover administrative costs” as enrolment fell. SB 176 (2025), which would have restructured OMMP financing/administration, died (see §1.2.1). No enacted OMMP financing fix was located for 2026. Verify OHA budget documents for the current shortfall figure — none is quoted here as an official number.

1.5 Hemp and intoxicating hemp

1.5.1 Hemp definition and THC measurement (Oregon, as of 1 Nov 2026)

  • Statutory definition is delegated: ORS 571.269(9)(a) — industrial hemp “Means the plant species Cannabis sativa that has a tetrahydrocannabinol concentration that complies with the concentration specified by the department [ODA] by rule” (plus further ODA rule definition); “does not mean industrial hemp commodities or products” (571.269(9)(b)).
  • ODA rule measurement — total THC: OAR 603-048: “‘Total THC’ means the sum of the concentration or mass of delta-9-THCA multiplied by 0.877 plus the concentration or mass of delta-9-THC.” I.e. Total THC = (Δ9-THCA × 0.877) + Δ9-THC. ODA’s federal-changes bulletin confirms: “Oregon calculates total THC using: (delta-9-THCA × 0.877) + delta-9-THC” and “Oregon already uses a total THC standard.”
  • The 0.3% figure: Oregon hemp products sold to consumers must contain no more than 0.3% total THC (OLCC/ODA guidance; HB 3000 summary: sale prohibited for products exceeding 0.3% total Δ9-THC or the federal concentration, whichever is greater, and exceeding OLCC/OHA/ODA adult-use cannabinoid concentrations by rule). The older HB 3000 summary phrasing (“average post-decarboxylation concentration of Δ9-THC not exceeding the greater of 0.3% dry weight or the federal concentration”) is the pre-delegation formulation — the current operative definition is the ODA-rule total-THC definition above. Verify the current OAR 603-048 hemp definition section (not just the (516) total-THC definition) for the 0.3% threshold’s rule citation.
  • Federal vs Oregon total THC — the open calculation gap (ODA’s own warning): the new federal language “does not yet specify how total THC must be calculated” and “does not clarify whether it will use a similar conversion factor or simply add the raw laboratory values. Depending on how federal agencies interpret the requirement, the federal definition of ‘total THC’ could become higher or lower than Oregon’s current calculation.” Do not assume federal total THC = Oregon total THC.
  • USDA plan status (for Part 7, noted here because §1.5 requires it): HB 3000 (2021) directed ODA to administer an Oregon Hemp State Program in accordance with the 2018 Farm Bill (i.e. a USDA-approved state plan, not USDA-direct licensing). Verify the current USDA AMS state-plan approval listing for Oregon before stating the plan’s approval date/status — the plan’s existence is established by HB 3000, its current USDA approval status was not re-checked in this run.

1.5.2 Artificially derived cannabinoids — the ban, the approval gate, and delta-8

  • Definition (HB 3000 summaries): “artificially derived cannabinoid” = a chemical compound manufactured by chemical reaction with any chemical compound derived from plants in the Cannabis family. OLCC consumer guidance: “substances that are created synthetically from a cannabis-derived starting material, like a hemp extract, rather than naturally occurring substances extracted from cannabis.”
  • General rule: artificially derived cannabinoids in hemp products for general-market sale are prohibited unless approved. OLCC wholesaler fact sheet (Aug 2026, official — https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/CBD/FS_CBD_Wholesalers.pdf ): “Products are generally prohibited from containing any artificially derived cannabinoids. At this time, none have received approval under OAR 845-026-0415. THC created by chemical conversion from CBD is prohibited for use in products sold to [Oregon consumers].”
  • Delta-8 as the paradigm: “because nearly all commercial Delta-8 is synthesized from CBD through a chemical conversion process, it falls squarely within [the] prohibition” (secondary — AtlRx summary of HB 3000/OAR, consistent with the OLCC fact sheet’s CBD-conversion sentence). Delta-8, delta-10, HHC, THC-O, THC-P are listed in secondary 2026 briefs as banned artificially derived / intoxicating cannabinoids in Oregon — Verify each compound against OAR 845-026-0415 / OLCC approved-list (none approved) rather than treating a secondary list as the rule text. Naturally occurring delta-8 in trace amounts vs converted delta-8 is a testing/origin question — flagged as a practical enforcement ambiguity, not resolved by the rule excerpts returned.
  • Timeline: OLCC rules implementing HB 3000 took effect July 2022: “selling artificially derived cannabinoids products that do not comply with [the applicable OAR] is illegal from July 2022” and “Any hemp product that exceeds the THC limits in OAR 845-026-0400 or contains artificially derived cannabinoids may no longer be sold to consumers on or after July 1, 2022, even if the product contains less than 0.3% THC” (OLCC CBD guidance via Manuals Plus PDF — https://manuals.plus/m/3ab07776fdd04f69077621fc34e476fba6ae6373e5390f81c766c2ce73eecaca.pdf ). Note the rule-number conflict for that guidance (845-025-1310 vs 845-026-0400 series) — see Conflicts.
  • CBN — the 2025 tightening: “Beginning July 1, 2025, products containing artificially derived CBN can no longer be sold in Oregon, either in the OLCC system or in the general (hemp-derived) market, unless the manufacturer has made a ‘Generally Recognized as Safe’ (GRAS) determination, or submitted a New Dietary Ingredient Notification to the FDA and received a ‘no objections’ response.” (Harris Sliwoski State of the State 2025, secondary.) HB 4121 (2024) had “re-established authority for the sale of non-intoxicating artificially derived cannabinoids in the general market, in particular CBN” (industry summary) — i.e. the legislature restored OLCC’s authority to set approval standards for CBN, and the subsequent rule outcome was the July 2025 GRAS/NDIN-gated ban. Verify the CBN rule text (OAR 845-026-0415 as amended / OLCC CBN bulletin) — the GRAS/NDIN condition is secondary-only here, and the interaction between HB 4121 §9 (“not more restrictive than adult-use retail rules”) and the CBN ban needs the rule text to reconcile.
  • What HB 4121 §9 does and does not do: it directs OLCC (with ODA) to adopt standards for approving retail hemp products containing artificially derived cannabinoids, capped at adult-use retail restrictiveness. It does not approve CBN, delta-8 or any other compound, and it does not repeal OAR 845-026-0415’s approval requirement.

1.5.3 Adult-use cannabinoids and the 21+ rule — correcting the brief

  • “Adult use cannabinoid” (HB 3000, via ORS 475C.009 / ORS 571.269(1)): includes delta-8 THC, delta-9 THC, optical isomers of delta-8 or delta-9 THC, and any artificially derived cannabinoid reasonably determined to have an intoxicating effect (HB 3000 -A5 summary). “Tetrahydrocannabinol” (THC) is defined to include all artificially or naturally derived tetrahydrocannabinols including delta-8, delta-9, optical isomers, and any artificially derived cannabinoid that may have an intoxicating effect.
  • “Adult use cannabis item”: a marijuana item, or an industrial hemp commodity/product that exceeds the concentration of adult-use cannabinoids established by OLCC (in consultation with OHA) by rule — i.e. the hemp/marijuana line for intoxicating products is a concentration rule, not a plant-origin rule. That is why high-THC hemp items are regulated as adult-use items.
  • 21+ sale rule: HB 3000 (2021) — “Prohibits sale of adult use cannabis items to a person under 21 years of age.” Not HB 4121 (2022) — there is no HB 4121 (2022) in this framework; HB 4121 is 2024 and its age-related provision is the minor-decoy uniform standards direction (operative 1 Jan 2025), not the creation of the 21+ rule. Any downstream file citing “HB 3000 (2021)” for the 21+ rule must be corrected to HB 3000 (2021).
  • The 0.5 mg minor-sale test (OAR 845-026-0300, OLCC fact sheet verbatim substance): “Certain cannabinoid hemp products cannot be sold to a minor under 21 years of age. A product can only be sold to a minor if: • It contains less than 0.5 mg total THC in the entire unit of sale; • The compliance testing was sensitive enough to demonstrate that the product contains less than 0.5 mg total THC; and • The product doesn’t contain any artificially derived cannabinoids (like delta-8-THC made synthetically from CBD). If a product contains more than 0.5 mg THC or other intoxicating cannabinoids, or if the testing was not sensitive enough to show that it does not exceed 0.5 mg of THC, or the product contains any artificially derived cannabinoids, it cannot be sold to minors.”
  • Practical age summary (secondary, consistent with the rule): no statewide age limit for most non-intoxicating CBD products (oils, tinctures, gummies, capsules, topicals with non-intoxicating cannabinoid levels) — retailer policy may still impose 21+; 21+ required for consumable hemp items containing THC above the 0.5 mg test, inhalable hemp products (vapes, smokable flower/pre-rolls), and any adult-use cannabis item. CBD vapes / hemp flower / pre-rolls: 21+ by Oregon law (AtlRx summary — Verify OAR 845-026-0300’s inhalable scope).
  • Minor decoy operations: HB 4121 (2024) directed OLCC to establish uniform standards for minor decoy operations to investigate sales of adult-use cannabinoid products (operative 1 Jan 2025). Verify the decoy-standards rule citation.

1.5.4 OLCC vs ODA authority — who regulates what hemp

Activity / product Regulator Basis
Hemp production (growing, harvest, crop THC compliance) ODA — grower/handler/seed licences under ORS 571.281; OAR 603-048; pre-harvest testing; crop inspection ORS 571.260–571.348; HB 3000 state-plan direction
Hemp commodities/products for human/animal consumption — THC/cannabinoid concentration limits per serving/package OLCC, in consultation with OHA (and ODA for the registry) — OAR 845-026-0400/0410/0415 ORS 571.309 (as amended by HB 4121 §9); HB 3000
Hemp product registration, labelling, packaging for consumer sale OLCC Hemp Registry (from 1 Jan 2026, enforced 1 June 2026) HB 4121 (2024) §§7–14; HE2025-01
Marijuana items (including hemp items that exceed adult-use cannabinoid limits and are therefore adult-use cannabis items) OLCC — full marijuana licensing, testing, CTS, retail rules ORS 475C.005–475C.586
Medical marijuana (OMMP) OHA (registration) + OLCC (CTS administration) ORS 475C.770–475C.919
Testing methods / reference lab ODA establishes the cannabis reference lab, in consultation with OHA and OLCC ORS 475C.523
Interagency enforcement / inspections of hemp operations Re-enacted HB 3000 enforcement provisions (HB 4121 §§1–6) — OLCC/ODA/OHA collaboration HB 4121 staff summary

The recurring confusion to avoid: ODA licenses hemp growing; OLCC registers hemp products for consumer sale and sets their THC limits. A product can be ODA-compliant as a crop and still be unsellable to Oregon consumers if it exceeds OLCC’s per-serving/per-container limits or contains an unapproved artificially derived cannabinoid.

1.5.5 Testing, labelling, THC beverages (hemp)

  • Hemp testing/labelling (general): Hemp Registry requires test results be made accessible to consumers; edible hemp products follow food-style labelling (OLCC Hemp Registry announcement, Nov 2025). Compliance testing must be sensitive enough to prove the <0.5 mg minor-sale test where relied upon (OAR 845-026-0300). Full hemp testing panel (pesticides, solvents, etc.) — the OLCC CBD guidance lists as registry/consumer-sale conditions that the product was properly tested for pesticides/solvents, does not exceed 0.3% total THC, contains no artificially derived cannabinoids (if sold on/after 1 July 2022), and does not exceed OAR 845-026-0400 THC limits (if sold on/after 1 July 2022). Verify the current testing-panel rule (OAR 603-048 vs 845-026) — Part 11 territory.
  • Hemp THC limits (OAR 845-026-0400 Table 3, OLCC fact sheet): “In addition to the 0.3% limit on total THC: • Hemp edibles, including beverages, are limited to 2 mg total THC per serving and 20 mg total THC per ‘container’ (generally equivalent to a unit of sale). • A full list of THC limits can be found in Table 3 of OAR 845-026-0400 and 845-026-0410 … Products that exceed these limits by more than 10% cannot be sold to Oregon consumers.” The 2 mg / 20 mg beverage limit is the hemp limit — do not confuse it with the marijuana edible limit (10 mg / 100 mg) or with any other state’s hemp-beverage limit. The >10% tolerance means a product at 22 mg/container (20 mg + 10%) is the boundary — Verify whether the tolerance is a testing-variance rule or a sale-prohibition threshold as worded in Table 3.
  • THC beverages (marijuana vs hemp): marijuana beverages sold at OLCC retailers follow marijuana edible/liquid rules + bottle-bill labelling (“OR 10¢” where ORS 459A.702 applies); hemp beverages sold in the general market follow the 2 mg / 20 mg hemp limits + Hemp Registry + food-style labelling. A hemp beverage over 20 mg/container (beyond tolerance) is not a lawful general-market hemp beverage in Oregon, even if it is under 0.3% total THC by percentage — the per-container milligram cap is a separate constraint.
  • Alcohol + THC: secondary material notes Oregon prohibits alcoholic beverages with THC (and a proposed expansion in another state’s bill is irrelevant here). Verify the Oregon alcohol-THC prohibition section before citing it — not located in this run.

1.5.6 Oregon’s response to the new federal hemp definition (12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026) — as of 1 Nov 2026

From ODA’s GovDelivery bulletin “Recent Federal Hemp Changes: What They Mean for Oregon” (https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/ORODA/bulletins/3fc8e8e ) — the only Oregon-agency response located in this run:

  1. “Key Point: Most federal changes do not take effect until November 2026.”
  2. “During this transition period, Oregon’s hemp program will continue operating under current Oregon laws and rules, including Oregon’s existing definition of total THC.”
  3. “ODA is also currently accepting public comments on hemp rule updates. These proposed changes were developed before the federal legislation was passed and are not related to the federal changes.” (Comments to 30 Dec 2025 on the miscellaneous hemp-rule updates.)
  4. “New federal definition of hemp and total THC: Hemp will be defined as cannabis containing no more than 0.3% total THC on a dry-weight basis. … Unlike Oregon’s current calculation, the federal bill does not yet specify how total THC must be calculated.”
  5. “Cannabinoids must naturally occur in the plant to qualify as ‘hemp-derived.’ Cannabinoids created or altered through chemical or synthetic processes would fall outside the hemp definition.” — This federal naturally-occurring requirement aligns in direction with Oregon’s existing artificially-derived-cannabinoid ban, but it is a federal definition change, not an Oregon rule change, and its interaction with Oregon’s OAR 845-026-0415 approval path is Verify.
  6. “Hemp product ‘containers’ will be limited to no more than 0.4 mg total THC per container.” — ODA’s bulletin states the cap as 0.4 mg (the baseline as supplied says “0.4 mg total THC per container cap” after 11 Dec 2026). The bulletin text as returned says “on a dry-weight basis” after the container cap — that phrasing is reproduced here as returned but looks like a conflation of the 0.3% dry-weight definition with the per-container milligram cap; Verify the federal text (PL 119-37 §781 as limited by PL 119-103 §2019) for the cap’s exact unit before quoting it.
  7. “Oregon statute gives ODA flexibility. ORS 571.269 allows ODA to define THC concentration requirements in rule, giving Oregon room to adjust once federal guidance is released.”
  8. “ODA’s current rulemaking is not tied to federal legislation.”

What was NOT located as of 1 Nov 2026: any Oregon statute, ODA rule, OLCC rule, Governor’s executive order, or Attorney General opinion conforming Oregon law to the federal 0.4 mg/container cap or to a federal total-THC calculation method; any Oregon guidance on what happens to hemp products between 0.4 mg and Oregon’s current 20 mg/container hemp-edible limit after 11 Dec 2026; any Oregon enforcement-position statement for the 12 Nov–11 Dec 2026 window (when PL 119-37 §781 takes effect but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it). All three are follow-ups for Part 7 / a post-11 Dec 2026 update. Do not fill the gap by assuming Oregon will simply adopt the federal cap by rule — ODA has said only that it has rule flexibility and will wait for federal guidance.

Interaction with the baseline’s other federal dates: USDA DEA-lab-testing enforcement delay to 31 Dec 2026 and the medical rider through 11 Dec 2026 have no Oregon-law counterpart located in this run; Oregon hemp testing continues under ODA/OLCC rules until a conforming change is adopted. Verify whether ODA has issued a testing-lab guidance referencing the 31 Dec 2026 date — none was located.

1.6 Packaging, labelling, advertising, delivery, zoning and buffer distances

1.6.1 Packaging and labelling — OAR 845-025-7000 to 7190 (operative excerpts)

OAR 845-025-7030 — Labelling for sale to consumer (verbatim excerpts — https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_845-025-7030 ):

“(1) A label required by these rules must: (a) Be printed on or affixed to the container holding the marijuana item or industrial hemp commodity or product and printed on or affixed to any outer package or container that is used to display the marijuana item or industrial hemp commodity or product for sale or transfer to a consumer, patient or designated primary caregiver; (b) Comply with [NIST Handbook 130 (2016), Uniform Packaging and Labeling Regulation, incorporated by reference]; (c) Contain all required information in any typed, legible font that is easy to read and contrasts sufficiently with the background and is at least 1/16th of an inch in height based on the uppercase ‘K’; (d) Be in English, though it can be in other languages; … (2) A label may not: (a) Contain any untruthful or misleading statements including, but not limited to, a health claim that is not supported by the totality of publicly available scientific evidence … and for which there is significant scientific agreement, among experts qualified by scientific training and experience to evaluate such claims; or (b) Be attractive to minors, as that is defined in OAR 845-025-7000 … (3) Principal Display Panel. … Every container … must have a principal display panel … [containing] the product identity, net quantity of contents, and universal symbol or hemp symbol, whichever is applicable. … If the product is a medical grade cannabinoid product, concentrate or extract processed by a licensee, or medical marijuana processing site, the principal display panel must also include the medical grade symbol. If the product is an industrial hemp commodity or product processed by a licensee, the principal display must include the hemp symbol in place of the universal symbol. (4) Product Identity … (a) The potency value shall be expressed as an average of the samples taken and tested under OAR 333-007-0360 … A label may not have a THC value that exceeds the applicable maximum con[tent … — truncated in return].”

OAR 845-025-7090 — Cannabinoid edible labelling (verbatim excerpts — https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_845-025-7090 ): before sale/transfer, the edible container label must include (numbering as returned): (6) net weight/volume in U.S. customary and metric units; (7) serving size and number of servings per container; (8) amount, in milligrams, of THC and CBD in each serving and in the container; (9) ingredients in descending order of predominance by weight/volume; (10) major food allergens; (11) calories, sodium, protein, added sugars, cholesterol, total carbohydrates, total fat per serving; (12) refrigeration/frozen statement if perishable; (14) activation time in words or pictogram; (16) “This product is not approved by the FDA to treat, cure, or prevent any disease”; (17) adult-use warnings (21+, keep out of reach of children; do not drive while under the influence; “BE CAUTIOUS” + “Cannabinoid edibles can take up to 2 hours or more to take effect.”); (18) medical-grade warnings + medical-grade symbol (“For use by OMMP patients only…”); (19) “OR 10¢” for beverage containers subject to ORS 459A.702.

OAR 845-025-7160 — Pre-approval (verbatim excerpt — https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_845-025-7160 ):

“(1) Prior to selling, offering for sale, or transferring a marijuana item or industrial hemp commodity or product that is for ultimate sale to a consumer, patient, or designated primary caregiver, a licensee, a license applicant or a registrant must submit both a package and a label application to and receive approval from the Commission. … The licensee … must submit a physical prototype upon request … (2) Except as provided in sections (5) to (7) …, the packaging and label applications must be accompanied by: (a) A fee as specified in OAR 845-025-1060 …; and (b) Information including but not limited to: (A) Documentation that the package has been certified as child resistant as defined by 16 CFR 1700 by a qualified third party child-resistant package testing firm. (B) A picture of and description of the item … (C) For label applications for inhalable cannabinoid products that contain non-cannabis additives: (i) The non-cannabis additive’s list of ingredients as required by 845-025-3265(1); … (4) … The Commission must review the packaging and labeling and notify the licensee … whether [it is] approved, and if not approved, a description of the … deficiencies. … [Approval may be denied if the package/label] Is attractive to minors or is marketed in a manner attractive to minors; Contains untruthful or misleading content; [or] Will contain a marijuana item or industrial hemp commodity or product that is not compliant with ORS 475B [now 475C], OAR 333, Divisions 7 and 8, or OAR 845, Division 25. … (12) Labels … do not require pre-approval if they are generic label[s … — truncated].”

Child-resistant packaging: “All marijuana edibles in Oregon must be sold in child resistant packaging. If not, the retailer must place it in an exit bag at the point of sale. This requirement applies to all marijuana and hemp items (except for usable marijuana and usable hemp). See OAR 845-025-7020.” (Salem News summary of OLCC rules, Apr 2022 — secondary; Verify 845-025-7020 text.)

Hemp Registry labelling overlay (2026): registered hemp products must follow the same kinds of labelling as ordinary foods for edibles, with consumer-accessible test results (OLCC Hemp Registry announcement). The registry does not replace OAR 845-025-7000-series labelling for OLCC-licensed items — it adds a registration + transparency layer for general-market hemp items.

1.6.2 Advertising

  • Statutory test as amended 2025: HB 3724 (2025 Laws ch. 68) directs OLCC to expand advertising/packaging rules to prevent marketing appealing to minors and changes the ORS 475C test from “attractive to minors” to advertising “likely to cause minors to unlawfully possess marijuana or marijuana items” (amending ORS 475C.017 and 475C.612 per OLCC overview). Verify the amended ORS text and whether OAR 845-025-8000-series rules have been conformed — the OAR text was not returned in this run, so no advertising prohibition is quoted verbatim here.
  • Secondary summary of the OAR position (use with caution): advertising restricted under OAR 845-025-8000, with signage limits and a ban on content designed to appeal to minors (including cartoon imagery); permitted: ads in adult-oriented media with reasonable age-audience targeting (CannBus summary — secondary, not a rule quote). Do not advise on a specific ad format from this summary alone.
  • Retailer signage (rule, not advertising generally): OAR 845-025-2840(2) requires prominent signs: “No Minors Permitted Anywhere on the Premises”; “No On-Site Consumption”; “Security Cameras in Use”; plus an exit sign: “Marijuana or Marijuana Infused Products May Not Be Consumed In Public”. See §1.6.4.

1.6.3 Delivery

ORS 475C.117 — Delivery of marijuana items to consumer (verbatim excerpts — https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_475C.117 ; history “[2021 c.155 §3]”):

“(1) A marijuana retailer that holds a license issued under ORS 475C.097 … may make deliveries to a consumer pursuant to the consumer’s bona fide order received by the marijuana retailer. The delivery … may be made to a consumer: (a) Within the same city or unincorporated area of the county in which the marijuana retailer is located; or (b) In a city or the unincorporated area of a county that is adjacent to the city or unincorporated area of the county in which the marijuana retailer is located, provided the adjacent city or county has adopted an ordinance allowing for the delivery of marijuana items by a marijuana retailer located in an adjacent city or unincorporated area of a county … (2) … Upon request, provide to the [Commission] information on each vehicle used to make deliveries …, including the make, model, year, color, vehicle identification number and registration plate number. (3) An individual who makes deliveries … [must]: Hold a permit issued under ORS 475C.273 … and carry the permit while making deliveries …; Present to the consumer a printed or electronic delivery manifest and obtain on the manifest the consumer’s written or electronic signature verifying completion of the delivery …; Except in the case of an emergency or unsafe road conditions or as necessary for fuel, rest or vehicle repair, travel only between the premises of the marijuana retailer and the locations at which the deliveries … are made. … May not: (A) Leave a delivery vehicle that contains marijuana items unattended unless the delivery vehicle is locked and equipped with an active vehicle alarm system. (B) Carry more than $10,000 worth of marijuana items in a delivery vehicle at any one time. (C) Consume, or be under the influence of, marijuana while making deliveries … (4) A delivery vehicle must: (a) … be equipped with an active global positioning system device that tracks the location of the delivery vehicle and enables the marijuana retailer … to identify the location of the delivery vehicle. (b) Be equipped with a lockable container in a secured cargo area … of a size appropriate to contain the marijuana items being delivered. (c) Be free of any markings that may indicate that the delivery vehicle is used for the purpose of delivering marijuana items. (5) A delivery of marijuana items may not be made to a consumer who is located on land owned or leased by the federal government. (6) The commission may adopt rules to carry out the purposes of this section.”

Delivery hours / frequency (secondary, from OLCC FAQ summaries): deliveries between 8:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m.; a retailer may deliver to the same address only once per day; daily sale limits apply equally to delivery and in-person sales. Verify the hours/frequency rule citation (OAR 845-025-2800 series / delivery rule) — the hours figure comes from a secondary FAQ summary, not a quoted rule here. Retailer operating hours generally (7 a.m.–10 p.m. in one secondary summary) are likewise Verify — do not state store hours as statute without the rule.

Adjacent-jurisdiction opt-in: delivery into an adjacent city/county requires that jurisdiction’s opt-in ordinance. A jurisdiction that has opted out of retail (Part 3) has not thereby opted into delivery — the two ordinances are distinct. Verify the OLCC “Cannabis Adjacent Jurisdiction Opt-In Home Delivery” list for the current opt-in jurisdictions (Part 3 territory).

1.6.4 Zoning and buffer distances (state floor; local rules are Part 3)

Retailer location — ORS 475C.097(2) (via CaseMine summary of the statute — https://www.casemine.com/act/us/65dc76a2d780611919130f18/amp ):

“(2) A marijuana retailer must have a retail license … To hold a retail license …, a marijuana retailer: … (c) May not be located in an area that is zoned exclusively for residential use; (d) Except as provided in ORS 475C.101, may not be located within 1,000 feet of: (A) A public elementary or secondary school for which attendance is compulsory under ORS 339.020; or (B) A private or parochial elementary or secondary school, teaching children as described in ORS 339.030(1)(a); …”

ORS 475C.101 — Proximity exception (verbatim substance — https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_475B.109 [old number in URL; current number 475C.101]):

“Notwithstanding ORS 475C.097 … (2)(d), a marijuana retailer may be located within 1,000 feet of a building described in ORS 475C.097 … (2)(d) if: (1) … (a) The marijuana retailer is not located within 500 feet of: (A) A building where a public prekindergarten or kindergarten program is provided by a school district or an education service district; (B) A public elementary or secondary school …; or (C) A private or parochial elementary or secondary school …; and (b) The [Commission] determines that there is a physical or geographic barrier capable of preventing children from traversing to the premises of the marijuana retailer; or … The marijuana retailer was established before August 1, 2017, in accordance with a city or county ordinance adopted under section 29b, chapter 83, Oregon Laws 2016. [Formerly 475B.109; 2022 c.81 §23]”

SB 162 (2025) interaction (conflicted — see §1.2.1): the OLCC overview describes SB 162 as repealing SB 1522’s PreK/kindergarten-only 1,000-ft bar and restoring the prior standard (i.e. the 475C.101 framework above, without PreK/kindergarten-only locations counting as “schools” for the 1,000-ft bar), plus grandfathering/reissue where a new school appears within 1,000 ft after licensing. The OLCC 2025 draft rules implement that as: “The Commission may allow a marijuana retailer to change its location if, after issuing the license, the Commission becomes aware that a school or a building where a public prekindergarten or kindergarten program is provided … that was established prior to issuance of the license is located within 1,000 feet of the retailer’s premises.” Do not apply the SB 162 version until OLIS confirms SB 162 as enacted.

OAR 845-025-2840 — Retailer premises (verbatim excerpts — https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_845-025-2840 ):

“(1) The licensed premises of a retailer: (a) May not be located in an area that is zoned exclusively for residential use. (b) Notwithstanding ORS 475B.105 [now 475C.097] (Retail license)(2)(d) may be located within 1,000 feet of a school if: (A) The marijuana retailer is not located within 500 feet of: (i) A public elementary or secondary school …; or … A private or parochial elementary or secondary school …; and (B) The Commission determines that there is a physical or geographic barrier capable of preventing children from traversing to the premises …; or (C) The marijuana retailer was established before August 1, 2017, in accordance with a city or county ordinance adopted under section 29b, chapter 83, Oregon Laws 2016. … Must be enclosed on all sides by permanent walls and doors. (2) A retailer must post in a prominent place signs that read: (a) ‘No Minors Permitted Anywhere on the Premises’; (b) ‘No On-Site Consumption’; and (c) ‘Security Cameras in Use’. (d) Exit … that reads: ‘Marijuana or Marijuana Infused Products May Not Be Consumed In Public’. … A retailer must designate a consumer sales area … [which] is the sole area … where consumers are permitted. … All inventory must be stored on the licensed premises. (5) For purposes of determining the distance between a retailer and a school …, ‘within 1,000 feet’ means a straight line measurement in a radius extending for 1,000 feet or less in any direction from the closest point anywhere on the boundary line of the real property comprising a school to the closest point of the licensed premises of a retailer. If any portion of the licensed premises is within 1,000 feet of a school … an applicant will not be licensed.”

Producer premises (from the 2025 draft-rules excerpt): “The licensed premises of a producer applicant may not be on: (a) Public land; or (b) The same tax lot as another producer licensee under common ownership; or (c) The same physical location or address as a medical marijuana grow site registered under ORS 475C.792.” Verify the current producer-premises rule number (OAR 845-025-2000 series) — the excerpt is from a draft, not the adopted rule text.

Local overlay (state floor, not ceiling): cities/counties may set additional zoning, time/place/manner rules and local taxes, and may opt out of licence types by ordinance referred to voters (ORS 475C.600-series framework; Part 3). The state 1,000-ft school buffer is a floor — a locality may impose a larger buffer or additional buffers (e.g. parks, churches, treatment facilities) by local ordinance. No statewide buffer for parks/churches was located in this run — do not state one.

1.7 Seed-to-sale tracking (Metrc / CTS)

  • System: Metrc — “Marijuana Enforcement Tracking and Compliance” — is the name of Oregon’s state-administered Cannabis Tracking System (CTS). OLCC CTS page (indexed official text — https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/pages/ommp_cts_guide.aspx ): “Metrc is the name of the state-administered cannabis tracking system (CTS). This system is used by both recreational marijuana licensees and medical marijuana registered grow sites, processing sites, and dispensaries, with some exceptions.”
  • Statutory duty: ORS 475C.177 (duty to develop/maintain a system for tracking transfer of marijuana items). Licensees that introduce untracked cannabinoids/marijuana into the regulated industry commit a revocation ground under ORS 475C.265(1) (see §1.2.2).
  • Who must use it (OLCC licensees): all OLCC licensees — producers, processors, wholesalers, retailers, laboratories — must track inventory in Metrc from propagation through final retail sale (secondary CannBus summary of OLCC rules; consistent with the CTS guides). No alternative CTS is permitted for OLCC licensees.
  • Who must use it (OMMP sites) — the 3-patient rule: “Any medical marijuana grow site that is registered to produce marijuana for three or more patients (regardless of the number of growers) is subject to tracking in CTS.” (OLCC CTS page.) Grow sites that qualify must designate a Grow Site Administrator (GSA) and pay the CTS user fee within 15 days of OMMP notification (OHA reporting page); the older CTS checklist cites a $480 CTS user fee to OMMP for medical sites (checklist PDF — Verify current fee; the $480 figure is from an undated checklist and may be stale).
  • OMMP sites that report monthly instead (OMMOS): registered grow sites with two or fewer patients must submit monthly reports in the Oregon Medical Marijuana Online System (OMMOS) if any of the listed triggers applies (the OHA page lists triggers including: patient growing for self at a non-residence address; transfers to a processing site/dispensary/PRMG required to use CTS — full trigger list not reproduced here, Verify OHA reporting page). A Person Responsible for a Medical Marijuana Grow site (PRMG) must report the previous month’s transfers and on-site inventory by the 10th of each month (OAR 333-008-0630).
  • Exempt from both CTS and OMMOS: all of the following must be true: patient only growing for self at own residence; two or fewer patients registered at the grow site; and the patient indicated on the application that they will not transfer to a medical processing site or dispensary (OHA reporting page). Reporting does not apply to a patient growing only for self at own residence unless transferring to a registered processing site/dispensary/PRMG required to use CTS (OAR 333-008-0630(1) as cited on the OHA page).
  • Day-to-day duties (OLCC CTS guide): set up item categories/strains; order Unique Identifier (UID) plant and package tags; enter starting inventory within 10 calendar days of CTS administrator activation (medical checklist); perform daily reconciliation — “any time a change occurs relating to marijuana inventory at your facility, you must reflect that change in CTS” — but “if no inventory changes or transfers occur during a day, there are no changes to make in CTS. There is no requirement to report ‘no activity’.” All CTS administrators (GSA / PRP / PRD) must complete Metrc training (via metrc.com/oregon, “Schedule Training Now”; webinars several times a month).
  • 2026 CTS process change: Compliance Education Bulletin CE2026-01, effective 1 Sep 2026, changes how secondary lab sample (sub-contracted / composited) test results are entered in Metrc: the primary lab records all compliance results under primary samples; the secondary lab records only “Composite Testing Complete” on the composite sample; failure after 1 Sep 2026 “will result in missing test results for the source package.” Source: OLCC bulletin page https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/Pages/CE2026-01.aspx (indexed official text). The bulletin “does not supersede any OLCC rule.”
  • Cost note (secondary, Verify): one secondary guide states OLCC covers all Metrc costs except RFID tags ($0.45 per plant tag, $0.25 per package tag). Verify against the current OLCC/Metrc fee schedule — tag prices change and the OLCC-subsidy statement may be dated.
  • Hemp tracking: HB 4121 (2024) repealed the requirement that ODA make rules for tracking/transfer of industrial hemp commodities/products intended for human consumption (OLIS HB 4121 summary). Hemp products are therefore tracked via the Hemp Registry (registration), not via Metrc CTS. Do not state that hemp products are Metrc-tracked. (Hemp crops under ODA licensing have their own ODA reporting — Part 7.)

1.8 Employment and drug-testing protections

Short answer: Oregon has no general statutory protection for off-duty cannabis use or for a positive cannabis test, for either adult-use consumers or OMMP patients, as of 1 Nov 2026. The 2025 bill that would have created medical-patient employment protections died. What exists is a set of non-accommodation / non-interference provisions plus general anti-discrimination and safety-sensitive / federal overlays.

Proposition Authority / source
Medical programme does not require workplace accommodation ORS 475C.780 (secondary summary, American Screening Corp — https://www.americanscreeningcorp.com/blogs/news/drug-testing-laws-oregon ): “nothing in the Oregon Medical Marijuana Act requires an employer to accommodate the medical use of marijuana in the workplace.” Verify verbatim 475C.780 text.
Adult-use programme does not amend employment law ORS 475C.013 (same secondary summary): adult-use statutes “may not be construed to amend or affect state or federal law pertaining to employment matters.” Verify verbatim text.
No comprehensive private-employer drug-testing statute Secondary analysis (American Screening Corp, 2026): “Oregon does not have a single statute that tells private employers how to run a drug testing program… There is no state licensed drug free workplace certification program and no comprehensive law that spells out notice periods, panel requirements, or lab accreditation for private sector testing.” An employer’s written policy, consistently applied, carries most of the legal weight. This is a secondary legal analysis, not a statute — treat as guidance, not as a quoted rule.
Employers may test and may act on a positive THC result, including off-duty use Same secondary analysis + Advanced Training Products Oregon guidance (Dec 2025, secondary PDF — https://advancedtrainingproducts.com/files/state-guidance/Oregon%20-%20State%20Specific%20Information-2025_1220.pdf ): “Oregon remains a ‘pro-employer’ state regarding drug testing. There are no state statutes that restrict a private employer’s right to test for marijuana. Employers may conduct pre-employment, random, and post-accident testing… Employers are free to maintain zero-tolerance policies and terminate employees for positive THC results, regardless of whether the use was off-duty.” Secondary — Verify against current case law (notably Emerald Steel Fabricators, Inc. v. Bureau of Labor & Industries, 348 Or. 159 (2010), cited in CannBus as the leading Oregon case — that case predates Measure 91 and concerns medical use / disability accommodation; its current application after Measure 91 and after federal Schedule III is Verify, not assumed).
Alcohol-testing restrictions do NOT extend to cannabis Same secondary analysis: Oregon regulates alcohol testing (consent / reasonable suspicion) but “these same restrictions do not apply to cannabis.” Verify ORS 652 / breathalyzer-polygraph provisions before advising.
Disability / reasonable-accommodation overlay General disability-discrimination law (ORS 659A, ADA) may protect an underlying condition but, on the Emerald Steel line, does not require accommodation of marijuana use itself. This is a general principle stated at summary level — specific accommodation advice requires current case-law research (Part 12 / employment counsel).
Safety-sensitive / federal overlay Federal DOT rules override state law for DOT-regulated safety-sensitive transportation jobs; federally funded agencies must comply with the federal Drug-Free Workplace Act; ORS 352.008 (cited in secondary guidance) prohibits unlawful drug use in the (university) workplace context. Verify ORS 352.008’s scope — the secondary citation may be to the public-university system, not all workplaces.
Unemployment / workers’ compensation overlays Secondary analysis notes the pieces that “bear directly on testing” include the unemployment-insurance misconduct rule and the workers’-compensation compensable-injury definition. No specific rule text was returned — Gap: do not state an unemployment-misconduct or comp rule for cannabis without the ORS/OAR citation.
SB 176 (2025) employment protections — DIED Would have “prohibited employers from making hiring or firing decisions solely based on an individual’s status as a medical cannabis patient or a positive test result for cannabis metabolites” (MPP summary). Died in Joint Ways and Means, 27 June 2025. Advocates expected to pursue similar legislation in the next session (MPP) — no such 2026 employment-protection enactment was located in this run; Verify the 2026 session’s employment bills on OLIS before stating the position changed in 2026.
Cannabis-industry workers (licensee staff) Separate regime: OLCC worker permits (ORS 475C.269/273, OAR 845-025-5500 series — §1.2.2) and, for licensees, the (now repealed prospectively) Measure 119 labour-peace requirement (HB 4162, effective 1 Jan 2027) and the 2025 “United For Cannabis Workers” ballot-measure note appended to ORS 475C.523 in Justia (a measure note, not enacted law — do not confuse with a worker-protection statute). Industry-worker collective-bargaining / wage protections beyond general Oregon labour law were not established in this Part 1 run.
Schedule III effect on employment (federal baseline interaction) Verify — not determined here. The federal move of state-licensed medical marijuana to Schedule III does not by itself create an Oregon employment protection (ORS 475C.780 / 475C.013 remain state law), but whether federal Schedule III status changes any federal contractor / DOT / drug-free-workplace analysis for medical patients is a federal question outside Parts 0–1 and was not researched. Do not advise that Schedule III creates Oregon job protection.

1.9 Pending legislation — status confirmed on OLIS / session record as far as this run allows

Oregon session structure (for reading every status below): Oregon has a long session in odd-numbered years (up to 160 days) and a short session in even-numbered years (up to 35 days; 2026 short session: 2 Feb–6 Mar 2026, sine die 6 Mar 2026). A bill that dies in a short session is not “pending” — it is dead unless reintroduced in the next session. A bill “in committee upon adjournment” is dead. A bill “referred to Ways and Means and never heard” in a short session is dead. No bill is described below as “pending” unless a source affirmatively shows it carried over or was pre-filed for 2027 — none was located.

Status-verification limit: OLIS bill pages were reached in this run only via OLIS staff summaries / measure documents returned in search (HB 3000, HB 4121, HB 4142) and via secondary session summaries (Harris Sliwoski, MPP, OLCC overview, BillTrack50). A full OLIS status check (each bill’s “current status” field) was not completed for every bill below because direct OLIS page opens were not available in this session. Every status below must therefore be re-checked on OLIS (https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov) before republication, and any bill whose OLIS status differs from the table governs over the table. This limit is stated here rather than hidden behind a false “confirmed on OLIS” claim.
