Oregon corporate excise/income tax — 280E decoupling Subtraction for deductions barred federally by IRC §280E Corporate filer in an ORS 475C-authorised marijuana business Same scope as above ORS 317.363, per DOR Form OR-20 instructions (2025): https://www.oregon.gov/DOR/forms/FormsPubs/form-OR-20-INS-instructions_102-129-1_2025.pdf
Oregon Corporate Activity Tax (CAT) General CAT rules apply; no cannabis-specific CAT rate was located — see §2.8, Verify Businesses over the CAT threshold generally — Verify — no DOR cannabis-specific CAT guidance located in searches tried
General state sales tax None — Oregon has no general sales tax; the 17% is a cannabis-specific retail tax — — DOR marijuana pages; widely stated, but the operative point is that no general sales-tax statute applies to these sales

2.2 State retail tax — statute, verbatim operative text, history

Citation: ORS 475C.674, “Imposition of tax on retail sale of marijuana items” [Formerly 475B.705]. Chapter: ORS 475C.670–475C.734, “Taxation of Cannabis and Cannabis Products.” Official text via Oregon Legislature ORS Chapter 475C page (see numbering warning above); section text as republished at https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_475c.674 and https://law.justia.com/codes/oregon/volume-14/chapter-475c/section-475c-674/ (both accessed 2026-11-01, both citing the Legislature’s page).

Verbatim operative text — ORS 475C.674(1)–(2), (4):

“(1) A tax is hereby imposed upon the retail sale of marijuana items in this state. The tax imposed by this section is a direct tax on the consumer, for which payment upon retail sale is required. The tax shall be collected at the point of sale of a marijuana item by a marijuana retailer at the time at which the retail sale occurs.”

“(2) The tax imposed under this section shall be imposed at the rate of: (a) 17 percent of the retail sales price of usable marijuana; (b) 17 percent of the retail sales price of immature marijuana plants; (c) 17 percent of the retail sales price of a cannabinoid edible; (d) 17 percent of the retail sales price of a cannabinoid concentrate; (e) 17 percent of the retail sales price of a cannabinoid extract; (f) 17 percent of the retail sales price of a cannabinoid product that is intended to be used by applying the cannabinoid product to the skin or hair; and (g) 17 percent of the retail sales price of cannabinoid products other than those described in paragraph (f) of this subsection.”

“(4) Except as otherwise provided by the Department of Revenue by rule, the amount of the tax shall be separately stated on an invoice, receipt or other similar document that the marijuana retailer provides to the consumer at the time at which the retail sale occurs.”

Subsection (3) (rounding): “If the tax imposed under this section does not equal an amount calculable to a whole cent, the tax shall be equal to the next higher whole cent.”

What is taxed, in plain English: Only the retail sale by an OLCC-licensed retailer to a consumer. Wholesale, producer-to-processor and processor-to-wholesaler transfers are not subject to this 17% tax. The tax is on the consumer, not on the business’s gross receipts — the retailer is the collector/trustee. DOR’s August 2024 distributions paper states this expressly: “The marijuana tax is collected from consumers by retailers and held in trust until remitted to the department.” Source: DOR, Marijuana Tax Distributions (Aug 2024): http://cms.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/HB3610/Marijuana-Tax-Distributions-Dept-Revenue-Aug2024.pdf (accessed 2026-11-01 via search result).

History — do not confuse the three rates: - Measure 91 (2014) as passed imposed producer-level taxes ($35/oz flower, $10/oz leaves, $5/immature plant). That scheme was replaced before OLCC retail licensing began. - HB 2041 (2015) created the retail tax; HB 3400 (2015) built the licensing/local framework. Governor signed HB 2041 on 5 October 2015 (secondary summary, Foster Garvey/JD Supra, accessed 2026-11-01 — used only for the signing date, not for law). - 1 January 2016 – 31 December 2016 (early start): recreational sales through medical dispensaries taxed at a temporary 25%. DOR Calendar Year 2016 report: “January 2016: State marijuana taxation begins on recreational sales from medical dispensaries to adults under Early Start, at a temporary rate of 25 percent of the retail sales price.” The two months of adult-use sales before that (Oct–Dec 2015) were untaxed. - From 1 January 2017: 17% permanent state rate for OLCC retailers (earlier for a retailer once OLCC-licensed and operating). Local 3% taxes voted in November 2016 generally took effect in 2017, giving the familiar 20% combined ceiling. - No state-rate change was located for 2018–2026. The 17% rate on DOR’s current page (opened 2026-11-01) is unchanged. Verify: whether any 2025/2026 bill changed the rate — none was found in the searches tried, and the 2026 omnibus HB 4139 as introduced proposed a new 17% tax on industrial hemp-derived cannabinoid products (see §2.9), not a change to the marijuana 17%. HB 4139’s later status is itself Verify (see §2.9).

Collection mechanics (DOR, opened 2026-11-01): - Every OLCC-licensed retailer must register separately with DOR as a marijuana tax collector for each location, as soon as it receives its OLCC retail licence, via Revenue Online or Form OR-MTR. - Monthly payments (payment voucher required; electronic, cash/check/money order; in-person cash only by appointment at the Salem Revenue Building, Mon–Fri 8 a.m.–4 p.m.) plus quarterly returns filed electronically in Revenue Online. Monthly vouchers do not replace the quarterly return. - If DOR administers the locality’s local tax, the quarterly return in Revenue Online automatically calculates both state and local tax. If DOR does not administer it, the retailer must contact the city/county directly. - Retailer retention: “As a marijuana retailer, you may keep 2 percent of the 17 percent state marijuana tax to cover administrative costs.” (DOR page.) Statutory basis, ORS 475C.710: “For the purpose of compensating marijuana retailers for expenses incurred in collecting the tax imposed under ORS 475C.674, each marijuana retailer is permitted to deduct and retain two percent of the amount of taxes that are collected by the marijuana retailer from all retail sales of marijuana items conducted by the marijuana retailer.” [Formerly 475B.745.] Note: the 2% is 2% of the tax collected, not 2 percentage points off the rate — i.e. on $100 of price, $17 tax, retailer keeps $0.34. For local tax, DOR states: “Some local jurisdictions allow retailers to retain administrative costs, while others do not.” The per-locality retention is in the DOR locality table (see §2.4 limitation). - Consumer overcharge remedy: consumer must first write to the retailer within 30 days with receipt and proof of excess tax; if the retailer does not refund, contact DOR at the marijuana-tax mailbox on the DOR page. - Tax compliance certificates: some retailers must provide OLCC with a DOR tax compliance certificate to obtain/renew a licence; requested through Revenue Online. This is the enforcement link between tax delinquency and licence renewal — see also Part 4/11 in the full dossier (not covered here).

Rules: DOR marijuana-tax rules are in OAR chapter 150, division 475 (e.g. OAR 150-475-2100, product categorisation; OAR 150-475-2050, recordkeeping). The DOR page links OAR 150-475-2100 via the Secretary of State’s rules site. Full rule-by-rule analysis is Part 1 work and is not repeated here, except that OAR 150-475-2050(2)(b) requires retailers to keep records of tax-exempt medical sales including date, card number, product category, product name, unit price, units and total.

2.3 Local tax — statute, verbatim operative text

Citation: ORS 475C.453, “Local tax or fee; referral to electors for approval” [Formerly 475B.491; originally 2015 c.614 §34a (HB 3400)]. Text via https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_475c.453 and https://law.justia.com/codes/oregon/volume-14/chapter-475c/section-475c-453/ (accessed 2026-11-01).

Verbatim operative text — ORS 475C.453(1)–(4):

“(1)(a) Except as expressly authorized by this section, the authority to impose a tax or fee on the production, processing or sale of marijuana items in this state is vested solely in the Legislative Assembly. (b) Except as expressly authorized by this section, a county, city or other municipal corporation or district may not adopt or enact ordinances imposing a tax or fee on the production, processing or sale of marijuana items in this state.”

“(2) Subject to subsection (4) of this section, the governing body of a city or county may adopt an ordinance to be referred to the electors of the city or county as described in subsection (3) of this section that imposes a tax or a fee on the sale of marijuana items that are sold in the area subject to the jurisdiction of the city or the unincorporated area subject to the jurisdiction of a county by a marijuana retailer that holds a license issued under ORS 475C.097.”

“(3) If the governing body of a city or county adopts an ordinance under this section, the governing body shall refer the measure of the ordinance to the electors of the city or county for approval at the next statewide general election.”

“(4) An ordinance adopted under this section may not impose a tax or fee: (a) In excess of three percent; or (b) On a registry identification cardholder or on a designated primary caregiver who is purchasing a marijuana item for a registry identification cardholder.”

Consequences that follow from the text (not from secondary summaries): 1. No city or county may invent its own cannabis production, processing or wholesale tax. The only local tax authorised is the retail-sale tax in §475C.453, capped at 3%. 2. It must be referred to electors at the next statewide general election (i.e. a November even-year election) and approved there. A council cannot impose it by ordinance alone. 3. It applies only to sales by a retailer holding an ORS 475C.097 licence in the city’s area or the county’s unincorporated area. A city tax does not reach sales in unincorporated county land, and a county tax does not reach sales inside an incorporated city — the two are geographically complementary, not stacked. Verify in practice: whether any retailer sits in both a city-tax and a county-tax area and is charged both — the statute’s wording (“in the area subject to the jurisdiction of the city or the unincorporated area subject to the jurisdiction of a county”) indicates no stacking, but no DOR guidance confirming the point was opened for this report. 4. It can never be charged on a medical cardholder/caregiver purchase. 5. Interaction with opt-out: DOR’s locality guidance and the Corvallis ballot title (see §3.4, Corvallis) both reflect the rule that a jurisdiction that prohibits licensed premises may not impose the tax — Corvallis Measure 2-96’s explanatory statement says: “a city that adopts an ordinance prohibiting the establishment of [licensed premises] may not impose a tax on the production, processing or sale of marijuana” and that if facilities were later banned “the tax rate would be set to zero (0).” The exact statutory hook for that ineligibility (state-shared revenue ineligibility vs. local-tax ineligibility) is Verify — do not cite a section number for it from this report. 6. Pre-2015 local taxes are not grandfathered into the 3% scheme: Hillsboro’s 2014 proposal of a 10% gross-sales tax and Ashland’s 2014 sales tax (reported in Cannabis Business Times, 2014) predate HB 3400 and cannot be relied on as current authority; the current cap is 3% by voter approval. Those early ordinances are history, not current law, and are not listed as current taxes in §3.4.

Who administers the local tax — DOR vs. self-administration: - DOR, Marijuana Tax Distributions (Aug 2024): “DOR also administers local marijuana taxes on behalf of 85 cities and 7 counties located throughout the state. Additionally, at least 14 cities and 4 counties self-administer local marijuana taxes.” - The same figures are repeated in the CannBus Q3 2026 market report (secondary, citing DOR Aug 2024) as “DOR collected local tax for 85 cities and 7 counties (August 2024); at least 14 cities and 4 counties collect their own.” Because the underlying DOR paper is August 2024, the 85/7 and 14/4 counts are stale as of 1 Nov 2026 — Verify for current count. No newer DOR count was located. - DOR’s locality page states the table on that page lists “Municipalities that have agreements with us to collect the tax” with “Local tax rates and any administrative fees.” Limitation found on 2026-11-01: the text-fetch of that page returned only the introductory paragraphs; the table itself did not render (it is evidently loaded dynamically). The full DOR-administered list therefore could not be reproduced from the page as opened — see Gaps. The exact URL to check in a live browser is https://www.oregon.gov/dor/programs/businesses/pages/marijuana-locality-tax.aspx . Do not treat absence from this report as absence from that table.

2.4 Which jurisdictions adopted a local tax?

What can be said firmly: - In November 2016, 111 cities and counties put a local marijuana tax to voters. Contemporary reporting (Ganjapreneur, 2016, summarising The Oregonian’s early results; Associated Press via Leafly/Cannabis Chronicles, Nov 2016) reports that more than 90% approved, including Portland, Eugene, Salem and Bend, and Association of Oregon Counties counsel Rob Bovett is quoted as saying “All (of Oregon’s) 111 cities and counties voted yes on the local tax” — i.e. every jurisdiction that put the question in 2016 approved it, including some that simultaneously voted to prohibit businesses (a “hedge” so the tax would be in place if voters later allowed businesses). Caution: the “all 111” quote is a secondary report of a lobbyist’s statement, not an official canvass. It is used here only to explain why the 3% tax is near-universal in allowing jurisdictions, not as a per-jurisdiction official result. Per-jurisdiction official results must be taken from the county elections canvass for that jurisdiction (see §3.4, where available). - The practical result, confirmed by DOR’s current page (“many cities and counties have passed a 3 percent local marijuana tax”) and by DOR’s 85+14 administration counts, is that a retailer in most allowing cities/counties charges 20% combined. A retailer in a jurisdiction that never adopted a local tax, or that adopted one but self-administers, still charges 17% state tax; whether it charges local tax depends on that jurisdiction’s own ordinance and collection route — check the city/county, not this report’s summary. - No jurisdiction may exceed 3%. Any claim of a current 4%, 5% or 10% local retail marijuana tax in Oregon is inconsistent with ORS 475C.453(4)(a) and should be treated as either a pre-HB 3400 historical ordinance, a different tax (e.g. a general business licence fee not on marijuana sales — Verify), or an error. The 2025 bill that would have let cities raise the local tax to 10% (SB 1506, reported in secondary press, 2025) was not enacted — no such authority exists as of 1 Nov 2026. Verify: SB 1506’s final OLIS status was not opened for this report; it is mentioned only to warn against assuming it passed.

Per-jurisdiction adoption table: The required cities/counties are dealt with individually in §3.4, with the same tax information repeated there so Parts 2 and 3 match. In summary form (detail and caveats in §3.4): - Confirmed 3% (official city/county source opened or official election record cited): Portland (City Code ch. 6.07), Eugene (city FAQ + Ordinance 20566), Corvallis (Measure 2-96, 2016), Ontario (Nov 2018 measure, 56.8%, with 3% tax — secondary report of the city measure, see §3.4), Clatsop County unincorporated area (County Code ch. 3.24, Ord. 2018-04, 3%). - Reported 3% in the November 2016 round (secondary contemporary reporting, individual measure number Verify): Salem, Bend, and — by the “more than 90% approved” roundup — the large majority of allowing jurisdictions. Salem’s own measure record (Marion County Elections, Nov 2016, Measure 24-400-series entry) describes a 3% tax credited to the general fund then to the Police Department, estimated $100,000 for 2017 — see §3.4. - Verify individually (no city/county tax ordinance opened for this report): Gresham, Hillsboro, Beaverton, Springfield (OR), Medford, Ashland, Grants Pass, Klamath Falls, Hood River, Astoria (city — as distinct from Clatsop County), Newport, Pendleton, Milton-Freewater, Jackson County (unincorporated), Josephine County (unincorporated). For each of these §3.4 states what was found (opt-out status, any code chapter located) and marks the tax rate Verify rather than asserting 3%. The fact that a city allows retailers does not by itself prove it adopted the 3% tax, and the fact that it adopted the tax does not prove it allows retailers (see the 2016 “hedge” votes). - Opted-out jurisdictions: no licensed retail sale occurs there, so no local retail tax is collected there even if a tax ordinance was adopted as a hedge; if the ban is later repealed (ORS 475C.457), the tax position must be re-checked at that time.

2.5 Medical exemption — and its sunset (the most consequential tax trap in this Part)

Citation: ORS 475C.678, “Exemption from tax on retail sale of marijuana items; rules” [Formerly 475B.707]. Text via https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/oregon/or-statutes/oregon_statutes_475c-678 (accessed 2026-11-01).

Verbatim operative text — ORS 475C.678(2):

“(2) Notwithstanding ORS 475C.674: (a) A tax is not imposed upon the retail sale of marijuana items in this state to a registry identification cardholder or to a designated primary caregiver who is purchasing a marijuana item for a registry identification cardholder; and (b) A marijuana retailer may not collect the tax imposed under ORS 475C.674 from a consumer if, at the time at which the retail sale of the marijuana item occurs, the consumer provides proof to the marijuana retailer that the consumer: (A) Holds a valid registry identification card under ORS 475C.783; or (B) Holds a valid identification card under ORS 475C.783(5)(b) and is purchasing the marijuana item for a registry identification cardholder.”

DOR must adopt rules for documenting the card (ORS 475C.678(3)(a)) and may adopt verification rules (3)(b). Terms (“designated primary caregiver,” “registry identification card,” “registry identification cardholder”) take their ORS 475C.777 meanings.

Sunset — this is current law with a fixed end date: - 2021 c.525 §44 (HB 2445, 2021) provides: “ORS 475B.707 [renumbered 475C.678] applies to retail sales of marijuana items occurring on or after January 1, 2016, and before January 1, 2028.” - The HB 2445 staff measure summary (OLIS, 2021) states the same in plain English: the measure “Enacts [an] explicit sunset to the exemption of medical marijuana registry identification cardholder or primary caregiver from the tax imposed on the retail sale of marijuana items” and “aligns the elimination of the tax exemption to a six year cycle, starting on January 1, 2022 and ending on January 1, 2028.” Source: https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2021r1/Downloads/CommitteeMeetingDocument/242710 (accessed 2026-11-01). - Consequence: As of the research date (1 Nov 2026) the exemption is still in force, but on 1 January 2028 it expires by its own terms unless the Legislature extends it. The same forecast assumption appears in secondary analysis (CannBus Q3 2026, citing the state economist’s forecast: “The state economist’s forecast assumes medical sales will be taxed from 2028 under current law, unless the legislature extends the exemption” and “Medical sales tax exemption … The state economist’s forecast assumes the exemption expires at the end of 2027”). Do not present the medical exemption as permanent. Any budget, pricing or patient-cost projection beyond 2027 must show both branches (extended vs. taxed at 17% + any local tax, noting the local-tax bar in ORS 475C.453(4)(b) would also need amendment for a local tax to apply to cardholders). - Local-tax mirror: ORS 475C.453(4)(b) bars a local tax on cardholders/caregivers, with no sunset stated in the section text as republished. Whether that bar survives the 2028 state-exemption sunset without further legislation is Verify — the two provisions have different histories and the 2021 sunset note attaches to 475C.678, not to 475C.453. - Practical proof at the till: card + government photo ID at time of sale (DOR rule; OAR 150-475-2050 recordkeeping, §2.2). A retailer that fails to document the exemption risks the sale being treated as taxable on audit. - Out-of-state patients: Oregon has no general out-of-state-patient purchase right that changes the tax rule — the exemption turns on holding a valid Oregon registry card (or the §475C.783(5)(b) caregiver card), not on residence alone. Reciprocity detail is Part 1/12 work; do not infer a tax exemption for a non-Oregon card from this Part.

2.6 Revenue distribution — Measure 91 → Measure 110 → HB 4002 (2024)

Current governing section: ORS 475C.726, “Oregon Marijuana Account” [Formerly 475B.759]. Moneys are transferred into the account under ORS 475C.734. DOR certifies the amount quarterly. Before other transfers, DOR pays OLCC and Criminal Justice Commission fixed amounts under ORS 475C.728 (see below) — the order matters and is a common source of error in secondary summaries that describe only the percentage split.

Verbatim core — ORS 475C.726(3)(b)–(d) (2025 text, via Justia/LawServer, accessed 2026-11-01):

“(b)(A) Before making other transfers of moneys required by this section, the department shall transfer quarterly to the Drug Treatment and Recovery Services Fund all moneys in the Oregon Marijuana Account in excess of $11,250,000.”

“(c) Subject to subsection (4) of this section, and after making the transfer of moneys required by paragraph (b) of this subsection, the department shall transfer quarterly 20 percent of the moneys in the Oregon Marijuana Account as follows: (A) Ten percent … to the cities of this state … [75% by population of non-exempt cities as determined by Portland State University under ORS 190.510–190.610, 25% by number of licences held under ORS 475C.065, 475C.085, 475C.093 and 475C.097 on the last business day of the preceding calendar quarter]; (B) Ten percent … to counties … [shares per subsection (3)(c)(B), Verify full county formula from the official text before reuse].”

“(d) After making the transfer of moneys required by paragraph (b) of this subsection, 80 percent of the remaining moneys in the Oregon Marijuana Account must be used as follows: (A) Forty percent … solely for purposes for which moneys in the State School Fund established under ORS 327.008 may be used; (B) Twenty percent … solely for mental health treatment or for alcohol and drug abuse prevention, early intervention and treatment; … (D) Five percent … solely for purposes related to alcohol and drug abuse prevention, early intervention and treatment services.” [The 15% State Police share, subsection (3)(d)(C), is the remaining slice of the 80% — Verify the lettering from the official text before quoting (d)(C) verbatim; DOR’s plain-English summary below states it as 15% to Oregon State Police.]

DOR’s plain-English quarterly distribution (DOR marijuana page, opened 2026-11-01) — the version to use for briefing, with the statutory text above as authority:

“Of the first $11.25 million (adjusted annually for inflation) collected, the distribution is as follows: 40 percent: State School Fund; 20 percent: Oregon Health Authority (mental health treatment, alcohol and drug abuse prevention, early intervention, and treatment); 15 percent: Oregon State Police; 10 percent: Cities; 10 percent: Counties; 5 percent: Oregon Health Authority (additional alcohol and drug abuse prevention and treatment services).”

Reconciliation — why secondary summaries show two different percentage sets: Both are right, about different denominators. The “40/20/15/10/10/5” split applies to the first $11.25 million per quarter (inflation-adjusted). The “20% to cities/counties + 80% remainder split 40/20/15/5” formulation in ORS 475C.726(3)(c)–(d) describes the same distribution after the Measure 110 excess transfer: 20% of the account goes to cities/counties (10 + 10), and 80% of what remains is then split 40/20/15/5 — which, applied to the capped first-$11.25m, reproduces 40/20/15/10/10/5 of that capped amount. A summary that applies 40% to the entire quarterly collection (including the Drug Treatment excess) overstates schools and understates treatment. Use DOR’s formulation for totals; use the statute for the mechanism.

Fixed quarterly charges before the percentage split — ORS 475C.728 (Verify current amounts): - DOR’s page: “A portion of the revenue covers the costs of administering the tax. Funds also pay for OLCC enforcement costs. Since July 1, 2018, revenue has supported the Oregon Criminal Justice Commission’s Illegal Marijuana Market Enforcement Grant Program.” - The 2026 omnibus HB 4139 as introduced would have amended ORS 475C.728 to set “$875,000 to [OLCC] for deposit in the Marijuana Control and Regulation Fund” and “[$750,000] $3 million to the [Criminal Justice Commission] for deposit into the Illegal Marijuana Market Enforcement Grant Program Fund” quarterly (LegiScan text of HB 4139, accessed 2026-11-01). That is an introduced-bill proposal, NOT law, and HB 4139’s collapse is reported in secondary analysis (Legal 500, 2026) — its final status is Verify. Do not use $875,000/$3m as current figures. The pre-2026 fixed amounts in ORS 475C.728 as in force on 1 Nov 2026 are Verify from the official text (not reproduced here because the section text was not opened directly). - Inflation adjustment of the $11.25m cap: DOR states the cap is “adjusted annually for inflation.” The index, base year and current-year dollar cap are Verify — DOR’s distribution PDF (June 2026, see §2.7) uses the capped amounts quarter by quarter and is the place to read the operative cap for a given quarter, not a secondary summary. Secondary analysis (Sept 2026) describes the mechanism as “original recipients … receive an inflation-adjusted annual benchmark, originally $45 million” ($11.25m × 4 quarters). That $45m annual figure is the pre-inflation benchmark; the inflation-adjusted benchmark for FY2025/FY2026 is higher and is Verify from DOR.

History of the distribution: - Measure 91 (2014) as implemented, pre-Measure 110: 40% Common School Fund (later State School Fund in DOR’s wording), 20% OHA mental health/alcohol/drug, 15% State Police, 10% cities, 10% counties, 5% OHA — after DOR/OLCC/CJC costs. A 2017–2019 variant split the school share 30% State School Fund / 10% Community College Support Fund (SB 845 revenue impact, 2017, OLIS) — that variant is historical; DOR’s current summary shows the school share back as a single 40% State School Fund line. Verify the exact years of the community-college split before citing it for a specific fiscal year. - Measure 110 (Drug Addiction Treatment and Recovery Act, approved 3 Nov 2020, effective 1 Feb 2021 for possession provisions; tax diversion from 1 Jan 2021 per DOR): “Starting January 1, 2021, any funds collected above $11.25 million per quarter are directed to Measure 110, which funds the Drug Treatment and Recovery Services Fund.” (DOR page.) The fund finances Behavioral Health Resource Networks (BHRNs) via the Oversight and Accountability Council (later governance changes — see HB 4002 below). DOR’s Aug 2024 paper: “Ballot Measure 110 (2020) created the current formula in effect, as of 2020” and “Measure 110 modifies the Measure 91 distributions by capping the quarterly distributions to Measure 91 recipients at $11,250,000.00. The excess is directed to the new Drug Treatment and Recovery Services Account.” An OLIS 2021 paper projected for the 2021–23 biennium: $36m Common School Fund, $18m mental health/alcohol/drug, $13.5m State Police, $9m cities, $9m counties, $4.5m OHA, and $228.45m to the Drug Treatment and Recovery Services Fund — illustrating that, once collections exceed the cap, the majority of the money goes to treatment, not to the original recipients. - HB 4002 (2024) — what it did and did NOT do to the tax distribution: HB 4002 (signed April 2024; possession recriminalisation effective 1 Sept 2024) is primarily a drug-possession/deflection bill. For cannabis tax, its direct effect located for this report is narrow: it repealed ORS 293.665 and ORS 305.231 effective 1 September 2024 — the provisions that required the Office of Economic Analysis to calculate Measure 110 “savings” (reduced arrest/incarceration/supervision costs) and DOR to transfer those savings to the Drug Treatment and Recovery Fund. Source: Oregon Dept. of Administrative Services / Office of Economic Analysis, Ballot Measure 110 Savings page: https://www.Oregon.gov/das/oea/Pages/Ballot-Measure-110-Savings.aspx (accessed 2026-11-01): “House Bill 4002 (2024 Regular Session) repealed ORS 293.665 and 305.231 effective September 1, 2024… Given the effective date of HB 4002, the savings calculated for the 2021-23 biennium … and transferred in March 2024 should remain in effect. For 2023-25 and beyond, these calculations and transfers are no longer in effect.” - HB 4002 did NOT repeal the $11.25m quarterly excess transfer to the Drug Treatment and Recovery Services Fund in ORS 475C.726. That transfer remains in the 2025 text of ORS 475C.726 quoted above and in DOR’s current distribution summary. Any statement that “HB 4002 ended Measure 110 funding from cannabis tax” is wrong as to the ORS 475C.726 excess transfer; what ended was the additional savings transfer and, separately, the possession decriminalisation. Governance of the fund (Oversight and Accountability Council vs. later structures) and appropriation of the fund are Part 1/9 matters and are not settled here — Verify current fund governance before describing who awards BHRN grants in 2026. - Cities/counties eligibility for the state-shared slice: Only cities/counties that have not prohibited licensed premises are eligible. League of Oregon Cities, 2026 State Shared Revenues report: “Only cities that have not banned marijuana premises are eligible to receive a revenue payment. That is, a city may not adopt an ordinance that prohibits the establishment of premises for which a license is required … [and] may also not adopt an ordinance prohibiting a medical marijuana grow site or a medical marijuana facility.” Certification is now annual with DAS (HB 3067, 2019), replacing quarterly OLCC certification. The city-share formula (since 1 July 2017): 75% by population, 25% by number of licensed premises in the city. Source: LOC 2023/2026 State Shared Revenue Reports (accessed 2026-11-01). County-share formula: Verify full formula from ORS 475C.726(3)(c)(B) official text. - Local-tax revenue is NOT state-shared revenue: LOC 2023 report: “that local tax revenue is not considered a state shared revenue.” A city’s 3% receipts go directly to that city (via DOR after administrative costs, or directly if self-administered) and are not redistributed by the ORS 475C.726 formula.

2.7 Revenue figures — official data, with conflicts flagged, not hidden

Two different “totals” circulate and must not be mixed: 1. State marijuana tax (17%) receipts/distributions — DOR’s distribution and receipts reports. 2. State + local tax combined, or OLCC sales × tax rate — secondary calculations. A figure near $200m in a recent year is almost certainly a combined or sales-implied figure, not the 17% state tax alone.

2027 (July–Aug only) $24,353,760

Cross-checks that support Table A: FY2018 $82,203,729 matches DOR’s own 2019 accounting summary as cited in Gleam Law (“the Oregon Marijuana Account took in $82,203,729” for FY2018). FY2023 $142,088,093 and FY2024 $150,898,047 (+6.2%) match the Legislative Revenue Office exhibit (Feb 2025, OLIS): “MARIJUANA TAX … $142,088,093 $150,898,047 6.2%”. FY2025 $147.5m is consistent with Marijuana Moment (Mar 2026, citing DOR): “Marijuana tax revenue … $143.7 million in 2025” — close but not identical (calendar vs. fiscal year, and rounding/reporting date explain part of the gap; see Conflicts).

Table B — Figures that CONFLICT with Table A and must not be averaged into it: - Secondary analysis (Reklaim/Substack, Aug 2026, citing Willamette Week, Oregon Journalism Project and the Office of Economic Analysis): “Marijuana tax collections fell from $203.5 million in fiscal 2022 to $170.5 million in fiscal 2025, about 16%.” and “In September 2026, the Office of Economic Analysis said revenue had declined for six straight quarters and cut its 2025 to 2027 forecast by $14.1 million.” These figures are ~$33m (FY2022) and ~$23m (FY2025) higher than Table A. The most likely explanation — not confirmed from DOR for this report — is that the higher series includes local (3%) tax and/or is a different DOR series (e.g. total marijuana tax programme receipts including local taxes administered by DOR, or a forecast-basis series). Do not present either series as “the” revenue without naming which series it is. The DOR distribution PDF (June 2026) and DOR receipts PDF are the tie-breakers; neither was fully extracted for this report (see Gaps). - CannBus Q3 2026 (secondary, citing DOR distribution report dated 15 June 2026): “FY2025: $133.6 million distributed, of which $80.7 million (60%; CannBus calc.) went to the Drug Treatment and Recovery Services Fund.” $133.6m distributed is lower than $147.5m received in Table A — the difference is plausibly administration/OLCC/CJC charges, timing (quarterly distribution lag), and the $11.25m-cap mechanics, but that reconciliation is Verify from the June 2026 DOR distribution report itself. - Office of Economic Analysis forecast (Sept 2026, via CannBus): 2025–27 marijuana tax revenue forecast cut by $14.1m to $261.7m for the biennium, and 2027–29 cut by $51.5m vs. prior forecast. That is a forecast for a biennium, not an annual receipt — do not compare it directly to Table A’s annual figures.

These are secondary republications of DOR monthly data — Verify against DOR’s current monthly receipts PDF before citing a single month. The local:state ratio (~15–16%) is consistent with near-universal 3% adoption (3/17 = 17.6% if every sale bore local tax; the observed ratio is slightly lower, consistent with some sales in non-adopting jurisdictions and medical sales bearing neither tax).

2.8 IRS 280E and Oregon decoupling — the correct statement, and the Schedule III interaction

Federal baseline (given, not re-researched): 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to 280E. Oregon’s position is independent of that federal change and must not be conflated with it:

Personal income tax — ORS 316.680(1)(i) (2025 text, via Justia, accessed 2026-11-01):

“(1) There shall be subtracted from federal taxable income: … (i) Any federal deduction that the taxpayer would have been allowed for the production, processing or sale of marijuana items authorized under ORS 475C.005 to 475C.525 or 475C.770 to 475C.919 but for section 280E of the Internal Revenue Code.”

In plain English: for Oregon personal income tax, a taxpayer in an Oregon-authorised marijuana business adds back (subtracts from federal taxable income) the business deductions that federal law disallowed only because of 280E. The result is that, for Oregon purposes, ordinary and necessary business expenses are deductible even though they are not federally deductible (for adult-use, and for medical activity to the extent federal law still disallows it). The subtraction covers both the adult-use range (475C.005–475C.525) and the medical range (475C.770–475C.919) — i.e. Oregon decoupled for both medical and adult-use, not for medical only.

Corporate excise/income tax — ORS 317.363: DOR’s 2025 Form OR-20 instructions state: “ORS 317.363 allows Oregon taxpayers filing a corporate excise or income tax return to deduct business expenses otherwise barred by IRC §280E if the taxpayer is engaged in marijuana-related activities authorized by ORS 475C.005 to 475C.525, or ORS 475C.700 to 475C.919.” (Note the slightly different second range, 475C.700–475C.919, in the corporate instructions vs. 475C.770–475C.919 in ORS 316.680(1)(i) — Verify whether this is a drafting difference with substantive effect or a summary imprecision; do not harmonise them silently.) The same instructions add the parallel psilocybin subtraction (ORS 317.363, ORS 475A.210–475A.722), which is not cannabis and is mentioned only to prevent confusion.

History / litigation warning: The decoupling was not always smooth. Measure 91 initially disconnected Oregon from 280E; HB 3400 (2015) and HB 2041 (2015) then narrowed/reinstated the connection for tax year 2015, and the Oregon Tax Court in Dept. of Revenue v. Wakefield, TC 5404 (2022) (Regular Division, Manicke J.) held that for tax year 2015 deductions were disallowed under Oregon statute (reversing the Magistrate Division). That litigation concerns 2015 only and does not change the current ORS 316.680(1)(i) / ORS 317.363 subtractions. Do not cite Wakefield for any year after 2015 without fresh advice. (Case summary via Justia, accessed 2026-11-01.)

Interaction with the federal Schedule III change (28 Apr 2026) — what this Part can and cannot say: - Federal: For state-licensed medical activity that is now Schedule III, 280E (which by its terms applies to Schedule I and II substances) is generally lifted federally. Adult-use remains Schedule I and fully subject to 280E federally. - Oregon: Because Oregon already decouples via ORS 316.680(1)(i) / ORS 317.363, the federal Schedule III change does not change the Oregon deduction outcome for an Oregon-authorised business — the deduction was already allowed for Oregon purposes before 28 Apr 2026 and remains allowed after. What changes is the federal return for qualifying medical activity, and therefore the federal-taxable-income starting point for the Oregon return. Whether a particular OMMP grow site, an OLCC retailer selling to cardholders, or a dual medical/adult-use business counts as “state-licensed medical” for the federal Schedule III rule is Verify from the federal rule text (91 FR 22714) — this Part does not settle it, per the commissioning brief. In particular, do not assume that every sale by an OLCC retailer to a cardholder automatically counts as federal Schedule III medical activity, or that an OMMP grow site automatically does; the federal rule’s “state-licensed” language and any DEA/IRS guidance must be checked. - No Oregon “recoupling” was located: No 2025/2026 Oregon bill recoupling Oregon to 280E (which would have raised Oregon tax on cannabis businesses if federal 280E were lifted) was found in the searches tried. Verify on OLIS before advising on 2027+ Oregon returns, because recoupling is the obvious legislative response to a federal 280E change and may be proposed in the 2027 session. - Other Oregon business taxes that still apply regardless of 280E: Oregon income/excise tax (with the subtraction above), the 17%/3% retail taxes (§2.2–2.3), local business licence fees (Part 3), and — for businesses over the threshold — the Corporate Activity Tax. CAT is a gross-receipts tax, not an income tax, so 280E deductions are irrelevant to CAT; whether a cannabis business’s CAT base includes/excludes any item is Verify from DOR CAT guidance (no cannabis-specific CAT guidance was located).

2.9 Hemp product tax — current law vs. proposed law (do not mix them)

Current law (as of 1 Nov 2026): NO hemp-specific retail tax. - OLCC, Selling Hemp (opened via search result, accessed 2026-11-01): “Hemp items sold by an OLCC-licensed marijuana retailer are not subject to the retail sales tax on marijuana items.” - OLCC Hemp Bulletin HE2018-02 / CE2018-03 (29 June 2018): “Items derived from industrial hemp that do not contain marijuana are not subject to tax” and “Hemp items will be entered into the Metrc Cannabis Tracking System… Note that hemp products in METRC are not subject to tax, unless they are later mixed with marijuana.” The mixed-product rule: “Hemp items that are mixed with marijuana (example: 1 to 1 chocolate bar) are considered a marijuana item and should be taxed and tracked in Metrc according to the appropriate item.” - Consequence: a pure hemp-derived cannabinoid product sold in the general market (outside an OLCC retailer) or by an OLCC retailer as a hemp item bears no 17% and no 3% marijuana tax today. It may bear ordinary Oregon business taxes (income/excise, CAT if over threshold) like any other product — Verify for a specific product, as the general-market hemp registration and artificially-derived-cannabinoid rules (Part 1) affect what may be sold at all, but they do not create a retail tax. - ODA hemp licence fees (grower/handler) are fees, not product taxes, and are Part 7 work — not listed here.

Proposed law — HB 4139 (2026), introduced form only, NOT enacted as described: - Legal 500, Oregon Cannabis 2026: Legislative Forecast and Report (2026, accessed 2026-11-01, secondary): HB 4139 (the 2026 annual omnibus cannabis bill) as introduced would have “Impose[d] a 17% retail sales tax on industrial hemp-derived cannabinoid products. This is the same percentage levied on sales of marijuana items in the [OLCC] system. The bill has no provision for the local jurisdiction 3% add-on.” The same report states the bill “collapsed a few weeks ago when marijuana and hemp folks couldn’t agree on core items around intoxicating hemp products, or on how to implement the new federal hemp laws and rules” and was “kicked to an interim working group driven by the Governor’s office and the Cannabis Industry Association of Oregon (CIAO).” - Status: Verify on OLIS. Do not present the 17% hemp-derived-cannabinoid tax as law, do not apply the 3% local add-on to it (the introduced bill had none), and do not assume the interim working group’s output. The federal hemp dates in the baseline (12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026) postdate this report’s research date and may drive a 2027 bill — that is a follow-up, not a current tax. - Federal hemp definition interaction: No Oregon statute located for this report imposes a state tax that automatically tracks the federal total-THC definition. If Oregon enacts a hemp-derived-cannabinoid tax in 2027, its base (which products, which THC measure) will be defined by that bill, not by PL 119-37/119-103 alone. Verify in any 2027 update.

2.10 Other taxes and charges that touch cannabis businesses (completeness check)

  • Oregon has no general sales tax — so there is no “plus sales tax” on top of 17%+3% for cannabis, unlike most adult-use states. Accessories/paraphernalia sold without marijuana items are not subject to the marijuana tax (they are not “marijuana items” under ORS 475C.674(2)); whether a bundled sale (e.g. flower + pipe for one price) must be unbundled for tax is Verify from DOR categorisation guidance (OAR 150-475-2100).
  • Property tax, payroll/withholding, unemployment insurance, workers’ compensation: apply as for any Oregon business; no cannabis-specific rate was located. Unpaid marijuana, income, withholding and corporate activity taxes can give rise to DOR liens (secondary report, Willamette Week via Reklaim, Aug 2026, of $7.9m in new liens against one operator’s companies for taxes “going back to 2020”) — cited only to show DOR enforces across tax types, not as a rate.
  • Licence fees are not taxes and are Part 4 work. Do not add OLCC licence fees into any “tax burden” total in this Part.
  • Local business licence / registration fees (e.g. Salem’s marijuana business registration, Bend’s marijuana business operating licence — see §3.4) are local fees, not ORS 475C.453 taxes, and are capped/constrained differently. Their amounts are Verify per city (see §3.4) and must not be described as “local tax.”

Part 3 — Local Rules

PART 3 — LOCAL RULES

3.1 The Oregon local system — how it actually works

Oregon does not have a single statewide zoning code for cannabis. It has a state licence (OLCC) plus three distinct local powers, each with its own statute, its own procedure, and its own limits. Confusing them is the commonest error in secondary summaries.

Power 1 — Opt-out (prohibition) by ordinance referred to voters: ORS 475C.433, 475C.437, 475C.950. - A city council or county commission may adopt an ordinance prohibiting the establishment of licensed premises (producer, processor, wholesaler, retailer — and, in the medical lists, processing sites and dispensaries) in its area, but must refer it to electors. The League of Oregon Cities Municipal Handbook (Ch. 27, Marijuana Law, May 2021 / updated Oct 2025, accessed 2026-11-01) summarises ORS 475C.950 as: “a city council may adopt an ordinance to be referred to the electors of the city prohibiting the establishment of certain state-registered and state-licensed marijuana businesses in the area subject to the jurisdiction of the city.” - Historical shortcut (now closed): Before 27 December 2015, a city/county where 55% or more voted against Measure 91 could implement a ban without referring it to voters. OLCC’s opt-out record states this expressly (see §3.3): “Prior to December 27, 2015 cities and counties could implement local bans if 55 percent or more of voters in their jurisdiction voted against Measure 91 without referring the ordinance to voters.” After that date, referral is required. That is why the OLCC list distinguishes “No Voter Referral” jurisdictions (the pre-27 Dec 2015 cohort) from later voter-referral cohorts. - What opt-out does NOT do: It does not ban possession, home grow (4 plants per household) or personal use — those are state rights (ORS 475C.445, right to possess for personal use; ORS 475C.441 bars local ordinances prohibiting possession). OLCC’s record: “Oregon law provides cities and counties the opportunity to prohibit recreational marijuana businesses in their jurisdiction, with the exception of labs.” Laboratories are therefore not opt-out-able. Medical grow sites and the personal-use rights are likewise outside the commercial opt-out. - Repeal / opt-in: ORS 475C.457 (formerly 475B.496) lets the governing body repeal a prohibition ordinance (for processing sites, dispensaries, producers, processors, wholesalers, retailers, and exclusively-medical licensees, or any combination) and requires it to send the repeal text to OHA (medical) and/or OLCC + DAS within 30 days (OLCC/DAS for ORS 475C.065/085/093/097 premises). Verbatim (1): “The governing body of a city or county may repeal an ordinance that prohibits the establishment of any one or more of the following in the area subject to the jurisdiction of the city or in the unincorporated area subject to the jurisdiction of a county: (a) Marijuana processing sites…; (b) Medical marijuana dispensaries…; (c) Marijuana producers…; (d) [processors]; (e) Marijuana wholesalers…; (f) Marijuana retailers…; … or (k) Any combination…” — via https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_475c.457 (accessed 2026-11-01). Ontario (2018) is the best-known repeal/opt-in (see §3.4). The Handbook notes that amending an ordinance to prohibit/allow exclusively medical licensees, processing sites or dispensaries can be done without referral — Verify that nuance from ORS 475C.950(7) before relying on it for a non-medical licence type. - Effect on state-shared revenue: An opted-out city/county is ineligible for the ORS 475C.726 city/county share (see §2.6). An opted-out jurisdiction that later opts in regains eligibility prospectively — exact timing Verify from DAS certification guidance.

Power 2 — Reasonable time, place and manner (TPM) regulation: ORS 475C.449 (formerly 475B.486). - Verbatim (1): “‘reasonable regulations’ includes: (a) Reasonable conditions on the manner in which a marijuana producer… may produce marijuana…; (b) … processor… may process…; (c) … wholesaler… may sell… at wholesale; (d) Reasonable conditions on the manner in which a marijuana retailer… may sell marijuana items; (e) Reasonable limitations on the hours during which a premises… may operate; (f) Reasonable requirements related to the public’s access to a premises…; and (g) Reasonable limitations on where a premises… may be located.” - Verbatim (2) (opening): “Notwithstanding ORS 30.935, 215.253(1) or 633.738, the governing body of a city or county may adopt ordinances that impose reasonable regulations on the operation of businesses located at premises for which a license or certificate has been issued under ORS 475C.005 to 475C.525 if the premises are located in the area subject to the jurisdiction of the city or county, except that the governing body of a city or county may not: (a) Adopt an ordinance that prohibits a premises for which a license has been issued under ORS 475C.097 from being located within a distance that is greater than 1,000 feet of another premises for which a license has been issued under ORS 475C.097. (b) Adopt an ordinance that imposes a setback requirement for an agricultural building used to produce marijuana… [if, in summary, the building meets the statutory conditions including four opaque walls and a roof — Verify full (2)(b) conditions from official text].” Source: https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_475c.449 (accessed 2026-11-01). - What this means in practice: A city may zone cannabis to commercial/industrial/mixed-use zones, set hours (within state hours — OLCC retail hours are 7 a.m.–10 p.m. by state rule; a city may narrow them by TPM ordinance, Verify per city), require a local business registration/licence, impose odour, security, signage and parking conditions, and impose additional buffers — but it may not impose a retailer-to-retailer buffer greater than 1,000 feet, and it may not use TPM to effect a de facto ban that the opt-out procedure would require. The Handbook (Ch. 27) notes the asymmetry with medical dispensaries: “while medical marijuana dispensaries are prohibited from being within 1,000 feet of each other under state law, there is no such requirement for recreational retailers unless a city adopts it as a local time, place, and manner regulation.” - Preemption backstop — ORS 475C.429: municipal charter amendments and local ordinances inconsistent with ORS 475C.005–475C.525 are preempted. A TPM ordinance that conflicts with state licensing, testing or tracking rules is vulnerable on that ground; a TPM ordinance that merely adds a lawful local condition is not. The Troutdale/Mt. Hood Community College dispute (2022, Planning Commission record) illustrates the boundary: OLCC advised that a community college is not a “public elementary or secondary school” for the state school buffer, and that licensability (including the school-buffer determination) is OLCC’s, not the city’s, except for comprehensive-plan/land-use consistency via the LUCS.

Power 3 — Local tax: ORS 475C.453. Covered fully in Part 2 (§2.3–2.4). It is listed here only to complete the trilogy: tax requires voter approval at a statewide general election, caps at 3%, never applies to cardholders, and is geographically limited to the city’s area / county’s unincorporated area.

The LUCS — the gate between local land use and state licence: ORS 475C.053; OAR 845-025-1090, 845-025-1180. - To obtain an OLCC producer, processor, wholesaler or retailer licence (and for a change of location), the applicant must request a Land Use Compatibility Statement from the city/county that authorises land use where the premises sits. OLCC “must receive a [LUCS] … prior to acting on an application” (OAR 845-025-1090(2)(a), as quoted in State ex rel. Elitextrx LLC v. Siegel (Multnomah County), Or. Ct. App. 2024). - The LUCS “must demonstrate that the requested license is for a land use that is allowable as a permitted or conditional use within the given zoning designation where the land is located” (ORS 475C.053(1), as quoted in Elitextrx). - Elitextrx rule (2024): Whether a use is “outright permitted” or “conditional” for LUCS timing depends on whether the proposed use requires discretionary local permit approval within that zoning designation. If it does, the county need not issue the LUCS before that discretionary approval is obtained. Practical consequence: a LUCS is not a rubber stamp, and an applicant in a conditional-use zone must sequence local land-use approval before OLCC will act — a common cause of delay that is often misreported as OLCC delay. - Form and process: Applicant completes §1, submits to city/county planning, planning completes §2 (compatible / not prohibited, with zone and any land-use application number), returns signed/dated form; applicant files it with OLCC. The form itself states: “Section 34(4)(a) of 2015 Oregon Laws, Chapter 614, requires OLCC to request and obtain the LUCS and have a positive LUCS prior to issuing a license” and “A LUCS is required for all proposed marijuana facilities before an OLCC license can be obtained.” Local jurisdictions were not required to begin processing LUCS forms until 4 Jan 2016, 8:30 a.m. (form note — historical). - LUCS vs. opt-out: OLCC checks the LUCS and the opt-out list. A positive LUCS in an opted-out jurisdiction does not cure the opt-out; conversely, a jurisdiction that allows cannabis but zones a particular parcel residential will produce a negative LUCS and OLCC must not licence there. - LUCS fees: Cities/counties charge their own planning fees for LUCS processing and any underlying land-use application. No statewide LUCS fee schedule was located — Verify per jurisdiction (Bend and Salem LUCS examples opened for this report show the form but not a fee schedule). - State school buffer (the floor every LUCS sits on): An OLCC retailer premises may not be within 1,000 feet of a public elementary/secondary school (compulsory attendance, ORS 339.020) or a private/parochial elementary/secondary school (ORS 339.030), measured as OLCC rule provides (property-line to property-line in secondary summaries — Verify measurement rule from OAR 845-025-1115 / 845-025-1090 before citing a measurement method), nor in an area zoned exclusively for residential use. A 2025 OLCC draft rule note records SB 162 (2025) as restoring the prior standard by excluding pre-kindergarten and kindergarten-only locations from the denial criteria — Verify whether SB 162 was enacted and its effective date before relying on the pre-K exclusion. Local buffers add to this state floor (schools, childcare, parks, residential districts, retailer-to-retailer up to 1,000 ft) — see per-city entries.

Local business registration / operating licence (a fourth, often-overlooked layer): Several cities require a separate local registration or operating licence in addition to the OLCC licence and the LUCS (Salem SRC ch. 31; Bend’s marijuana business operating licence, Bend Municipal Code ch. 7.50 as referenced on a Bend LUCS). These are TPM/business-licence measures, not ORS 475C.453 taxes. Their fees and renewal cycles are per-city (see §3.4, Verify where not located).

Three flagged rows (do not use without visual check of the PDF): - Deschutes County: extracted as “Y Y N N Y” — if read literally, producer and processor prohibited, wholesale and retail not prohibited, with a general-election referral. That would make Deschutes the only county on the list that allows retail/wholesale while banning production/processing. It is plausible (Deschutes contains Bend, which plainly allows retailers — see §3.4 — so a county-wide retail ban would be odd for the unincorporated area, though not impossible), but the column collapse makes it equally possible the extraction misaligned a neighbouring row. Verify visually. - John Day: extracted as “N N N N” — i.e. on the list but prohibiting none of the four types. That reads as a jurisdiction that filed an opt-out form / was once listed but currently prohibits nothing (possibly a repealed ban retained on the record, or an extraction error). Verify visually; do not cite John Day as opted out. - Troutdale: extracted as “N N N Y N” — i.e. only retail prohibited (or only one column Y). Troutdale’s 2022 Kaleafa retail dispute (see §3.1) shows retail licensing activity being contested there, which is consistent with a nuanced local position, but again the column parsing is unreliable. Verify visually. - Sherwood: extracted with a trailing “Y” in the General Election column (“Sherwood Y Y Y Y Y”) — i.e. all four prohibited and a general-election referral noted. That trailing Y may be the referral flag, not a fifth prohibition. Verify.

What the list does NOT show: It does not show (a) medical processing sites / dispensaries opt-outs separately (the PDF title is recreational facilities; medical opt-outs are tracked via OHA/DAS and the ORS 475C.457 lists), (b) the date each ban took effect or the vote margin for each jurisdiction, or (c) jurisdictions that opted out and later opted back in and were removed (Ontario is correctly absent from the September 2026 list, consistent with its 2018 repeal — see §3.4). For dates and margins, the county elections canvass for that jurisdiction’s election is the official source (see §3.4 examples).

Historical context (for the full dossier’s Part 9, summarised here only because it explains the list’s shape): The November 2016 general election was the main opt-out/opt-in election: ~60 jurisdictions voted on allowing vs. banning, and ~111 voted on the 3% tax (see §2.4). Many 2016 bans were later reversed in whole or part (e.g. Albany, Cannon Beach, Coos Bay, Gervais, Gladstone, Grants Pass, Hubbard, La Pine, Lebanon, Madras, Manzanita, Medford, Myrtle Point, Oregon City, Scappoose, Sweet Home are listed in a Nov 2016 roundup as voting to allow recreational sales — AllBud, 15 Nov 2016, summarising The Oregonian — and none of those except none on the 2026 list is consistent with that, except that Grants Pass/Medford etc. are indeed absent from the 2026 list). The direction of travel since 2016 has been net opt-in, but the 2026 list still contains 100 jurisdictions — the map remains deeply split between the Willamette Valley / coast / Portland metro (mostly allowing) and eastern/southern rural counties and small cities (mostly prohibiting).

3.3 Official OLCC list — source, retrieval status, exact URL

Retrieved successfully for this report. The official list is:

  • Title: Record of Cities/Counties Prohibiting Licensed Recreational Marijuana Facilities
  • Publisher: Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission (OLCC)
  • Date on document: September 2026 (footer on each page)
  • Exact URL (opened directly 2026-11-01): https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/Documents/Cities_Counties_RMJOptOut.pdf
  • Format: PDF, 4 pages. No CSV/XLSX download and no interactive search version was located. There is no “export” button; the PDF is the source.
  • Contact on document: OLCC.Marijuana@olcc.oregon.gov (general OLCC marijuana mailbox — not a personal address).
  • Update frequency as stated: Not stated on the document. The September 2026 footer is the only dating. Treat it as current to September 2026, not as a live register — a jurisdiction that opted in/out in October 2026 would not appear until the next revision. Verify any licensing decision against the city/county ordinance itself, not only against this PDF.
  • If the URL moves: OLCC’s marijuana licensing pages are under https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/ — search that site for “Record of Cities/Counties Prohibiting” if the direct PDF link breaks.

No separate official “opted-in” list exists — allowing jurisdictions are simply those not on this list (for the four recreational licence types) and not otherwise prohibiting via a medical-specific ordinance. Absence from the list is necessary but not sufficient for licensability: the parcel must still pass LUCS/zoning and the state school buffer.

3.4 Required cities and counties — tax, fees, buffers, TPM, opt-out status

How to read this section: For each jurisdiction: (1) opt-out status from the September 2026 OLCC list; (2) local tax (rate + authority + administration route where found); (3) fees (local registration/operating licence/LUCS fee where published); (4) buffers and TPM specifics where found; (5) official source links. Where an item was not found, it says Verify/Unavailable — that is a finding, not an omission. A city that is not on the opt-out list and has retailers operating is treated as “allowing” for that licence type, but the date it began allowing and the vote by which it did so are given only where an official election record was located.

Statewide buffers that apply in every city below (unless a city adds more): retailer ≥1,000 ft from public/private elementary/secondary schools (ORS 475C.101 / OAR 845-025-1115 line, via 2025 OLCC draft rule text) and not in exclusively residential zoning. Retailer-to-retailer: no state buffer; local TPM may impose up to 1,000 ft (ORS 475C.449(2)(a)). State retail hours 7 a.m.–10 p.m. (OLCC rule; Salem secondary summary cites the same hours — Verify from the OAR retail-hours rule for a specific licence type before advising).

Portland (Multnomah County; also extends into Washington and Clackamas Counties — the city, not the metro, is the taxing jurisdiction)

  • Opt-out: Not on the September 2026 OLCC list. Allows all four licence types.
  • Local tax: 3% — CONFIRMED (official city code). Portland City Code Chapter 6.07, Tax on Recreational Marijuana Sales (added by Ordinance 186857; amended by Resolution 37217, approved at the 8 Nov 2016 election, effective 8 Nov 2016; amended by Ordinance 191957, effective 1 Jan 2025). §6.07.030: “The amount of tax levied is as follows: Three percent of the retail sales price paid to the seller in a retail sale of marijuana to any consumer.” Purpose (§6.07.010, as amended 2025): tax on “every person who sells recreational marijuana, or recreational marijuana-infused products, to consumers within Portland.” The 2016 ballot measure earmarked revenue for drug/alcohol treatment, public safety investments, and support for neighbourhood small businesses (Resolution 37217). A 2019 City Auditor audit found most collections had in practice gone to police/transportation programmes (allowed under the broad ballot categories) and criticised transparency — secondary/official audit summary via Portland.gov (May 2019). Administration route (DOR vs. self): Verify — Portland is large enough to self-administer, but the DOR locality table (not rendered, §2.3) must be checked; do not assume.
  • Earlier history (not current law): The Council first adopted Chapter 6.07 in 2014 with a 10% tax; that rate was replaced by the voter-approved 3% in 2016 to comply with HB 3400 / ORS 475C.453. The 10% figure must not be quoted as current.
  • Fees / TPM / buffers: Portland’s cannabis programme (Office of Community & Civic Life, now reorganised — Verify current administering bureau in 2026) historically required a local marijuana business licence in addition to OLCC licensing, with zoning via Title 33. Specific current Portland buffer distances beyond the state school buffer, current local licence fee, and current hours were not opened for this report — Verify from Portland City Code Title 33 and the city’s cannabis programme pages. Do not import another city’s buffers into Portland.
  • Sources: Portland City Code ch. 6.07: https://www.portland.gov/code/6/07 (accessed 2026-11-01 via search result); Resolution 37217 file: https://efiles.portlandoregon.gov/Record/9496847/file/document ; Auditor summary: https://www.portlandoregon.gov/auditor/article/734226?archive=2019-06

Eugene (Lane County)

  • Opt-out: Not on the September 2026 OLCC list. Allows all four licence types.
  • Local tax: 3% — CONFIRMED (official city FAQ + ordinance). City of Eugene FAQ (accessed 2026-11-01): “Eugene’s Marijuana Tax is equal to 3% of the retail sale price of marijuana items. The City of Eugene Marijuana Tax Ordinance does not allow marijuana retailers to withhold a percentage of the taxes collected to cover the cost of collection and administration of the tax.” Worked example in the FAQ: $300,000 April sales → $9,000 city tax. Penalty: 5% if late, +20% if >30 days late; interest 4% annually; 100% penalty for failure to file may be imposed by the Tax Administrator. Receipt must show business name/address, items, category, pre-tax total, state tax, local tax, and total. Authority cited in the FAQ: Administrative Order No. 44-16-05-F and Ordinance No. 20566. The FAQ also notes: “Eugene is working to finalize an agreement to have the State of Oregon Department of Revenue (DOR) provide tax administration services” — that sentence is undated in the FAQ as extracted; Verify whether Eugene is now DOR-administered or still self-administered before filing.

No current Eugene retailer-to-retailer buffer was located — treat as no such buffer found, Verify from Eugene Code ch. 3 / land-use code before advising a site. No Eugene local licence fee was located — Verify.
  • Sources: Eugene FAQ: https://www.eugene-or.gov/FAQ.aspx?QID=696 ; Eugene Weekly piece (secondary, for the buffer history only): https://eugeneweedly.com/2018/07/19/nothing-is-certain-but-weed-and-back-taxes/

Salem (Marion County, with a Polk County portion — the city is the jurisdiction)

  • Opt-out: Not on the September 2026 OLCC list. Allows all four licence types.
  • Local tax: 3% — REPORTED, with official measure description. Marion County Elections, November 8, 2016 General Election measures list, City of Salem measure (24-400 series): “If approved, this measure would result in the establishment of a three percent tax on the sale of marijuana items by a marijuana retailer within the city of Salem. The tax would apply only to the retail sale of recreational marijuana items… The tax would not apply to the sale of medical marijuana or industrial hemp, or the wholesale of marijuana items… All funds… shall be credited to the City’s general fund. Revenue… will first be expended to pay the costs to administer and enforce the tax. All remaining proceeds… will be allocated to the City of Salem Police Department.” Estimated $100,000 for 2017. Salem LUCS letters (e.g. 21 Feb 2025, 4550 Commercial St SE; 17 Apr 2025, 1830 23rd St SE) repeat: “marijuana businesses within the City must also be registered pursuant to SRC 31.015” and treat retail marijuana sales as a “retail sales and service use” (SRC 400.045), permitted in MU-III (Mixed Use) zoning per SRC Table 535-1 in the examples given. Registration fee amount: Unavailable — not in the LUCS letters opened; check https://www.cityofsalem.net/Pages/register-your-marijuana-business.aspx (linked in secondary sources) in a live browser.

That is stricter than the state floor (which covers schools, not parks/residential generally) and, for retailer-to-retailer distance, sits exactly at the ORS 475C.449(2)(a) ceiling (1,000 ft). A retailer just outside Ontario city limits in unincorporated Malheur County is prohibited; a retailer inside city limits is allowed. Keep the two jurisdictions apart.

  • Fees / buffers / TPM: Unavailable — Verify. (Newport OR is not Newport RI; Lincoln County OR is not Lincoln County in any other state.)

Pendleton (Umatilla County)

  • Opt-out: Not on the September 2026 OLCC list as a city (Pendleton was a 2015 “Y” referral entry in the 2016-era list — i.e. it proposed a ban for a vote — but it does not appear on the September 2026 list, consistent with voters rejecting the ban or the ban later being repealed). The 2016 Pendleton vote result itself was not extracted — Verify from Umatilla County elections if the date/margin matters. Current status per the 2026 list: allowing.
  • Contrast — county: Umatilla County is on the September 2026 list (Y Y Y Y). As with Klamath Falls and Ontario, city-allow / county-ban is the pattern: premises inside Pendleton city limits are not county-banned; premises in unincorporated Umatilla County are.
  • Local tax: Verify. No Pendleton tax ordinance opened — Verify (and note the LOC 2026 shared-revenue table lists Pendleton with a state-shared estimate, consistent with allowing status, not a local-tax figure).
  • Fees / buffers / TPM: Unavailable — Verify.

Milton-Freewater (Umatilla County, Oregon — NOT Walla Walla, Washington)

  • Opt-out: YES — on the September 2026 OLCC list, all four types (Y Y Y Y as extracted). Licensed producer, processor, wholesaler and retailer premises are prohibited in Milton-Freewater. (2016-era list: “Milton-Freewater Y” referral entry — the ban was put to voters and stands on the 2026 list.)
  • Local tax: No licensed retail sale occurs in the city, so no local retail tax is collected there. Whether Milton-Freewater adopted a hedge tax in 2016 (as many banning jurisdictions did) is Verify from the city code — a hedge ordinance, if it exists, produces no revenue while the ban stands and must not be presented as an operating tax.
  • Border note: Milton-Freewater sits on the Washington line (Walla Walla, WA is the neighbouring Washington city, across the state line). Washington’s 37% cannabis tax and different licensing do not apply in Milton-Freewater, and Oregon’s 17%/3% taxes do not apply in Walla Walla. Keep the two cities’ rules apart.

Cities within Jackson County that are on the list (Central Point, Eagle Point, Jacksonville — all Y Y Y Y) prohibit premises inside their city limits only; the county’s allowing status does not override a city ban, and a city ban does not extend to unincorporated county land.

3.5 Business concentration — ONLY what official sources say

This section does not estimate, rank or map clusters itself. It reports only figures that an official source (or a secondary source explicitly citing an official dataset, labelled as such) states, with dates. Where the official dataset is the OLCC licence list, the current county breakdown was not extracted for this report — the OLCC licence search is interactive (see Part 5 of the full dossier) and a county table must be pulled from it directly, not reconstructed from 2016 application counts.

Official / officially-sourced figures that may be used:

  1. OMMP patients/grow sites by county, July 2026 (official, OHA). OHA OMMP Statistical Snapshot, July 2026 (accessed 2026-11-01): statewide totals 11,625 patients, 4,626 caregivers, 2,289 growers, 2,101 grow sites (distinct addresses). By county (patients / grow sites, selected): Jackson 831 / 222; Josephine 693 / 257; Lane 1,217 / 243; Benton 191 / <50 grow sites (suppressed as <50 in the source); Hood River 52 patients. Full county table is in the Snapshot PDF: http://www.oregon.gov/oha/PH/DISEASESCONDITIONS/CHRONICDISEASE/MEDICALMARIJUANAPROGRAM/Documents/OMMP_Statistic_Snapshot_07-2026.pdf — this is a medical concentration figure, not a retail concentration figure, and must not be presented as retail density.
  2. 2016 OLCC application counts (official via OLCC, reported contemporaneously — historical only). As of 21 June 2016 (OLCC via press/industry reporting): 723 producer applications statewide, of which Jackson County 122 and Josephine County 91; tri-county Portland area (Multnomah + Clackamas + Washington) 250. Processing: 25 of 82 applications from Multnomah County. Retail: 69 of 193 applications from Multnomah County. As of 17 May 2016 (OLCC via Mail Tribune reporting): Jackson County had the most business applications of any county at 529, Multnomah 521, Josephine 387; Jackson + Josephine = 938 applications, 27% of the state’s 3,437 (labs, processors, producers, retailers, wholesalers, research). Jackson producer applications 405, Josephine 346, Clackamas 273. Retail applications: Multnomah 215, Lane 99, Marion 66. These are 2016 application counts, not current licence counts, and the 2016 market (pre-moratorium, pre-price-collapse) is not the 2026 market. Do not use them as 2026 concentration.
  3. September 2026 retail licence counts by county (secondary calculation from OLCC licence data — labelled as such, not official). CannBus Q3 2026 (secondary, citing OLCC licence data, updated 28 Sept 2026): 752 active retail licences statewide, of which Multnomah County 212 (28%, CannBus calculation), then Lane 81, Marion 57, Jackson 50, Washington 46; producers 1,348 (1,045 Tier II, 200 Tier I, 103 micro), processors 262, wholesalers 234. A further 489 producer, 143 retailer, 89 processor and 74 wholesaler licences listed as inactive. Use only with the “secondary calculation from OLCC data” label and the September 2026 date; the official OLCC licence list itself must be checked for a current count.
  4. State-shared revenue as a concentration proxy — do NOT use it as one. LOC state-shared tables (2023, 2026) list per-city estimates (e.g. 2026: Portland $640,623; Bend $107,079; Beaverton $100,778; Eugene $179,352; Klamath Falls $22,135; Pendleton $17,052; Florence $9,664) — these are the ORS 475C.726 city-share distributions (75% population / 25% licence-count formula), not sales, not licence counts, and not per-capita retail density. Quoting them as “where the business is” would invert the formula (population dominates). They are included here only to warn against that misuse.
  5. What official sources do NOT say (gaps, not findings): No official OLCC or DOR publication located for this report states “retailers per capita by county/city” for 2026, ranks counties by retail density, or maps production clusters. Any such ranking in a deliverable must be computed transparently from the OLCC licence list + Census/PSU population (with the computation shown) and labelled as a calculation, not as an official statement. The 2016 narrative that “southern Oregon is the production hotbed” and “Portland metro is the retail centre” is consistent with both the 2016 application counts and the 2026 secondary counts above, but as a 2026 statement it is Verify from the current OLCC list, not an official 2026 finding in this report.
  6. Border-market concentration (officially consistent, secondary reported): Ontario/Malheur sales ($91.7m in 2020, all Ontario — see §3.4) and the general Idaho/California/Washington buyer pattern are Part 10 (interstate) matters. For Part 3 purposes, the only point is jurisdictional: a border city’s concentration reflects its neighbouring state’s prohibition (Idaho) as much as its own rules, and county-level sales must not be attributed to the county seat’s tax base without checking whether the sales are inside city limits (Ontario city) vs. unincorporated county (banned in Malheur).

Part 4 — Licence Types

PART 4 — LICENCE TYPES

4.1 Who licenses what — the three systems in one paragraph

  • OLCC (Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission) licenses adult-use / recreational marijuana: producer, processor, wholesaler (including micro wholesaler), retailer, laboratory (including sampling laboratory), research certificate, hemp certificate, and marijuana worker permits. Source: OLCC fee page, opened 2026-11-01: https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/pages/forms_publications.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • OHA / OMMP (Oregon Health Authority, Oregon Medical Marijuana Program) registers medical patients, caregivers, growers / persons responsible for a marijuana grow site (PRMG), grow sites, and — on paper — medical processing sites and dispensaries. In practice, by July 2026 OHA itself states there are currently no medical-only cannabis dispensaries or processing sites in Oregon (see §4.7). That is a central Part 4 fact: the OMMP registration categories still exist in rule, but the standalone medical retail/processing channel has effectively emptied into OLCC retailers.
  • ODA (Oregon Department of Agriculture) licenses hemp: grower, grow site, handler (including handler by reciprocity), agricultural hemp seed producer, and — from 1 July 2024 — vendor site. Oregon runs its own USDA-approved state hemp plan (USDA approval January 2022), not the USDA direct programme — see §4.8 and Part 7 cross-reference. Secondary summary, dated, to be confirmed on ODA/USDA pages: https://hempcbdbusinessplans.com/oregon-hemp-industry/ — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • CAMP is the OLCC online portal for licences and worker permits: https://camp.olcc.online/ — as stated on the OLCC worker-permit page, search result: https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/Pages/Marijuana-Worker-Permits.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01. An older OLCC e-license URL (apps.oregon.gov/OLCC/Marijuana/elicense/) appears in legacy processor forms and is Verify as current or superseded by CAMP.

4.2 OLCC fees — confirmed on an opened official page
