The same fee list appears in OAR 845-025-1060 as rendered in search results, including a Medical Canopy producer fee of $100 (see §4.3.7). Because the OAR 845-025-1060 direct open failed in this run, the $100 medical-canopy figure is snippet-derived — Verify against the current OAR text before budgeting. A separate secondary report (October 2026) states OLCC proposes a 75% fee increase from 1 July 2027 in its 2027–29 Agency Request Budget, citing a ~$17.25 million shortfall and 53 positions at risk, and that fees have been unchanged since 2015: https://www.cannabisnews.org/united-states-cannabis-news/oregon-olcc-75-percent-marijuana-license-fee-increase-17-million-shortfall/ — secondary, accessed 2026-11-01. That increase is a proposal only, NOT current law — Verify its status; do not budget it as the 2026–27 fee.

4.3 OLCC producer licences

What it allows. A producer licence authorises planting, cultivating, growing, trimming, harvesting and drying marijuana, and transfer/sale to other licensees (not direct sale to consumers). A person may hold more than one licence type, subject to OLCC rules — secondary summary of the League of Oregon Cities Municipal Handbook, ch. 27 (May 2021, updated October 2025): https://www.orcities.org/application/files/3117/6851/9196/Municipal_Handbook_-Chapter_27-_Marijuana.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01. Verify the current multiple-licence / financial-interest rules in OAR 845-025 before relying on them.

Canopy tiers — indoor, outdoor, mixed. From OAR 845-025-2040 as rendered in search results (direct open failed — snippet-derived, Verify): https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_845-025-2040 — accessed 2026-11-01.

Tier Indoor mature canopy Outdoor mature canopy
Micro Tier I Up to 625 sq ft Up to 2,500 sq ft
Micro Tier II 626–1,250 sq ft 2,501–5,000 sq ft
Tier I 1,251–5,000 sq ft 5,001–20,000 sq ft
Tier II 5,001–10,000 sq ft 20,001–40,000 sq ft

Mixed production = growing both indoors and outdoors at the same licensed premises; the Commission uses a 4:1 ratio (outdoor:indoor) to allocate canopy, not to exceed the sum limits above. Immature canopy limits for licences issued/renewed after 1 April 2018 (snippet-derived, Verify): Micro I 625 sq ft; Micro II 1,250 sq ft; Tier I 5,000 sq ft; Tier II 10,000 sq ft. A producer must document size, method, measurements and shapes for each canopy area; a mature plant may only be in a designated mature canopy area; changing a canopy location/shape, producer type, method or tier needs prior written Commission approval. No more than 20 quadrilateral canopy areas (or 20 canopy areas of any shape under the alternative prong, text truncated in the snippet — Verify the full paragraph).

Micro-tier processing privilege. Micro Tier I and II producers may hold a micro-tier processing endorsement (concentrate only, per the Portland code summary and retailer/processor rules — Verify the current endorsement list in OAR 845-025). Portland’s code, which mirrors OLCC definitions, defines a micro-wholesaler as a person who only purchases/receives seeds, immature plants or usable marijuana from a micro Tier I/II producer for resale to a person other than a consumer: https://www.portland.gov/code/14/b130 — accessed 2026-11-01.

Medically designated canopy (producer privilege). An OLCC producer may register to produce usable marijuana for registered OMMP cardholders, provided at least 75% of the annual yield from the medically designated canopy is provided to OMMP cardholders for no consideration. The medically designated canopy may be up to 10% of the tier’s maximum mature canopy in addition to the licensed canopy (e.g. Tier II outdoor: up to 4,000 sq ft in addition to 40,000 sq ft; Micro Tier I indoor: up to 62.5 sq ft in addition to 625 sq ft). A producer may also transfer immature plants to a PRMG at the PRMG’s grow site, or to a cardholder/caregiver at the producer’s premises, under OAR 845-025-2550. OLCC will not issue a licence to a site registered with OHA for medical production; any OHA registration for the site must be surrendered at licensure. Source: OLCC form instructions: https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/Documents/Licensing_Forms/mj_opt_pro_medcanopy.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01. Fee for this privilege is stated as $100 in the OAR 845-025-1060 snippet (Verify).

Requirements (general, all OLCC licences). In outline, and Verify each item in current OAR 845-025 and the CAMP application: Oregon residency / entity requirements as in force (residency rules have been litigated and amended — do not assume the pre-2023 residency bar still applies in the same form); Land Use Compatibility Statement (LUCS) from the city/county; local government recommendation where required; premises diagram and security plan; background checks ($50 per individual if not part of an initial/renewal application, per §4.2); worker permits for all plant-touching staff (§4.6); Metrc seed-to-sale tracking; tax-compliance certificate on renewal/transfer (retailers must be current on taxes or on a qualifying payment plan before renewal — secondary, Harris Sliwoski, 2025, and OLCC practice reported 2023–2025; Verify the current rule text). Premises may not be in a jurisdiction that has opted out of that licence type (Part 3, not covered here).

4.4 OLCC processor licences and endorsements

One licence, multiple endorsements, one fee. A processor may only process and sell a product type if it holds the endorsement for that type. Endorsement types (OAR 845-025-3210, snippet-derived — Verify against current OAR): https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_845-025-3210 — accessed 2026-11-01.

  • Cannabinoid edible processor
  • Cannabinoid topical processor
  • Cannabinoid concentrate processor
  • Cannabinoid extract processor (listed in the processor form; the OAR snippet’s enumeration is truncated at “(c) Cannabinoid concentrate processor; and (2) Industrial Hemp processor” — Verify whether extract is a separate endorsement or subsumed, and the exact current list)
  • Industrial hemp processor

Only one application and licence fee is required regardless of how many endorsements are requested or when. An endorsement may be requested on the initial application or added/removed later; adding an endorsement requires OLCC approval and, for concentrate/edible/topical/extract, a LUCS showing the endorsement is not a prohibited use (a new LUCS is not required if only adding the industrial-hemp endorsement). Surrendering an endorsement requires written notice with the cessation date. The Commission may deny/revoke an endorsement if the processor does not meet OAR 845-025-3200 to -3290 for that endorsement. Any cannabinoid product intended to be consumed/ingested orally or applied in the mouth counts as an edible for endorsement purposes.

Extract-specific requirements. For the extract endorsement, the applicant must also submit: proof of Certificate of Occupancy for the intended use; an Extract Processing Equipment form identifying all equipment; and, for hydrocarbon solvents, proof the installed equipment has been inspected by a certified mechanical/electrical engineer, industry-recognised third party, or manufacturer. Source: legacy processor application form via secondary host: https://data.templateroller.com/pdf_docs/2174/21740/2174065/main_form-mj17-3020-marijuana-processor-application-oregon.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 (form date old; Verify current CAMP form).

Edible/topical food-establishment overlay. A processor endorsed for edibles may only process edibles in a food establishment licensed by ODA, meeting security and licensed-premises requirements; an ODA commercial-kitchen licence is required for edibles processing. Secondary summary: https://oregonstatecannabis.org/licensing/processing — accessed 2026-11-01 (Verify in OAR 845-025 and ODA food-safety rules).

Alternating proprietor (“shared kitchen”). Available only for edible/topical endorsements; not granted if the application was submitted on/after 1 January 2019, if the premises was not licensed under an alternating-proprietor arrangement before 1 January 2019, or if the extract endorsement is requested. Source: same legacy processor form, above (Verify current status — this may be a closed legacy category).

Medical processing by OLCC processors. An OLCC processor may, for a fee, process a patient’s/caregiver’s usable marijuana into cannabinoid products/concentrates/extracts for transfer back to that patient/caregiver (legacy form statement — Verify current OAR 845-025 medical-processing provisions).

4.5 OLCC wholesaler, micro wholesaler, retailer, laboratory, research certificate

Wholesaler. Buys/receives marijuana items from producers/processors and sells/transfers to other licensees (retailers, other wholesalers, processors). Fee $4,750/year (§4.2). A wholesaler may also hold a for-hire trimming privilege (legacy supplemental form MJ17-4200 — Verify current availability). Wholesaler is one of the two licence types whose moratorium is now the subject of a possible lift (see §4.9).

Micro wholesaler. Fee $1,000/year (§4.2). Limited to purchasing/receiving seeds, immature plants or usable marijuana from micro Tier I/II producers for resale to a person other than a consumer (Portland code definition, §4.3). Verify the full micro-wholesaler privilege/limits in OAR 845-025.

Retailer. Sells/transfers/delivers marijuana items and hemp items to consumers 21+ (and, with a medical endorsement, to OMMP patients/caregivers aged 18–21 with a valid OMMP card) between 7:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m. local time, from the licensed premises and by bona fide delivery order. Source: OAR 845-025-2800, snippet-derived — Verify: https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_845-025-2800 — accessed 2026-11-01. Retailer endorsements/registrations: - Medical endorsement (no separate fee stated in the sources located — Verify): allows sale for medical purposes under OAR 845-025-2900 and sale to 18–21-year-old cardholders; a retailer with a medical endorsement may, at its discretion, provide cannabis at no charge to qualifying patients/caregivers (secondary summary of Washington/Oregon comparison — Verify for Oregon specifically). - Home-delivery endorsement/registration: allows delivery pursuant to a bona fide order under OAR 845-025-2880; delivery into adjacent jurisdictions is subject to local opt-in rules (Part 3, not covered here — Verify the current adjacent-jurisdiction programme). - Hemp items sold by a retailer must have been received from a Commission-certified hemp handler, a processor with an industrial-hemp endorsement, a wholesaler, or a retailer owned by the same/substantially same persons, per OAR 845-025-2800 snippet. - Retailers may accept returns only of usable marijuana, marijuana items, hemp items, immature plants and seeds, only from the original supplying licensee or the purchasing customer/cardholder, accurately recorded in the CTS, and may not resell items returned by customers (same snippet).

Laboratory and sampling laboratory. Laboratory fee $4,750/year; sampling laboratory $2,250/year (§4.2). Laboratories must be accredited through ORELAP (OHA’s Oregon Environmental Laboratory Accreditation Program) and licensed by OLCC, and may not hold a producer, processor or retail licence (secondary summary, CannBus Q3 2026: https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/or_cannmir.html — accessed 2026-11-01; Verify the current conflict-of-interest rule in OAR 845-025). From 1 September 2026 labs must follow a new process for entering results on secondary lab sample packages (same secondary source — Verify in current OLCC lab guidance). The licensed-lab list itself is a Part 5 source (§5.3).

Research certificate. Fee $4,750 for a three-year term (§4.2). Allows research with marijuana/hemp items, including transfers with licensees as permitted by rule. Only 1 research certificate was active in the September/December 2025 counts (§5.8). Requirements, application route, and whether new research-certificate applications are open are Verify — no current OLCC research-certificate application page was confirmed in this run; do not assume it is closed under HB 4121, which by its terms addresses producer/processor/wholesaler/retailer caps.

Hemp certificate (OLCC). Fee $1,000/year (§4.2). This is the OLCC certificate for a hemp handler to transfer hemp items into the OLCC retail system (see League of Oregon Cities handbook summary, §4.3, and the legacy form MJ18-2700 “Industrial Hemp Certificate Application”). It is distinct from an ODA hemp handler licence (§4.8). Verify the current hemp-certificate application route in CAMP and its relationship to the 2026 OLCC Hemp Registry (see §4.9, Hemp Registry).

4.6 Marijuana worker permits

Who needs one. Persons employed in the OLCC-licensed recreational marijuana industry, including licensees themselves, must have a valid Marijuana Worker Permit. All employees, including seasonal employees, need one. Source: OLCC worker-permit page, search result: https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/Pages/Marijuana-Worker-Permits.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01.

Eligibility and process. - 21 years of age or older to be eligible. - Apply through CAMP: https://camp.olcc.online/ (stated on the OLCC page). - Review the Recreational Marijuana Worker Permit Education material and pass the test with at least 70%; upload the Certificate of Completion and a valid photo ID (secondary, Vangst state-requirements page: https://app.vangst.com/reports/state-requirements/oregon — accessed 2026-11-01; Verify the current education/test steps on the OLCC page itself). - Fee $100, due on application submission; permit term five years (§4.2). - A separate background check is required for the worker-permit application, processed directly by OLCC (OLCC page, search result). - If OLCC requests additional information, the applicant has two weeks to provide it / complete corrections; failure results in the application being considered incomplete and inactivated, and any Temporary Permit becomes invalid at inactivation — the applicant must reapply (OLCC page, search result). - All marijuana workers take the same test, allowing movement between jobs in the industry (OLCC page, search result).

Denial grounds (secondary, Vangst summary — Verify in OAR 845-025-5500 et seq.). Must deny if: under 21; or a marijuana licence/worker permit was revoked for violation of ORS 475C.005–475C.525 (now ORS 475C — Verify the current citation) within two years of application. May deny if: felony conviction for possession/manufacture/delivery of a controlled substance within three years; felony crime of violence within three years; felony crime of dishonesty/deception (theft, fraud, forgery) within three years; more than one conviction for listed crimes within five years; violation of the marijuana statutes/rules; or false statement to the Commission.

Scale. OLCC’s May 2026 licensing presentation reports 51,800 worker permits in its 2025 licensing snapshot and “160k+ active permits” in a separate slide (the latter appears to include alcohol service permits — conflict/ambiguity flagged, do not quote 160,000 as marijuana worker permits): http://cms.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/commission_agendas/2026/OLCC-Licensing-Program-Presentation-May2026.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01. A 2027–29 budget narrative reported in October 2026 puts the programme at roughly 2,665 recreational licensees and 50,000 permittees (secondary: https://www.cannabisnews.org/united-states-cannabis-news/oregon-olcc-75-percent-marijuana-license-fee-increase-17-million-shortfall/ — accessed 2026-11-01). Use 51,800 (OLCC May 2026 presentation) as the most recent OLCC-sourced permit figure located; the 50,000 figure is a rounded secondary restatement.

4.7 OHA / OMMP registrations — patients, caregivers, growers, grow sites, processing sites, dispensaries

Patient card fees (secondary, to be confirmed on an opened OHA page — Verify). Standard application fee $200; reduced fees: Oregon Health Plan (OHP) members $50, SNAP $60, SSI $20, veterans $20 (and $0 for veterans with 50%+ service-connected disability, per one secondary summary). Replacement card $100 unless proof of SSI ($20) etc. Sources: https://www.safeaccessnow.org/becoming_a_patient_in_oregon and https://sativauniversity.com/cannabis-laws/oregon/ — both accessed 2026-11-01, both secondary. Do not quote these fees as official until confirmed on oregon.gov/ommp.

Grower / PRMG and grow site. - A designated grower (PRMG) must be 21+, may grow for no more than eight registered patients at one time, and is subject to a criminal-history check by OMMP. - Per registered patient, a grow site may produce up to 6 mature plants, 12 immature plants 24 inches or more in height, and 36 immature plants less than 24 inches in height (secondary, Safe Access Now, above). A grow site that is the patient’s residence, where the patient (or that patient’s caregiver) is the designated grower, may not have more than 12 mature plants if more than two patients are registered to the site (OHA change-form instructions, Dec 2025: http://egov.oregon.gov/oha/PH/DISEASESCONDITIONS/CHRONICDISEASE/MEDICALMARIJUANAPROGRAM/Documents/form/Change_form_and_Instructions_12-16-25.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01). - Grow site registration fee $200, paid by the grower, except $0 where the patient grows for themselves at their own residence with 12 or fewer mature plants and will not transfer to an OMMP dispensary/processing site. The $200 fee is triggered if: the grower is not also the patient; the site is not the patient’s residence; the site has more than 12 mature plants; or the grower is transferring to a dispensary/processing site (same OHA form instructions). - From 1 January 2026, where the patient/grower does not own the property, a notarised Medical Marijuana Grow Site Consent form from the property owner is required (SB 907, 2025 session, per secondary summary — Verify the bill and the OAR text). - Proof of zoning is required if the grow site address is within city limits; a grow site must have a physical Oregon address and must not be located at a medical or retail marijuana dispensary (legacy OHA form statements — Verify current OAR 333-008). - Grow sites are subject to inspection. Reporting: growers report monthly via OMMOS (Oregon Medical Marijuana Online System) if the site has 1–2 patients and a reporting trigger applies, or in real time via the OLCC Cannabis Tracking System (CTS/Metrc) if the site has 3+ registered patients, unless exempt — per the OMMP July 2026 Statistical Snapshot, p. 5 (see §5.5). - Grandfather petitions under OAR 333-008-0520 exist for certain grow-site addresses (legacy form reference — Verify current availability).

Medical processing sites (OHA). Endorsements mirror the OLCC processor endorsements, plus a fifth: cannabinoid tincture, capsule, suppository, or transdermal patch processor. Source: OAR 333-008-1700, snippet-derived — Verify: https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_333-008-1700 — accessed 2026-11-01. Only one application/registration fee regardless of endorsements; endorsements may be added after registration. Current fee, application route, and whether any new medical processing-site registrations are being accepted are Verify, and the July 2026 snapshot statement below suggests the category is empty in practice.

Medical dispensaries (OHA) — effectively zero. OHA’s July 2026 Statistical Snapshot, p. 8, states: “There are currently no medical-only cannabis dispensaries or processing sites in Oregon” and “The Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission (OLCC) licenses all retail cannabis dispensaries in Oregon” (snapshot PDF: http://www.oregon.gov/oha/PH/DISEASESCONDITIONS/CHRONICDISEASE/MEDICALMARIJUANAPROGRAM/Documents/OMMP_Statistic_Snapshot_07-2026.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01). A secondary history notes 48 strictly medical dispensaries in April 2017, falling to one medical-only dispensary business in Josephine County by October 2024 (Oregon Employment Department / Southern Oregon Business Journal, 2024): https://southernoregonbusiness.com/oregons-marijuana-industry-and-employment-trends-3/ — accessed 2026-11-01. For Part 4 purposes: do not list OMMP dispensaries as a live route to market in 2026; patients buy at OLCC retailers (with a medical endorsement) or grow via a registered grow site.

OMMP counts (July 2026, official snapshot — see §5.5 for full table). Patients 11,625 (1 July 2026); caregivers 4,626; growers 2,289; grow sites 2,101 (CannBus Q3 2026 restatement of the OHA snapshot: https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/or_cannmir.html — accessed 2026-11-01; cross-check against the snapshot PDF itself, which was located but its p. 1 totals were not fully rendered in search output). The snapshot’s grow-site-address table totals 2,723 on p. 4 of the July 2026 PDF as rendered — this conflicts with the 2,101 figure and is flagged in §5.5/§6.5; do not quote either without noting the conflict, until the PDF is opened in full.

4.8 ODA hemp licences and registrations

Legal basis. ORS 571.260–571.348; OAR chapter 603, division 48. Oregon’s USDA-approved state plan was approved in January 2022 (secondary: https://hempcbdbusinessplans.com/oregon-hemp-industry/ — accessed 2026-11-01; confirm on USDA AMS state-plan list — Verify).

Fees — OAR 603-048-0700 as rendered (snippet-derived, Verify; current through Register Vol. 64, No. 6, 1 June 2025 per the Justia rendering). Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/oregon/chapter-603/division-48/section-603-048-0700/ — accessed 2026-11-01.

ODA hemp licence Fee
Grower application $350
Each grow site application $875
Handler application $2,275
Handler by reciprocity application $875
Agricultural hemp seed producer application $875
Key participant fee $75 each (per the 11/2025 grower application form)
Late fee, grow site application received after 31 May but no later than 31 July $250
Change fee (specified changes under OAR 603-048-0400) $125 per change
Vendor site licence $100 / year, valid 1 July–30 June (OAR 603-048-0175, effective 1 July 2024 — secondary: https://sativauniversity.com/cannabis-laws/oregon/ — Verify)

Older secondary pages quote $250 grower / $500 grow-site / $1,300 handler fees (e.g. https://oregonstatecannabis.org/cbd and https://fortunahemp.com/hemp-seeds/states/oregon-hemp-seeds/ — accessed 2026-11-01). Those are superseded — use the OAR 603-048-0700 figures above, subject to the Verify flag.

Grower / grow site. - Valid for one year, 1 January–31 December unless revoked/cancelled. Renewal application and full fee payment must be received no later than 1 December of the current licence year. No new grow sites may be added after 31 May, or after 31 July with the late fee. Fees are non-refundable and not prorated; applications without full payment by the deadline will not be processed. Source: ODA grower/grow-site application, rev. 11/2025: https://www.oregon.gov/oda/Documents/Publications/Hemp/Grower_Application.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 (and stage mirror: https://stage.oregon.gov/oda/Documents/Publications/Hemp/Hemp_Grower_App_Fillable.pdf). - Applicants must list key participants (members, officers, owners, any other key participants authorised to make changes); growers must meet ORS 571.260–571.348 and OAR 603 division 48; growers must register their grow site with the USDA Farm Service Agency (FSA) (application text, same source). - No additional grower licence fee is required when licensing additional grow sites (application fee note, same source).

Handler. - Valid for one year, 1 January (or issue date)–31 December unless revoked/cancelled. Renewal must be received, with premises map, property-owner authorisation, LUCS, endorsement approvals (with additional documentation for extraction, if applicable) and full fee payment, no later than 1 December of the current licence year. Source: ODA handler application, rev. 9/2026: https://www.oregon.gov/oda/Documents/Publications/Hemp/Hemp_Handler_App_Fillable.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01. - Handler by reciprocity ($875) applies only to OLCC recreational marijuana processors with a hemp endorsement; attach a copy of the OLCC processor licence and hemp endorsement certificate (same application). - Verify the current handler endorsements (e.g. extraction) and whether a handler licence alone authorises retail sale — the vendor-site licence below is the retail/wholesale registration.

Agricultural hemp seed producer. Application fee $875 (OAR 603-048-0700 snippet). What it allows, seed-certification requirements, and application form are Verify — no current ODA seed-producer application page was confirmed in this run.

Vendor site (retail/wholesale). - Required from 1 July 2024 for hemp retailers or wholesalers who store, transfer or sell industrial hemp or hemp items for resale to another person; applies to out-of-state vendors as well (ODA Board of Agriculture presentation, March 2025: https://stage.oregon.gov/oda/about-us/Documents/Board%20of%20Agriculture/2025_03/BOA%20March%202025_PPCD%20Update.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01). - Fee $100/year, licence cycle 1 July–30 June, aligned with other ODA programmes (same presentation; secondary confirmation: https://sativauniversity.com/cannabis-laws/oregon/). - Verify the current vendor-site application form and whether the vendor licence is distinct from the OLCC Hemp Registry registration (§4.9) — the two are different regimes (ODA vendor = seller registration; OLCC Hemp Registry = product registration) and must not be conflated.

OLCC hemp roles (for completeness, cross-referenced). OLCC hemp certificate ($1,000/year, §4.5) for handlers transferring hemp into the OLCC system; OLCC processor industrial-hemp endorsement (§4.4); OLCC retailer sale of hemp items (§4.5). From 1 January 2026, OLCC Hemp Registry product registration is additionally required for cannabinoid hemp products sold to consumers in Oregon (see §4.9).

4.9 Moratorium, caps, and whether applications are open — the decisive Part 4 question

Short answer (1 November 2026): NO — new applications for producer, processor, wholesaler and retailer licences are NOT being accepted, except as the caps below allow and except for changes to existing licences (ownership, location, structure, amendments). Wholesale is the one category where a lift is in active rulemaking, but applications remain closed until rules are adopted.

Timeline. - 2019: moratorium on new producer licences (SB 218, 2019 — curtailment authority; secondary summaries). - 2022: moratorium broadened to producer, processor, wholesaler and retailer; new applications stopped (one secondary source gives 4 April 2022 as the stop date — Verify the exact 2022 instrument). - 20 March 2024: Governor Kotek signed HB 4121. It extended the moratorium past its 30 March 2024 sunset to 31 December 2024, after which a permanent per-capita cap system took effect. Source: secondary legal summary: https://cannabislaw.report/olcc-cannabis-license-moratorium-extended-with-passage-of-hb-4121-new-license-caps-also-implemented/ — accessed 2026-11-01; and OLCC licensed-businesses page (search result): https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/pages/recreational-marijuana-licensee-reports.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01, which states: “New Applications for Producer, Processors, Wholesalers, and Retailers are not being accepted at this time. ‘Marijuana License Caps and Moratorium,’ House Bill 4121 (2024)”. - Caps (HB 4121, from 1 January 2025): no more than 1 active producer or retailer licence per 7,500 residents aged 21+; no more than 1 active processor or wholesaler licence per 12,500 residents aged 21+. The cap does NOT apply to renewal applications or to new licences resulting from a change in location or ownership — so buying/transferring an existing licence remains the entry route. Sources: same HB 4121 summary; MPP Oregon page: https://www.mpp.org/states/oregon/ — accessed 2026-11-01. - Some secondary sources describe the moratorium as “extended until at least HB 4121 per-capita caps (no calendar sunset)” (MPP; CannBus legal summary: https://www.cannbus.org/lsum/or_lsum.html — accessed 2026-11-01). Conflict flagged: HB 4121’s own structure is a permanent cap system from 2025, not a HB 4121 per-capita caps (no calendar sunset) sunset; the “HB 4121 per-capita caps (no calendar sunset)” phrasing appears to conflate HB 4121 with an earlier sunset or with a 2025 extension bill. Verify on OLIS whether any 2025 bill re-imposed a HB 4121 per-capita caps (no calendar sunset) date, and quote HB 4121’s cap mechanism as the operative rule unless OLIS shows otherwise. - Wholesale lift in progress (August–September 2026). OLCC opened a permanent rulemaking track and a Rules Advisory Committee (RAC) specifically on lifting the wholesale moratorium; the call for RAC volunteers closed 28 August 2026 at 5 p.m.; the RAC met 25 September 2026; OLCC staff concluded active wholesale licences had fallen below the HB 4121 population threshold, clearing a statutory path to lift the moratorium for wholesale alone. New wholesale applications stay closed until rules are drafted, noticed, commented on and adopted by the Commission. Processor, producer and retailer applications remain closed while the wholesale rewrite moves forward. Sources: https://www.cannabisnews.org/united-states-cannabis-news/oregon-starts-rulemaking-that-could-lift-cannabis-wholesale-license-moratorium/ (29 Aug 2026) and https://themarijuanaherald.com/2026/08/oregon-begins-rulemaking-process-that-could-lift-marijuana-wholesale-license-moratorium-for-first-time-since-2022/ (28 Aug 2026) — both accessed 2026-11-01, both secondary reporting of OLCC action. Verify the current RAC/rulemaking status on the OLCC rulemaking page before advising any wholesale applicant. - What IS still being processed. OLCC’s licensed-businesses page (search result, above) states applications are currently being assigned/processed from submission dates including 20 October 2026 for Changes for all licence types (Change of Ownership, Change of Location, Business Structure, and other amendments). Use the Application Status Request form to inquire about an application awaiting a licensing action (same page). OLCC’s May 2026 presentation reports 11,000+ marijuana licensing actions in 2025, mostly transfers/ownership changes (see §4.6 source). - Licences NOT covered by the HB 4121 caps (Verify each): laboratory, sampling laboratory, research certificate, hemp certificate, worker permits, and ODA hemp licences are not stated in the sources located to be subject to the HB 4121 producer/processor/wholesaler/retailer caps. Do not assume they are closed — but also do not assume they are open without checking CAMP / ODA, because laboratory accreditation and other gates may limit them in practice.

Hemp Registry (OLCC) — a 2026 registration, not a licence, but it gates hemp sales. Under HB 4121, from 1 January 2026 all cannabinoid hemp products sold to consumers in Oregon, online or in brick-and-mortar stores, must be registered with OLCC in a Hemp Registry, with test results accessible to consumers and food-style labelling for edibles. Product registration applications opened 1 January 2026; enforcement of the registry was delayed to 1 June 2026 as a transition/grace period; OLCC continued enforcing existing laws (sales to minors, THC over legal limits, intoxicating/adulterated cannabinoids) during the grace period. There is a fee to register, with similar products registrable under one fee in some cases (exceptions apply). The registry applies to cannabinoid hemp items intended for human or animal consumption/use (gummies, beverages, tinctures, capsules, vapes, smokable flower). Source: OLCC GovDelivery bulletin: https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/OLCC/bulletins/3fc3d7a — accessed 2026-11-01. A September 2026 proposed rulemaking would revise OAR 845-026-6100 to allow greater flexibility on resubmission deficiencies (filed 29 Sept 2026, comment to 30 Oct 2026): https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/rules/2026-Hemp%20Registry%20Perm%20Notice%20092926.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01. Verify the final hemp-registry rules and fee schedule in OAR 845-026 before advising a hemp brand.

4.10 Ownership, transfer, residency, and financial-interest rules — what was confirmed and what was not

  • Transfers / change of ownership are the live entry route. Because new producer/processor/wholesaler/retailer applications are closed under the caps, entry is by buying an existing licence and filing a change-of-ownership (and, if applicable, change-of-location, $1,000 per licence, §4.2) application in CAMP. OLCC processes change-of-ownership applications from the 20 October 2026 assignment date noted in §4.9.
  • Tax compliance as a transfer/renewal gate. Retailers must show a certificate of tax compliance to renew or transfer a licence (secondary, CannBus Q3 2026, citing OLCC practice; the underlying rule — retailers current on taxes or on a qualifying payment plan before renewal, adopted 2023 and upheld by the Oregon Court of Appeals in 2025 — is Verify in current OAR 845-025).
  • Residency. Oregon’s former residency requirement for OLCC licensees has been the subject of litigation and legislative change; multiple secondary sources in this run describe “residency requirements” as still shaping entry, while others describe a “residency wall … under direct dormant-commerce-clause attack” (secondary, Drug Policy Watch 2026 brief: http://drugpolicywatch.info/states/oregon.html — accessed 2026-11-01). Residency is therefore marked Verify in full — do not advise any applicant on residency until the current ORS 475C / OAR 845-025 text and any pending litigation are checked.
  • Ownership caps / multiple licences / financial interest. No current Oregon ownership cap (e.g. a maximum number of licences per person) was confirmed on an opened official page in this run. MPP (secondary) reports OLCC “tightened transfer restrictions to curb license speculation and consolidation” in 2025 (https://www.mpp.org/states/oregon/ — accessed 2026-11-01). Ownership caps, vertical-integration limits, and financial-interest disclosure rules are all Verify — they belong in a Part 11 follow-up, not assumed here.
  • Local approval. A LUCS and, where applicable, a local government recommendation are required before OLCC licensure (see §4.3). Local opt-out status for the licence type must be checked first (Part 3).

4.11 Social equity provisions

There is no Oregon state social-equity licence tier comparable to Illinois, New York or New Jersey. Findings: - The Oregon Secretary of State Audits Division audit (April 2023, reported via GovDelivery: http://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/ORSOS/bulletins/3578e6e — accessed 2026-11-01) found Oregon “did not consider or include targeted equity provisions when developing the recreational cannabis program” and OLCC’s licensing system “is not capable of tracking demographic data”. - A consulting summary states plainly: “As Oregon has not yet implement[ed] any social equity programs, businesses must check with their cities and municipalities if they have special programs” (https://canndelta.com/us/oregon/ — accessed 2026-11-01, secondary). - CannBus Q3 2026 (secondary, https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/or_cannmir.html) finds: lower fees for small (micro) producers, state income-tax relief for federal 280E costs, reduced medical-card fees, and one local equity programme — Portland’s NuLeaf Project ($5,000–$30,000 per business, $150,000 city pool from cannabis tax revenue, launched September 2018, for Portland-headquartered businesses at least 51% owned by people of colour; current availability NOT confirmed). No open state grant or loan fund was verified; a 2023 audit noted Business Oregon did not engage with cannabis businesses. - A conflicting secondary claim (MPP Oregon page) that “The Cannabis Equity Program received $15 million in 2025 for BIPOC-owned businesses” is flagged as conflicting and Unverified — it does not match the CannBus “no open state fund verified” finding, and no Oregon statute, budget line or programme page for a $15 million Cannabis Equity Program was located in this run. Do not quote the $15 million figure without an official source. - Moratorium exceptions for social equity: none was located. HB 4121’s caps, as summarised, contain no social-equity exception for new producer/processor/wholesaler/retailer applications. If any equity exception exists in rule or in a 2025–26 bill, it is Verify and must be found on OLIS/OLCC before it is claimed. - Related but distinct: record set-aside/expungement (SB 420, 2019) is a Part 12 topic, not a licence-equity programme, and is not covered here beyond this note.

No official OLCC/ODA startup-cost estimate was located. The following are illustrative, non-official, order-of-magnitude planning figures compiled from the fee schedule in §4.2/§4.8 plus ordinary business costs — they are NOT official and must not be quoted as OLCC figures:

Route (illustrative only) Licence/registration fees (official, §4.2/§4.8) Other costs to budget (non-official estimate — Verify with vendors)
Buy an existing OLCC retailer licence (transfer) $250 application + $4,750 annual + $1,000 if changing location Licence purchase price itself is a private market price and, under a capped market, is typically the dominant cost — no reliable public price was located; Verify via brokers/closed transactions, do not guess. Plus premises, build-out, inventory, Metrc, security, insurance, working capital, tax-compliance clearance.
Buy an existing OLCC Tier II producer licence (transfer) $250 + $5,750 annual (+ $1,000 location change if applicable) Land/premises, water rights (see Part 5, WRD), cultivation build-out, testing, labour, Metrc — no official total exists.
New ODA hemp grower + 1 grow site (new application, open) $350 + $875 + $75/key participant Seed/clones, land, irrigation, testing (pre-harvest THC), harvest/drying, handler fees if processing.
New ODA hemp handler (new application, open) $2,275 Premises, equipment, extraction endorsements/documentation, food-safety licensing if edibles, testing.
New ODA hemp vendor site (new application, open) $100/year Retail/wholesale premises and OLCC Hemp Registry product registrations (fee Verify).
OLCC worker permits (staffing) $100 per person per 5 years Education/test time; background-check handling.

Do not present any total startup figure (e.g. “$X to open a dispensary in Oregon”) as a fact. Under the moratorium, the transfer price of an existing licence — which is not published by OLCC — swamps the $5,000 licence fee, so any single-number estimate would be misleading.

  2. OMMP patient-card fee schedule is secondary-only — confirm on oregon.gov/ommp.
  3. Residency, ownership caps, financial-interest and transfer-restriction rules are Verify.
  4. Research-certificate and sampling-laboratory application routes are Verify.
  5. ODA seed-producer application and handler endorsement details are Verify.
  6. The “HB 4121 per-capita caps (no calendar sunset)” moratorium date conflicts with HB 4121’s permanent-cap structure — resolve on OLIS.
  7. The $15 million “Cannabis Equity Program” claim conflicts with “no open state fund verified” — resolve with an official budget/programme source.

Part 5 — Licence Data Sources

PART 5 — LICENCE DATA SOURCES

Scope note: This part inventories sources; it does NOT list every licence holder, per the task. Where a source is an interactive search/dashboard with no bulk download, that is stated explicitly. Where a direct download link was located verbatim, it is given with its file name; where it was not located verbatim, the entry says so and gives the portal/search route instead of inventing a URL. “Latest data date” means the latest date stated in the source material located in this run, not a live check on 2026-11-01 — the live browser was not available to this subagent, and Socrata/portal pages that failed to open directly are flagged accordingly.

5.1 OLCC — Marijuana Businesses and Endorsements (Oregon Open Data Portal)

  • URL: https://camp.olcc.online/ (stated on the OLCC worker-permit page: https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/Pages/Marijuana-Worker-Permits.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01).

5.8 Total licence counts by type and status — official figures located

Two snapshots are given because they differ by date and by source; do not merge them.

A. Late September 2026 — OLCC Open Data dataset q32u-cmam, updated 28 September 2026, as restated by CannBus Q3 2026 (secondary, https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/or_cannmir.html — accessed 2026-11-01). Distinct active licences: - Producers: 1,348 (1,045 Tier II, 200 Tier I, 103 micro) - Retailers: 752 (692 with medical endorsement; 599 with home-delivery endorsement — endorsement counts overlap, they are not separate licences) - Processors: 262 - Wholesalers: 234 - Laboratories: 9 - Research certificate: 1 - Inactive licences in the same dataset: 489 producer, 143 retailer, 89 processor, 74 wholesaler (laboratory/research inactive counts not stated in the restatement — Verify). - Active total from these figures (calculation, not an OLCC-stated total): 1,348 + 752 + 262 + 234 + 9 + 1 = 2,606. Note this excludes sampling laboratories and hemp certificates, which CannBus’s segment table does not break out — Verify those two categories on the dataset before stating a grand total.

B. December 2025 — as restated by a secondary market page (https://cannabusinessplans.com/oregon-cannabis-market/ — accessed 2026-11-01), attributed to OLCC data: - Total licensed recreational businesses: 2,649, comprising producers 1,349, processors 276, retailers 770, wholesalers 243, laboratories 9, sampling laboratory 1, research facility 1. (Arithmetic check: 1,349+276+770+243+9+1+1 = 2,649 — consistent.) - Conflict/transition note: December 2025 (2,649) vs September 2026 active distinct licences (2,606 on the six categories above, plus any sampling-lab/hemp-certificate actives) shows a modest decline, consistent with the “declined marginally across the board” narrative in Harris Sliwoski’s State of the State 2025 (https://harris-sliwoski.com/cannalawblog/oregon-cannabis-state-of-the-state-2025/ — accessed 2026-11-01) and with OLCC’s May 2026 presentation snapshot (retailer 764, wholesaler 239, processor 270 — http://cms.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/commission_agendas/2026/OLCC-Licensing-Program-Presentation-May2026.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01). The May 2026 presentation figures sit between the December 2025 and September 2026 figures, which is coherent for a slowly declining market, but all three are secondary restatements of OLCC data except where the presentation itself is the source — the dataset (§5.1) is the authoritative check. - Older benchmarks (for the trend in §6.3): “Over 3,000 active marijuana licensees” as of July 2025 (MPP, https://www.mpp.org/states/oregon/ — accessed 2026-11-01); ~2,900 active licences in December 2022 including 833 retailers (Cannabis Business Times, https://Www.cannabisbusinesstimes.com/business-issues-benchmarks/cannabis-price-compression/news/15688004/oregon-shy-of-1-billion-in-cannabis-sales-for-first-time-since-2019 — accessed 2026-11-01); 1,152 producers and 664 retailers at end-2019 (Harris Sliwoski State of the State 2019, via https://harris-sliwoski.com/ar/cannalawblog/oregon-cannabis-state-of-the-state-3/ — accessed 2026-11-01).

Because Oregon operates under its own USDA-approved state plan (January 2022, §4.8), the authoritative Oregon hemp licence list is ODA’s (§5.6), not a USDA producer list. USDA NASS hemp statistics (acreage/value) are a Part 6 market source (§6.6), not a licence-holder source. Local tax records are held by DOR for state-collected local taxes (see §5.7) and by individual cities/counties for locally collected taxes — Verify jurisdiction by jurisdiction; no consolidated local cannabis-tax dataset was located.

These are alcohol datasets and must not be counted as cannabis licences.

Part 6 — Market Data

PART 6 — MARKET DATA

Reading note on tax vs sales: OLCC sales figures (Metrc retail sales at OLCC retailers, recreational + patient) and DOR tax receipts (payments received in the month, net of refunds, retailers retaining 2% for collection costs, state/local split estimated from February 2017) are different series. Do not divide one by the other to “derive” a tax rate without stating both series’ definitions (see §5.7 notes). Monthly sales for the month in progress are incomplete in the OLCC file (§5.3) and must be excluded from year-to-date totals.

6.3 Licence counts over time and closures

  • Trend narrative (official/secondary): Licence numbers were essentially static 2023–2024, then “declined marginally across the board” in 2025 (Harris Sliwoski State of the State 2025). The September 2026 dataset (§5.8) shows 489 inactive producer, 143 inactive retailer, 89 inactive processor and 74 inactive wholesaler licences alongside the active counts — inactive in the dataset is not the same as “closed in 2026”; a licence may be inactive for non-renewal, surrender, revocation, or pending change, and the dataset does not state the reason — Verify the status definitions on the dataset.
  • Counts over time (active licences, as located):
  • End-2019: producers 1,152; retailers 664 (Harris Sliwoski 2019).
  • December 2022: ~2,900 active licences total, including 833 retailers, ~19.6 dispensaries per 100,000 people (Cannabis Business Times, above).
  • October 2024: 795 active retail licences (Oregon Employment Dept. analysis, above).
  • July 2025: over 3,000 active licensees (MPP).
  • December 2025: 2,649 total (1,349 producers, 276 processors, 770 retailers, 243 wholesalers, 9 labs, 1 sampling lab, 1 research).
  • May 2026 (OLCC presentation snapshot): retailers 764, wholesalers 239, processors 270.
  • Late September 2026: producers 1,348, retailers 752, processors 262, wholesalers 234, labs 9, research 1 (§5.8).
  • Retailers with sales (a better “open shops” measure than licences): 651 shops transacted as of July 2026 (Cannabis Data Project, from OLCC dataset kctd-stii); 599 retailers held a home-delivery endorsement in September 2026 (§5.8). A retailer may hold a licence but record no sales in a month — do not equate licences with open stores.
  • Closures: No official OLCC closure count (surrenders + revocations + non-renewals by year) was located in this run. Closures by year are Unavailable from the sources located — the inactive counts in §5.8 are a stock, not a flow, and must not be presented as “closures in 2026”. Follow-up: request the OLCC licensing-actions series or derive year-on-year active-count changes from successive dataset snapshots, labelling the derivation as such.

6.4 Inventory, oversupply, harvest and price data

Harvest (wet weight, OLCC Metrc data): - 2023: harvest up 15% on 2022 (Harris Sliwoski 2023 summary); October 2023: 4,835,736 lb (vs 4,175,004 lb October 2022) — Oregon Employment Dept. analysis. - 2024: 12.27–12.3 million lb for the year (OLCC 2025 Supply & Demand Report via MJBizDaily/secondary: https://mjbizdaily.com/news/oregon-cannabis-prices-fall-to-record-low-but-consumer-demand-steady/613926/ — accessed 2026-11-01; Medium/Reklaim summary gives 12.27M). October 2024 alone was then the record month. - 2025: over 13 million lb (MJBizDaily: “more than 13 million pounds”; Reklaim/Medium: 13.56M, up 10.5% on 2024 and 41.3% on 2023). Range flagged: “over 13M” vs 13.56M — Verify on OLCC dataset kqws-k3cp. - October 2025 (“Croptober”): 6,289,890 lb, Oregon’s largest Metrc harvest month ever, +8.9% on October 2024 (Harris Sliwoski State of the State 2025).

Supply vs demand (OLCC 2025 Recreational Marijuana Supply & Demand Report, ORS 475C.529 biennial report, 1 February 2025): - “Currently, the OLCC estimates the wet weight equivalent of demand was 71% of actual annual supply in 2023 and 57% in 2024.” Source: OLCC Ways & Means Q&A excerpting the report: http://apps.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2025R1/Downloads/CommitteeMeetingDocument/290871 — accessed 2026-11-01. In plain terms: supply was ~1.4× demand in 2023 and ~1.75× demand in 2024. - Report conclusion (quoted in secondary summaries): “The Oregon recreational marijuana market … is continually disadvantaged by the marketplace being limited to Oregon. Year after year, supply has outpaced demand. … Until the federal government creates pathways to interstate commerce, the Oregon recreational marijuana market will be characterized by variations on the same theme: a competitive marketplace that features low prices for consumers but low margins for businesses.” (Harris Sliwoski oversupply post: https://harris-sliwoski.com/cannalawblog/oregon-cannabis-oversupply-in-2025/ — accessed 2026-11-01.) - Inventory stockpile: The 2024 harvest “indicates there will be larger inventory stockpiles in the system going forward, putting more downward pressure on prices” (OLCC report via secondary, Feb 2025). No official point-in-time inventory (pounds on hand) figure was located — Unavailable; do not infer inventory from harvest minus sales without a Metrc inventory series.

6.6 Retailers per capita

No official “retailers per capita” series was located. The following are calculations from the figures in this file, labelled as calculations, not official statistics: - December 2022: ~19.6 dispensaries per 100,000 people (833 retailers — Cannabis Business Times, above; this IS a published per-capita figure, secondary). - September 2026: 752 active retailer licences. Against Oregon’s population (approx. 4.3 million — population figure itself is Verify; no population source was opened in this run), that is roughly 17–18 retailer licences per 100,000 residents, or roughly 1 retailer per ~5,700 residents. Against the 651 retailers with sales (July 2026), roughly 15 per 100,000. Do not quote these as official; quote the 19.6 (Dec 2022) figure with its date, or present the September 2026 calculation explicitly as a calculation. - Under HB 4121’s cap (1 retailer per 7,500 residents 21+), Oregon at ~752 retailers is above the cap-implied level for the adult population alone if the adult (21+) population is taken as ~3.2–3.3 million (≈427–440 retailers at cap) — which is why new retailer applications remain closed. This arithmetic is illustrative; the OLCC’s own cap calculation (which adult-population denominator and which licence count it uses) is Verify.

6.7 Out-of-state buyers — Idaho, California, Washington (officially reported vs anecdotal)

What is officially reported: OLCC publishes sales by county (dataset 5prm-2vmn). It does not publish buyer residency. Every “X% from Idaho” figure below is therefore an operator estimate or a county-sales inference, NOT an OLCC buyer-residency statistic. That distinction must be kept in any deliverable.

Ontario / Malheur County (Idaho border) — the documented case: - Ontario, Oregon (Malheur County) is the only city in Malheur County that allows marijuana sales, after voters overturned the county ban by initiative in 2018 (56.8% vote, per secondary history). Malheur County voted 68.7% against Measure 91 in 2014, the highest opposition of any Oregon county (same history). - Malheur County sales: ~$8 million/month or more for seven months to late 2020 (OLCC data via Radical Russ history: https://radicalruss.com/idaho-marijuana-sales-top-100m-in-ontario-oregon/ — accessed 2026-11-01); ~$9.1–9.2M/month average in 2021–2022 (nine Ontario shops, Jan 2022 $9.1M: https://radicalruss.com/marijuana-sales-remain-steady-at-the-idaho-oregon-border/ — accessed 2026-11-01); 2021 total $111.2M (up from $91.7M in 2020), a $19.5M increase that was 27.6% of Oregon’s entire 2021 sales increase ($70.9M), with Malheur County’s 21.3% growth the highest of Oregon’s 36 counties (https://radicalruss.com/idaho-accounted-for-a-quarter-of-oregons-marijuana-sales-growth-in-2021/ — accessed 2026-11-01). In 2021 Malheur ($111.2M) ranked third among counties, behind only Multnomah ($310.2M) and Washington ($112M), ahead of Lane ($108.6M). - 2023: Ontario dispensary sales ~$100M, ~$3,125 per Malheur County resident, “by far the highest per-capita sales amount of any county in Oregon” (Portland Monthly, recent article: https://www.pdxmonthly.com/news-and-city-life/ontario-oregon-idaho-marijuana-cannabis-business/ — accessed 2026-11-01). Ontario has at least a dozen dispensaries; one operator estimates more than 90% of customers come from Idaho (same article — operator estimate, not OLCC data). A 2022 legislative testimony letter similarly states ~90% of Ontario sales are to Idaho citizens, ~892,857 transactions/year, ~2,500 sales/day, average transaction $112, and that Ontario is the second-largest retailer of cannabis in Oregon behind Portland, accounting for ~10% of all Oregon sales (testimony: https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2022R1/Downloads/PublicTestimonyDocument/34828 — accessed 2026-11-01; that testimony is advocacy, not an official sales audit — label it as such). - Do not confuse Ontario, Oregon with Fruitland/Payette, Idaho (across the Snake River) or with Ontario, Canada. The Boise metro (750,000 people, ~55 miles east on I-84) is the demand source cited in every account. - December 2023 county check: Malheur County $8.8M that month (Herald Jan 2024, §6.1) — consistent with the ~$9M/month Ontario run-rate, not with a collapse.

California and Washington buyers: No official OLCC buyer-residency figure for California or Washington buyers was located. Border markets in southern Oregon (Brookings, Grants Pass, Medford/Ashland area) and northern Oregon (Portland metro, Milton-Freewater/Walla Walla) are routinely described in industry commentary as serving cross-border demand, but no quantified, sourced figure for California or Washington buyers was located in this run — Unavailable, do not estimate. The lawful point is narrower: an adult 21+ may buy at an OLCC retailer regardless of residency (Oregon does not impose a residency requirement on retail purchasers — Verify in OAR 845-025-2800), but transporting marijuana out of Oregon remains unlawful under the destination state’s law and federal law.

Diversion: Whitney Economics’ estimate (via secondary, Oct 2026) that Oregon sends ~2.7 million pounds to other states, and that licensed retailers’ share of Oregon cannabis sales fell from 75% (2020) to 68% (2024), is an analyst estimate, not official enforcement data (Substack analysis, §6.2). Official diversion/enforcement data (seizures, illegal-grow enforcement) are a Part 10/11 topic and were not quantified here.

6.10 Cannabis-friendly banks and credit unions

Federal context (given baseline): There is no federal cannabis banking law. Banks serving cannabis-related businesses (CRBs) operate under FinCEN guidance, Bank Secrecy Act / anti-money-laundering obligations, Suspicious Activity Reports and enhanced due diligence. Visa/Mastercard prohibit cannabis transactions (secondary summary) — card processing for marijuana remains unavailable through the card networks.

Institutions named for Oregon (secondary sources only — no institution’s current CRB programme was confirmed on the institution’s own site in this run; Verify with the institution before referring a client): - Maps Credit Union (headquartered Salem) — the best-documented Oregon CRB programme: began serving cannabis businesses in 2014 under FinCEN guidance; still banks nearly 500 cannabis-related businesses (Register-Guard, Dec 2025: https://www.registerguard.com/story/business/2025/12/19/marijuana-reclassified-as-schedule-iii-cannabis-business/87836133007/ — accessed 2026-11-01, reporting Maps COO Rachel Pross); “removed more than $3.5 billion in cannabis-related cash deposits from the streets” over a decade, transported directly to the Fed, not stored at Maps locations (same article). Dedicated cannabis banking, deposit accounts and payment processing (secondary: https://www.solvent.io/cannabis-banking/oregon — accessed 2026-11-01). - Wauna Credit Union — named in multiple secondary lists as one of (formerly) only two Oregon institutions accepting cannabis business accounts, with Maps (Green Eugene, student journalism: http://greeneugene.com/3675/science-legal/barriers-to-banking-in-the-cannabis-industry/ — accessed 2026-11-01). Current Wauna CRB status is Verify — the “only two” claim is old and conflicts with the longer lists below. - Central Willamette Credit Union — named in Solvent’s Oregon list (https://www.solvent.io/cannabis-banking — accessed 2026-11-01) as “Central Willamette Credit Union” (Solvent’s Oregon page renders it as “Bank Central Willamette Credit Union” — name garble flagged). - Other names appearing on secondary Oregon lists (all Verify individually): Herring Bank, Safe Harbor Financial (fintech), Amalgamated Bank, First Citizens Bank, Salal Credit Union (Washington-based, serves Oregon per secondary), Numerica Credit Union (Washington-based; early cannabis banking from 2014, ~200 cannabis accounts per one secondary history), KeyPoint Credit Union, Twin City Bank, Bison State Bank, Green Check (fintech), Lighthouse Biz Solutions (CUSO). Source for the consolidated list: https://oregonstatecannabis.org/business/banking — accessed 2026-11-01 (secondary, undated). - Cost signal (secondary, dated): A Eugene processor owner quoted cannabis account costs at ~$400–$500/month vs $15–$50/month for a normal small-business account (Green Eugene, above). Dated and anecdotal — Verify current pricing with the institution. - Lending gap (secondary): Credit unions accepting cannabis businesses in Oregon “do not issue loans” to them, per the Green Eugene piece (attributed to an Oregon cannabis attorney). Part 7 — Hemp Licences

PART 7 — HEMP LICENCES

(All sections below are complete for this part; items marked Verify remain open — see §7.18.)

7.1 The headline answer: Oregon runs its own USDA-approved state plan

Oregon does NOT use the USDA programme. Oregon operates under its own USDA-approved state plan, administered by the Oregon Department of Agriculture (ODA). This is confirmed on the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service list itself, updated 17 February 2026, which lists “Oregon | OR Approved Plan (pdf)*” — the asterisk meaning approved under the final rule effective 22 March 2021 — and NOT “USDA Hemp Producer License” for Oregon. Source: https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review — accessed 2026-11-01 (page opened directly in this run).

The plan was approved in January 2022. Secondary reporting of the approval (Hemp Industry Daily, 7 January 2022; ODA/Greenhouse Product News summaries) states the approval “allows the state through ODA to continue as the primary regulator of hemp production in Oregon” and that from 1 January 2022 hemp production had to comply with the 2018 Farm Bill provisions and USDA Domestic Hemp Production Program regulations, including grower registration with USDA Farm Service Agency (FSA). Sources: https://hempindustrydaily.com/?p=134802 ; https://gpnmag.com/news/oregon-department-of-agriculture-receives-approval-on-plan-to-regulate-hemp-production/ — accessed 2026-11-01. ODA’s own hemp law/rules hub links the “State of Oregon hemp plan (2022)” directly. Source: https://www.oregon.gov/oda/hemp/pages/hemp-law-rules.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01 (page opened directly in this run).

Consequence: the authoritative Oregon hemp licence list is ODA’s, not a USDA producer list (consistent with Run 1 Part 5 §5.9). A grower licensed only by USDA in another state does not thereby hold an Oregon licence. Conversely, an Oregon ODA licence is the state-plan licence; USDA FSA registration is an additional reporting step, not a substitute licence (see §7.4).

Plan-amendment rule (for §7.15): USDA’s list page states that once approved a plan “remains in effect unless withdrawn by the State or Tribal government or revoked by USDA” and that if a state “makes substantive revisions to its plan or its laws which alter the way the hemp plan functions, the State or Tribal government must re-submit the revised plan for USDA approval.” Source: USDA list page above — accessed 2026-11-01. This is why ODA’s federal-changes bulletin says ODA will “evaluate the changes needed to Oregon’s USDA-approved state plan” once USDA updates its requirements (§7.15).

7.2 Statutory and rule framework — verbatim operative text

Statutes: ORS 571.260 to 571.348 (Industrial Hemp). Source index: https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors571.html — accessed 2026-11-01. Key sections located in this run: ORS 571.269 (definitions), 571.281 (grower and handler licence), 571.282 (interagency agreement), 571.285 (revocation/refusal), 571.287 (criminal records check on grower applicant), 571.289 (ineligibility/denial grounds), 571.290 (propagation), 571.291 (crop location), plus 571.295/571.296 (Hemp Registry-related provisions as cited in OLCC rule 845-026-6100), 571.309 (OLCC concentration/approval standards), 571.330/571.339 (testing), 571.336/571.337 (OLCC hemp certificate/endorsement authority).

Hemp definition — delegated, not fixed at 0.3% in the statute. ORS 571.269(9)(a), as quoted in Run 1 Part 1 §1.2.3 and re-confirmed here:

“‘Industrial hemp’: (A) Means the plant species Cannabis sativa that has a tetrahydrocannabinol concentration that complies with the concentration specified by the department by rule; and (B) Has the meaning given that term as it is further defined by the department by rule. (b) ‘Industrial hemp’ does not mean industrial hemp commodities or products.”

That delegation is the legal reason ODA could say ORS 571.269 “allows ODA to define THC concentration requirements in rule, giving Oregon room to adjust once federal guidance is released” (ODA federal-changes bulletin, §7.15). Do not quote “0.3% in ORS 571.269” as a statutory fixed figure — 0.3% operates through ODA rule and OLCC product limits (see §7.11).

Who must be licensed — ORS 571.281 and OAR 603-048-0100. OAR 603-048-0100 (as rendered in the October 2025 RAC draft and older rule text): “Only a grower registered [now licensed] with the department may produce industrial hemp. Only a handler registered [licensed] with the department may process industrial hemp.” Registrations/licences are personal and may not be transferred: “A registrant may not sell or transfer an industrial hemp or agricultural hemp seed production registration.” Source: https://stage.oregon.gov/oda/agriculture/Documents/Rulemaking/draft_october_2025_rac_hemp_rules.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 (draft rules — the non-transfer principle is stated there; Verify the current adopted OAR 603-048-0100 text on the Secretary of State OAR site before advising on transferability, because the draft is not the adopted rule). This non-transferability contrasts sharply with OLCC marijuana licences, where change-of-ownership transfer is the live entry route under the caps (Run 1 Part 4 §4.10). Do not assume an ODA hemp licence can be sold like an OLCC licence.

Criminal-history bar — ORS 571.287 / 571.289, 10 years. ORS 571.289(1), as rendered from the Legislature’s ORS page:

“Except as provided in subsection (2) of this section: (a) If a person has been convicted of a felony related to a controlled substance under state or federal law, the person is ineligible for a license under ORS 571.281 to grow hemp for 10 years following the date of the person’s conviction.”

The exception in subsection (2) (as described in the 2021 HB 2281 staff summary) does not apply the bar to a person registered to grow hemp with ODA before 20 December 2018 / 31 October 2019 in the various drafts — the exact exception date in current ORS 571.289(2) is Verify; the October 2025 RAC draft states the denial rule as: the Department must deny a grower application if “the applicant or any key participant has been convicted of a felony relating to a controlled substance within the last ten years from the date of application unless the conviction also occurred before December 20, 2018, the convicted individual was growing hemp lawfully under a pilot program authorized by Section 7606 of the Agricultural Act of 2014 before December 20, 2018, and documentation of the participation is submitted with the application.” Sources: https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors571.html ; https://stage.oregon.gov/oda/agriculture/Documents/Rulemaking/draft_october_2025_rac_hemp_rules.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01. ODA’s grower page states the rule in plain language: “In Oregon since 2022, all hemp growers must go through a background check. This means all key participants need to get checked, including fingerprinting. Only those without recent felony drug convictions (in the last 10 years) can get a license to grow hemp.” Source: https://www.oregon.gov/oda/hemp/Pages/hemp-growers.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01 (page opened directly). Scope note: the bar as written applies to a grower licence; whether it applies identically to handler, seed-producer and vendor applicants is Verify in ORS 571.289 / OAR 603-048-0225 — do not assume it does.

Rules: OAR Chapter 603, Division 48 (ODA hemp programme rules, including licence requirements, pre- and post-harvest testing, and violations); OHA testing rules OAR 333-007 and OAR 333-064 (accreditation) as incorporated by OAR 603-048-2300 to 603-048-2500; OLCC rules OAR Chapter 845, Division 25 (hemp certificates/endorsements, OAR 845-025-2700 to 845-025-2785) and Division 26 (concentration limits and Hemp Registry, OAR 845-026-0300/0400/0410/0415 and 845-026-6000 to 845-026-6120). ODA hub source: https://www.oregon.gov/oda/hemp/pages/hemp-law-rules.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01 (opened directly).

Fees are OAR 603-048-0700, current through Register Vol. 64, No. 6, 1 June 2025 on the Justia rendering opened directly in this run. They match Run 1 Part 4 §4.8 exactly — no fee change is claimed here. Older fee schedules ($250 grower / $500 grow site / $1,300 handler, and the 2016 $500/$500/$25 schedule) are superseded and must not be quoted as current.
