Fees are non-refundable and not prorated (grower application, ODA). Source: https://www.oregon.gov/oda/Documents/Publications/Hemp/Grower_Application.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01.

No hemp retail tax, no ODA “CBD retail licence” as a standalone type: Run 1 Part 2 §2.9 found no current hemp retail tax. For completeness here: a person selling hemp items to consumers in Oregon needs (a) an ODA vendor site licence if they store/transfer/sell for resale (§7.7), and (b) OLCC Hemp Registry registration for each cannabinoid product (§7.9) — there is no separate ODA “CBD shop licence.” A vendor licence “does not authorize further processing, repackaging or relabeling” (secondary summary of ODA vendor FAQ — Verify the vendor FAQ text; the FAQ is linked from the ODA law/rules hub).

7.4 ODA grower licence and grow sites — what it allows, requirements

What it allows: producing (growing, harvesting, drying — see handler distinction in §7.5) industrial hemp at the licensed grow site(s) listed on the licence. A grower licence number must be held before growing starts. ODA grower page, verbatim key points (opened directly):

“Hemp growing licenses expire on December 31 each year. Fees are not prorated.” “You must submit your grower application (renewal or new) to the ODA by May 31 of the year you plan to grow. Late submissions, received by the Department no later than July 31, are subject to a $250 late fee for each grow site application.” “You must have your license number before you start growing.” “Growing hemp without a license can lead to not getting a license and possible fines.”

Source: https://www.oregon.gov/oda/hemp/Pages/hemp-growers.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01.

Application contents (grower/grow site application, rev. 11/2025): business/entity information and Oregon Secretary of State registration number (if applicable, not the tax ID); grow-site information and maps; list of key participants — “members, officers, owners, and any other key participants authorized to make changes to the license” — each subject to fingerprint background check (§7.2); grow-site registration with USDA Farm Service Agency (FSA) — the application states growers “will need to register their grow site with the [USDA FSA]”; attestation that ODA may enter any field/facility/greenhouse used for hemp production and take samples and test for total THC; pre-harvest testing for total THC under OAR 603-048-0600 for each production area before harvest (§7.10); compliance with ORS 571.260–571.348 and OAR Chapter 603, Division 48; seed-law compliance (ORS 633.500–633.996, OAR 603-056-0490) where applicable. Source: https://www.oregon.gov/oda/Documents/Publications/Hemp/Grower_Application.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01.

Deadlines, restated precisely (two different deadlines — do not conflate): - Grower/grow-site new or renewal application deadline for the growing year: 31 May; late grow-site applications accepted to 31 July with the $250 late fee per site; “No new grow sites may be added after May 31 or July 31 with the late fee” (application text). - Renewal payment deadline: “Renewal applications must be received with full fee payment no later than December 1st” of the current licence year, or licensure will expire (application text). The secondary summary that renewal is due “no later than December 8” for growers/handlers/seed producers conflicts with the application form’s December 1 date — use December 1 from the ODA form; the December 8 date is flagged as a secondary conflict, Verify in OAR 603-048-0200/0225.

Grower endorsements without a handler licence (proposed/draft — do NOT cite as adopted law without checking): the October 2025 RAC draft would let a licensed grower, without a handler licence, (a) trim hemp produced by the grower at the licensed grow site if a valid LUCS stating trimming is permitted is submitted first and handler requirements for usable hemp are met; (b) manufacture kief from the grower’s own hemp at the grow site on the same LUCS + handler-requirements conditions; (c) manufacture pre-rolled hemp under stated conditions. Source: https://stage.oregon.gov/oda/agriculture/Documents/Rulemaking/draft_october_2025_rac_hemp_rules.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01. The current grower application (rev. 11/2025) already asks: “Do you plan to trim hemp, produce kief, or make pre-rolls? If yes, circle desired endorsements above and check corresponding boxes on a new LUCS form” — so endorsement-by-LUCS is operating in the form even though the draft-rule status of the underlying rule is Verify. A grower who wants to do anything beyond the grower’s own trimming/kief/pre-roll endorsements needs a handler licence (§7.5).

Research grower: ODA’s grower page lists a separate “Research grower and grow site license application” (and Spanish version), which “must be submitted with both a research plan and a destruction plan for review prior to approval.” Source: ODA grower page above — accessed 2026-11-01. The RAC draft defines “licensed research grower” as a person licensed to produce hemp for research purposes only under OAR 603-048-0126. Fee, term and whether research growers are counted in the grower totals in §7.14 are Verify — no research-grower fee line was located in OAR 603-048-0700 as opened.

What a grower licence does NOT allow: processing into commodities/products (handler licence required, except the endorsements above); retail sale for resale without a vendor-site licence where §7.7 requires one (a grower selling only its own product from a notified location is excepted from vendor licensing — see §7.7); transfer into the OLCC adult-use system without an OLCC hemp certificate (§7.8); growing at an unlisted site; growing after 31 December without renewal.

7.5 ODA handler licence, endorsements, and reciprocity

What it allows: receiving industrial hemp for processing into commodities, products or agricultural hemp seed, and any other activities identified by ODA by rule (ORS 571.269 definition of “handler,” Run 1 §1.2.3). “Only a handler registered [licensed] with the Department may process industrial hemp” and “a hemp handling registration applies to only one handling site. A handler must obtain a separate registration for each handling site” (OAR 603-048-0150, as rendered). Source: https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_603-048-0150 — accessed 2026-11-01.

Application (rev. 9/2026) contents: owner/member information (ownership interest as described in OAR 603-048-0010(41)); handling-site information; premises map; property-owner authorisation; LUCS; endorsement approvals; full fee payment. Renewal: “completed renewal application including premises map, property owner authorization, LUCS, approval of endorsements (with additional required documentation for extraction, if applicable), and full fee payment no later than December 1st of the current license year.” Source: https://www.oregon.gov/oda/Documents/Publications/Hemp/Hemp_Handler_App_Fillable.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01.

Endorsements shown on the handler application form: Hemp Edible; Hemp Topical; Flower or biomass — Drying/trimming; Hemp Concentrate; Hemp Extract; Other (describe). Two endorsement rules matter: - Hemp Extract “additionally requires proof of passing inspection of extraction equipment by a professional engineer and certificate of occupancy from the local governing body. 603-048-0151(3)(c).” - No endorsement required for: “Flower or biomass — Drying/trimming/pre-rolls.” - LUCS timing change: “Effective June 30, 2026, handler applications must include an approved LUCS for specific endorsements. Extraction endorsements require a passing equipment inspection certified by a professional engineer and certificate of occupancy from the local governing body. OAR 603-048-0151(3)(c).” And: “DO NOT BEGIN OPERATIONS until written notification of license approval is received from the Department.” Source: handler application above — accessed 2026-11-01. Verify the full current OAR 603-048-0151 endorsement list in the adopted rule — the form is the best evidence located, but a form is not the rule text, and the October 2025 RAC draft was still revising endorsement language (including a LUCS “permitted” vs “not prohibited” wording dispute noted in OLCC feedback on the draft).

Handler by reciprocity ($875): “A marijuana processor licensed under ORS 475C.085 with a hemp endorsement as described in OAR 845-025-3210 from the OLCC may be registered by reciprocity with the Department as a handler in accordance with OAR 603-048-0225” (OAR 603-048-0150(3)). A reciprocity handler “is deemed to be in compliance with the recordkeeping requirements in OAR 603-048-0500 if the marijuana processor tracks all industrial hemp and industrial hemp products and commodities in the Cannabis Tracking System as required by OAR Chapter 845, Division 25” and “is deemed to be in compliance with testing requirements for hemp items if the marijuana processor tests all hemp items as required in OAR Chapter 845, Division 25.” Source: OAR 603-048-0150 rendering above — accessed 2026-11-01. The handler application confirms the practical requirement: attach “a copy of the OLCC processor licence and hemp endorsement certificate” (Run 1 §4.8). Reciprocity is one-way in the text located: OLCC processor → ODA handler. The reverse (ODA handler → OLCC system) is via the OLCC hemp certificate (§7.8), not via “reciprocity.”

Additional handler obligations located: handlers must ensure an authorised laboratory conducts testing under OAR 603-048-2300 to 603-048-2500 (§7.10); scales used must be certified by ODA Measurement Standards (ORS 618.121, per handler application); “An ODA Food Safety license must be obtained prior to handling or manufacturing any article used, or intended for human consumption” (handler application text, truncated in rendering — Verify the full food-safety condition in the application/rule); “Cannabinoid containing hemp items intended for human or animal consumption are required [to] be enrolled in the OLCC Hemp Registry prior to offering for sale to Oregon consumers, regardless of THC content. OAR 845-026-…” (handler application text). Records: “Keep a copy of this application and all other records associated with your hemp business, as required by Oregon law, for at least three years from disposition of hemp inventory” (handler application).

7.6 Agricultural hemp seed producer licence

What it allows: producing agricultural hemp seed as a registered grower or handler (RAC draft definition: “‘Agricultural hemp seed producer’ means a registered grower or handler that…” — definition truncated in rendering, Verify full definition in OAR 603-048-0010). In practice, ODA’s grower page states: “If you plan to produce agricultural hemp seed, you’ll also need an agricultural hemp seed license” — i.e. it is an additional licence on top of grower/handler status, not a standalone right to grow. Source: ODA grower page — accessed 2026-11-01.

Fee: $875 application (OAR 603-048-0700(1)(e), opened directly — §7.3). Application form: ODA’s grower page lists a “Hemp seed application” (and Spanish version) as a separate form. Source: ODA grower page — accessed 2026-11-01. Seed-law overlay: seed production is also subject to ORS 633.500–633.996 and OAR 603-056-0490 (grower application text). What it does NOT establish: seed certification (as distinct from licensing), variety approval, or interstate seed shipment conditions were not located in this run — all Verify in OAR 603-048 and OAR 603-056 before advising a seed producer. Run 1 §4.8 flagged the same gap; it remains open.

Nursery overlay (Verify): the RAC draft states sales/transfers of growing immature hemp plants are permitted only if the seller is a licensed grower holding a valid ODA nursery licence under ORS 475.065 (rendering garbled as “571.055” in one passage — Verify the correct nursery statute) and the buyer is a licensed grower. Do not advise on live-plant sales from this draft alone.

7.7 ODA vendor site licence (retail/wholesale) — from 1 July 2024

Rule: OAR 603-048-0175. ODA law/rules hub, verbatim (opened directly):

“Starting July 1, 2024: In Oregon, any hemp retailers or wholesalers who store, transfer, or sell industrial hemp or hemp items for resale to another person must get a hemp vendor license from the Oregon Department of Agriculture (ODA), as per OAR 603-048-0175. The vendor license costs $100 per year and is valid from July 1 – June 30.”

Source: https://www.oregon.gov/oda/hemp/pages/hemp-law-rules.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01. The hub note that “any hemp vendor site license applied for will be registered under the 2025/2026 licensing year (effective July 1st)” is stale as of the 1 November 2026 cut-off (the 2026/2027 year began 1 July 2026) — Verify the current licensing-year note on the live hub page; the $100 / 1 July–30 June cycle itself is confirmed by the rule text in OAR 603-048-0700(1)(h).

Scope and exceptions (proposed-rule text, November 2025 — the adopted 0175 text should be re-checked, but the structure is consistent across secondary summaries): a vendor must have a licence for each vendor site before storing, transferring, offering for sale, or selling industrial hemp or hemp items to consumers in Oregon, except: (a) a person who only facilitates sale/transfer by connecting buyers and sellers and never stores the product; (b) a licensed grower, handler, or agricultural hemp seed producer is not required to be licensed as a vendor site to store/transfer/sell industrial hemp or hemp items the licensee produced or processed, if the licensee first notifies ODA of the location in the licence application or otherwise. Source: http://egov.oregon.gov/oda/agriculture/Documents/Rulemaking/misc_hemp_rule_updates.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01. Secondary summaries (Harris Sliwoski via Lexology/Mondaq, June 2024) add: the rule was adopted 5 June 2024 after HB 4121; originally proposed at $200/site, reduced to $100 after wholesaler/small-retailer pushback; fee not prorated mid-year; each unlicensed vendor site is a separate violation. Sources: https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=4bfa8824-6a26-4417-9ea2-54b5eb69fe88 — accessed 2026-11-01. Distinction that must not be lost: ODA vendor licence = seller/site registration. OLCC Hemp Registry = product registration (§7.9). A vendor still needs Registry registration for each cannabinoid product it sells to Oregon consumers, and Registry registration does not replace the vendor licence.

Application: two-page vendor application (business name/location/contact, primary contact, Secretary of State number, $100 fee); submission by email to ODA hemp applications or fax, or mail cheque/money order; “License will not be issued until application has been approved”; fees non-refundable, not prorated. Source: vendor application as rendered in the OLCC/ODA CBD guidance PDF bundle — https://manuals.plus/m/3ab07776fdd04f69077621fc34e476fba6ae6373e5390f81c766c2ce73eecaca.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 (Verify the standalone vendor application PDF linked from the ODA hub, since this rendering is inside a bundled PDF).

7.8 OLCC roles for hemp items — hemp certificate, processor endorsement, retailer sale

These are OLCC (adult-use system) roles, NOT ODA licences. They are the only lawful bridge for hemp into OLCC-licensed premises. Run 1 Part 4 §4.5/§4.8 figures are confirmed and extended here.

OLCC hemp certificate (OAR 845-025-2700 to 845-025-2785). OLCC hemp-certificate page (opened via search rendering; Verify on the live OLCC page, since the direct open in this run was the search rendering):

“Obtaining an OLCC hemp certificate is necessary for any business that will transfer hemp or hemp items to an OLCC-licensed marijuana business. Only a hemp grower or hemp handler licensed with [ODA] can receive an OLCC hemp certificate.”

Privileges differ by underlying ODA licence: - Grower with certificate: “can only transfer ‘harvested industrial hemp’ to OLCC licensees. Harvested industrial hemp means hemp that has not been processed or been only minimally processed. It does not include ‘usable hemp’ (smokable flower). OAR 845-025-2750.” - Handler with certificate: “can transfer ‘harvested industrial hemp’ as well as ‘hemp items’ to OLCC licensees. ‘Hemp items’ includes ‘usable hemp’ (smokable flower), hemp concentrates and extracts, and cannabinoid hemp products like edibles, tinctures, and topicals. OAR 845-025-2755.”

Source: https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/Pages/Hemp-Certificate-Application-Process.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01.

Fees: “Applicants for an Industrial Hemp Certificate must pay a $250 non-refundable application fee and a $1,000 certificate fee.” Applications via CAMP (https://camp.olcc.online/). Source: same OLCC page — accessed 2026-11-01. This confirms Run 1’s “$1,000/year” hemp certificate figure (the $250 application fee is the addition here; the annual vs one-time character of the $1,000 fee beyond the first year is Verify in OAR 845-025-1060, which Run 1 could not open directly).

Certificate mechanics: certificate holders receive a Metrc (CTS) account and enter hemp items to be transferred to OLCC licensees into Metrc; the item “must undergo certain required compliance testing prior to being transferred to an OLCC marijuana licensee. At minimum, it needs to pass a potency test to make sure it’s below the THC thresholds for hemp items that OLCC licensees are allowed to receive,” plus any other test required for the equivalent marijuana item (OAR 845-025-5800 to 845-025-5850). “A test performed by an out-of-state lab, or any lab not licensed by OLCC, cannot satisfy this requirement. The sampling and testing must be performed by an OLCC-licensed, ORELAP-accredited lab” and recorded in CTS. Transfers may go only to OLCC wholesalers, processors (with hemp endorsement), and retailers as the certificate privileges allow. Sources: OLCC hemp-certificate page and OLCC Adult-Use Hemp FAQ — https://WWW.OREGON.GOV/olcc/marijuana/Pages/Adult-Use-Hemp-FAQ.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01.

OLCC processor industrial-hemp endorsement (OAR 845-025-3210): a processor holding this endorsement may receive/transfer hemp and hemp items under OAR 845-025-3215; it is also the gateway to ODA handler-by-reciprocity (§7.5). A wholesaler may receive/transfer hemp under OAR 845-025-3500; a retailer may sell/transfer/deliver hemp items to consumers under OAR 845-025-2800, under the same hours/age rules as marijuana items (21+, or 18–21 for OMMP cardholders at a medically endorsed retailer). Source: OAR 845-025-2785 rendering (2019 proposed-amendments PDF, citing the rule structure) — https://cannabislaw.report/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/Industrial_Hemp_Package_FINAL.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 (Verify the current 845-025-2785/3210/3500/2800 text; the endorsement fee, if any beyond the processor licence fee, was not located and is Verify).

THC limits for hemp entering the OLCC system: OAR 845-025-2760 (THC Concentration Limits for Industrial Hemp and Hemp Items). A certified grower “may not transfer… any batch of harvested industrial hemp to a licensee that exceeds the THC limits specified in OAR 845-025-2760” (OAR 845-025-2750 rendering). The Table in 845-025-2760 itself was not opened in this run — Verify Table 845-025-2760 before quoting any OLCC-system hemp limit; do not substitute the general-market Table 3 limits (§7.11) for it.

Interaction with the HB 4121 caps: OLCC hemp certificates are NOT producer/processor/wholesaler/retailer licences and are not stated in the sources located to be subject to the HB 4121 per-capita caps (Run 1 §4.9). ODA hemp licences are likewise not subject to those caps. New ODA hemp applications and OLCC hemp-certificate applications were therefore open in 2026 while new OLCC marijuana licences were closed — subject to the application deadlines in §§7.4–7.5 and to CAMP/ODA processing.

7.9 OLCC Hemp Registry — product registration, not a licence (OAR 845-026-6000 to 845-026-6120)

Legal basis and dates: HB 4121 (2024), 2024 Oregon Laws ch. 16, directed OLCC to establish a registration system for industrial hemp products containing cannabinoids for human/animal consumption, with labelling/packaging minima and civil penalty up to $10,000 per violation. OLCC adopted the Registry rules in OLCC 7-2025 (approved 20 November 2025, effective 1 January 2026). Enforcement of the Registry was delayed to 1 June 2026 as a transition/grace period; during the grace period OLCC continued enforcing existing laws (sales to minors, THC over legal limits, intoxicating/adulterated cannabinoids). Sources: OLCC 20 November 2025 announcement — https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/OLCC/bulletins/3fc3d7a — accessed 2026-11-01; OLCC June 2026 enforcement bulletin — https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/OLCC/bulletins/41940ef — accessed 2026-11-01; permanent order summary — http://egov.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/rules/2025-Hemp-Product-Registry.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01.

What must be registered: OLCC Hemp Registry FAQs (opened via search rendering — Verify on the live FAQ page):

“Hemp items must be registered with the OLCC if: They are for sale to a consumer in Oregon; They are intended for human or animal consumption or use; and They are not exclusively for topical application to skin or hair.”

Source: https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/Pages/hemp-registry-faqs.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01.

What is excluded: hemp items that do not contain cannabinoids; hemp items intended only for topical use (lotions, soaps); hemp grain or fibre products that do not contain added cannabinoids; commercial feed products for animals registered under ORS 633.006–633.089 (regulated exclusively by ODA); hemp items transported through Oregon en route to a final destination in another state; hemp items sold only out of state (no Oregon registration/labelling required for out-of-state-only sales). Source: same FAQs — accessed 2026-11-01. The November 2025 announcement confirms: “Topical products like lotions and soaps, as well as hemp grain and fiber products that do not contain cannabinoids are excluded from the registration.” Note the tension to flag: the FAQ says “not exclusively for topical application” — a product that is both topical and ingestible/inhalable is not excluded. Verify the exact topical boundary in OAR 845-026-6020 before advising on dual-use products.

What registration requires (OAR 845-026-6100, as amended by temporary order OLCC 2-2026, effective 24 May–19 November 2026, and proposed permanent 29 September 2026): before selling/offering/transferring/delivering a hemp item to a consumer or retailer in Oregon, the responsible party must submit an electronic registration application and receive Commission approval. The application must include: the fee in OAR 845-026-6010; name/type of hemp item; manufacturer and responsible-party name/phone/email/physical/mailing address; a certificate of analysis for a batch (for human-consumption items, demonstrating compliance with ORS 571.339 testing and passing each required test); a copy of the label; a statement whether the item is an adult-use cannabis item; for inhalable products with non-cannabis additives, the additive ingredient list and manufacturer attestation; for items containing an artificially derived cannabinoid allowed by OAR 845-026-0415, the §7.12 documentation. OLCC may refuse registration if the application/item does not comply with the rules or 2024 ch. 16 §§11–12 (ORS 571.295/571.296), contains untruthful/misleading content, is adulterated, exceeds OAR 845-026-0300/0400/0410 concentration/serving limits, or the label does not comply with OAR 845-026-6030 to 845-026-6090. Renewal: “a registration renewal application and fee specified by OAR 845-026-6010 must be received no later than 395 days after the date the registration was previously approved.” A single application fee may cover a hemp item in different flavours, colours, cannabinoids or sizes if otherwise identical, but may not combine adult-use cannabis items with non-adult-use items. Sources: https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/rules/Hemp-Temp-Admin-Order-845-026-6100.pdf ; https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/rules/2026-Hemp%20Registry%20Perm%20Notice%20092926.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 (both opened directly).

Fees (OAR 845-026-6010) — resolved here, filling Run 1’s gap: the proposed fee was $420, lowered after public comment to $400 initial registration and $400 annual renewal, with a $25 amendment fee for modifications to an approved registration. Sources: OLCC November 2025 commission rules update — https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/commission_agendas/2025/Rules-Update-112025.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 (“the registration and renewal fees were lowered from $420 to $400 and a $25 amendment fee was created”); corroborated by secondary summaries — https://www.thebrothersapothecary.com/we-support-responsible-hemp-regulation-we-oppose-prohibition/ ; https://sativauniversity.com/cannabis-laws/oregon/ — accessed 2026-11-01. Verify the adopted OAR 845-026-6010 text itself on the OAR site — the $400/$400/$25 figures rest on the OLCC commission update and secondary restatements, not on a direct open of 6010 in this run.

Resubmission reform (2026): under the rules as first adopted, OLCC had to deny an application if the applicant failed to correct every deficiency on the first resubmission. Temporary order OLCC 2-2026 (filed 21 May 2026, effective 24 May–19 November 2026) and the proposed permanent amendment filed 29 September 2026 (comment to 30 October 2026, hearing 21 October 2026) give OLCC discretion to authorise additional resubmissions in writing without collecting additional application fees. Source: September 2026 proposed-rulemaking notice above — accessed 2026-11-01 (opened directly). Status at cut-off: the temporary order expired 19 November 2026 (after the 1 November cut-off) and the permanent rule’s adoption was pending at cut-off — Verify whether the permanent 6100 amendment was adopted, since a reader after 19 November 2026 cannot rely on the temporary order.

Uptake — first official count (new in this part, not in Run 1): OLCC’s September 2026 proposed-rulemaking fiscal statement says: “In 2025, OLCC estimated that approximately 4,500 hemp items would require registration. Of the registration applications approved in 2026, each applicant has an average of 2.7 approved registrations. Based on the 2025 estimate, this could impact around 1,600 businesses.” And: “As of September 28, 2026, 141 applications have been submitted of which 89 have been approved.” Source: September 2026 notice above — accessed 2026-11-01 (opened directly). Read this correctly: 89 is approved applications at 28 September 2026, not 89 products on the market and not a compliance rate — the denominator (products actually offered to Oregon consumers) is unknown, and the 4,500/1,600 figures are 2025 estimates, not counts. Do not present “89 of 4,500” as a compliance percentage.

Registry search: Hemp Registry Product Search via CAMP: https://camp.olcc.online/ [search URL quarantined on audit — see Audit Q28] (as cited in the September 2026 notice). Format/download: CAMP is an interactive search, not a bulk download — whether a Registry export exists is Verify in CAMP (Run 1 Part 5 flagged the same gap for CAMP generally).

No new testing at registration: “There is no additional product testing required as part of the Hemp Registry; testing of hemp products remains a requirement of the Oregon Department of Agriculture’s Hemp Program.” Source: June 2026 enforcement bulletin above — accessed 2026-11-01. Registry registration therefore does not cure an untested product — testing is ODA’s gate (§7.10), registration is OLCC’s gate.

Labelling: Registry items must be labelled under OAR 845-026-6030 to 845-026-6090 (general + product-type labelling), with test results accessible to consumers and food-style labelling for edibles. The full labelling rule text was not opened in this run — Verify OAR 845-026-6030 to 6090 before advising on a label. Civil penalties for Registry violations are in OAR 845-026-6110 (rule number from secondary summary — Verify).

7.10 Hemp testing and labs — pre-harvest, post-harvest, and the lab gate

Pre-harvest (crop) testing — OAR 603-048-0600. Operative rules as rendered (oregon.public.law):

“(1) A grower may not harvest a harvest lot until it has been sampled in accordance with these rules.” “A grower must arrange for and ensure the sampling of a harvest lot no more than twenty-eight (28) calendar days prior to harvest for the purpose of ensuring that the harvest lot does not exceed permissible THC concentration levels on a dry weight basis.” “To be sufficient… all sampling and testing must be performed by the Department or a laboratory” meeting LOQ and method requirements, including: “Can demonstrate that its limit of quantification (LOQ) for THC is at or below 0.3 percent THC” and tests/reports “total THC content… calculated in accordance with OAR 333-064-0100(4).”

Source: https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_603-048-0600 — accessed 2026-11-01. OSU Extension’s plain-language summary adds the harvest window: “Harvest must be complete within 30 days from the date of sampling or the grower must arrange for additional sampling of the unharvested hemp,” and each strain/variety needs its own pre-harvest test (each harvest lot a single strain/variety). Source: https://extension.oregonstate.edu/catalog/when-hemp-harvest-nears-its-time-preharvest-testing — accessed 2026-11-01.

Fail threshold — CONFLICT, do not resolve by picking one: the OAR 603-048-0600 rendering states: “A sample fails testing if the test report indicates that the sample contains total THC content… of 0.35 percent or greater on a dry weight basis. If a sample from a harvest lot fails… the harvest lot fails.” OSU Extension states the failure test differently: “A sample will fail the preharvest test when the application of the measurement of uncertainty to the amount of total THC… produces a distribution or range that does not include 0.3 percent or less on a dry weight basis.” These are not the same test (0.35% bright line vs measurement-of-uncertainty range around 0.3%). Both are reported here; the current adopted 0600 text must be opened to determine which governs at cut-off. The older 0600 text may predate a measurement-of-uncertainty amendment, or the OSU summary may paraphrase a different subsection — either way, do not quote a single fail threshold as settled.

Retesting / resampling — OAR 603-048-0630. If a sample fails, the grower may pursue retesting at the grower’s own cost: request within 7 days of the failed-test notice; retest completed within 30 days of request; if the retest passes, a second laboratory (or the Department) must retest the remaining file sample and also pass to confirm. Alternatively, resampling of the standing production area may be requested within 7 days (resampling within 10 days, results within 30 days), with subdivision into separate harvest lots required if the initial test exceeded 1.0% total THC. A harvest lot that fails after resampling may pursue retesting but not further resampling. Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/oregon/chapter-603/division-48/section-603-048-0630/ — accessed 2026-11-01.

Detention / destruction — OAR 603-048-0900, 603-048-0640, 603-048-8031. ODA “may detain, seize, embargo, or dispose of the harvest lot as provided in ORS 561.605 to 561.620” (OAR 603-048-0900). Destruction may be ordered if the lot was not sampled/tested in compliance, fails and no timely retest/resampling is requested, or fails retesting. Separately, OAR 603-048-8031 allows a final order requiring destruction of all cannabis determined to be “presumptively marijuana” under OAR 845-026-4110 where at least 50% of composite samples from mature plants test at/above 10% total THC, or the average tests at/above 10% — rebuttable only by Department pre-harvest sampling/testing under OAR 603-048-0600 (laboratory testing alone is not sufficient to rebut). Sources: https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_603-048-0900 ; https://regulations.justia.com/states/oregon/chapter-603/division-48/section-603-048-8031/ — accessed 2026-11-01.

Post-harvest (product) testing — OAR 603-048-2300 to 603-048-2500, incorporating OHA rules. OAR 603-048-2300(1): “A grower or handler may not sell or transfer industrial hemp for human consumption or a hemp item unless it is first tested by a laboratory as required by these rules.” The rules require sampling/testing/reporting “in a manner consistent with the Authority’s marijuana sampling and testing rules in OAR 333-007-0300 to 333-007-0500 and OAR 333-064,” with hemp treated as its marijuana equivalent under OAR 603-048-2310. The laboratory must, by testing agreement/contract: sample under OAR 333-007-0360 and OAR 333-064-0100; test under OAR 333-007-0390 to 333-007-0440 and OAR 333-064-0100; meet proficiency-testing requirements in OAR 333-064-0120; and demonstrate THC LOQ at or below 0.3%. Source: https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_603-048-2300 — accessed 2026-11-01. ODA’s hub confirms: “All hemp commodities or products used for human consumption — eating/drinking, smoking, or applications to skin/hair — must be tested to the same standards as marijuana as established by [OHA].” Source: ODA hub — accessed 2026-11-01.

Which lab may test — the ORELAP/OLCC gate, and the federal DEA question: for retail sale, OAR 603-048-1500(4) provides testing may only be conducted by “(a) A laboratory licensed by [OLCC] under ORS 475B.560 [now 475C] and accredited by [OHA] under ORS 475B.565 [now 475C]; or (b) A laboratory accredited to the same or more stringent standards… if the hemp item was processed outside the state of Oregon.” Source: https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_603-048-1500 — accessed 2026-11-01 (note: the rendering still cites 475B numbers — read as 475C). For transfer into the OLCC system, sampling/testing “must be performed by an OLCC-licensed, ORELAP-accredited lab” (OLCC FAQ, §7.8). Federal DEA-registered lab testing: the baseline delays USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing to 31 December 2026. Whether any Oregon rule already requires DEA registration for hemp labs, or whether Oregon will add it when the federal delay expires, was not located in this run — Verify in OAR 603-048-0600/2300 and any ODA lab bulletin. Do not tell an Oregon hemp lab it must be DEA-registered as of 1 November 2026 on the basis of the federal baseline alone.

No separate “hemp testing licence” type was located: testing is performed by OLCC-licensed, ORELAP-accredited laboratories (the same labs that test marijuana items, Run 1 Part 4 §4.5: 9 laboratories in September 2026). There is no ODA-issued hemp-only lab licence in the sources located — Verify on ODA/OHA lab pages whether any hemp-specific lab authorisation exists.

7.11 THC measurement and product limits — Oregon as of 1 November 2026

Crop measurement: Oregon total THC = (delta-9-THCA × 0.877) + delta-9-THC. Sources: ODA federal-changes bulletin (opened directly) — https://apps.oregon.gov/oregon-newsroom/OR/ODA/Posts/Post/Recent-Federal-Hemp-Changes-What-They-Mean-for-Oregon — accessed 2026-11-01; OAR 603-048 definition (516) as quoted in Run 1 §1.2.4. ODA’s bulletin warns the federal bill “does not yet specify how total THC must be calculated” and the federal figure “could end up higher or lower than Oregon’s” (simple sum of THC + THCA + other natural THC isomers, unconfirmed) — see §7.15.

General-market product limits (OAR 845-026-0400 Table 3 / 845-026-0410, OLCC wholesaler fact sheet, rev. August 2026): - Consumer hemp products must contain no more than 0.3% total THC (plus the per-serving/per-container milligram caps below — both constraints apply). - “Hemp edibles, including beverages, are limited to 2 mg total THC per serving and 20 mg total THC per ‘container’ (generally equivalent to a unit of sale).” - “Products that exceed these limits by more than 10% cannot be sold to Oregon consumers” — i.e. the 10% figure is a tolerance on the limit, not a separate higher limit; whether it operates as a testing-variance rule or a sale-prohibition threshold as worded in Table 3 is Verify (Run 1 §1.5.5 flagged the same point). - Full Table 3 (tinctures, topicals, inhalables, concentrates, etc.) was not opened in this run — Verify Table 3 in OAR 845-026-0400/0410 before quoting any non-edible category limit. Do not apply the marijuana edible limit (10 mg/serving, 100 mg/package) to hemp products. Source: https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/CBD/FS_CBD_Wholesalers.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 (OLCC fact sheet, August 2026, as cited in Run 1).

Minor-sale test (OAR 845-026-0300): a hemp product may be sold to a minor only if it contains less than 0.5 mg total THC in the entire unit of sale, compliance testing was sensitive enough to prove it, and it contains no artificially derived cannabinoids. Anything above 0.5 mg, or with insufficiently sensitive testing, or containing any artificially derived cannabinoid, cannot be sold to minors. In practice this makes consumable hemp items above 0.5 mg, inhalable hemp products, and adult-use cannabis items 21+ (Run 1 §1.5.3). Source: OLCC wholesaler fact sheet above — accessed 2026-11-01.

Retail-sale gate (OAR 603-048-1500): a person may not sell an industrial hemp commodity/product to a consumer unless the hemp used complied with the growing jurisdiction’s laws to ensure the 0.3% THC limit; may not sell a hemp item to a consumer unless it was tested under OAR 603-048-2300 to 2500 or the seller holds documentation that the commodity/product was so tested and does not exceed 0.3% total THC; and “may not sell an industrial hemp product that contains more than 0.3 percent total THC to a consumer unless licensed as a retailer by OLCC.” Source: https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_603-048-1500 — accessed 2026-11-01. In plain terms: over-0.3% hemp product is not a general-market product at all — it belongs in the OLCC system (if it qualifies there) or not at all.

7.12 Artificially derived cannabinoids — the approval gate (OAR 845-026-0415 and OAR 845-025-1310)

General rule (unchanged from Run 1): artificially derived cannabinoids in hemp products for general-market sale are prohibited unless approved. OLCC wholesaler fact sheet (August 2026): “Products are generally prohibited from containing any artificially derived cannabinoids. At this time, none have received approval under OAR 845-026-0415. THC created by chemical conversion from CBD is prohibited for use in products sold to [Oregon consumers].” Source: https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/CBD/FS_CBD_Wholesalers.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01.

The approval standard — OAR 845-026-0415 (draft text, August 2024 RAC — the adopted text must be re-checked, but the standard is consistent across the 2024 draft, the 2025 CBN order, and the 2026 Registry form): “An industrial hemp product that contains an artificially derived cannabinoid may be approved on or after January 1, 2026, if: (1) The artificially derived cannabinoid: (a) Is not a controlled substance under OAR chapter 855, division 80; (b) Was manufactured in compliance with applicable laws relating to food safety; (c) In the Commission’s judgment, is not impairing or intoxicating at the intended concentration in the product; and (d) Has been reported as a naturally-occurring component of the plant Cannabis family Cannabaceae in at least three peer-reviewed publications…” plus manufacturer GRAS/NDI documentation (see below). Source: http://egov.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/rules/2024-Hemp-Implementation-Draft-Rule-RAC081324.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01.

Manufacturer documentation (OLCC Artificially Derived Cannabinoid Label Application Form, rev. 11/2025, for use with OAR 845-026-6100 Registry applications): the manufacturer must provide one of: a GRAS determination for the cannabinoid; an FDA letter responding to a GRAS notice for the cannabinoid manufactured by the same method, affirming FDA has no question; or an FDA letter of acknowledgment with no objections in response to a New Dietary Ingredient (NDI) notification for the cannabinoid manufactured by the same method. Citations to at least three peer-reviewed publications showing the cannabinoid has been reported as a naturally-occurring component of Cannabis family Cannabaceae (author, publication, date, DOI link each). Plus a copy of the ODA food-establishment licence (or equivalent food-safety compliance documentation under ORS 616.695–616.755 standards). Source: http://cms.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/Documents/Hemp/Artificially-Derived-Cannabinoid-Label-Application-Form-Hemp-Registry-.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01.

CBN — the unresolved tension (flagged, not resolved): the same form contains checkboxes stating the GRAS and peer-review requirements “do not apply because the artificially derived cannabinoid is cannabinol (CBN) allowed by OAR 845-026-0415.” Meanwhile, the OLCC CBN order (OLCC 1-2025, effective 20 May 2025, amending OAR 845-025-1310, 845-026-0400, 845-026-0410) shows CBN transitional windows: items manufactured before 1 July 2023 could be sold until 2 January 2025, and items manufactured on/after 1 July 2023 could be sold until 1 July 2025, in each case only if not for human inhalation, not a controlled substance, manufactured in food-safety compliance, and (for the later window) manufactured by a person with written Commission approval affirming substantial steps toward the full §7.12 criteria. Run 1 §1.5.2 summarised this as: from 1 July 2025, artificially derived CBN may no longer be sold unless the manufacturer has a GRAS determination or FDA NDI no-objections response (secondary source). Reconciliation required: if CBN is “allowed by OAR 845-026-0415” without GRAS/peer-review on the 2026 form, then either (a) 0415 as adopted contains a CBN-specific allowance that the wholesaler fact sheet’s “none approved” summary does not capture, or (b) the form checkbox is a legacy/conditional box that does not itself approve any CBN product. Do not advise that CBN is approved, and do not advise that all CBN is banned, until the adopted OAR 845-026-0415 text and any OLCC CBN approval list are opened. This is the single most important Verify item in Part 7 for any hemp brand.

OLCC-system ADC rule (OAR 845-025-1310): for OLCC licensees, the same substantive criteria apply (not a controlled substance; food-safety manufacture; not impairing/intoxicating in the Commission’s judgment at the intended concentration; reported as naturally occurring in at least three peer-reviewed publications; not for human inhalation; manufacturer GRAS/FDA documentation). The 2025 CBN order is the latest amendment located. Source: http://cms.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/rules/CBN-Final-052025.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01.

Delta-8 specifically: delta-8-THC made synthetically from CBD is the paradigm prohibited case — it is an artificially derived cannabinoid, it has not received 0415 approval on the evidence located, and it cannot be sold to minors under any circumstances (OAR 845-026-0300). Possession is not itself criminalised in the sources located; sale is the prohibited act. Do not conflate the two.

7.13 Transport, records, and interagency enforcement

Transport: ORS 571.281 (as summarised in the 2021 HB 2281 staff summary) authorises a licensed grower/handler to transport to or receive from a licensed person within state boundaries, and ODA was directed to establish by rule requirements for a shipment manifest for commercial hemp shipments. The current manifest rule number and form were not located in this run — Verify in OAR 603-048 before advising on transport paperwork. For transfer into the OLCC system, transport must comply with OLCC marijuana-item transport rules (OAR 845-025-7700) as incorporated by OAR 845-025-2750 (§7.8). Interstate hemp shipment is a Part 10 topic; for Part 7, note only that Oregon’s USDA-approved state plan authorises interstate transfer of hemp/hemp products in the USDA approval summaries (§7.1), subject to the receiving state’s law — Verify the plan PDF itself for its interstate clause.

Records: handler application: retain application and all business records “for at least three years from disposition of hemp inventory.” Grower recordkeeping is in OAR 603-048-0500 (harvest-lot identifiers, etc.); reciprocity handlers are deemed compliant if they track in CTS (§7.5). Pre-harvest test reports must be reported to ODA within 24 hours on the Department form/portal (OAR 603-048-0630 rendering). Growers must also report crop acreage to USDA FSA (§7.4).

Interagency enforcement: HB 3000/HB 4121 re-enacted interagency inspection/enforcement provisions (OLCC/ODA/OHA collaboration, including law-enforcement accompaniment of inspectors under ORS 571.283). ODA may enter fields/facilities/greenhouses and sample/test for total THC (grower application). OLCC civil penalty for Registry violations up to $10,000 per violation (HB 4121). ODA civil penalties for hemp violations are in ORS 571.348 and OAR 603-048-0800 series (2016 text: up to $2,500 per violation — Verify the current penalty ceiling; do not quote $2,500 as current without checking the adopted rule).

7.15 Effect of the federal 12 November / 11 December 2026 dates on Oregon hemp licensing — as of 1 November 2026

The only Oregon-agency response located, opened directly in this run: ODA bulletin “Recent Federal Hemp Changes: What They Mean for Oregon” (linked from ODA’s hemp law/rules hub as “Nov. 21, 2025” — the bulletin text itself does not carry a visible publication date in the rendering; the hub date is therefore Verify against the bulletin metadata, since the federal bill it describes postdates November 2025 in the baseline’s framing). Verbatim operative passages:

“Key Point: Most federal changes do not take effect until November 2026.“ “During this transition period, Oregon’s hemp program will continue operating under current Oregon laws and rules, including Oregon’s existing definition of total THC.” “ODA is also currently accepting public comments on hemp rule updates. These proposed changes were developed before the federal legislation was passed and are not related to the federal changes.” “Oregon calculates total THC using: (delta-9-THCA × 0.877) + delta-9-THC“ “ORS 571.269 allows ODA to define THC concentration requirements in rule, giving Oregon room to adjust once federal guidance is released.” “Practical Effects for Oregon (Right Now) — No immediate changes are required for Oregon hemp licensees. — ODA’s current rulemaking is not tied to federal legislation. — ODA anticipates that the [USDA] will need to update the national hemp program to reflect the new federal definitions. — Once USDA updates its requirements, ODA will evaluate the changes needed to Oregon’s USDA-approved state plan.”

Source: https://apps.oregon.gov/oregon-newsroom/OR/ODA/Posts/Post/Recent-Federal-Hemp-Changes-What-They-Mean-for-Oregon — accessed 2026-11-01 (opened directly).

What the federal changes would do, per ODA’s summary (baseline dates applied): hemp defined as cannabis with no more than 0.3% total THC dry weight; cannabinoids must naturally occur in the plant to qualify as hemp-derived (synthetic/manufactured cannabinoids fall outside the definition); hemp product “containers” limited to no more than 0.4 mg total THC (federal definition of “container” to be detailed by FDA); first-time federal distinction between intermediate and final hemp-derived cannabinoid products; FDA to publish within 90 days lists of naturally occurring Cannabis sativa cannabinoids, THC-class cannabinoids, and other THC-like cannabinoids, plus container specificity. ODA’s anticipated Oregon consequences: revised testing requirements (depending on the federal total-THC calculation); possible movement of some hemp-derived products into Oregon’s OLCC adult-use system; market disruption, particularly for products exceeding the 0.4 mg container limit; crop-destruction requirements if USDA directs states to apply the new total-THC standard at pre-harvest testing. Any future Oregon rule change will go through public rulemaking.

Application to licensing at the 1 November 2026 cut-off (i.e. BEFORE 12 November / 11 December 2026): - No Oregon conforming statute or rule for the federal dates was located as of 1 November 2026. Do not describe Oregon hemp products as already subject to the 0.4 mg/container cap, and do not describe the cap as an Oregon rule (Run 1 §1.5.6, confirmed here). - ODA licences issued for 2026 remain under current Oregon law through their term (grower/handler to 31 December 2026; vendor to 30 June 2027 for the 2026/2027 year — Verify the vendor year on renewal). Renewal for 2027 will be the first cycle in which a federal-conforming change could bite, if USDA/ODA act — but no such change was adopted at cut-off. - The PL 119-103 §2019 limitation (baseline) means the operative federal date for the full definition + cap is 11 December 2026, not 12 November 2026 alone — do not advise clients that 12 November 2026 is the compliance cliff without explaining the limitation. - USDA DEA-registered lab testing enforcement delayed to 31 December 2026 (baseline): as of cut-off, Oregon’s lab gate is OLCC licence + ORELAP accreditation (§7.10), not DEA registration on the evidence located. - State-plan consequence: if Oregon substantively revises its plan/laws to conform (e.g. a new total-THC calculation or container cap that alters how the plan functions), USDA requires re-submission of the revised plan for approval (§7.1). That re-submission step is the procedural reason ODA says it will “evaluate” changes after USDA acts, rather than conforming unilaterally on 12 November.

7.16 Tribal hemp plans — separate from the state plan

USDA’s list (updated 17 February 2026, opened directly) shows two Oregon tribes with their own USDA-approved hemp plans, distinct from Oregon’s state plan: - Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs — “Approved Plan (pdf)” - Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians — “Approved Plan (pdf)” Source: https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review — accessed 2026-11-01.

Growers operating under a tribal plan are licensed under that tribe’s plan, not by ODA — do not count them in ODA totals and do not advise them from ODA forms. The substantive terms of the Warm Springs and Cow Creek plans, their licence fees, and whether either tribe operates a medical cannabis programme are Verify in the plan PDFs and tribal government sources (Part 10 territory). In particular, whether any tribal medical programme counts as “state-licensed” for federal Schedule III / 280E purposes is Verify — the federal baseline does not settle it, and no tribal medical programme was confirmed in this part.

7.17 What is NOT an Oregon hemp licence — common confusions

  • OLCC marijuana licences are not hemp licences. A producer/processor/wholesaler/retailer licence does not authorise ODA hemp growing/handling, and vice versa — the bridges are the hemp certificate (§7.8) and handler-by-reciprocity (§7.5).
  • Hemp Registry registration is not a licence to grow, handle, or sell. It is product registration (§7.9). A registered product still needs an ODA-licensed grower/handler supply chain and, for resale, a vendor-site licence where required.
  • A vendor-site licence is not a handler licence. It does not authorise processing, repackaging or relabelling (secondary summary of ODA FAQ — Verify).
  • FSA registration is not a licence. It is federal acreage reporting (§7.4).
  • An OLCC medical endorsement is not a hemp authorisation. It governs marijuana-item sales to OMMP cardholders at OLCC retailers (Run 1 Part 4), not hemp items.
  • No “hemp dispensary licence” type was located. Hemp items are sold at general retail (with vendor + Registry gates) or at OLCC retailers (under OLCC rules) — there is no ODA hemp-dispensary licence in the sources located.

Part 8 — Cannabis-Zoned Properties

PART 8 — CANNABIS-ZONED PROPERTIES

8.1 Strict verified standard — stated before any listing

This part uses the same strict standard as the other state dossiers in this series. A property counts as strict-verified only if ALL five conditions are met on evidence opened in this run:

  1. Active and recent on the listing itself: the listing page itself shows ACTIVE status with a listed/updated date within 90 days before the 1 November 2026 cut-off (i.e. after about 3 August 2026), not merely a search-index date.
  2. Full street address stated in the listing body: a street number + street + town, not a town only, not a road name inferred from an attachment filename, and not an address printed in a broker-page title while the listing body says location is withheld pending NDA.
  3. Zoning corroborated independently: the zoning designation is stated in the listing AND corroborated for that parcel by an independent official source opened in this run (county zoning map, city/county code, a LUCS document, or an OLCC/ODA licence record at that address).
  4. Licence corroborated independently: any claimed OLCC/ODA licence at that address is confirmed in OLCC Open Data / CAMP or an ODA list, not merely claimed in marketing copy.
  5. No material contradiction: the listing is not simultaneously OFF MARKET elsewhere, “previously licensed” while described as licensed, or price/status-conflicted across duplicate listings for the same property.

A property that fails any one condition is marketed-only, however detailed its marketing copy is. In particular:

  • “EFU” is not cannabis zoning. Exclusive Farm Use (EFU) is Oregon farm zoning. Cannabis production on EFU land additionally requires a LUCS from the county/city with land-use jurisdiction and an OLCC licence (Run 1 Part 3 §3.1, Part 4 §4.10); a local opt-out for that licence type must also be checked. A listing that says “EFU, perfect for cannabis” has stated a farm zoning, not a cannabis zoning approval.
  • No Oregon jurisdiction was found in the searches tried with a distinct “cannabis zone” district (e.g. a “Cannabis Overlay” or “Marijuana Zone” as a zoning designation). Properties below are therefore described as “zoned or marketed for cannabis or hemp use” in the brief’s sense — marketed for that use on stated (usually EFU or commercial/industrial) zoning — not as carrying a cannabis-specific zoning code. If a city/county cannabis overlay exists, it was not located in this run and is a follow-up, not an assumption.
  • Water-rights statements are claims, not verifications. “Senior 1890 water rights,” “MID water rights,” “1857 water rights,” and “seasonal water rights” below are reproduced exactly as the listing states them. None was checked against Oregon Water Resources Department water-rights records in this run. An irrigation-district service area is not itself proof of a water right, and a “seasonal” right is not a year-round right.

8.2 Headline result: ZERO properties meet the strict verified standard

ZERO properties in Oregon meet all five strict-verified conditions on the evidence opened in this run.

That is NOT a finding that no cannabis-suitable property is for sale in Oregon. The searches tried returned a large marketed inventory, concentrated in southern Oregon (Jackson County / Medford / Ashland / Grants Pass / Jacksonville), plus Eugene, Portland (Sellwood), Florence, and smaller southern-Oregon towns. What is missing for every one of them is condition 3 and/or 4 (independent zoning/LUCS and licence corroboration at a full stated address), and for several, condition 2 (full address) or 5 (no contradiction) also fails. The closest candidates are listed separately in §8.4 so a reader can see exactly how close each one gets and what check would promote it to strict-verified.

Why the gap is structural, not a search failure: cannabis-business listings routinely withhold the exact premises address pending NDA / proof of funds (expressly stated in the Grants Pass Crexi listing, §8.3), and OLCC CAMP is a search-only tool with no bulk address-matching export (Run 1 Part 5). A researcher cannot therefore corroborate licence-at-address for NDA listings without contacting the broker — which this run did not do, and which would not in any case make the listing itself strict-verified. The honest statement is ZERO strict-verified, with a full marketed inventory below.

OREGON CANNABIS AND HEMP — PART 9 ONLY: REGULATORS AND HISTORY

Research / access date: 1 November 2026. Cut-off: 1 November 2026. Do NOT import 3 November 2026 election results. No 3 November 2026 result is included in this file. Scope: Part 9 only. Other Parts (0–8, 10–12) are NOT covered here.

How to read this file — consistency, sourcing, and flags

Consistency with Run 1 (do not silently change)

The following Run 1 anchors are carried forward unchanged. Where a source below appears to conflict, the conflict is flagged, not resolved by silent substitution:

  • HB 4121 is 2024, not 2022. The 21+ adult-use cannabinoid framework is HB 3000 (2021).
  • Per-capita caps under HB 4121: 1 producer/retailer per 7,500 aged 21+, 1 processor/wholesaler per 12,500 (aged 21+).
  • 17% state tax on retail sale of marijuana items; local tax up to 3%; medical exemption sunsets 1 January 2028.
  • OMMP 11,625 cardholders, July 2026 — Run 1 figure, carried forward. It was not re-verified from a fresh OHA statistical release in this Part 9 track; see §1.2, Verify note.

  • Measure 110 (2020) and HB 4002 (2024) recriminalisation with deflection from 1 September 2024; cannabis limits unchanged by that recriminalisation. Measure 110’s drug-possession decriminalisation is distinct from cannabis legalisation under Measure 91.

Federal baseline (as given — not re-researched in this track)

  • Schedule III for state-licensed medical effective 28 April 2026; adult-use Schedule I.
  • 280E lifted for Schedule III medical; adult-use fully subject to 280E.

Other official material is cited from search-result excerpts of official domains (oregon.gov, olis.oregonlegislature.gov, sos.oregon.gov / records.sos.state.or.us, oregonlegislature.gov) and is labelled as such where the full page text was not opened in this track.

1. EVERY STATE AGENCY REGULATING CANNABIS AND HEMP

1.1 Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission (OLCC) — lead regulator, adult-use marijuana + hemp in the adult-use system + general-market hemp registration

What it does. OLCC licenses and regulates recreational (adult-use) marijuana businesses — producers, processors, wholesalers, retailers, laboratories and research certificates — plus marijuana worker permits, packaging/labelling, compliance and enforcement in the licensed system, the Cannabis Tracking System (Metrc/CTS), and, since HB 3000 (2021) and HB 4121 (2024), hemp items that enter the adult-use system and general-market cannabinoid hemp products sold to Oregon consumers (Hemp Registry, §1.1.1). It also continues to regulate alcohol and the Bottle Bill; cannabis is an addition to, not a replacement of, that mission. The agency was created in 1933 after Prohibition repeal; it began regulating recreational marijuana after Measure 91 (2014).

Legal basis. ORS chapter 475C (formerly 475B, renumbered 2021); OAR chapter 845, division 25 (marijuana) and division 26 (hemp/cannabinoid products). OLCC’s own May 2026 commission presentation states its marijuana authority as “Marijuana (ORS 475C)” and lists businesses as “Growers, Processors, Distributors, Retailers & Special Events” and employees as worker permittees.

Governance. Nine commissioners appointed by the Governor and confirmed by the Senate (per 2025 SB 557 staff summary). A 2025 proposal (SB 557) would have required at least one member to hold a marijuana producer, processor, wholesaler or retailer licence — Verify whether SB 557 was enacted; the staff summary alone does not establish enactment.

1.1.1 Hemp Registry (OLCC) — the 2026 change

  • OLCC news release 20 November 2025: Commissioners finalised new hemp product registration rules under HB 4121, effective 1 January 2026, requiring all cannabinoid hemp products sold to consumers in Oregon, whether online or in brick-and-mortar locations, be registered with the OLCC in a Hemp Registry. Enforcement delayed until 1 June 2026. See Hemp Education Bulletin HE2025-01 for detail.
  • This matches Run 1 exactly (effective 1 January 2026, enforcement 1 June 2026) and is therefore Confirmed as a Run 1 anchor.
  • Secondary summaries add a $400 per registration per year figure — Verify against the OLCC Hemp Registry fee schedule before budgeting; the OLCC release excerpt in this track does not state the fee.
  • Source: OLCC news release 20 Nov 2025 (via republication excerpt, accessed 2026-11-01); OLCC Hemp Registry guidance. Accessed 2026-11-01.

1.1.2 OLCC–ODA split on hemp (do not conflate)

OLCC’s own Adult-Use Hemp FAQ states, verbatim in substance:

“The primary agency that regulates hemp in Oregon is the Oregon Department of Agriculture (ODA). Persons who want to grow or process hemp in Oregon must obtain the appropriate license with ODA. ODA is also responsible for the testing requirements that apply to most hemp items. OLCC is responsible for some of the regulations that apply when hemp items are sold to consumers.”

OLCC issues Industrial Hemp Certificates to ODA-licensed growers/handlers so they obtain a CTS account to transfer hemp into the OLCC system; an OLCC-licensed producer cannot grow hemp on its licensed premises (a control plan / premises-removal route applies for the same tax lot). Processor Industrial Hemp endorsement is governed by OAR 845-025-3320; transferred hemp items must have passed compliance testing and cannot exceed 0.3% total THC (as stated in the FAQ excerpt).

Source: OLCC Adult-Use Hemp FAQ, https://WWW.OREGON.GOV/olcc/marijuana/Pages/Adult-Use-Hemp-FAQ.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01 (search excerpt; full page not re-opened in this track — Verify wording against live page before quoting in a publication).

1.2 Oregon Health Authority (OHA) — medical marijuana (OMMP), testing/labelling/concentration limits (historically), public health

What it does. OHA administers the Oregon Medical Marijuana Program (OMMP): registration, regulation and oversight of medical marijuana, including patients/cardholders, caregivers, growers, grow sites, processing sites and dispensaries (as described on OHA’s own pages). OHA also historically set testing, labelling and concentration-limit rules (OAR 333-007) and oversees the Oregon Environmental Laboratory Accreditation Program (ORELAP) for cannabis testing labs. In 2017, SB 1057 transferred from OHA to OLCC oversight of tracking/reporting of grow-site activities and inspections for tracking/reporting errors at large OMMP grow sites — OHA retained the cardholder programme.

OMMP cardholder figure (Run 1 anchor). Run 1: 11,625 cardholders, July 2026 (peak ~80,000). This Part 9 track did not open a fresh OHA statistical release confirming 11,625; the OMMP index page opened 2026-11-01 shows only application-processing status (reviewing applications received 15–20 October 2026; cards mailed within 7–10 business days for complete applications) and a 30-day receipt rule under ORS 475C.783(2) (receipts issued from 2 June 2016 have the same legal effect as a registry card for 30 days). Therefore: 11,625 (July 2026) is carried as a Run 1 figure, flagged Verify against the next OHA OMMP statistical report before republication.

The same letter (Oct 2025) warns of an OMMP revenue shortfall, declining enrolment/revenue, and recommends reducing OHA’s role to a medical cannabis registry only and ending cultivation oversight — this is an advisory recommendation, not enacted law in this track; Verify whether any 2026 legislation adopted it.

1.3 Oregon Department of Agriculture (ODA) — lead agency for hemp

What it does. ODA administers the Oregon Hemp Program: licensing/registration of hemp growers, hemp handlers and agricultural hemp seed producers, pre- and post-harvest testing, recordkeeping, and enforcement. ODA states: “The Oregon Health Authority (OHA) and the Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission (OLCC) are the lead agencies for medical and recreational marijuana, respectively. ODA is the lead agency for hemp.”

Legal basis. ORS 571.260 to 571.348; OAR 603-048 (hemp programme rules, including OAR 603-048-0010 definition and OAR 603-048-0175 vendor licence). Definition (OAR 603-048-0010, via ODA page): hemp means all non-seed parts and varieties of the Cannabis plant, whether growing or not, that contain an average THC concentration not exceeding 0.3% on a dry weight basis.

1.4 Oregon Department of Revenue (DOR) — marijuana tax collection and distribution

What it does. DOR collects the state retail marijuana tax (ORS 475C.674, 17%) and any local marijuana tax that a city/county has adopted (up to 3%) where DOR administers it, and distributes state revenue under the statutory formula as amended by Measure 110 and later legislation (see §2.12 for the formula conflict — the pre-Measure 110 40/20/15/10/10/5 split is not the current distribution after Measure 110’s Drug Treatment and Recovery Services Fund carve-out).

1.5 Oregon Water Resources Department (OWRD) — water rights, water hauling, illegal-grow water enforcement

What it does. OWRD administers water rights (all water in Oregon belongs to the public and may be appropriated only under an OWRD permit, subject to exempt-use exceptions in ORS 537.545). For cannabis, OWRD enforces: (a) that a grow must hold a lawful water right or qualify for an exempt use; (b) the 2022 water-hauling laws (HB 4061); (c) unlawful use/storage/diversion of water for illegal cannabis operations (funded in part via SB 766 (2023) — $5 million to OWRD for that purpose, per the SB 766 staff summary).

Key page (opened directly 2026-11-01): https://www.oregon.gov/owrd/programs/regulation/Pages/2022-Water-Hauling-Laws-and-Cannabis-Laws.aspx

Operative provisions (HB 4061, effective 3 June 2022, per OWRD page):

  • A person purchasing water from a supplier at a hydrant, fill station or other distribution location to haul for irrigation or nursery purposes must maintain records for 12 months and present them to law enforcement or OWRD on request (date, purchase location, recipient name/contact, intended use including plant type, quantity, delivery location/date).
  • It is prohibited to haul water or arrange to haul water to any cannabis site with more than four cannabis plants (marijuana or hemp) not licensed with OLCC, ODA or OHA.
  • Providing false information wilfully or negligently to OWRD or law enforcement about water hauling to a cannabis site is prohibited.
  • Penalties as stated on the OWRD page: use of water without a water right at an unregistered cannabis site with >4 plants may be punishable by a Class A misdemeanor with a maximum fine of $25,000; hauling/arranging to haul to such a site may be a Class A misdemeanor (up to 1 year / $6,250) and a maximum $25,000 fine if the arranger is the responsible party for the grow site; false information may draw civil penalties (OAR 690-260) and up to a Class A misdemeanor (up to 1 year / $6,250). Failure to retain/present records may draw civil penalties (OAR 690-260). Water suppliers selling to the public must retain sale records up to 12 months (name/contact, quantity, vehicle plate, purchase date) with stated exemptions (state/local government purchasers, CCB-licensed contractors, firefighting) and immunity for releasing records to OWRD/law enforcement or in proceedings — not immunity from water-law compliance itself. Notice-of-violation period extended from 5 days to 10 business days after observing a violation.
  • Cannabis grower licence information page: https://www.oregon.gov/owrd/programs/regulation/pages/cannabis-grower-license-information.aspx — states ODA is the licensing agency for hemp and OLCC for recreational marijuana, and links ODA’s hemp licence list.
  • 2025 exempt-use change (Verify final enrolled text): HB 3372 (2025) added an exempt groundwater use for a commercial garden up to ½ acre / 3,000 gal/day (combined commercial + garden cap 5,000 gal/day). The staff summary and OWRD testimony show a drafting fight over whether cannabis counts: OWRD testified the bill as written excluded only unregistered cannabis, while the stated intent was to exclude marijuana (registered or not) and unregistered hemp, leaving only ODA-registered hemp (ORS 571.281) eligible; the -A7/-A11 amendments define “commercial garden” to exclude Cannabaceae locations unless grown by a licensed person, and Lower Umatilla Basin commercial-garden eligibility is delayed to 2 January 2028 (sunset). Do not state a final HB 3372 cannabis rule without opening the enrolled/chapter text — Verify.
  • Historical enforcement note (secondary, 2019–2020): OWRD hired an assistant watermaster in February (2020, per contemporary reporting) just for hemp in southwest Oregon; 40 of 41 registered Williams Valley sites visited, 12 with no water rights using well water without a commercial permit. This is context, not a current staffing figure.
  • Public contact: OWRD directs cannabis questions to the local Watermaster (via the page above). OWRD’s general contact page was not opened in this track — Verify main phone/address before publication.

Source: OWRD 2022 Water Hauling and Cannabis Laws page, opened 2026-11-01; HB 3372 staff summary / OWRD testimony (2025). Accessed 2026-11-01.

1.6 Oregon State Police (OSP) — criminal enforcement, illegal-market assistance, tax-revenue recipient

What it does. OSP is the state-level law-enforcement agency for illegal cannabis operations: investigation/prosecution support to county/local agencies, participation in multi-agency teams (e.g. Illegal Marijuana Enforcement Team, IMET, in Jackson County — JCSO, Medford Police, District Attorney, with OSP/MADGE assistance), and enforcement against unlicensed grows, diversion and associated labour-trafficking/water-theft harms. OSP is also a statutory recipient of marijuana tax revenue (15% under the original Measure 91 formula; capped/benchmarked after Measure 110 — see §2.12).

Funding history (official legislative summaries):

  • SB 1544 (2018) established the Illegal Marijuana Market Enforcement Grant Program (IMMEGP) Fund to assist local law enforcement against illegal marijuana markets/operations; administered by the Oregon Criminal Justice Commission (CJC), awarding grants by statutory priority levels.
  • SB 893 (2021, second special session) expanded IMMEGP to include grants for local law enforcement to partner with community-based organisations addressing humanitarian crises from unlawful cultivation/distribution; HB 4074 (2022) allowed grants directly to community-based organisations. Contemporary reporting put SB 893 at $25 million for state law enforcement and local community organisations — Verify the $25m figure against the enrolled SB 893 fiscal note; the SB 766 summary does not state it.
  • SB 766 (2023) would have added a further IMMEGP category for OSP costs (equipment, contract services, personnel for investigation/prosecution), allocating $51 million in general funds to CJC for IMMEGP grants, $5 million to OWRD, and $750,000 to the Department of Justice for labour-trafficking prosecutions associated with illegal cannabis operations. Verify whether SB 766 was enacted as summarised; the staff summary alone does not establish final passage.
  • Seizure context (CJC, via secondary reporting): 551,000 marijuana plants seized in Jackson, Josephine and Deschutes counties, 1 July 2020–30 June 2021.
  • Public contact: OSP’s general contact page was not opened in this track — Verify before publication. Do not publish an OSP cannabis-specific mailbox from secondary sources.

Source: SB 766 staff summary (2023, olis.oregonlegislature.gov); SB 893 reporting (2021). Accessed 2026-11-01.

1.7 Governor’s offices and other state bodies

  • Governor (Tina Kotek, in office through the cut-off). Signed HB 4002 on 1 April 2024 (see §2.10); signed HB 4016 on 4 April 2022 (see §2.9); signed HB 2111 name-change (effective 2 August 2021). The Governor appoints OLCC commissioners (Senate-confirmed) and the OHA director. The Governor’s office is also a consultee in cannabis planning exercises (e.g. HB 2997 (2021) proposal directing DOR, OHA, OLCC, ODA and the Governor’s office to consult OCC — proposal status Verify).
  • Oregon Criminal Justice Commission (CJC). Administers IMMEGP (§1.6); under HB 4002, directed to oversee/standardise county deflection programmes (see §2.10). Also produced the racial/ethnic impact statement for Measure 110 (2,139 misdemeanour + 1,918 felony possession convictions in 2019, per LPRO brief).
  • Oregon Department of Justice (DOJ). Prosecution support for labour trafficking associated with illegal cannabis operations (SB 766 allocation, §1.6); defends state cannabis laws in federal court (e.g. Measure 119 litigation, §3.5). DOJ main phone from place listing: 503-378-5555, 1162 Court St NE, Salem — Verify against DOJ’s own contact page.
  • Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ), Oregon Occupational Safety and Health (OSHA), county code enforcement, fire marshals. Appear as assisting agencies in illegal-grow enforcement (e.g. IMET operations with OSHA, county code enforcement, fire district marshals) and in cannabis waste/water-quality matters (ODA Agricultural Water Quality Program for cannabis/water quality). Their cannabis roles are ancillary, not lead-regulator roles — Verify any specific DEQ/OSHA cannabis rule citation before use.
  • Oregon State University (OSU) / Extension. Research role only (e.g. spent hemp biomass feeding studies; hemp agronomy). Not a regulator.
  • Secretary of State, Elections Division. Conducts statewide ballot elections and publishes official abstracts (see §3). Public Service Building, 255 Capitol St. NE, Suite 126, Salem, OR 97310; Elections phone 503-986-1518 (from SOS historical-data page). Historical data hub: https://sos.oregon.gov/elections/pages/historical-data.aspx
  • Oregon courts. Oregon Tax Court (1241 State St, Salem; 503-986-6455, courts.oregon.gov/tax) for tax disputes; circuit courts for criminal/expungement matters; U.S. District Court for the District of Oregon for federal challenges (Measure 119, §3.5). No cannabis-specific court exists.

1.8 Interagency task forces and advisory bodies (complete as located)

Body Created by Mandate / status at cut-off
Task Force on Cannabis-Derived Intoxicants (later Task Force on Cannabis-Derived Intoxicants and Illegal Cannabis Production) HB 3000 (2021); expanded to include Illegal Cannabis Operations by SB 1564 (2022) Recommend legislative changes supporting law enforcement response to illegal cannabis operations; examine funding/command structure, labour trafficking, water theft, genetic-engineering regulation of cannabis. First met May 2022 (video link). Its recommendations fed SB 766 (2023). Sunset / final report date: Verify — no sunset date was confirmed in this track.
Oregon Cannabis Commission (OCC) Statutory advisory commission in OHA (see §1.2.1) Advises OHA and OLCC on medical-cannabis rules and retail cannabis as it pertains to patients/caregivers. Still active Oct 2025 (letter to Governor).
Illegal Marijuana Enforcement Team (IMET) — Jackson County multi-agency team CJC grant-funded; JCSO + Medford Police + Jackson County DA, with OSP/MADGE, OSHA, county code enforcement, fire marshal assistance Operational enforcement against black-market grows (e.g. Sept 2021: two sites, ~20,000+ plants, 15,000 lb processed, ~$643k–$650k cash — figures vary by report; treat as approximate, secondary). Not a statewide agency.

Funding fell as marijuana revenue fell (secondary, Jan 2026: BHRN funding down 38% since 2021 — Verify against OHA/CJC reports).
