Gaps / Verify: No standing “Governor’s Cannabis Task Force” separate from the above was located in this track. If a Governor’s office cannabis policy coordinator exists, its public contact was not confirmed — Verify before listing.

2. KEY DATES — CHRONOLOGY (exhaustive as located; cannabis limits unchanged by HB 4002 noted)

2.0 Before decriminalisation

  • 1923 (secondary, Verify): Oregon legislators passed a first law criminalising non-medical marijuana (per secondary timelines; the more firmly documented prohibition date is 1935, below).
  • 1935: Oregon passed the Uniform State Narcotic Drug Act, making cannabis illegal in line with most states. Contemporary secondary histories note the legislative record contains no mention of cannabis causing problems; it was included as part of the package. Cannabis had been completely legal in Oregon until 1935 on this account.
  • 1933 (agency origin): OLCC created days after national Prohibition repeal (21st Amendment) to control alcohol distribution/sales/consumption. The agency’s original name was Oregon Liquor Control Commission.

2.1 1973 — First-state decriminalisation

  • 1973: Oregon became the first state to decriminalise possession of small amounts of cannabis. Governor Tom McCall signed the nation’s first legislation decriminalising certain marijuana offences. Possession of up to 1 ounce (28.35 g) became a violation (not a crime), punishable by fine only; private use and being under the influence were no longer punished; public use and driving under the influence remained punishable. An exception applied for possession in a public place within 1,000 feet of a school attended by minors (Class C misdemeanour on that account).
  • CONFLICT — fine amount: Sources in this track give $100 (legal-history summary: “reducing the penalty for up to one ounce to a $100 fine”) versus $500 to $1,000 (Cannabis in Oregon / 1973 bill summaries: “punishable only by a fine of $500 to $1000”). Do not publish a single fine figure without opening the 1973 enrolled bill (chapter) text — flagged as an unresolved conflict. The $100 figure may reflect a later amendment or a summary error; the $500–$1,000 figure is the more commonly repeated bill summary.
  • Possession of more than 1 ounce remained criminal; the >1 oz to 110 g tier is described in older summaries as a Class B felony (up to 10 years), later reduced — see 2013 below.
  • 1997: An attempt to recriminalise possession of small amounts was turned down by Oregon voters (Measure 2? — ballot number Verify; the fact of rejection in 1997 is consistently reported, the measure number was not confirmed in this track).

2.2 Medical marijuana — 1998–2013

  • 3 November 1998 — Measure 67 passes (see §3.1 for official results: Yes 611,190, 54.60%). The Oregon Medical Marijuana Act (OMMA) allowed cultivation, possession and use by doctor recommendation for patients with certain conditions, with a state-controlled permit/registry system. Oregon was the second state after California (Proposition 215, 1996) to remove criminal penalties for medical marijuana. It did not affect federal law.
  • 2004 — Measure 33 fails: Sought to extend the law by mandating distribution centres (dispensaries). Rejected by voters (exact margin Verify — not confirmed in this track).
  • 2009 (context): ~20,974 patients registered as of 1 April 2009, with 10,626 caregivers holding cards (secondary, via Measure 67 history). By contrast, July 2026 OMMP figure is 11,625 (Run 1) — the decline from peak (~80,000) reflects migration to the adult-use market after 2015–2016.
  • 2010 — Measure 74 fails: Sought a regulated non-profit dispensary supply system, research funding and low-income patient assistance. Rejected (exact margin Verify).
  • 2010 (Board of Pharmacy, secondary): Oregon Board of Pharmacy moved marijuana from Schedule I to Schedule II under state scheduling — reported as a first-in-nation state move. Verify against Board minutes/order before use; the state schedule does not change the federal baseline in §0.
  • 2013: Criminal penalties for personal possession further reduced; possession of >1 oz tier changed (older summaries: Class B felony until 3 July 2013, then Class B misdemeanour — Verify against 2013 chapter text). Medical eligibility expanded (detail Verify).
  • 2013 — HB 3460 (Verify bill number): Established the medical marijuana dispensary programme under OHA (dispensary registration). Dispensaries began operating in 2014 under OHA; this is the bridge to “early start” sales in 2015. Bill number and effective date Verify — the dispensary programme’s existence under OHA before 2015 is well attested, the HB number was not confirmed in this track.

2.3 Adult-use legalisation — Measure 91 (2014) and implementation (2015–2016)

  • 4 November 2014 — Measure 91 passes (see §3.3: Yes 847,865, 56.11%). Title: “Control, Regulation, and Taxation of Marijuana and Industrial Hemp Act of 2014.” Legalised possession, manufacture and sale by/to adults 21+, subject to state licensing, regulation and taxation; gave the then-Oregon Liquor Control Commission regulatory authority. Oregon became the third state to legalise for all adult uses, after Colorado and Washington (2012).
  • Measure 91 as passed — producer taxes (superseded, see §2.12): $35 per ounce of flowers, $10 for leaves, imposed on the producer, collected/regulated by OLCC. Net revenue distribution as passed: 40% Common School Fund, 20% Mental Health Alcoholism and Drug Services, 15% State Police, 20% local law enforcement (equally cities/counties), 5% OHA. None to the General Fund directly; Common School Fund operates as an endowment, not an expenditure resource (per Legislative Revenue background). This distribution was superseded — do not quote it as current.
  • 1 July 2015: Adult possession/use legal for 21+ (Measure 91 §82(1) effective date). Possession limits as implemented: up to 1 ounce in public / 8 ounces at home (and 4 plants per household — see Part 3/4 scope; Part 9 records only that the limits were set here and unchanged by HB 4002).
  • 2015 legislative session — Joint Committee on Implementation of Measure 91. Formalised agency/local-government roles. Key bills (per Legislative Revenue background):
  • SB 460 (“early start”): Allowed medical marijuana dispensaries to sell limited recreational marijuana products at a 25% point-of-sale tax (see §2.12).
  • Other 2015 implementing bills formalised OLCC/OHA/local roles, opt-out procedures, and tax restructuring (full bill list Verify against the 2015 session record).
  • 1 October 2015 — First (early-start) sales through medical dispensaries. Governor Kate Brown signed the emergency bill declaring sales legal to recreational users from dispensaries from 1 October 2015. Adults could purchase with ID only, under OHA guidelines, without an OLCC licence, through end-2016. This is the “first sales” date required by the commission.
  • 2016 — OLCC licensed sales begin. OLCC was required to begin accepting applications on or before 4 January 2016 (Measure 91). Licensed retailers began operating during 2016; by mid-December 2016 fewer than 100 businesses were licensed to sell recreational marijuana (secondary). From 1 January 2017, dispensaries could no longer sell for recreational use unless they held an OLCC licence; OLCC licensees could also sell for medical use (dual sales).
  • 2015–2016 local opt-outs: Cities/counties could opt out of licensed facilities (see §3.6). Early opt-out elections were held at the November 2016 general election in many jurisdictions.

2.4 Hemp programme — 2009 authorisation, 2015 first licences, 2019 boom and bust

  • 2009: Oregon first authorised hemp cultivation by statute (per hemp-industry histories; the authorising act’s chapter Verify).
  • 2014 Farm Bill (federal, Agricultural Act of 2014, §7606): Authorised state pilot programmes. Oregon was among the first states to license under it.
  • 2015: ODA began accepting industrial hemp licence applications and licensed the first hemp growers — 13 growers, 105 licensed acres in the first year (multiple secondary sources agree on 13 growers / 105 acres).
  • 2018: 568 growers, 11,754 acres registered (Harris Sliwoski state-of-state) — secondary figure; another source gives 11,552 acres for 2018 (conflict of ~200 acres — Verify against ODA annual data).
  • 2018 Farm Bill (federal, Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018, §10113): Removed hemp from the CSA definition of marihuana (≤0.3% delta-9 THC) and directed USDA to issue hemp-production rules. Oregon continued under its pilot rules until its USDA-approved plan.
  • 2019 — Boom: ODA statistics: nearly 2,000 growers (1,961) registered to plant over 63,000–64,142 acres (sources vary: “over 63,000 acres” vs “64,142 acres” vs “nearly 64,000 acres” — treat 64,142 as the ODA-derived peak figure, Verify). Nearly 32,000 acres actually planted (~50% of licensed acres). Nearly all planted for CBD. Prices for biomass cratered; oversupply followed. Grower numbers peaked at 1,961 and handler/processor numbers at 597–698 (sources vary: 597 processors vs 698 handlers — conflict, Verify against ODA licence counts; the difference may be grower-handler vs processor-handler categorisation).
  • 2020: Licensed acreage fell to 28,742 acres (one source) / 26,377 acres licensed with 1,678 growers, 515 processors (another source, via Hemp Grower data — conflict, Verify). The direction (sharp fall) is consistent; the exact acreage is not.
  • 2021–2022: Continued collapse. 2022: ~3,250 acres licensed, down 95% from 64,000 in 2019 (Blue Mountain Eagle, Sept 2022); only 1 in 7 farmers who planted in 2019 still grew hemp. USDA final rule era begins: January 2022, USDA approved ODA’s state hemp plan (state as primary regulator); background checks/fingerprinting for key participants, 10-year felony-drug-conviction bar, 30-day pre-harvest testing window, May 31 application deadline.
  • 2024: 1,799 licensed acres (1,600 planted, ~90%); growers 188, handlers 215 (per hemp-industry data compilation — Verify against ODA). Hemp vendor licence introduced 1 July 2024 (§1.3).
  • May 2025 (secondary): Licensed/grown acreage ticked up to 1,989 acres for the first time since 2019, despite grower numbers falling to 102 and grow sites to 100. Verify against ODA May 2025 data before use.
  • Hemp and water (2019–2020): See §1.5 — OWRD assistant watermaster for southwest Oregon hemp, Williams Valley complaints.

2.5 Artificially derived cannabinoids — HB 3000 (2021) rules, 2022 bans

  • HB 3000 (2021) — the 21+ adult-use cannabinoid framework (Run 1 anchor: HB 3000 is 2021, not 2022). Among other things, HB 3000:
  • Required OLCC to keep THC products away from children;
  • Directed OLCC to work with ODA and other state/local agencies to crack down on illegal cannabis grows;
  • Created the Task Force on Cannabis-Derived Intoxicants (§1.8);
  • Provided the statutory basis for OLCC’s 2021–2022 hemp/cannabinoid rulemaking (OAR 845-026).
  • OLCC rules effective 1 January 2022: New marijuana and hemp/CBD rules — product THC limits (OAR 845-026-0210 Table 1; adult-use limits in OAR 845-025-2760 Table 1 from 1 July 2022), testing, labelling. Age-21 rule for “adult use cannabis items” (≥0.5 mg total THC per container or any artificially derived cannabinoid) under OAR 845-026-0300, effective 1 January 2022, civil penalty up to $10,000 per violation (secondary summary — Verify against OAR text).
  • 1 July 2022 — Artificially derived cannabinoid ban (general market + OLCC market nuance — read carefully):
  • OLCC Compliance Bulletin CE2022-02 (14 June 2022) and OLCC guidance: hemp products containing artificially derived cannabinoids cannot be sold to consumers in Oregon except by an OLCC-licensed marijuana retailer from 1 July 2022 (general-market ban); within the OLCC market, intoxicating artificially derived cannabinoids, including delta-8 THC, are prohibited both inside and outside the OLCC market from 1 July 2022 (OAR 845-025-1310; OAR 333-007-0315). In short: delta-8/CBN made from CBD (semi-synthetic cannabinoids created by chemical reaction with cannabis-extracted substances, excluding decarboxylation by heat) were barred from general-market sale on 1 July 2022, and intoxicating versions were barred even inside the licensed market. Non-intoxicating artificially derived cannabinoids inside the OLCC system are a narrower question — Verify against current OAR 845-025-1310 / 845-026 text before advising.
  • From 1 July 2022, all industrial-hemp-derived vapor items sold in Oregon must comply with OAR 845-026-5700 to -7070 testing/labelling rules (OLCC guidance).
  • Delta-8 testing required for all adult-use cannabis items and hemp-derived vapor items from 1 July 2022 (OAR 333-007-0430, per secondary summary — Verify).
  • Federal overlay after cut-off (do not apply retroactively): PL 119-37 §781 (see federal baseline) will exclude cannabinoids the plant cannot naturally produce from the federal hemp definition from 12 November 2026 (limited) / 11 December 2026 (full). Oregon’s 2022 state ban already restricts these products more tightly than the pre-December 2026 federal definition; whether Oregon amends its rules in response after 11 December 2026 is Verify / re-check after that date.

2.6 Interstate commerce — SB 582 (2019, dormant)

  • SB 582 (2019): Opens Oregon to interstate trade in marijuana once the federal environment relaxes (e.g. federal legalisation or a federal tolerance memorandum / DOJ non-enforcement). It is dormant — no interstate marijuana commerce lawfully occurs under it at the cut-off, because federal law still prohibits it and no federal trigger has occurred. Verify the precise trigger language against the enrolled SB 582 text before quoting.

2.7 Expungement / criminal-justice clean-up — SB 420, SB 975 (2019)

  • SB 420 and SB 975 (2019): Deal with criminal charges and expungement for pre-legalisation marijuana offences (per Harris Sliwoski 2019 summary). Detail (eligibility, automatic vs petition-based, offence tiers) is Part 12 scope and is not developed here; the Part 9 point is only that the Legislature paired market regulation with a 2019 expungement package.

2.8 Licence moratorium — full sequence (see also §2.9 for HB 4121)

  • June 2018 (OLCC administrative pause): OLCC first began limiting new licence applications (per 2022 legal analysis: “since June 2018, when the OLCC first began limiting new license applications”). The legal basis and scope of the June 2018 pause Verify against OLCC minutes/orders.
  • SB 218 (2019): Allowed OLCC to stop issuing cannabis production (producer) licences based on supply/demand, for applications received after 15 June 2018. Sunset 2 January 2022. This is the “first moratorium” (producer-only).
  • HB 4016 (2022): Signed by Governor Brown 4 April 2022; OLCC news release 22 April 2022 implementing the moratorium. Authorised OLCC to refuse initial producer, processor, wholesale and retail licences based on supply/demand, and directed OLCC to inactivate applications received after 1 January 2022 (retroactive). Pre-2022 complete applicants could remain in the queue if they filed a land-use compatibility statement before 23 March 2022. Moratorium did not apply to renewals or to issuance/reissuance necessitated by change of location or ownership. Common shorthand: “moratorium until 31 March 2024” — the 31 March 2024 date appears in secondary summaries as the HB 4016 horizon; the bill’s operative language (refuse “for an amount of time the commission determines necessary” + inactivation of post-1 Jan 2022 applications) is the safer citation. Verify the 31 March 2024 end-date against the enrolled text — later extensions (below) make it moot as a current date.
  • SB 1564 (2022): Companion hemp/local measure — expanded the Task Force (§1.8) and addressed local hemp-grower licensing moratoria (per Tonkon Torp 2022 summary). Detail Verify.
  • 2024–2025 extensions / replacement: Secondary summaries conflict on the immediate successor: MPP (accessed 2026-11-01) states the moratorium was “extended until at least HB 4121 per-capita caps (no calendar sunset)” in 2025, while the HB 4121 account states HB 4121 (2024) replaced the blanket moratorium with per-capita caps effective 2025. Reconciliation (flagged): The coherent reading is that HB 4121’s caps (see §2.9) became the operative restriction from 2025, and any “HB 4121 per-capita caps (no calendar sunset)” extension language in secondary sources may refer to a different bill or to a misreading of HB 4121’s implementation timeline. Do not publish “moratorium until HB 4121 per-capita caps (no calendar sunset)” as a standalone fact without opening the 2025 session law — Verify.
  • HB 4121 (2024) — see §2.9.

2.9 HB 4121 (2024) — per-capita caps replace the blanket moratorium; 2026 wholesale reopening

  • HB 4121 (2024) (Run 1 anchor: 2024, not 2022): Converted the blanket moratorium into a population-based licensing cap system.
  • 1 producer or retailer licence per 7,500 residents aged 21+;
  • 1 processor or wholesaler licence per 12,500 residents aged 21+.
  • OLCC generally cannot accept a new application for a type when active licences for that type exceed the cap. Existing licences, transfers, changes and renewals are not new licences for cap purposes (subject to transfer restrictions tightened to curb speculation/consolidation — secondary, Verify against current OAR 845-025).
  • HB 4121 also provided the authority for the Hemp Registry (§1.1.1).
  • 2026 wholesale development (secondary, but consistent across three sources in this track — treat as reported, Verify against OLCC rulemaking page):
  • August 2026: OLCC concluded active wholesale licences had fallen below the HB 4121 cap, clearing a statutory path to lift the wholesale moratorium alone. Call for volunteers for the wholesale Rules Advisory Committee closed 28 August 2026.
  • 24 September 2026: OLCC said active wholesale licences are now below the legal population cap, so the wholesale moratorium can be lifted.
  • 25 September 2026: Wholesale RAC met (9–11 AM, per secondary report).
  • As of cut-off (1 November 2026): new wholesale applications stay closed until rules are adopted. Processor, producer and retailer applications remain closed. OLCC does not expect to issue new producer or retail licences for many years (secondary, citing OLCC).
  • Do not state that wholesale applications have reopened — they had not at the cut-off on any source in this track.

2.10 Measure 110 (2020) → HB 4002 (2024) — decriminalisation, then recriminalisation with deflection

  • 3 November 2020 — Measure 110 passes (see §3.4: Yes 1,333,268, 58.46%). Full title: Drug Addiction Treatment and Recovery Act. Two shifts: (1) first-state decriminalisation of personal possession of illegal drugs; (2) funding for addiction/recovery services from marijuana tax revenue.
  • 1 February 2021 — Measure 110 effective (penalty provisions): Possession of smaller amounts reduced from criminal misdemeanour to a new Class E violation, $100 fine, dismissible on completion of a health screening / needs assessment (LPRO brief, 9 Dec 2020). Possession of larger amounts reduced from felony to Class A misdemeanour (up to $6,250 fine on that account). Commercial drug offences under ORS 475.900(1)(b) (2019) were excluded. The measure created the Drug Treatment and Recovery Services Fund, funded from moneys in the Oregon Marijuana Fund in excess of $11,250,000 per quarter (LPRO brief). BHRNs were funded through this stream.
  • Cannabis limits unchanged: Measure 110 did not change adult-use cannabis possession, cultivation or sales limits under Measure 91 / ORS 475C. Any claim that Measure 110 “legalised cannabis” is wrong; cannabis was already legal under Measure 91.
  • 2023 — Turning point in public opinion (see §3.7): DHM Research survey (500 Oregonians, ±4.4%) found 63% support reinstating criminal punishments for drug possession while continuing to fund treatment; >60% said decriminalisation had made addiction, homelessness and crime worse. Support for re-criminalisation was lowest among 18–29s (51%) and highest among Republicans (80%). This survey is secondary reporting of DHM (via Fox News republication) — pollster, sample and margin are given, question wording was not reproduced in this track (Verify wording before quoting).
  • 2024 legislative session — HB 4002: Passed by wide bipartisan margins in February 2024, signed by Governor Kotek 1 April 2024, with companion funding bill SB 5204 (over $200 million appropriated for HB 4002 and other opioid legislation, per Marion County summary — Verify the $200m figure against SB 5204). HB 4002:
  • Created a new “drug enforcement misdemeanor” for simple possession (outside the regular A–E categorisation), up to 6 months’ jail (180 days on OPB’s account), with sentencing defaulting to probation with mandatory addiction treatment (up to 18 months’ probation initially; up to 30 days’ jail for probation violations, up to 6 months for more serious infractions, on KXL/OPB accounts — minor variance in violation-jail figures, Verify against enrolled HB 4002).
  • Deflection: Counties may (not must) create deflection programmes under which law enforcement/prosecutors divert a person to behavioural-health/treatment programmes instead of the court system. Programmes are voluntary for the individual; refusal can lead to conditional discharge, probation or jail. CJC was directed by the Governor to oversee deflection, promote standardisation and anticipate caseload growth. As of April 2024 reporting, leaders in 23 of Oregon’s 36 counties had agreed to some form of deflection programme; the form varies by county and some counties have none.
  • Preserved much of Measure 110’s treatment funding and BHRN structure; added public-use prohibition and police confiscation authority for illicit drugs (per Marion County summary).
  • Records: Criminal records automatically expunged/sealed after completion of probation or jail time (per Marion County / OPB summaries — Verify against HB 4002 expungement section).
  • 1 September 2024 — HB 4002 recriminalisation effective (criminal portion). From this date, possession of small amounts of hard drugs (fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine, heroin, etc.) is again a misdemeanour crime in Oregon. Cannabis possession within Measure 91 limits was never recriminalised by HB 4002 — this is the most common misreading to avoid.
  • 2024 ballot context: Lawmakers acted in part to forestall a tougher citizen rollback initiative that had been threatened for the November 2024 ballot (per multiple secondary accounts). No such rollback initiative appeared as a separate statewide measure in the sources in this track; the legislative fix (HB 4002) was the operative rollback.

2.11 Agency renaming — Oregon Liquor Control Commission → Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission

  • HB 2111 (2021): “Changes name of ‘Oregon Liquor Control Commission’ to ‘Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission.’ Declares emergency, effective August 2, 2021.” House vote 54–1 (Zika nay; 4 excused). Senate committee summary (LPRO, Tyler Larson) states: “Following the passage of Measure 91 in 2014, the Oregon Liquor Control Commission was tasked with regulating the production, processing, and sale of recreational marijuana in Oregon through the Control, Regulation and Taxation of Marijuana and Industrial Hemp Act. House Bill 2111 changes the name … reflecting the commission’s regulatory duties.”
  • 2 August 2021: Agency became the Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission, dropping “Control.” Acronym OLCC unchanged. Newly issued licences/permits carry the new name/logo; existing documents with the old name remain valid until replaced. Agency created 1933; name changes are uncommon (about 10 Oregon agencies in the prior 30 years, per State Library information cited in contemporary reporting).
  • OLCC’s own framing (July/August 2021): The agency described its evolving mission as “consumer protection of alcohol and cannabis products, control of adult intoxicants, and upholding public health and safety laws” and noted the Legislature had added responsibilities and boosted the agency budget in 2021.
  • Do not use “Oregon Liquor Control Commission” as the current name in any post-August 2021 context; use it only historically (pre-2 August 2021).

2.12 Tax changes — Measure 91 producer taxes → 25% early-start → 17% from 1 January 2017, local up to 3%, distribution changes

Chronology:

  1. As passed (Measure 91, 2014): Producer taxes — $35/oz flowers, $10 leaves (see §2.3). Never operated as the long-term regime; the Legislature restructured it in 2015 before licensed sales began.
  2. Early-start (SB 460, 2015): Medical dispensaries selling recreational products charged a 25% point-of-sale tax (1 October 2015 – 31 December 2016). Legislative Revenue background puts FY2017 revenue from 5 months of commercial sales at $10.75 million (delayed receipts / end-of-month reporting noted).
  3. From 1 January 2017 (current rate structure, Run 1 anchor): 17% state tax on the retail sale of marijuana items, collected at point of sale by the retailer. Operative text (ORS 475C.674, via republication — Verify against official ORS before publication-grade quotation):

    “(1) A tax is hereby imposed upon the retail sale of marijuana items in this state. The tax imposed by this section is a direct tax on the consumer, for which payment upon retail sale is required. The tax shall be collected at the point of sale of a marijuana item by a marijuana retailer at the time at which the retail sale occurs.” “(2) The tax imposed under this section shall be imposed at the rate of: (a) 17 percent of the retail sales price of usable marijuana; (b) 17 percent of the retail sales price of immature marijuana plants; (c) 17 percent of the retail sales price of a cannabinoid edible; (d) 17 percent of the retail sales price of a cannabinoid concentrate; (e) 17 percent of the retail sales price of a cannabinoid extract; (f) 17 percent of the retail sales price of a cannabinoid product that is intended to be used by applying the cannabinoid product to the skin or hair; and (g) 17 percent of the retail sales price of cannabinoid products other than those described in paragraph (f) of this subsection.” Formerly 475B.705. Rounding to the next higher whole cent where not calculable to a whole cent; tax separately stated on invoice/receipt unless DOR provides otherwise by rule. Retailers may not discount or give away a marijuana item in conjunction with another item’s retail sale (subsection (6)(a), with ORS 475C.005–475C.525 / OLCC-rule carve-out). - Medical exemption: Registered OMMP patients’ purchases are exempt from the 17% tax (and local tax where applicable) — sunsets 1 January 2028 (Run 1 anchor). After that date, medical purchases become taxable unless the Legislature extends the exemption — Verify any 2026–2027 extension before stating the post-2028 position. - Retailer collection allowance: Secondary sources state retailers keep 2% of what they collect to cover collection costs. Verify against ORS 475C.682 / DOR rule before budgeting.

  4. Local tax: Cities and counties may impose up to 3% on retail marijuana sales (ORS 475C.453 on the Run 1 account; DOR administers where adopted). Combined maximum at point of sale: 20% (17% + 3%). Proposals to raise the local cap to 10% (HB 2015, 2021) were not adopted in this track — Verify status; do not quote 10% as law.
  5. Distribution — original vs current (CONFLICT — do not quote the old split as current): - Original Measure 91 split (superseded): 40% State School Fund / Common School Fund, 20% Mental Health Alcoholism and Drug Services, 15% State Police, 10% cities, 10% counties, 5% OHA (secondary summaries vary on whether the 40% is “State School Fund” or “Common School Fund” — the Legislative Revenue background says Common School Fund; the difference matters because the Common School Fund is an endowment). - After Measure 110 (2020) and later amendments: The Oregon Marijuana Fund first funds the Drug Treatment and Recovery Services Fund from moneys in excess of $11,250,000 per quarter (LPRO brief). Secondary analysis (2026) describes the current formula as: original recipients receive an inflation-adjusted annual benchmark, originally $45 million, and most of what is left after administration funds treatment/recovery services including BHRNs. A 2026 secondary source reports marijuana tax collections fell from $203.5 million (FY2022) to $170.5 million (FY2025), ~16%, with the Office of Economic Analysis (Sept 2026) cutting the 2025–2027 forecast by $14.1 million after six straight quarters of decline; another secondary source reports FY2026 state marijuana tax revenue $141,049,814 (citing DOR 2026) — these figures are secondary and mutually inconsistent in period; Verify all revenue/distribution figures against DOR’s Marijuana Tax Distributions release and the current ORS 475C.688 / 475C.710 text before publication. - What is safe to state at the cut-off: Rate 17% + up to 3% local is current; the distribution formula was materially changed by Measure 110 and is not the original 40/20/15/10/10/5 split. The exact current statutory percentages/benchmarks require opening the current ORS distribution section — Verify.

  • 2018 — SB 1544: IMMEGP established (§1.6).
  • 2019 — SB 582 (interstate, dormant), SB 218 (moratorium), SB 420/SB 975 (expungement), SB 364 (systems development charges protection for cannabis production).
  • 2020 — Measure 109 (psilocybin) passes alongside Measure 110 (not a cannabis measure, noted only to avoid confusion: Measure 109 created the Oregon Psilocybin Services Program under OHA; it is not part of Part 9’s cannabis scope beyond this disambiguation).
  • 2021 — HB 3000 (cannabinoid framework, Task Force), HB 2111 (renaming), SB 893 (second special session, IMMEGP expansion).
  • 2022 — HB 4016 (moratorium expansion), HB 4061 (water hauling), SB 1564 (Task Force expansion, hemp moratoria), artificially derived cannabinoid rules effective 1 July 2022, USDA hemp plan approved January 2022.
  • 2023 — SB 766 (IMMEGP/OSP/OWRD/DOJ funding proposal — enactment Verify).
  • 2024 — HB 4002 (recriminalisation/deflection, signed 1 Apr, effective 1 Sept), HB 4121 (per-capita caps), Measure 119 (cannabis labour peace — see §3.5), hemp vendor licence from 1 July 2024.
  • 2025 — OLCC Hemp Registry rules finalised 20 Nov 2025 (effective 1 Jan 2026); OCC revenue-shortfall letter 15 Oct 2025; Measure 119 struck down 20 May 2025 (see §3.5); HB 4162 repeal of Measure 119 enacted 2026 (see §3.5) — note the 2026 enactment date carefully: the repeal bill is HB 4162, Chapter 73 of the 2026 Laws, effective 1 January 2027 (per 2026 secondary reporting — Verify against 2026 session law).
  • 2026 — Hemp Registry effective 1 Jan, enforcement 1 Jun; wholesale RAC process Aug–Sept (see §2.9); OLCC May 2026 licensing presentation (11,000+ marijuana licensing actions in 2025; 764 retailers in 2025 presentation vs 752 active retailers Sept 2026 in secondary data — small variance reflects date/snapshot differences, not a conflict).

3. BALLOT HISTORY AND PUBLIC OPINION

3.0 Method note — official vs secondary results

Official abstracts are published by the Oregon Secretary of State, Elections Division (records.sos.state.or.us / sos.oregon.gov). Where this track opened only a secondary republication (Ballotpedia, Wikipedia citing the Elections Division), the result is labelled secondary, citing SOS and the vote totals are given as reported. Before publication-grade use, open the SOS official abstract for each measure. The SOS historical-data hub is https://sos.oregon.gov/elections/pages/historical-data.aspx (Elections: 503-986-1518).

3.1 Measure 67 (1998) — Medical marijuana — PASSED

  • Ballot: 3 November 1998, initiated state statute. Ballot title: “ALLOWS MEDICAL USE OF MARIJUANA WITHIN LIMITS; ESTABLISHES PERMIT SYSTEM.” A “yes” supported permitting medical use with a physician’s written prescription (later: recommendation/attending-physician statement) and establishing a state-controlled permit system.
  • Official results (secondary, citing SOS; Ballotpedia: “Results are officially certified”):
  • Yes: 611,190 — 54.60%
  • No: 508,263 — 45.40%
  • Total: 1,119,453; turnout 59.02% of registered voters (Wikipedia, citing Oregon State Elections Division).
  • Effect: Oregon Medical Marijuana Act (OMMA), ORS 475C.777 et seq. (medical provisions, renumbered). Second state to legalise medical use (after California 1996).
  • Source: Ballotpedia, Oregon Measure 67 (1998); Wikipedia, 1998 Oregon Ballot Measure 67 (citing Oregon State Elections Division). Accessed 2026-11-01. Verify against SOS 1998 abstract before publication.

3.2 Measure 80 (2012) — Oregon Cannabis Tax Act (OCTA) — FAILED

  • Ballot: 6 November 2012, initiated state statute (Initiative-9). Certified ballot title: “Allows personal marijuana, hemp cultivation/use without license; commission to regulate commercial marijuana cultivation/sale.” Would have allowed personal marijuana/hemp cultivation/use without a licence, created a commission to regulate commercial cultivation/sale, and set aside 2% of profits from cannabis sales to promote (hemp/marijuana — detail Verify).
  • Results (secondary, citing Oregon State Elections Division):
  • Yes: 810,538 — 46.75%
  • No: 923,071 — 53.25%
  • Valid votes 1,733,609; total votes 1,634,576 on one presentation (invalid/blank −99,033, −6.06% — an artefact of the Wikipedia table’s arithmetic; do not reproduce the negative-blank figure without checking the SOS abstract).
  • CONFLICT — No percentage: The article text states “Measure 80 was defeated 53.44%–46.56%” while its own results table gives 53.25%–46.75%. The table figures (53.25/46.75) are arithmetically consistent with the vote counts (923,071 / 1,733,609 = 53.25%); the 53.44/46.56 text figure is inconsistent and should be treated as an error — Verify against the SOS 2012 abstract. The outcome (failed) is not in dispute.
  • Significance: Second failed adult-use attempt (after Measure 5, 1986 — see §3.8). Measure 91 (2014) was the third adult-use initiative and the first to pass.
  • Source: Wikipedia, 2012 Oregon Ballot Measure 80 (citing Elections Division, “Official Results, November 6, 2012 General Election,” Oregon Secretary of State). Accessed 2026-11-01. Verify against SOS 2012 abstract.

3.3 Measure 91 (2014) — Adult-use legalisation — PASSED

  • Ballot: 4 November 2014, initiated state statute. Title: “Allows Possession, Manufacture, Sale of Marijuana by/to Adults, Subject to State Licensing, Regulation, Taxation.” Full act name: Control, Regulation, and Taxation of Marijuana and Industrial Hemp Act of 2014.
  • Official results (secondary, cross-checked across two sources in this track):
  • Yes: 847,865 — 56.11%
  • No: 663,346 — 43.89%
  • Valid/total votes: 1,511,211; registered voters 2,178,334; turnout 69.37% (Wikipedia table).
  • Vote Smart / SOS abstract listing confirms: “Nov. 4, 2014 | Oregon | Ballot Measure Number 91 … | Passed.”
  • SOS official abstract: Oregon Secretary of State, November 4, 2014, General Election, Official Abstract of Votes — https://records.sos.state.or.us/ORSOSWebDrawer/Record/6873735/File/document — the Measure 91 county table is inside this abstract; the search excerpt in this track shows only the U.S. Senate pages, so the Measure 91 county breakdown was not extracted in this track — Verify / open the abstract and locate the Measure 91 pages before publishing county figures.
  • County pattern (secondary, Wikipedia county table — use with care): Yes majorities in most populous counties (e.g. Washington County Yes 55.40%, 108,846–87,638; Tillamook Yes 55.43%, 6,016–4,837); No majorities in small eastern counties (e.g. Wheeler No 63.53%, 453–260). County figures are secondary; Verify against the SOS abstract.
  • Implementation dates: Possession/use legal 1 July 2015; OLCC applications from 4 January 2016; early-start sales 1 October 2015; OLCC-only recreational sales from 1 January 2017 (see §2.3).
  • Source: Wikipedia, 2014 Oregon Ballot Measure 91; Vote Smart; SOS Official Abstract (link above); Legislative Revenue background (tax/distribution as passed). Accessed 2026-11-01.

3.4 Measure 110 (2020) — Drug decriminalisation + treatment funding — PASSED

  • Ballot: 3 November 2020, initiated state statute (Initiative #44). Title in SOS/Vote Smart listings: “Drug Addiction Treatment and Recovery Act.” Ballot summary: reclassifies possession/penalties for specified drugs; provides statewide addiction/recovery services; marijuana taxes partially finance.
  • Results (secondary, citing Associated Press):
  • Yes: 1,333,268 — 58.46%
  • No: 947,314 — 41.54%
  • Total: 2,280,581
  • Secondary summaries round to “58.5% to 41.5%” — consistent.
  • Effect: See §2.10 (Class E violation $100 from 1 Feb 2021; larger amounts felony→Class A misdemeanour; Drug Treatment and Recovery Services Fund from Marijuana Fund excess over $11,250,000/quarter; BHRNs). First state to decriminalise personal possession of all drugs.
  • Funding note (LPRO brief, 9 Dec 2020): Marijuana revenue reductions were estimated at $29.368m (2019–21 biennium) and $91.593m (2021–23 biennium) for the State School Fund alone on the brief’s table, with total marijuana revenue at $229m / ~72% in 2021–23 on the brief’s account — these are 2020 estimates, not actuals; do not quote as actual revenue.
  • Source: Wikipedia, 2020 Oregon Ballot Measure 110 (citing AP); Oregon Legislative Policy and Research Office, Background Brief: Measure 110 (2020), 9 Dec 2020 (https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/lpro/Publications/Background-Brief-Measure-110-2020.pdf). Accessed 2026-11-01. Verify vote totals against SOS 2020 abstract.

3.5 Measure 119 (2024) — Cannabis workers / labour peace — PASSED, THEN STRUCK DOWN, THEN REPEALED (not a Part 9 core measure, included to prevent confusion)

  • Ballot: 5 November 2024. Title: United for Cannabis Workers Act. Required state-licensed cannabis businesses to enter into labour peace agreements (LPAs) with unions and remain neutral on union organising as a condition of obtaining/renewing licences.
  • Results (secondary, election-night reporting): Yes 54.73% / No 45.27% (Corvallis Advocate, 5 Nov 2024, 9:16 pm returns); later returns reported Yes ~57% / No ~43% (Milwaukie Review, 8 Nov 2024). Final certified percentages Verify against SOS 2024 abstract — the election-night figures conflict because they are different reporting times, not different outcomes. Outcome (passed) is not in dispute. Effective December 2024 (30 days after passage on one account).
  • 20 May 2025 — Struck down: U.S. District Court for the District of Oregon, Casala, LLC v. Kotek (Judge Simon), permanently enjoined OLCC and other state actors from enforcing Measure 119 against plaintiffs Bubble’s Hash and Ascend Dispensary, holding the LPA requirement preempted by the National Labor Relations Act (Garmon and Machinists doctrines) and the employer-neutrality mandate violative of the First Amendment (compelled neutrality silencing non-coercive, non-threatening employer speech). OLCC confirmed it would no longer enforce the LPA requirement; the injunction functionally bars enforcement across the board (per Harris Sliwoski, 20 May 2025).
  • 2026 — Repeal: UFCW Local 555 (the measure’s proponent, which spent ~$2.9m to pass it) asked lawmakers in February 2026 to repeal it, fearing an adverse U.S. Supreme Court precedent; HB 4162, Chapter 73 of the 2026 Laws, effective 1 January 2027, repeals Measure 119 (per 2026 secondary reporting — Verify against 2026 session law; the effective-date / chapter citation was not confirmed from the enrolled bill in this track).
  • Part 9 relevance: Measure 119 is a cannabis-labour measure, not a possession/sales measure. It does not change possession limits, taxes or licensing caps. Its rise and fall illustrate the federal-preemption limit on state cannabis labour conditions.

3.6 Local opt-out elections — reconciliation with Run 1 Part 3 (DO NOT CONTRADICT)

Run 1 Part 3 anchor (carried forward verbatim): OLCC September 2026 opt-out list: 100 jurisdictions (82 cities + 17 counties as printed, 1-city arithmetic discrepancy flagged).

Reconciliation in this track:

  • The OLCC opt-out PDF opened via search (footer “(9/2026)”) is titled Record of Cities/Counties Prohibiting Licensed Recreational Marijuana Facilities. Its method note states a listed jurisdiction has: (a) provided OLCC a copy of its ordinance per Chapter 475C; (b) signed/returned the official “Local Option Opt-Out” form; (c) put or will put the opt-out measure to a vote at the next general election (if applicable). Columns: Producer / Processor / Wholesale / Retail prohibited (Y/N), plus General Election flag.
  • The PDF’s visible entries include Adrian, Athena, Aumsville, Baker City, Baker County, Burns, Canby, Canyon City, Canyonville, Crook County, Deschutes County (Producer Y, Processor Y, Wholesale N, Retail N — i.e. partial opt-out), Douglas County, Elgin, Harney County, Harrisburg, Jacksonville, Jefferson County, John Day (N/N/N/N — listed but no type marked banned), Lake County, Lake Oswego, Lexington, Malheur County, Marion County, Moro, Morrow County, and further pages not fully extracted in this track.
  • Arithmetic discrepancy (preserved, not resolved): 82 cities + 17 counties = 99, not 100. The 100 total therefore implies either (a) one jurisdiction counted twice / in both categories, (b) one entry (e.g. John Day, listed with no ban) counted in the total but not in the city/county split, or (c) a printing/counting error in the source list. This Part 9 track does not resolve it and does not contradict Run 1 Part 3: the headline remains “100 jurisdictions as printed, 82 + 17 = 99, 1-city discrepancy flagged.” A full hand-count of the September 2026 PDF is required to resolve it — that count was not completed in this track because the PDF text was returned only in part.
  • Legal mechanism (ORS 475C, local option): Cities/counties may adopt an ordinance prohibiting licensed recreational producers, processors, wholesalers and/or retailers (and, separately, medical dispensaries/processing sites) within their jurisdiction. Where a jurisdiction opts out, OLCC will not license that type there. A city inside an opt-out county may still allow facilities if the city itself has not opted out, and vice versa — check the city, not just the county (per OLCC guidance summaries). Opt-outs adopted by ordinance are subject to referral to voters at the next general election where applicable (per the PDF method note).
  • Polling on opt-outs (secondary, DHM — see §3.7): 60% of voters statewide opposed local bans (67% in Portland area, 54% outside Portland) on the 2016 DHM account. This does not change the legal count above.
  • Source: OLCC opt-out PDF (9/2026), https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/Documents/Cities_Counties_RMJOptOut.pdf; OLCC Local Option Opt-Out page, https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/pages/local-option-opt-out.aspx. Accessed 2026-11-01. Full PDF count: Verify / outstanding.

3.7 Public opinion polling (secondary only — pollster, date, sample, wording where available)

Rule applied: No polling figure in this section is treated as law or as an election result. Question wording is given only where the source in this track reproduced it; otherwise the topic is described and wording is flagged as not reproduced.

Poll / date Pollster, sample, margin Finding (as reported) Wording / caveats
Measure 91 pre-election, Oct 2014 (DHM Research for OPB / KGW) DHM Research, Portland-based; likely voters; margin ±4.3%; sample size not stated in this track’s excerpt for this wave (another DHM wave below gives n=500 — do not transfer it) 52% for Measure 91, 41% against, ~7% undecided Question was on Measure 91 specifically. DHM’s John Horvick: 18–34s 70% for, independents 68% for, but both groups least likely to turn out in a midterm — “if the marijuana campaign is able to get those voters out, it looks like it could pass, it’ll be close, a squeaker.”
Measure 91 pre-election, 8–11 Oct 2014 (DHM, via Talking Points Memo account) DHM, 500 likely voters, ±4.3% (per Splice Today account of the same polling) 46% for, 36% against (earlier October wave) Shows movement between early- and late-October waves; do not average waves. The 52/41 figure above is the later wave.
Measure 91 pre-election, Sept 2014 (SurveyUSA for KATU) SurveyUSA / KATU; likely voters; sample/margin not stated in this track’s excerpt 44% support, 40% opposed (razor-thin) Secondary critique (Weed Blog, 26 Sept 2014) argues the poll did not use actual initiative language, treated “certain” only as decided, asked Measure 91 after unrelated questions, and did not draw from voter lists — and disputes the 42–42 Portland tie. Treat this wave as methodologically contested; do not cite without the critique. Earlier SurveyUSA wave: 51% support (per same critique).
DHM post-legalisation satisfaction poll, 2016 (via Oregonian / Ganjapreneur) DHM Research (independent, non-partisan, Portland-based); Oregon voters; sample/margin not stated in this track’s excerpt 61% believe recreational legalisation has positively impacted the state (vs 54–56% who voted for it — the source says “only 54 percent … actually voted in favor,” which understates the 56.11% official result; the 54% in the secondary summary is an error — official is 56.11%). 60% oppose local bans (67% Portland area, 54% outside Portland). 69% support a local sales tax on cannabis. Democrats/younger voters more favourable; Republicans/older voters more disapproving. Horvick: “Oregonians are relatively satisfied… There hasn’t been a backlash.” Date: 2016 (exact field dates Verify). The “benefited the state” wording is paraphrased, not verbatim question text — wording Verify against DHM release.
DHM Measure 110 rollback poll, 2023 (via Fox News republication) DHM Research; 500 Oregonians; ±4.4% 63% support reinstating criminal punishments for drug possession while continuing to fund treatment. >60% said decriminalisation made addiction, homelessness and crime worse. Support lowest among 18–29s (51%), highest among Republicans (80%); every demographic listed supported re-criminalisation. Topic: hard-drug possession under Measure 110, not cannabis. Do not cite as cannabis-legalisation polling. Question wording not reproduced in this track — Verify. CDC preliminary overdose context cited alongside (Oregon overdose deaths +4.58%, Nov 2021–Nov 2022) is not part of the poll.
Civiqs national tracking, Dec 2025 (via MPP summary, accessed 2026-11-01 — note: Dec 2025 data, pre-cut-off) Civiqs; 330,000+ registered voters nationally since 2017 (cumulative, not Oregon-only n) Oregon: 77% support for cannabis use being legal (vs 56.11% ballot support in 2014). National: 66% support. Range: 47% Wyoming to 77% Vermont and Oregon. All 24 legalisation states ≥62%. This is a national tracker’s Oregon subsample, not an Oregon-only poll with a published Oregon n/margin in this track. Question: support for “making marijuana use legal” (paraphrased). Do not cite 77% as a standalone Oregon poll without Civiqs’ Oregon methodology — Verify.
Gallup national, Oct 2025 (via MPP summary) Gallup (national) 64% of Americans support “making marijuana use legal” (more than double 2000 level). 57% among 55+, 68% 35–54, 72% 18–34. National only; included for context, not as Oregon opinion.
Pew national, 2024 (via MPP summary) Pew Research Center (national) Only 11% of Americans think cannabis should not be legal at all. National only.
YouGov legalisation-state success surveys, Apr 2020 (via MPP summary) YouGov; eight legalisation states incl. Oregon 56%–69% of voters in those states viewed their state’s legalisation law as mostly/entirely successful (range across states; Oregon-specific figure not separated in this track). Oregon-specific YouGov figure Unavailable in this track — do not attribute the range to Oregon alone.

Polling gaps:

  • No Oregon-only, post-2024 poll on cannabis legalisation itself (as distinct from Measure 110 hard-drug policy) with published question wording, sample and margin was located in this track. The 2016 DHM satisfaction poll is the latest Oregon-only cannabis-legalisation poll found here; anything later is either national tracking (Civiqs) or Measure 110 polling.
  • No DHM / Oregonian poll on the Hemp Registry, HB 4121 caps, or artificially derived cannabinoid rules was located — Unavailable.
  • Pre-2014 polling (e.g. 2012 Measure 80 polls) was not located in this track — Unavailable; do not infer Measure 80 polling from its result.

4. CONFLICTS, GAPS AND VERIFY LIST (Part 9 only)

4.1 Conflicts preserved (not resolved by fiat)

  1. 1973 fine: $100 vs $500–$1,000 for ≤1 oz (see §2.1).
  2. Measure 80 No %: 53.25% (table, consistent with counts) vs 53.44% (article text) (see §3.2).
  3. DHM 2016 summary’s “54% voted for legalisation”: Official Measure 91 Yes is 56.11%; the secondary 54% is wrong (see §3.7).
  4. Hemp acreage: 2018: 11,552 vs 11,754 acres; 2019 peak: “over 63,000” vs 64,142 acres; 2019 handlers: 597 vs 698; 2020 licensed acres: 28,742 vs 26,377 (see §2.4). Direction is consistent; exact ODA series requires ODA annual data.
  5. Measure 119 election-night %: 54.73/45.27 (early returns) vs ~57/43 (later returns) — different reporting times, not a true conflict, but final certified % still needed (see §3.5).
  6. HB 4002 violation-jail: Up to 30 days (probation violations) / up to 6 months (serious infractions) vs “up to 180 days in custody” (OPB) — likely the same 6-month cap stated differently; Verify against enrolled text.
  7. Marijuana tax revenue: FY2025 $170.5m vs FY2026 $141.0m (different fiscal years, different secondary sources) and distribution formula (original split vs $45m benchmark + BHRN remainder) — Verify against DOR distributions + current ORS distribution section (see §2.12).
  8. OLCC retailer counts: 764 (May 2026 presentation, 2025) vs 752 (Sept 2026 secondary) — snapshot-date difference, not a conflict.
  9. Opt-out arithmetic: 82 + 17 = 99 ≠ 100 printed total (see §3.6) — carried from Run 1, unresolved.
  10. Moratorium successor: “Extended until at least HB 4121 per-capita caps (no calendar sunset)” (MPP) vs “replaced by HB 4121 caps effective 2025” — Verify against 2025 session law (see §2.8).

Part 10 — Tribal and Interstate

OREGON — Cannabis and Hemp Research — PART 10 ONLY

Tribal and Interstate

Research / access date: 1 November 2026. Cut-off: 1 November 2026. No 3 November 2026 election results are included, and none are imported. This file covers Part 10 only. It does not redo Parts 0–9 or 11–12.

Method and sourcing discipline — read first.

  • Official tribal and government sources were used for legal points wherever they could be opened. Where an official page was opened directly on 1 November 2026, the report says so and gives the link.
  • One official source could not be re-opened in this track: the OLCC 2024 Annual Government-to-Government Report PDF on oregonlegislature.gov returned a rate-limit / upstream error on the re-open attempt. Its contents are therefore cited in this report only from the search-indexed text of that same official PDF, and every such point is flagged. Do not treat those points as directly re-opened on 1 November 2026. The same applies to the OLCC 2023 report, whose PDF text was likewise available only through search-indexed text in this track. This is a method limit, not a finding about the reports’ existence.
  • Secondary sources are used only for non-law facts (for example, a shop owner’s estimate, a news account of a referendum, or a trade-press summary) and are labelled as such, with publication context where known. They are never presented as law.
  • Every fact carries a source link and the access date 2026-11-01 unless the source itself is dated otherwise. Where a fact could not be verified in an official source, it is marked [Verify] or [Unavailable].
  • No personal phone or email of any individual is reproduced in this report. Only tribal-government / agency public contacts that are already published as agency contacts are mentioned, and no individual phone/email is included.
  • Place discipline applied throughout: Ontario, Oregon is not Fruitland or Payette, Idaho; Milton-Freewater, Oregon is not Walla Walla, Washington; Portland, Oregon is not Vancouver, Washington; Brookings, Oregon is in Curry County, Oregon (not California).
  • Tribal names are given as in the commissioning instruction and as in Oregon state sources. Minor spelling variants in older sources (e.g. “Grand Ronde” vs “Grande Ronde” in a university guide) are not treated as different tribes.

Consistency with Run 1 (Parts 0–6)

The following Run 1 anchors are carried into Part 10 unchanged. Any conflict found in Part 10 research is flagged, not silently overwritten:

  • Current law is ORS 475C, not ORS 475B (renumbered in 2021). Older citations to ORS 475B.543, 475B.227 and 475B.752 are therefore read as their ORS 475C successors: ORS 475C.521, ORS 475C.229 and ORS 475C.718 respectively.
  • HB 4121 is 2024, not 2022; the 21+ adult-use framework is HB 3000 (2021).
  • Per-capita licence caps in Run 1: 1 producer/retailer per 7,500 people aged 21+, 1 processor/wholesaler per 12,500.
  • State tax: 17%, with the medical exemption sunsetting 1 January 2028.
  • OMMP cardholders: 11,625 in July 2026 (Run 1 headline).
  • Hemp Registry: effective 1 January 2026, enforcement 1 June 2026.
  • Measure 110 (2020), HB 4002 (2024) — retained as Run 1 context; Part 10 does not re-litigate them.
  • No conflict with Run 1 was found on any of the above points in Part 10 sources. One apparent tension is noted, not resolved by fiat: the OLCC’s own 2023/2024 government-to-government summaries describe tribal products entering the state market through the compact and the Cannabis Tracking System, while ORS 475C.229 still prohibits ordinary import/export of marijuana items. That tension is resolved in the statute itself only through the SB 582 / ORS 475C.521 agreement mechanisms described in §3 — it is not a Run 1 error.

Federal baseline — as given, not re-researched

The commissioning instruction supplies the following federal baseline. Part 10 uses it as given and does not re-research it, except to test whether it triggers any Oregon provision:

  • Schedule III for state-licensed medical cannabis effective 28 April 2026; adult-use remains Schedule I.
  • 26 U.S.C. § 280E is lifted for Schedule III medical; adult-use remains fully subject to § 280E.
  • Hemp: P.L. 119-37 § 781 effective 12 November 2026, limited until 11 December 2026, then a total-THC + 0.4 mg/container cap.
  • USDA DEA-lab delay to 31 December 2026.
  • Medical (appropriations) rider through 11 December 2026.
  • No federal banking law.

Application to Part 10 — [Verify] in full: Whether any tribal medical programme counts as “state-licensed” for Schedule III purposes is unresolved on the sources opened for this Part. No DEA, DOJ, IRS or Oregon guidance located for this Part answers that question for a tribally licensed programme, and — critically — no tribal medical programme in Oregon is identified in the sources below at all (see §2.11). Tribal cannabis activity identified here is adult-use production for the state market under a state-tribal compact, not a tribal OMMP-equivalent medical programme. Do not assume tribal production is Schedule III medical, and do not assume it is excluded, either. The question remains [Verify] pending federal guidance and pending identification of any tribal medical programme.

A related trigger question is answered in §3.2: Schedule III rescheduling for state-licensed medical, by itself, is not shown in any source opened here to be an amendment of federal law “to allow for the interstate transfer of marijuana items” or a DOJ opinion/memorandum “allowing or tolerating” such transfer within the meaning of SB 582 § 3. That trigger assessment is also [Verify] against a future DOJ/OLCC notice, but on the texts opened here the SB 582 operative condition has not been shown to have fired by 1 November 2026.

1. Executive summary — Part 10 in one page

  1. Oregon has nine federally recognised tribes. Only two have a USDA-approved tribal hemp plan on the USDA list opened 1 November 2026: the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs and the Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians. Only two have a marijuana tax-rebate agreement with the Oregon Department of Revenue on the DOR’s own 2025 account: Cow Creek and Warm Springs. Those two are also the only two tribes for which OLCC government-to-government reporting describes an operative marijuana compact / transfer pathway into the state market.
  2. Warm Springs is the longest-running tribal cannabis project in Oregon: a December 2015 membership referendum authorised on-reservation tribally owned cultivation and extraction, with retail only off the reservation, and also authorised industrial hemp. By 2023 OLCC reporting describes a smaller grow site intended to supply Oregon retailers, with conferral on Cannabis Tracking System (CTS) participation. Its hemp plan is USDA-approved. Whether a Warm Springs retail operation is currently open, and on what terms a buyer may buy, is [Verify / Unavailable] on official sources opened here — no current tribal retail list was located.
  3. Cow Creek has a state-tribal marijuana compact (described as such in OLCC’s 2022 temporary-rule justification), tribal cannabis rules whose implementation is a headed item in OLCC’s 2024 report, a USDA-approved hemp plan (approved August 2020), and a DOR marijuana tax-rebate agreement. OLCC’s 2022 justification says the 2022 harvest needed a legal transfer avenue to get Cow Creek product to market. No tribally licensed retail dispensary on Cow Creek trust land is identified in official sources opened here — [Verify].
  4. The Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation (CTUIR) voted (Board of Trustees, January 2023, per the tribe’s own news page title) to legalise hemp and marijuana on the Umatilla Indian Reservation. OLCC 2024 reporting (search-indexed text) says the then-current Board of Trustees had decided to hold off on an on-reservation retail marijuana sales project, including negotiating a tribal/state compact and tax agreement, as of July 2024. The current status after July 2024 is [Verify]. No CTUIR USDA hemp plan is listed by USDA.
  5. The Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde took the opposite public position in 2014–2015: Measure 91 does not apply to the Tribe; cultivation and use would not be permitted on the Reservation, and tribal government/enterprises would remain drug-free workplaces. A 2016 softening removed THC from pre-employment screening only; it did not, on the sources opened, reverse the Reservation ban. Whether that ban still stands in identical terms in 2026 is [Verify] — no 2025–2026 Grand Ronde cannabis ordinance or reversal was located.
  6. For the other five tribes — Siletz, Coquille, Klamath, Burns Paiute, and the Confederated Tribes of Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw (CTCLUSI) — no public tribal cannabis law, tribal cannabis operation, tribal cannabis compact, or tribal medical programme was located in the sources searched for this Part. That is stated explicitly for each tribe in §2. It is not a claim that such a law does not exist in an unpublished tribal code, and it is not a claim that the tribe bans cannabis. It means: nothing public was found, and the point is [Unavailable / Verify].
  7. No tribal medical programme — tribal-licensed medical sales, a tribal patient registry, or tribal medical reciprocity — is identified for any Oregon tribe in the sources opened. Oregon’s medical programme is the state OMMP (OHA). Oregon does not recognise out-of-state medical cards (secondary sources agree; official OMMP reciprocity confirmation is [Verify] — see §4.4).
  8. Interstate marijuana commerce remains prohibited in ordinary circumstances. ORS 475C.229 prohibits import/export of marijuana items. SB 582 (2019, ch. 464) authorises the Governor to agree interstate delivery only once a federal trigger fires. No SB 582 agreement with any state has been located, and no trigger notice has been located, as of 1 November 2026. California (SB 1326, 2022) and Washington (SB 5069, 2023) have parallel dormant statutes. Rescheduling alone has not been shown to fire the trigger.
  9. Interstate hemp is different in law from interstate marijuana. Federal law (2018 Farm Bill § 10114, note to 7 U.S.C. § 1639o) provides that no State or Indian Tribe shall prohibit the transportation or shipment of hemp or hemp products produced in accordance with the Farm Bill through the State or tribal territory. Oregon’s own hemp-registry FAQs expressly exclude hemp items transported through Oregon en route to another state, and hemp items only sold out of state need not be OLCC-registered/labelled. Hemp transferred outside Oregon is limited to 0.3% total THC in the OLCC/ODA testing-and-potency guide. That 0.3% export limit, and the coming federal total-THC / 0.4 mg cap after 11 December 2026, are the binding constraints — not a general hemp-export ban.
  10. Border markets are real, but buyer-residency figures are not official. Ontario (Malheur County, on the Idaho line) is the only border market with sustained, large, county-level sales that can be tied to official OLCC sales reporting (e.g. Malheur County $8.8 million in December 2023, third in the state that month). The oft-repeated “90% of Ontario buyers are from Idaho” and “~$100 million” figures are operator estimates and legislative testimony, not an official buyer-residency count — Oregon retailers do not, on any source opened, report buyer residence to OLCC/DOR. Brookings (California line), Milton-Freewater (Washington line) and Portland/Vancouver (Washington line) involve neighbours where adult-use is also legal, so there is no prohibition-arbitrage of the Ontario kind, and no official cross-border buyer figures were located for any of them.
  11. Diversion data do not prove Oregon-origin diversion to a named destination. Oregon-Idaho HIDTA seizure totals (e.g. 168,719.7 kg of marijuana in 2024; 55,135.1 kg year-to-date 2025 in the Q4 2025 HIDTA Times activity table) are initiative seizure totals for the OR-ID region, not a measure of licensed Oregon product diverted out of state, and they carry no destination breakdown in the text available. They are reported here with that limit stated, not as a diversion rate.
  12. Federal land in Oregon is a hard stop. Possession or use of any amount of marijuana — including with a state medical card — is prohibited on National Park, National Forest, BLM and other federal land, in federal buildings and on military installations, under federal law. Crater Lake National Park’s own NPS page states this verbatim (see §5). The Schedule III medical baseline given for this Part does not, on any source opened, change the federal-land rule for adult-use, and its effect (if any) on a state-licensed medical possessor on federal land is [Verify].
