2. Tribal cannabis and hemp — the nine federally recognised tribes

2.0 The nine tribes, and the state-tribal framework that applies to all of them

The nine. Oregon state sources list the same nine throughout. The Oregon Department of Consumer and Business Services (DCBS) page “Working with tribal nations” lists:

“Oregon’s nine federally recognized tribes: Confederated Tribes of the Grand Ronde; Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians; Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs / The Museum at Warm Springs; Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla / Tamástslikt Cultural Institute; Confederated Tribes of Coos, Lower Umpqua, and Siuslaw Indians; Burns Paiute Tribe; Coquille Indian Tribe; Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians; The Klamath Tribes: Klamath, Modoc, and Yahooskin.”

  • Source: Oregon DCBS, “Working with tribal nations” — https://www.oregon.gov/DCBS/deib/Pages/tribes-of-Oregon.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01 (search-indexed; direct open not completed in this track — flag as search-derived official list, corroborated identically by OHA/ODHS tribal consultation policy and by OLCC/DOJ government-to-government reports, see below).
  • Corroboration: OHA/ODHS Tribal Consultation Policy (ODHSOHA 010-028, eff. 6 Oct 2023) lists the same nine: Burns Paiute; Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw; Grand Ronde; Siletz; Umatilla; Warm Springs; Coquille; Cow Creek; Klamath — https://egov.oregon.gov/odhs/data/cwdata/cw-apsr-2025-att-66.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 (search-indexed).
  • OLCC’s 2023 report footnote 1 lists the same nine with abbreviations: Burns Paiute Tribe; CTCLUSI; CTWS / Warm Springs Tribe; Coquille Tribe; Klamath Tribes; Cow Creek Tribe; CTGR / Grand Ronde; Siletz Tribe; CTUIR / Umatilla Tribe — OLCC 2023 Annual Government-to-Government Report — https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/cis/GovToGovReports/Annual Report (OLCC) 2023.pdf — search-indexed text, see method note above.
  • Tenth-tribe caution: A University of Oregon research guide notes a tenth federally recognised tribe spanning the Nevada–Oregon border, Fort McDermitt Paiute and Shoshone. That tribe is not one of Oregon’s nine for state government-to-government purposes in the sources above, and it is not covered as a tenth entry here. No Fort McDermitt cannabis/hemp operation in Oregon was searched for as part of the nine-tribe commission. [Verify] if a future Part requires it.

Government-to-government baseline. ORS 182.164–182.168 requires state agencies to promote government-to-government relations with the nine tribes, and agencies file annual reports under ORS 182.166. OLCC’s tribal liaison function, the Governor’s tribal-relations memoranda, and the Legislative Commission on Indian Services (LCIS) cluster process are the standing channels through which cannabis conferral described below occurred. Those reports are the principal official source for tribal cannabis activity in this Part, because the compacts themselves are not published in full in any source located.

The state-tribal cannabis statute — verbatim operative text. ORS 475C.521 (formerly ORS 475B.543) is the whole of the state-side authority for a tribal marijuana agreement. Opened directly 1 November 2026:

“(1) The Governor, or the Governor’s designee, may enter into an agreement with the governing body of a federally recognized Indian tribe located in this state for the purpose of cross-jurisdictional coordination and enforcement of marijuana-related businesses licensed to conduct business on tribal trust land by the governing body of the federally recognized Indian tribe.

(2) An agreement entered into under this section:

(a) May provide for the cross-jurisdictional coordination and enforcement of marijuana producers, marijuana processors, marijuana wholesalers, marijuana retailers and marijuana testing laboratories licensed by the governing body of the federally recognized Indian tribe.

(b) May require the governing body of the federally recognized Indian tribe to establish the same or similar requirements on marijuana producers, marijuana processors, marijuana wholesalers, marijuana retailers and marijuana testing laboratories that are consistent with the policies set forth in: (A) ORS 475C.005 to 475C.525; (B) ORS 475C.540 to 475C.586; and (C) ORS 475C.600 to 475C.648.

(c) Must ensure enforceable public health and safety standards and include a system to regulate and track the purchase, sale, production, processing, transportation and delivery of marijuana items for marijuana producers, marijuana processors, marijuana wholesalers, marijuana retailers and marijuana testing laboratories that are licensed by the governing body of the federally recognized Indian tribe.

(d) May authorize an agency of this state to assist in the implementation and enforcement of the terms of the agreement. [Formerly 475B.543]”

  • Source: ORS 475C.521 — https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_475c.521 — opened directly 2026-11-01. Last-amended date: not stated on the page opened; the “[Formerly 475B.543]” tag confirms the 2021 renumbering. [Verify] last-amendment date against the official ORS publication before publication-grade citation.
  • What the statute does not do: It does not itself license any tribal business, does not authorise retail sale on trust land without a tribal licence and an agreement, and does not make tribal licensees OLCC licensees. OLCC’s consistent summary (2023 and 2024 reports, search-indexed) is: “The OLCC does not regulate marijuana within Tribal borders” / “OLCC does not regulate marijuana activities within tribal borders.” The compact is the bridge; the tribe regulates on trust land, the state regulates once product enters the state system.

The tax-rebate statute — verbatim operative core. ORS 475C.718 (formerly ORS 475B.752) is the companion tax provision:

“(1) The Department of Revenue may enter into an agreement with the governing body of a federally recognized Indian tribe that is qualified as described in this section for the purpose of making rebate payments for an estimate of the tax on marijuana items imposed under ORS 475C.674 as described in this section.

(2) The governing body of a federally recognized Indian tribe is qualified to enter into an agreement under this section if the governing body has entered into an agreement with the Governor, or the Governor’s designee, pursuant to ORS 475C.521.

(3) The department shall provide rebates under this section for: (a) Usable marijuana sold by a marijuana retailer that holds a license issued under ORS 475C.097 that is produced by a marijuana producer that is located on tribal trust land and licensed by the governing body of a federally recognized Indian tribe that has entered into an agreement with the Governor, or the Governor’s designee, pursuant to ORS 475C.521, provided that the licensing of the marijuana producer comports with the agreement; and (b) Cannabinoid concentrates, cannabinoid extracts or cannabinoid products sold by a marijuana retailer that holds a license issued under ORS 475C.097 that are processed by a marijuana processor that is located on tribal trust land and licensed by the governing body of a federally recognized Indian tribe that has entered into an agreement with the Governor, or the Governor’s designee, pursuant to ORS 475C.521, provided that the licensing of the marijuana processor comports with the agreement.”

  • Source: ORS 475C.718, via Justia’s 2021 ORS reproduction — https://law.justia.com/codes/oregon/2021/volume-14/chapter-475c/section-475c-718/ — accessed 2026-11-01 (search-indexed; official ORS text to be re-checked before publication-grade use — [Verify] against oregonlegislature.gov / ORS publication).
  • Consequence: A rebate agreement presupposes an ORS 475C.521 Governor’s agreement. DOR’s statement that it maintains marijuana tax-rebate agreements with only two tribes (Cow Creek and Warm Springs) is therefore also evidence that only those two are treated by DOR as qualified under § 475C.718. See §2.1–2.2 and DOR 2025 below.

The transfer rule. OLCC adopted a temporary rule in September 2022 to make the compact transfer pathway operable. The filing caption and justification (official OLCC filing via Secretary of State Archives) state:

“FILING CAPTION: Adopt rule that allows for the transfer of Marijuana Items Between State and Tribal Licensees … EFFECTIVE DATE: 09/23/2022 THROUGH 12/31/2022 … ORS 475C.521 enables the Governor to enter into an agreement with the governing body of a federally recognized Indian tribe … OLCC rules do not align with an agreement between the State and a federally recognized Indian tribe with regard to the transfer of marijuana items.”

And, on the rule’s operative core (temporary rule text in the filing):

“(1) For the purposes of these rules, ‘tribal licensee’ means an entity licensed or approved to produce, process, or wholesale marijuana items by the governing body of a federally recognized Indian tribe located in this state that has entered into an agreement with the Governor pursuant to ORS 475C.521. (2) Notwithstanding any provision in these rules relating to transfers of marijuana items: (a) A producer, processor, wholesaler or a retailer may: (A) Receive marijuana items from a tribal licensee; and (B) Transfer marijuana items to a tribal licensee that the producer, processor, wholesaler, or retailer has the privilege to transfer to licensees. (b) A laboratory licensee may engage in sampling and testing of marijuana items produced or processed by the tribal licensee. (3) Transfers of marijuana items must comply with applicable provisions of these rules.”

  • Source: OLCC 197-2022, Temporary Administrative Order, 22 Sept 2022 — https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/rules/Transfer-Marijuana-Items-Between-State-and-Tribal-Licensees-845025775.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 (search-indexed).
  • Critical limit — [Verify]: The filing opened is the temporary rule expiring 31 December 2022. Whether a permanent OAR Division 25 tribal-transfer rule superseded it, and its current OAR number, was not confirmed in this track. Do not cite the temporary rule as current law. The permanent-rule position is [Verify] against the current OAR Chapter 845, Division 25, before any compliance use.
  • The same justification names the two tribes who would suffer without the rule: “The Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Indians and the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs would not have a legal avenue to transfer marijuana items” and warns of delay to Cow Creek “stand[ing] up their marijuana operation” and to getting the 2022 harvest to market. That is the strongest official evidence in this Part that, as of September 2022, the operative compact/transfer work concerned exactly those two tribes.

OLCC’s compact summary (applies to every compact tribe). From OLCC 2023 (search-indexed):

“Under ORS 475C.521, the Governor may enter into an agreement … The IGA is often referred to as the Marijuana Compact and recognizes the authority of the State to regulate the participation of an Oregon tribe’s marijuana activities in the state regulated market. … The compact between OLCC and tribes does not specifically support or prohibit the direct transfer or sale of marijuana items from an entity authorized by the tribe to an OLCC licensee. The compact, however, expressly requires the tracking of the tribe’s marijuana items in OLCC’s cannabis tracking (seed to sale program) system in support of public safety and consumer health.”

OLCC 2024 repeats the same two sentences verbatim in substance: the compact does not explicitly permit or prohibit direct transfer/sale to OLCC licensees, but requires CTS tracking; OLCC does not regulate within tribal borders. Both reports are search-indexed only in this track (see method note).

Who may buy — general rule. No source opened states a tribal-retail buyer rule distinct from state law (21+ for adult-use; OMMP cardholder for tax-exempt medical sale at an OLCC retailer). For product that enters the state market via a tribal producer/processor and is sold by an OLCC-licensed retailer, the buyer rule is the state rule: 21+ (adult-use) or OMMP patient/caregiver (medical, tax-exempt). For any sale on trust land by a tribal licensee, the buyer rule would be the tribal rule under the compact — and no tribal retail buyer rule was located for any tribe (see per-tribe entries). Do not assume tribal on-reservation retail is open to the general public. That is [Verify] tribe by tribe.

Tribal regulators. The only tribal cannabis regulator named in official sources opened here is the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs Cannabis Commission (CTWS Cannabis Commission), described as conferring with OLCC, DOJ and the Governor’s Office. Cow Creek’s regulator is described only as “Cow Creek Tribes Cannabis Rules Implementation” in OLCC 2024 contents — the regulator’s name and the rules text were not located. CTUIR’s regulator, if any was created after its January 2023 vote, was not located. For the other six tribes, no tribal cannabis regulator was located. All such gaps are marked per tribe below.

2.1 Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs (CTWS)

Status in one line: The only Oregon tribe with both a USDA-approved hemp plan and a DOR marijuana tax-rebate agreement and a long-documented compact-conferral history — and the only tribe whose membership has voted, by referendum, to authorise tribal cannabis cultivation. Current operating/retail status is [Verify].

Hemp — USDA-approved plan: YES. - USDA’s “List of USDA-approved Hemp Plans,” updated 17 February 2026, lists under Tribes: “Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs | Approved Plan (pdf)” and, separately, *“Oregon | OR Approved Plan (pdf)“ for the State. - Source: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service — https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review — opened directly 2026-11-01. The page states an approved plan “remains in effect unless withdrawn by the State or Tribal government or revoked by USDA” or re-submitted after substantive revision. - History (secondary, for context only): Warm Springs submitted a hemp plan to USDA and awaited review in December 2019 (500Nations tribal-cannabis page, reporting the submission). The USDA list now shows it as approved; the approval date itself is not stated on the list page opened and is [Verify] against the plan PDF. - Plan content note (secondary, Harris Sliwoski tribal-plans analysis): the Warm Springs plan/regulation provides that hemp licence applicants be a “wholly-owned tribal entity,” with individual tribal members also apparently able to apply. That characterisation is secondary only — the plan PDF itself was not opened in this track, so the eligibility rule is [Verify] against the USDA-posted Warm Springs plan PDF before any reliance. - Commercial hemp brand (secondary): Oregon Business (“Hemp Hopes”) reports Warm Springs has sold CBD products under the brand Daminwa (described as a Kiksht word meaning “of all time”) since the prior summer (article context ~2024–2025). That is a secondary, dated brand fact, not a licence or product-registration finding, and current availability is [Verify].

Cannabis — referendum, commission, compact conferral: YES, documented; current operation: [Verify]. - December 2015 referendum (secondary accounts, consistent across multiple outlets). Tribal members were asked whether Tribal Council should be authorised to “allow, regulate and operate an on-reservation, tribally owned cannabis cultivation and extraction facility, with retail sales allowed only off the reservation.” The vote is reported as 1,252 in favour to 198 against (about 86% in favour), with a one-third turnout threshold (about 1,100 of about 3,300 eligible voters) — Spilyay Tymoo (Warm Springs tribal newspaper, via wsnews.org, July 2017 funding-plan article) and KWSO 91.9 (tribal radio, December 2015 ballot article) agree on the question wording and threshold; the AP account summarised in Cannabis Chronicles reports “about 80 percent” and “more than 1,400 of the 3,300 eligible voters turned out” — a minor turnout/percent discrepancy that does not affect the outcome (authorisation passed) but is flagged here rather than smoothed over. - Sources (secondary): https://wsnews.org/2017/07/funding-plan-for-cp-enterprise/ ; https://kwso.org/2015/12/ballots-coming-on-cannabis-referendum/ ; https://cannabis-chronicles.com/2015/12/warm-springs-tribe-approves-pot-sales-project/ — all accessed 2026-11-01. - Contemporaneous limit in the referendum plan: The proposal did not change the law banning marijuana possession on the reservation (AP account), and retail was only off the reservation (three proposed tribal-owned stores in the Portland and Bend areas in early reporting; a 36,000-square-foot greenhouse; 80+ jobs; early revenue projections of $11.7m first-year profit / $26m+ annual net revenue in trade-press reporting). Those revenue projections are 2015–2016 promotional/early estimates, not audited results, and are recorded here only as history. Do not cite them as current performance. - The referendum also authorised “the production, sale, wholesale, and retail sale of industrial hemp for future development” (Merry Jane summary of the referendum; Emerald Magazine indigenous-business list, citing Warm Springs Ventures). That hemp authorisation is consistent with the later USDA hemp plan, but the two should not be conflated: the referendum is tribal authorisation; the USDA plan is federal programme approval. - Tribal Cannabis Commission. OLCC 2023 (search-indexed) states: “CTWS has been conferring with the State since 2016 on their initial plans for a cannabis production. In 2023, CTWS opted for a smaller grow site, for purposes of transporting marijuana to Oregon retailers for sale. For 2023, the OLCC’s Executive Director and the Tribal Liaison continued the conferral process with the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs Cannabis Commission (CTWS – Cannabis Commission), the Department of Justice (DOJ), and the Governor’s Office under section IV.B.1.b of the Intergovernmental Agreement (Marijuana Compact).” On 12 July 2023 a CTWS representative updated OLCC on ongoing efforts and inquired about participation in CTS; on 7 August 2023 staff prepared to discuss implementing seed-to-sale tracking. - Source: OLCC 2023 Annual Government-to-Government Report — https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/cis/GovToGovReports/Annual Report (OLCC) 2023.pdf — search-indexed text only in this track. - OLCC 2024 contents likewise head a section “Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs (CTWS) Cannabis Commission” (p. 12 in the contents listing) — search-indexed only. - What this proves and does not prove: It proves conferral and a compact framework with a cited section (IV.B.1.b) existed through 2023, and that the 2023 direction was wholesale supply to Oregon retailers, not on-reservation retail. It does not prove a currently operating grow, a current CTS enrolment, or a current retail store. The full compact text, including § IV.B.1.b, was not located — [Verify]. - Financing history (secondary, tribal newspaper). Spilyay Tymoo (July 2017) reports Tribal Council approved formation of Warm Springs Financial Strategies LLC, wholly owned, to finance the Cannabis Project (CP Enterprise) with $3 million from carbon-sequestration revenue via Warm Springs Ventures/GeoVisions, after a narrow Council vote (2–2–2, Vice-Chairman breaking the tie). This explains the long gap between the 2015 vote and any operation; it is not evidence of a 2026 operation. - Later referendum report — conflict flagged, not resolved. Oregon Business (“Hemp Hopes”) states: “A referendum put before tribal members this spring that would allow the tribe to begin growing its own cannabis and open a dispensary didn’t get enough votes to move forward.” That appears to describe a later, separate referendum (spring, year not pinned in the excerpt) concerning growing + opening a dispensary — which sits in tension with the 2015 authorisation if read as the same question. The article does not, in the excerpt available, give the year, question wording, or vote count for that later referendum. Do not merge the two referenda. The later-referendum claim is [Verify] in full (year, wording, result, and whether it concerned on-reservation retail, which the 2015 referendum had excluded). - Source (secondary): https://oregonbusiness.com/hemp-hopes/ — accessed 2026-11-01. - “Warm Springs Cannabis” branding (secondary only). 500Nations states: “The Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs own Warm Springs Cannabis, which grows and processes cannabis for medical and recreational purposes” and “broke ground on Oregon’s first tribal-owned marijuana cultivation operation” and “hopes to open three outlet shops.” No official tribal or OLCC source opened in this track confirms a currently operating Warm Springs Cannabis grow, processor, or retail outlet, a licence number, or a product line in the state market. The brand claim is therefore recorded as secondary / [Verify], not as an operating fact. - Who may buy: [Verify / Unavailable]. If Warm Springs product is sold through an OLCC retailer, state buyer rules apply (21+; OMMP for medical). No tribal on-reservation retail buyer rule was located, consistent with the 2015 plan that retail be off-reservation and possession remain banned on the reservation at that time. Whether possession on the reservation is still banned in 2026 is [Verify] — no current Warm Springs tribal code provision on cannabis possession was located. - Medical programme: None identified. No Warm Springs medical registry, medical dispensary, or medical reciprocity arrangement was located. The “medical and recreational purposes” phrase in the secondary brand summary does not establish a tribal medical programme. Schedule III “state-licensed” question: [Verify] (see §2.11). - Tribal regulator: CTWS Cannabis Commission (named in OLCC reporting). Its current membership, rules, and licence list were not located — [Verify].

Tax rebate: YES. - DOR 2025 (search-indexed): “The department maintains marijuana tax refund agreements with two of the nine federally recognized tribal governments in Oregon: Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Indians and Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs. These agreements allow tribal governments to receive a rebate for an estimate of taxes paid on marijuana products produced or processed on tribal land.” - Source: Oregon Department of Revenue, 2025 Government-to-Government Activity Report (December 2025) — https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/cis/GovToGovReports/Annual Report (DOR) 2025.pdf — search-indexed text only in this track. Note: the report is dated December 2025, which post-dates the nominal research date in its file label but pre-dates the 1 November 2026 access date; it is the latest DOR tribal report located. The rebate amounts paid to Warm Springs are not stated in the excerpt — [Unavailable].

2.2 Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians

Status in one line: The second compact tribe: USDA hemp plan approved, tribal cannabis rules in implementation per OLCC 2024, DOR rebate agreement, and a 2022 harvest that needed the state transfer pathway. Operative tribal rules text and any tribal retail operation are [Verify].

Hemp — USDA-approved plan: YES. - USDA list (opened 1 Nov 2026, updated 17 Feb 2026): “Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians | Approved Plan (pdf)” — https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review - Approval timing (secondary/USDA announcement reporting): USDA announced approval of the Cow Creek plan in August 2020, together with Maine and Missouri state plans, bringing the approved-plan total to 58 at that time; the tribe was then “authorized to self-administer and self-regulate the production of hemp on its reservation without oversight or regulation from the State of Oregon” (500Nations summary of the USDA approval; Morning Ag Clips USDA announcement summary). - Sources (secondary): https://www.500nations.com/hemp.asp ; https://www.morningagclips.com/usda-approves-hemp-production-plans-2/ — accessed 2026-11-01. - Plan PDF content (licensing eligibility, testing, disposal, etc.) was not opened in this track — [Verify] against the USDA-posted Cow Creek plan PDF.

Cannabis — compact, rules, production for the state market: YES (framework); operative text [Verify]. - Compact existence: OLCC’s 2022 temporary-rule justification refers expressly to “the Tribal Compact with the Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Indians within the statutory regulation of cannabis” and warns that failure to adopt the transfer rule would delay Cow Creek “from being able to stand up their marijuana operation” and leave no legal avenue to transfer the 2022 harvest to market. - Source: OLCC 197-2022 — https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/rules/Transfer-Marijuana-Items-Between-State-and-Tribal-Licensees-845025775.pdf — search-indexed. - Rules implementation: OLCC 2024 contents head a section “Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Indians – Cow Creek Tribes Cannabis Rules Implementation” (p. 11 in the contents listing), under the Distilled Spirits / Tribal Intergovernmental Agreement area and before the Recreational Marijuana Program section (p. 12). The body text of that section was not available in the search-indexed excerpt beyond the contents heading — the rules’ adoption date, regulator, licence types, and buyer rules are [Verify / Unavailable]. - Source: OLCC 2024 Annual Government-to-Government Report — https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/cis/GovToGovReports/Annual Report (OLCC) 2024.pdf — search-indexed contents only in this track; direct re-open blocked (see method note). - Tribal code availability limit: The National Indian Law Library (NARF) Tribal Law Gateway page for Cow Creek states: “The tribe has not given permission for the full-text document to be made available online. The tribe has made limited materials available on their website.” The NILL table of contents on that page (based on print materials received April 2003) lists liquor, gaming, governmental-immunity and other titles, but no cannabis title is shown in that 2003-based contents list — which proves nothing about post-2022 cannabis rules, since they post-date the contents list. The operative Cow Creek cannabis rules are therefore [Unavailable in public full text in this track]. - Source: http://narf.org/nill//codes/cow_creek_umpqua/index.html — accessed 2026-11-01 (search-indexed). - Who may buy / retail: [Verify / Unavailable]. No Cow Creek tribal retail dispensary, on trust land or off, is identified in official sources opened. The Seven Feathers Casino Resort in Canyonville (Douglas County, off I-5 Exit 99) is a Cow Creek-owned gaming/hospitality property; no source opened ties Seven Feathers to a cannabis retail operation, and it must not be described as a dispensary. Any Cow Creek product reaching consumers in this track’s evidence does so via OLCC retailers after tribal-to-state transfer (hence state 21+ / OMMP buyer rules at the point of retail sale). - Medical programme: None identified. No Cow Creek medical registry or medical dispensary was located. Schedule III “state-licensed” question: [Verify] (see §2.11). - Tribal regulator: Not named in sources opened — [Verify]. Do not assume the gaming commission or any other named body is the cannabis regulator. - Tax rebate: YES (DOR 2025, same passage as Warm Springs — see §2.1). Rebate amounts [Unavailable].

2.3 Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation (CTUIR)

Status in one line: Legalisation voted on-reservation in January 2023; on-reservation retail project held off as of July 2024 per OLCC; no compact, no rebate, no USDA hemp plan identified. Current position after July 2024 is [Verify].

  • Legalisation vote (tribal source, title only). CTUIR’s own news page is titled “Board of Trustees Votes to Legalize Hemp and Marijuana on the Umatilla Indian Reservation” and links a file “FINAL PR Marijuana Legalization 1.30.23” (PDF, updated 9 Jan 2025 on the page).
  • Source: https://ctuir.org/news/board-of-trustees-votes-to-legalize-hemp-and-marijuana-on-the-umatilla-indian-reservation/ — opened directly 2026-11-01, but the page text as rendered contained only the title and file link; the press-release PDF body was not opened in this track. The vote date (30 January 2023, from the file name), the scope (hemp + marijuana, on-reservation), any possession/cultivation/retail limits, and any regulator created are therefore [Verify] against the PDF itself. Do not cite ordinance text that was not read.
  • OLCC conferral and hold-off (search-indexed OLCC 2024). OLCC 2024 reports, in substance: 20 February 2024 — CTUIR attorney requested discussion on (compact-related) matters; 24 April 2024 — CTUIR-State government-to-government meeting on a compact; 3 June 2024 — continued collaboration including other jurisdictions (Suquamish–Washington agreement and a Nevada tribe) as possible examples; 24 July 2024 — CTUIR attorney updated OLCC that “The current Board of Trustees has decided to hold off on moving forward with this project, including negotiating a tribal/state compact and tax [agreement]” in relation to an on-reservation retail marijuana sales project.
  • Source: OLCC 2024 Annual Government-to-Government Report — search-indexed text only in this track.
  • Interpretation limit: “Hold off” is not a ban and not a repeal of the January 2023 vote on the evidence available; it is a pause on the retail project and compact negotiation as of July 2024. Whether the Board later resumed, abandoned, or narrowed the project is [Verify] — no 2025–2026 CTUIR cannabis update was located.
  • Temporary sales licence note (OLCC 2024, search-indexed). On 8 May 2024 OLCC’s Pendleton regulatory specialist received a request for a Temporary Sales License (TSL) on Umatilla Indian Reservation lands, raising whether land-use approval is necessary for a TSL for events hosted by the Umatilla Tribe without tribal representatives’ knowledge/approval; OLCC’s note records that land-use/zoning regulations are not required for TSL issuance. This is an OLCC-licence (state) event question, not a tribal-licence retail finding, and it does not establish tribal retail. It is recorded here because it is the only CTUIR-specific OLCC licensing interaction in the 2024 excerpt.
  • Hemp plan: NO — not on USDA list. USDA’s list (opened 1 Nov 2026) contains no CTUIR tribal plan. CTUIR hemp producers on trust land would therefore fall, on the USDA framework, either under a future tribal plan or under the federal (USDA-licence) route — but no CTUIR hemp licence/production fact was located, so this is framework only, [Verify] if operational detail is needed.
  • Compact: NO (as of July 2024 hold-off). No CTUIR ORS 475C.521 agreement was located.
  • Tax rebate: NO. DOR 2025 names only Cow Creek and Warm Springs.
  • Who may buy: [Verify / Unavailable]. No CTUIR retail buyer rule was located. State rules would apply to any sale through an OLCC retailer; tribal rules would apply to any future on-reservation tribal retail, if resumed.
  • Medical programme: None identified. No CTUIR medical programme was located. Schedule III “state-licensed” question: [Verify].
  • Tribal regulator: Not located — [Verify].
  • PL 280 note (see §2.10): CTUIR is the tribe whose PL 280 criminal jurisdiction was retroceded in 1981 and whose civil jurisdiction was the subject of the 2025 SB 1011 process and a 2026 Governor’s proclamation (post-dating the nominal research year but pre-dating access — see §2.10 for dating care). That jurisdictional history is relevant to who enforces a future tribal cannabis code on the Umatilla Reservation, but it does not itself authorise or prohibit cannabis.

2.4 Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde (CTGR)

Status in one line: The clearest tribal ban position in Oregon: Reservation cultivation/use not permitted under the 2014–2015 Tribal Council position, with a narrow 2016 employment-screening softening. Current 2026 terms [Verify]; no compact, no hemp plan, no operation.

  • November 2014 statement (tribal newspaper). After Oregon voters approved Measure 91 (4 Nov 2014), the Grand Ronde Tribal Council stated (17 Nov 2014) that Measure 91 “does not apply to the Tribe. The Tribe is a sovereign nation. … until the Tribal Council decides otherwise, the use and possession of marijuana on the Grand Ronde Reservation is illegal.” The statement also cited federal illegality and federal-grant drug-free-workplace requirements.
  • Source (tribal newspaper, secondary for law but primary for the Council’s stated position): Smoke Signals, “Tribal Council releases statement on marijuana measure’s passage” — https://www.smokesignals.org/articles/2014/12/01/tribal-council-releases-statement-on-marijuana-measures-passage/ — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • July 2015 confirmation (tribal newspaper). “On July 1, 2015, Measure 91 took effect. The use and possession of recreational marijuana will be decriminalized in Oregon. Measure 91 does not apply to the Tribe. … After considerable work … the Tribal Council has determined that the Tribal government and enterprises – like Spirit Mountain Casino – will remain Drug Free Workplaces. Neither the cultivation nor use of marijuana will be permitted on the Reservation and, in housing units, the use, possession, and cultivation of marijuana will not be allowed. The Tribe will use available tools such as state criminal citations for public use, Tribal trespass, and housing evictions to enforce this policy. Spirit Mountain Casino has posted signs stating that marijuana is not permitted in the casino and lodge.”
  • Source: Smoke Signals, “Tribal Council: Tribe will remain a drug-free workplace, community” — https://www.smokesignals.org/articles/2015/07/10/tribal-council-tribe-will-remain-a-drug-free-workplace-community/ — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Quoted operative effect: This is a Council policy statement as reported in the tribal newspaper, not a tribal code section quoted verbatim from the code. The code provision (if codified) was not located — [Verify] against the Grand Ronde Tribal Code before citing it as an ordinance.
  • December 2016 softening — employment screening only. Smoke Signals reports the Tribe would no longer screen for marijuana (THC) in pre-employment processes at Spirit Mountain Casino and Tribal government, on a staff directive approved by six Tribal Council members, driven by casino recruitment difficulties. The same report stresses the Tribe would continue reasonable-suspicion, post-accident, and random safety-sensitive testing for marijuana, and it does not report any reversal of the Reservation cultivation/use ban.
  • Source: Smoke Signals, “Tribe to end testing for marijuana in pre-employment process” — https://www.smokesignals.org/articles/2016/12/01/tribe-to-end-testing-for-marijuana-in-pre-employment-process/ — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Do not over-read: Ending pre-employment THC screening is not legalisation, not a retail authorisation, and not permission to use/cultivate on the Reservation.
  • No compact, no rebate, no USDA hemp plan, no operation, no medical programme located for Grand Ronde in this track. OLCC 2023/2024 contents list no Grand Ronde cannabis item; DOR 2025 names no Grand Ronde marijuana rebate.
  • Who may buy: Not applicable on the Reservation under the 2015 position (no lawful tribal retail; no lawful possession/use on the Reservation as stated). Off-reservation, Grand Ronde members are subject to state law like any Oregon adult (21+ adult-use purchase at OLCC retailers; OMMP if cardholders). Current enforcement tools / current ban wording in 2026 [Verify].
  • Tribal regulator (cannabis): None — consistent with a ban position, no cannabis regulator was located.
