  • CTCLUSI appears in nine-tribe lists and in DOR tobacco/other-tobacco refund-agreement lists, but not in DOR’s marijuana-rebate list (only Cow Creek and Warm Springs), not on the USDA tribal hemp-plan list, and with no cannabis item in OLCC 2023/2024 contents excerpts searched.
  • No CTCLUSI cannabis ordinance, operation, retail, regulator, buyer rule, ban statement, or medical programme was located. Position: [Unavailable / Verify].
  • Tobacco-agreement caution: DOR maintains cigarette-tax refund agreements with all nine tribes and other-tobacco agreements with a subset including CTCLUSI (DOR 2024/2025). Those tobacco agreements are not marijuana agreements and must not be counted as cannabis compacts.

2.10 Legal framework common to all nine — Public Law 280, sovereignty, and enforcement

What PL 280 is. Public Law 83-280 (1953), codified principally at 18 U.S.C. § 1162 (criminal) and 25 U.S.C. §§ 1321–1323 (civil / retrocession), transferred certain criminal and civil adjudicatory jurisdiction over Indian country to six mandatory states, including Oregon, without tribal consent. It did not grant states general regulatory / legislative jurisdiction over tribes — a distinction Oregon’s own retrocession materials stress (see CTUIR letter summary below). Tribes retain concurrent jurisdiction, and federal jurisdiction (including the Major Crimes Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1153) is not divested by PL 280.

Oregon’s PL 280 map — as summarised in Oregon DOJ materials (secondary summary of Oregon law, [Verify] against federal retrocession notices). The Oregon Department of Justice 2026–2029 VAWA Implementation Plan (search-indexed) summarises:

“Public Law 280 extended state jurisdiction to all Indian country in Oregon except the Warm Springs Reservation, ‘over offenses committed by or against Indians.’ … Since that time, the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation and the Burns-Paiute Tribe have obtained exemptions from Public Law 280’s criminal jurisdictional provision through retrocession. In December 2020, after consultation … Former U.S. Attorney for Oregon Bill Williams notified DOJ that the Cow Creek Band of Indians is not subject to Public Law 280. Public Law 280 applies on lands of the other five Oregon tribes but does not divest tribes of concurrent jurisdiction over crimes by Indians. In 2025, the Oregon Legislature passed Senate Bill 1011, which created a formal process for tribes, currently subject to Public Law 280, to petition the state for retrocession.”

  • Source: Oregon DOJ, STOP VAWA Implementation Plan 2026–2029 — https://www.doj.state.or.us/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2026-2029-VAWA-IP-for-Oregon-FINAL.pdf — search-indexed, accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Arithmetic check (flagged, not smoothed): 9 tribes − Warm Springs (always exempt) − CTUIR (criminal retrocession) − Burns Paiute (criminal retrocession) − Cow Creek (not subject per 2020 notice) = 5 tribes remaining under PL 280 on the DOJ summary’s counting, which matches its “other five” phrase. A separate secondary account (Lincoln Chronicle, May 2025) says “six tribes still remain under Oregon state civil jurisdiction and five tribes remain under PL-280 criminal jurisdiction” — the civil/criminal split explains the 6 vs 5 difference (CTUIR retained civil jurisdiction until 2026 — see below). Do not collapse civil and criminal PL 280 into one number.
  • HIDTA corroboration (partial): The Oregon-Idaho HIDTA 2027 Threat Assessment (June 2026, search-indexed) describes Umatilla and Warm Springs as “non public Law 280” reservations in its HIDTA-county discussion — which, for Umatilla, reflects its criminal retrocession, not full civil retrocession at the time of that assessment’s data. The HIDTA footnote defines PL 280 as “a 1953 federal law that transferred criminal and civil jurisdiction from the federal government to certain states over Indian country in specific states including Oregon.”
  • Source: https://oridhidta.org/s/2027-Oregon-Idaho-HIDTA-Threat-Assessment-FINAL.pdf — search-indexed.

SB 1011 (2025) — the retrocession process. SB 1011 (Chapter 142, 2025 Oregon Laws; signed 22 May 2025) establishes a formal process for a federally recognised tribe in Oregon to request retrocession of PL 280 jurisdiction from the Governor, who then petitions the U.S. Secretary of the Interior under 25 U.S.C. § 1323. Secondary and Governor’s-office summaries agree: passed unanimously in the Senate 31 March 2025 and in the House 14 May 2025; bipartisan sponsorship led by Sen. Anthony Broadman.

  • Sources: Governor’s Office newsroom (CTUIR civil retrocession proclamation) — https://apps.oregon.gov/oregon-newsroom/OR/GOV/Posts/Post/governor-kotek-signs-proclamation-returning-civil-legal-jurisdiction-to-the-confederated-tribes-of-the-umatilla-indian-reservation — search-indexed; CTUIR retrocession joint release (5 June 2026) — https://ctuir.org/media/k0ydp032/retrocessionjointrelease_260605.pdf — search-indexed; Umatilla County agenda letter (CTUIR request 12 Nov 2025, Governor deadline 11 May 2026) — https://www.co.umatilla.or.us/fileadmin/user_upload/BCC/Agendas/Item4041726.pdf — search-indexed. All accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Dating care: The CTUIR civil-retrocession proclamation and joint release are dated June 2026 — after the 1 November 2026 research-date label in the sense of being later in the same year? No: June 2026 pre-dates 1 November 2026, so it is within the cut-off. The confusion to avoid is the reverse: no 2026 event after 1 November 2026 is included. The June 2026 proclamation is included, and it states: the signing “ends a 73-year history of the state having concurrent jurisdiction with the CTUIR in civil cases on the UIR. The state’s Public Law-280 criminal jurisdiction over the CTUIR was retroceded in 1981. Its PL-280 civil jurisdiction, however, remained in place until now.” The Governor “will now petition the U.S. Secretary of the Interior pursuant to 25 USC 1323 … to accept this retrocession.” Federal acceptance is therefore the remaining step — [Verify] whether the Secretary has accepted as of 1 November 2026. The proclamation alone does not complete retrocession under § 1323.
  • What retrocession does not do for cannabis: Retrocession returns adjudicatory jurisdiction; it does not by itself legalise cannabis, create a tribal cannabis licence, or amend ORS 475C.521. A tribe that obtains retrocession still needs its own cannabis code + (for state-market access) an ORS 475C.521 agreement. Conversely, a tribe still under PL 280 is not thereby barred from tribal cannabis regulation — PL 280’s criminal jurisdiction is concurrent, and Oregon’s cannabis statutes expressly contemplate tribal licensing on trust land via compact. The practical effect is enforcement complexity (who prosecutes what, on trust vs fee land, Indian vs non-Indian defendant), not a simple on/off switch. Fee land within reservation boundaries may be subject to state jurisdiction on different terms than trust land — parcel status must be checked in any real case. [Verify] with tribal counsel / BIA land-status records for any specific site.

Federal tribal-cannabis policy background (context, not Oregon law). In October/December 2014 the U.S. Department of Justice issued tribal marijuana guidance (the Wilkinson Memorandum, 28 Oct 2014) stating federal prosecutors would apply the Cole Memorandum priorities to tribal marijuana activity. That guidance was part of the backdrop to Warm Springs’ 2015 referendum and to early tribal cannabis discussions nationally. No source opened for this Part confirms the current (2026) status of that memorandum after successive administrations, and it is not relied on here as current enforcement policy — [Verify] before citing it as live policy. Federal enforcement discretion, the medical rider (through 11 Dec 2026 per the given baseline), and Schedule III rescheduling are all federal overlays; none of them creates an Oregon tribal licence.

State enforcement on tribal land — OLCC’s own limit restated. OLCC does not regulate marijuana within tribal borders (OLCC 2023/2024). Oregon State Police / county enforcement on trust land is governed by PL 280 status, tribal consent/agreement, and federal jurisdiction as above — not by OLCC licence authority. Any claim that OSP or OLCC “enforces OLCC rules on a reservation” without a compact/agreement should be treated as [Verify].

2.11 Tribal hemp plans — complete USDA picture, and tribal medical programmes

USDA tribal hemp plans in Oregon: exactly two, on the list opened. - Approved: Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs; Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians. - Not listed (therefore no USDA-approved tribal plan shown): Grand Ronde, Siletz, Umatilla (CTUIR), Coquille, Klamath, Burns Paiute, CTCLUSI. - State plan: Oregon — Approved Plan (pdf)* (final-rule approval, eff. 22 Mar 2021 framework). - Source: USDA AMS list, updated 17 Feb 2026 — https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review — opened directly 2026-11-01 (full tribal table reproduced in research notes; only the two Oregon tribal rows are Oregon-relevant). - What “not listed” means: It means USDA does not show an approved tribal plan for that tribe on that date. It does not prove the tribe never applied, never drafted a plan, or is barred from applying. A tribe without an approved plan whose members wish to produce hemp on trust land would need to check whether USDA direct licensing (USDA Hemp Producer Licence route, used by some tribes nationally) or a future tribal plan applies — [Verify] tribe by tribe; no such licence fact was located for the seven non-listed Oregon tribes. - Interaction with Oregon state hemp law: A USDA-approved tribal plan means the tribe self-administers hemp production on its reservation “without oversight or regulation from the State of Oregon” (USDA-approval reporting for Cow Creek). Oregon’s ODA hemp programme and OLCC hemp registry therefore do not govern production on those reservations under those plans — but they do govern sale to Oregon consumers / retailers in the state market (see §3.3). The boundary is production jurisdiction vs market jurisdiction; do not collapse them.

Tribal cannabis compacts — complete picture on sources opened. - Described as operative / in conferral: Warm Springs, Cow Creek. - Described as paused / held off (retail project incl. compact negotiation, July 2024): CTUIR. - No compact described: Grand Ronde, Siletz, Coquille, Klamath, Burns Paiute, CTCLUSI. - Full compact texts: not located for any tribe — [Verify / Unavailable]. All compact terms in this report (CTS tracking, tax rebate linkage, wholesale-to-retailer direction for Warm Springs 2023) come from OLCC/DOR summaries, not from the compacts themselves.

Tribal medical programmes — none identified; Schedule III question open. - No tribe is shown in any source opened to operate: a tribal medical marijuana registry/card, tribal medical dispensary sales distinct from adult-use sales, tribal medical grow-site licensing distinct from the compact adult-use pathway, or medical reciprocity with Oregon OMMP or any other state. - OMMP itself is a state programme (OHA), with 11,625 cardholders in July 2026 per Run 1. Tribal members who are Oregon residents may participate in OMMP as individuals; that is state participation, not a tribal programme. - Schedule III “state-licensed” assessment: On the given baseline (Schedule III for state-licensed medical eff. 28 Apr 2026), the question “does a tribally licensed medical programme count?” cannot be answered from Part 10 sources because (a) no such programme is identified, and (b) no federal guidance answering it was located. If a future tribal medical programme is created, the analysis would need to address at least: whether the programme is licensed by the tribe alone, by the tribe under an ORS 475C.521 agreement, or by the State; whether DEA treats tribal licensing as state licensing; and whether § 280E relief follows that characterisation. All [Verify] — do not publish a yes/no answer on current evidence. - Adult-use tribal product and § 280E: Tribal adult-use production for the state market is, on the given baseline, Schedule I adult-use and therefore fully § 280E-subject in the same way as state adult-use. No tribal exemption from § 280E was located. [Verify] with tax counsel for any specific tribal entity’s federal tax status (tribal-governmental vs tribal-entity distinctions are outside this Part’s sources).

3. Interstate issues — marijuana

3.1 The baseline prohibition: ORS 475C.229

ORS 475C.229 (formerly ORS 475B.227), “Prohibition against importing or exporting marijuana items,” provides in its core:

“(1) For purposes of this section: (a) ‘Export’ includes placing a marijuana item in any mode of transportation for hire, such as luggage, mail or parcel delivery, even if the transportation of the marijuana item is intercepted prior to the marijuana item leaving this state. (b) ‘Marijuana item’ includes an industrial hemp commodity or product that exceeds the greater of: (A) A concentration of 0.3 percent total delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol; or (B) The concentration of total delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol allowed under federal law. (2) A person may not import marijuana items into this state or export marijuana items from this state. (3) A violation of this section is a Class B violation, except: (a) As provided in subsection (4) …; or (b) If the item is industrial hemp and does not exceed a total delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol concentration of one percent. (4) A violation … is: (a) Class A misdemeanor, if [not for consideration and licensee, or amount exceeds ORS 475C.337(1)(a)–(f) maxima]; (b) Class C felony, if [for consideration and licensee; or amount exceeds 16× those maxima; or concerns a cannabinoid extract not purchased from an ORS 475C.097 retailer].”

  • Source: ORS 475C.229 text as reproduced in secondary compilation — https://www.oregoncrimes.com/oregon_marijuana_laws.html — accessed 2026-11-01, corroborated by SB 582 staff summary describing ORS 475B.227 (now 475C.229) in identical terms (“importing or exporting marijuana to or from Oregon is prohibited”). Official ORS text to be re-checked before publication-grade use — [Verify] against oregonlegislature.gov ORS Chapter 475C.
  • Two consequences that are often missed: 1. The “export” definition catches mail/parcel/luggage placement even if intercepted before leaving Oregon. Personal “I was only mailing it within Oregon” is not the test in subsection (1)(a) as written; the test is placement in a for-hire mode. 2. The “marijuana item” definition for this section sweeps in hemp commodities/products above 0.3% total delta-9 THC (or the federal allowance if greater). That is why the hemp-export limit in §3.3 (0.3% total THC) matters: hemp above that line is treated as a marijuana item for import/export prohibition purposes, subject to the 1% industrial-hemp carve-out in subsection (3)(b) for penalty classification — a penalty nuance, not a permission to export. Do not read (3)(b) as authorising export of 0.3–1% product.

3.2 SB 582 (2019) — the interstate-commerce law that has no effect yet

Enactment. Senate Bill 582, 80th Oregon Legislative Assembly, 2019 Regular Session (Chapter 464, 2019 Oregon Laws). Sponsors: Sen. Prozanski, Rep. Helm; Sen. Manning Jr (presession filed). Passed Senate 19–9–2 on 15 May 2019; House 43–16–1 on 11 June 2019 (vote figures from secondary legislative-record summary — [Verify] against OLIS journals); signed by Governor Kate Brown 20 June 2019.

  • Source for bill text: SB 582 A-Engrossed — https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2019R1/Downloads/MeasureDocument/SB582/A-Engrossed — accessed 2026-11-01 (search-indexed).
  • Source for staff summary: SB 582 A Staff Measure Summary, Senate Judiciary, action 3 Apr 2019 — https://apps.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2019R1/Downloads/MeasureAnalysisDocument/49500 — accessed 2026-11-01 (search-indexed).

What SB 582 does — operative text (A-Engrossed summary + § 2 note in ORS 475C.485). The Governor (or designee) may enter into an agreement with another state for:

“(a) Cross-jurisdictional coordination and enforcement of marijuana-related businesses authorized to conduct business in either this state or the other state; and (b) Cross-jurisdictional delivery of marijuana items between this state and the other state.”

An agreement must:

  • ensure enforceable public health and safety standards;
  • include a system to regulate and track the interstate delivery of marijuana items;
  • ensure any marijuana items delivered into Oregon, prior to sale to a consumer, are tested under ORS 475C.540–475C.586, and packaged/labelled under ORS 475C.600–475C.648 (renumbered from the 475B ranges in the original note).

Notwithstanding ORS 475C.229, and in accordance with such an agreement:

  • a marijuana producer, processor, wholesaler, or certified researcher may deliver marijuana items to a person located in, and authorised to receive them by, the other state;
  • a marijuana processor, wholesaler, retailer, or certified researcher may receive marijuana items from a person located in, and authorised to export them by, the other state.

Early SB 582 drafts that included a 30% excise tax and a structure pressing the Governor to act in defiance of federal law were removed during session (Gleam Law 2019 session roundup, secondary). The enacted law creates no excise or other tax. Do not cite the dropped 30% figure as law.

The federal-authorisation condition — the whole point. Section 3 of the 2019 Act provides, in substance (A-Engrossed + staff summary + ORS 475C.485 note agree):

“Section 2 of this 2019 Act becomes operative on the earlier of the date on which: (a) Federal law is amended to allow for the interstate transfer of marijuana items between authorized marijuana-related businesses; or (b) The United States Department of Justice issues an opinion or memorandum allowing or tolerating the interstate transfer of marijuana items between authorized marijuana-related businesses.”

If such an event occurs, OLCC must notify the Judiciary Committees and Legislative Counsel (staff summary). No such notice, federal amendment, or DOJ opinion/memorandum was located as of 1 November 2026.

Effect as of 1 November 2026: NONE — dormant. - No SB 582 agreement with Washington, California, Idaho, Nevada, or any other state was located in any source searched. The Governor has not, on the evidence in this track, entered into an interstate delivery agreement, because the operative condition has not fired. - Schedule III does not fire it on the evidence opened. The given baseline moves state-licensed medical to Schedule III eff. 28 April 2026. That is a scheduling change, not an amendment “to allow for the interstate transfer of marijuana items,” and no DOJ opinion/memorandum allowing/tolerating interstate transfer was located. A secondary 2026 industry brief states the point directly: “Rescheduling does not authorize interstate cannabis commerce, and none has begun. State enabling statutes (Oregon SB 582, California SB 1326, Washington SB 5069 …) all remain dormant, contingent on a federal trigger … that has not fired.” That brief is secondary and, in the copy indexed, hosted on GitHub — it is cited here only as corroboration, not as authority. The authoritative point is the absence of a located trigger notice/amendment/opinion, which leaves SB 582 inoperative. [Verify] against OLCC / Governor’s Office / OLIS for any trigger notice issued after the last search in this track. - Secondary corroboration: https://github.com/robofinsystems/robosystems-content-machine/blob/HEAD/campaigns/cannabis_coverage/CAMPAIGN_BRIEF.md (refresh date 20 June 2026 in the brief) — accessed 2026-11-01. - Parallel dormant statutes (for comparison, not Oregon law): - California SB 1326 (2022): Empowers the California Governor to agree interstate commerce between licensed businesses, but “shall not take effect unless” federal law is amended to allow interstate transfer, or federal law prohibits expenditure to prevent it, or DOJ issues a tolerating opinion/memorandum (formulations vary slightly by summary; the federal-condition structure mirrors Oregon’s). No California–Oregon agreement is in effect. - Washington SB 5069 (2023): Takes effect “on the earlier of the date on which federal law is amended to allow for the interstate transfer of cannabis between authorized cannabis-related businesses or the U.S. Department of Justice issues an opinion or memorandum allowing or tolerating” such transfer. Washington’s bill report itself notes Oregon SB 582 as the model and California SB 1326 as the parallel. - Sources (secondary/official bill analyses): Washington SB 5069 bill report — https://lawfilesext.leg.wa.gov/biennium/2023-24/Htm/Bill%20Reports/Senate/5069%20SBA%20LC%2023.htm ; California SB 1326 analysis — https://billtexts.s3.amazonaws.com/ca/ca-analysishttps-leginfo-legislature-ca-gov-faces-billAnalysisClient-xhtml-bill-id-202120220SB1326-ca-analysis-350872.pdf — both accessed 2026-11-01. - What SB 582 does not do even when operative: It does not authorise unlicensed interstate sale, does not authorise transport through a non-party state, does not authorise airspace / federally-regulated-mode transport on the early-draft terms (those restrictions were in early drafts and are not part of the enacted summary relied on here — [Verify] against the enrolled Act before citing transport-mode limits), and does not displace federal law. An SB 582 agreement, if ever made, would still need the other state’s authorisation and Oregon testing/packaging/labelling compliance for inbound product.

Litigation over the import/export ban — Jefferson Packing House — outcome [Verify / conflict flagged]. - In November 2022, Oregon cannabis distribution company Jefferson Packing House sued Oregon officials (then-Governor Kate Brown, Attorney General Ellen Rosenblum, OLCC Interim Executive Director Craig Prins, among others) seeking to overturn the state ban on interstate cannabis commerce on Dormant Commerce Clause grounds (Harris Sliwoski summary, secondary). - Source (secondary): https://harris-sliwoski.com/cannalawblog/changing-interstate-cannabis-sales/ — accessed 2026-11-01. - A complaint in the District of Oregon (Jefferson Packing House, LLC v. …) challenges ORS 475C.229 as facially discriminating against interstate commerce; a First Amended Complaint dated 26 February 2026, Case No. 3:25-cv-1791 (District of Oregon), against OLCC Executive Director Tara Wasiak (official capacity), Jackson County District Attorney Patrick Green, and Lake County District Attorney Paul Charas, was located in search results. - Source (pleading, secondary host): https://andrewdeweese.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/20260226-First-Amended-Complaint.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01. - Conflict: The June 2026 industry brief cited above states an Oregon wholesaler “withdrew its dormant-Commerce-Clause challenge in 2026, leaving the status quo intact.” Whether that refers to Jefferson Packing House, to a different wholesaler, or to a withdrawal after the February 2026 amended complaint is not resolved on the sources opened. The February 2026 amended complaint proves the challenge was live in February 2026; the June 2026 brief suggests a later withdrawal. Outcome as of 1 November 2026: [Verify] against the District of Oregon docket for 3:25-cv-1791. Do not state that ORS 475C.229 has been struck down, upheld, or that the case was dismissed, on current evidence. The statute is treated in this report as in force unless/until a court order to the contrary is located. - Related Ninth Circuit context (secondary pleading citation, not independently verified here): Peridot Tree WA, Inc. v. Wash. State Liquor & Cannabis Control Bd., Nos. 24-3481, 24-7196 (9th Cir. 2 Jan 2026), cited in the Jefferson pleading for the proposition that allowing the ban to stand does not “protect an illegal national marketplace.” That citation is pleading argument, not a holding about Oregon, and is flagged as such.

3.3 Interstate hemp — shipments, transport rules, enforcement

Federal transport protection (2018 Farm Bill). Section 10114 of the Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018 (P.L. 115-334) provides, codified at the note to 7 U.S.C. § 1639o:

“(a) Rule of Construction — Nothing in this title … prohibits the interstate commerce of hemp (as defined in [7 U.S.C. § 1639o]) or hemp products.

(b) Transportation of Hemp and Hemp Products — No State or Indian Tribe shall prohibit the transportation or shipment of hemp or hemp products produced in accordance with subtitle G of the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946 [7 U.S.C. §§ 1639o et seq.] through the State or the territory of the Indian Tribe, as applicable.“

  • Sources: USDA legal opinion / Farm Bill summaries as reproduced in court and secondary analyses — D.D.C. Memorandum Opinion, DeLorean 88 LLC v. District of Columbia, 1:25-cv-2458 (8 Oct 2025), quoting § 10114(b) verbatim — https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/district-of-columbia/dcdce/1:2025cv02458/283168/24/ — accessed 2026-11-01; JD Supra Farm Bill analysis quoting the same provision — https://www.jdsupra.com/post/contentViewerEmbed.aspx?fid=315b9153-b65c-46c5-a764-e3bcc0415839 — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Limits of the protection (important): Courts cited in those sources hold the clause addresses transportation/shipment through a state/tribe; it “says nothing about whether a state may prohibit possession or sale of industrial hemp” within its borders (C.Y. Wholesale, 965 F.3d at 546, as cited in DeLorean). A through-shipment that stops for sale in a destination state is governed by that state’s sale law, not by the transport clause. Roadside indistinguishability (hemp vs marijuana by sight/smell) is a practical enforcement friction noted in every secondary source; it is not a legal exception to the clause, but it explains seizures and testing delays.
  • Coming federal change (given baseline, not re-researched): After 11 December 2026, the federal hemp definition tightens to total-THC + 0.4 mg/container cap (P.L. 119-37 § 781). Product that qualifies as hemp for through-transport on 1 November 2026 under the delta-9 0.3% test may not qualify after that date. Through-transport protection after 11 December 2026 will therefore turn on the new definition. [Verify after 11 Dec 2026.]

Oregon through-shipment and out-of-state-sale rules (official, opened). - OLCC Hemp Registry FAQs (opened directly 1 Nov 2026) state the registry does not apply to: - “Hemp items transported through Oregon en route to a final destination in another state.” - And: “If the hemp items are only being sold out of state, then you do not need to register or label your products according to OLCC rules. The hemp registry’s requirements apply prior to selling, offering for sale, transferring, or delivering a hemp item to a consumer in Oregon or to a retailer for sale to consumers in Oregon.” - Source: https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/Pages/hemp-registry-faqs.aspx — opened directly 2026-11-01. - ODA draft-rule commentary (October 2025 draft rules, public comment) records a proposed OAR 603-048-0100 provision: “A license is not required to transport or ship hemp or hemp products produced in accordance with 7 USC 1639, et seq. through the state.” That is a draft-rule comment document, not an adopted rule — the adopted OAR text must be checked before compliance reliance. [Verify] current OAR 603-048-0100. - Source: https://stage.oregon.gov/oda/agriculture/Documents/Rulemaking/ODA_DRAFT_RULES%20_Input.docx.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 (search-indexed). - Export potency limit (OLCC/ODA guide, official). The joint OLCC/ODA “Hemp Testing and Potency: Quick Reference Guide” (Rev. 18 Dec 2025, search-indexed) states: “Hemp products transferred outside of Oregon are limited to no more than 0.3% total THC” and tabulates OAR 603-048-0545 for import/export, with OLCC-market (5% THC for ODA handlers in the guide’s Table 3 context) vs Oregon general market (0.3% total THC) vs wholesale import/export distinctions. The guide’s tables are complex and partly garbled in search-indexed form; the 0.3% export limit sentence is the only export proposition relied on here, and the full guide should be opened before any product-specific advice. - Source: https://stage.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/Documents/Hemp/Hemp-Testing-and-Potency-Guide.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 (search-indexed). - Intrastate vs interstate hemp sales (OAR 603-048-0100, search-indexed). For transfers/sales within Oregon, an ODA registrant may sell/transfer industrial hemp or agricultural hemp seed to another registrant or to an OLCC licensee under ORS 571.336 / 571.337. A registrant may not sell an industrial hemp product containing more than 0.3% total THC to a consumer unless OLCC-retailer-licensed. Those are intrastate rules; they do not govern a pure through-shipment or a pure out-of-state sale as above. - Source: https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_603-048-0100 — accessed 2026-11-01 (search-indexed; official OAR to be re-checked).

Idaho hemp-shipment seizures — historic, and why they matter to Oregon shippers. - In 2019, Idaho State Police seized Oregon-origin hemp shipments in transit through Idaho, including a 6,700-pound shipment from Boones Ferry Berry Farms (Oregon) in transit between Oregon and Colorado, with the driver jailed and facing (as reported then) a five-year mandatory minimum for drug trafficking; a separate Montana-origin shipment (Big Sky Scientific) was also seized and litigated; a 69-pound Canada–Boise–Oregon package was intercepted by Boise Police, tested at zero THC throughout by a Kentucky lab, and returned. - Source (secondary, dated 9 Sept 2019, updated 21 Oct 2024): https://ganjapreneur.com/idaho-police-agencies-take-different-approaches-to-hemp/ — accessed 2026-11-01. - Current Idaho position — [Verify] interaction: Idaho now appears on USDA’s list with an Approved Plan (pdf)* (opened 1 Nov 2026), which changes the 2019 framework (when Idaho had no approved plan and a 0.0% THC state stance). Whether Idaho’s current plan, state statute, and enforcement practice now permit Oregon hemp through-shipments without seizure is not established in this track and must not be assumed from the USDA listing alone. Oregon shippers transiting Idaho should still expect testing, documentation, and roadside-stop risk, and should carry lab certificates / bills of lading / USDA-plan compliance documentation. No 2025–2026 Oregon–Idaho hemp-seizure count was located — [Unavailable]. - Oregon enforcement of hemp shipments (inbound/outbound): No Oregon OSP/ODA seizure count for hemp shipments, and no Oregon hemp-shipment stop data, was located in this track. [Unavailable.] Do not present the Idaho 2019 seizures as Oregon enforcement data.

4. Out-of-state buyers and border markets

Headline limit — stated once, applies to the whole section: Oregon law does not require OLCC retailers to record or report buyer residence, and no official OLCC/DOR buyer-residency dataset was located in this track. Every “X% from [neighbour]” figure below is therefore an operator estimate, legislative testimony, or press observation, labelled as such. County sales totals (which are official OLCC sales data as reported) prove where sales occurred, not where buyers live. Do not convert a county sales total into a buyer-residency share without that label.

Buyer rules that do apply (state law, not border-specific). - Adult-use: any adult 21+ with acceptable ID may buy at an OLCC retailer, resident or not. Oregon imposes no residency requirement for adult-use purchase (contrast: OMMP participation requires Oregon residency — see §4.4). A non-resident 21+ buyer from Idaho, California, Washington, or anywhere else may lawfully buy in Oregon; what they may lawfully do after purchase is governed by their home state’s law and by federal interstate-transport law (see §3.1, §5). - Medical: OMMP purchases (tax-exempt) require OMMP patient/caregiver status. Out-of-state medical cards are not recognised (see §4.4). A visiting patient without OMMP status buys, if at all, as an adult-use 21+ buyer and pays tax. - Delivery: Oregon delivery is intrastate only under OLCC rules (delivery to an Oregon address); interstate delivery is prohibited by ORS 475C.229 outside an SB 582 agreement (none in effect). No border-market delivery-into-Idaho/Washington/California scheme is lawful on current law.

4.1 Ontario, Oregon — Idaho line (Malheur County) — the prohibition-arbitrage market

Geography (place discipline). Ontario is the largest city in Malheur County, Oregon, on the Snake River at the Idaho border, on I-84, about 55 miles west of Boise. Fruitland and Payette are in Idaho (Payette County, Idaho), across the line from Ontario; they are part of the same micropolitan area (Ontario, OR-ID Micropolitan Statistical Area: Malheur County, OR + Payette County, ID) but they are not Ontario and they are not in Oregon. Sales in Fruitland/Payette are Idaho sales (where marijuana remains illegal for all purposes on the evidence in this Part); sales in Ontario are Oregon sales.

How Ontario became a cannabis island. Malheur County opted out / banned marijuana businesses under the county opt-out framework (counties voting >55% against Measure 91 could ban licensees), and the county voted 68.7% against Measure 91 in 2014 (the highest opposition in Oregon, per secondary reporting). Ontario voted by initiative in November 2018 to overturn its ban (reported 56.8% in favour in one secondary account), becoming the only city in Malheur County that allows marijuana sales. Recreational sales began in Ontario in 2019 (first full year 2020).

  • Sources (secondary, consistent): Wikipedia “Ontario, Oregon” (cannabis section, citing Cannabis Business Times 9 Feb 2021) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario,_Oregon ; Portland Monthly (2026) — https://www.pdxmonthly.com/news-and-city-life/ontario-oregon-idaho-marijuana-cannabis-business/ — both accessed 2026-11-01. The 56.8% / 68.7% figures are secondary and [Verify] against Malheur County / City of Ontario election records before publication-grade use.

Official sales totals (OLCC sales data as reported — where, not who). - 2023: Portland Monthly (2026, secondary) reports Ontario dispensary sales “in 2023 … hit about $100 million — or about $3,125 for every resident in the county. It’s by far the highest per-capita sales amount of any county in Oregon. Only Multnomah and Washington Counties move more weed overall.” The “$100 million” here is presented in Portland Monthly as a sales total, not a buyer count. - December 2023 (official OLCC monthly reporting via trade press): “In December [2023] Multnomah County by far sold the most … at $18.3 million, followed by Washington County with $8.9 million and Malheur County with $8.8 million. Total sales for 2023 … $955 million” statewide; December statewide $81,332,264. - Source (secondary reporting of OLCC data): The Marijuana Herald, 2 Jan 2024 — https://themarijuanaherald.com/2024/01/oregon-81-million-in-legal-marijuana-sold-in-december-950-million-for-the-year/ — accessed 2026-11-01. - 2020–2021 (OLCC data as reported): Ontario shops topped $103 million in just over sixteen months of operation (to early 2021), averaging about $8 million/month over seven months to late 2020; Malheur County $111 million in 2021, about 10% of Oregon sales; Ontario’s first full year (2020) raised about $1.8 million in local tax revenue (3% local tax), with sales up 65% the next year (2021). - Sources (secondary reporting of OLCC data): https://radicalruss.com/idaho-marijuana-sales-top-100m-in-ontario-oregon/ ; https://radicalruss.com/idaho-doubles-marijuana-arrests-to-no-avail/ (February sales $8.7m, “average of about $9 million per month for the past year and a half” as of that article’s period) — accessed 2026-11-01. Dates/periods for the $8m vs $9m monthly averages differ by article period; both are preserved as period-specific, not averaged together. - Scale today (secondary, not official): Portland Monthly (2026) counts “at least a dozen dispensaries” in Ontario, including Weedology near the highway exit and Burnt River Farms, with lots “already packed with Idaho cars” on a spring-afternoon observation. Dispensary-directory listings located in search (Weedology, Hotbox Farms, Burnt River Farms, Treasure Valley Cannabis, High Supply, The Bud House, Elevation 2150, Cannabis & Glass, Nectar, Cookies Ontario, etc.) corroborate a dozen-plus retail presence but are directory listings, not an OLCC licence count — the OLCC licence count for Ontario as of 1 Nov 2026 is [Verify] against OLCC’s licence list / CAMP. - No official 2024, 2025, or 2026 Ontario/Malheur sales total is stated in this Part beyond the December 2023 county figure above, because no directly opened OLCC monthly sales table for those years was obtained in this track. Do not extrapolate $100m/year forward. [Unavailable for 2024–2026 in this track.]

Buyer-residency claims — labelled, not official. - Operator estimate (label: ANECDOTE / OPERATOR ESTIMATE): Steven Meland, co-owner of Hotbox Farms, who helped organise Ontario’s legalisation effort and is reported to control about a third of Ontario licences, estimates “more than 90 percent of customers come from Idaho” (Portland Monthly, 2026). That is one operator’s estimate, not a survey and not OLCC data. - Legislative testimony (label: TESTIMONY, not official count): Testimony in support of SB 1506 (2022, Ontario local-tax proposal) states: “Ontario cannabis retailers are grossing approximately $100 million in sales and 892,857 transactions per year. That’s nearly 2,500 sales daily with 90% of those sales being from citizens of Idaho.” The testimony also states Ontario is “the second largest retailer of cannabis behind only Portland and accounts for 10% of all Oregon sales” and that the average transaction is $112. - Source: OLIS public testimony, SB 1506 support (JL Wilson et al.) — https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2022R1/Downloads/PublicTestimonyDocument/34828 — accessed 2026-11-01. - Why this is not an official figure: Testimony is advocacy to a committee; the 90% figure’s methodology (licence-plate counts? customer surveys? operator reports?) is not stated in the excerpt. It is consistent with the operator estimate, which is why the 90% figure recurs — consistency between two non-official sources does not make it official. - Press observation (label: OBSERVATION): Portland Monthly’s reporter observes Idaho plates in dispensary lots; a 2021 Associated Press-derived account (via TimesNet) describes “hundreds of customers … mak[ing] the pilgrimage from Idaho to Ontario” daily and 11 dispensaries (about one per 1,000 people at that time). Plate observation proves some Idaho buyers, not a share. - Historic Idaho-law-enforcement claim (label: HISTORIC, SECONDARY, 2012-era): An NPR-derived 2012 account reported Idaho State Police records showing 40% of cannabis seizures in Idaho came from Oregon (53% in a border trooper’s sector), with only 196 Idahoans then holding Oregon medical cards. That is a medical-era, pre-adult-use-retail figure (2012) and must not be cited as a current adult-use diversion share. - Source: https://www.police1.com/drug-interdiction-narcotics/articles/more-are-sneaking-medical-marijuana-across-state-lines-nT86xANzuQsyjbO2/ — accessed 2026-11-01 (article text includes a “June 21, 2102” typographical error for 2012 in the excerpt; the underlying events are 2012). - What Ontario’s market does prove officially: Malheur County, population roughly 30,000, sustains the state’s third-highest county sales in December 2023 ($8.8m) and ~10% of statewide sales in 2021 — a per-capita outlier that is inconsistent with local demand alone and consistent with substantial out-of-county / out-of-state buying, without quantifying the Idaho share officially. That inference is stated as inference, not as a buyer count.

Ontario local-tax politics (context, not a border-flow finding). SB 1506 (2022) would have allowed Ontario voters to impose up to 10% local cannabis tax (vs the then-current 3% local cap), on the argument that importing 90% of buyers from Idaho imposes unique public costs (policing, infrastructure) not covered by 3%. SB 1506 passed one committee but never received a floor vote; a later SB 1524 cannabis-tax amendment (limited to counties bordering a prohibition state with population >30,000 — only Malheur County met the definition in that account) was removed from the final bill. The 3% local cap therefore remained the framework in those accounts. Current Ontario local tax rate as of 1 Nov 2026 is [Verify] against City of Ontario / DOR — do not assume 3% still applies without checking. - Sources (secondary): https://cannabislaw.report/legislative-victory-bill-increasing-cannabis-sales-tax-in-oregon-dies/ ; SB 1506 testimony above — accessed 2026-11-01.

Huntington (Baker County) — historic feeder market, not current Ontario data. Portland Monthly notes that before Ontario opted in, tens of thousands of Idahoans passed through Ontario to Huntington (Baker County, population ~500), where two shops (Hotbox and 420ville) “were basically supplying the entire greater Boise area.” Hotbox has since moved to Ontario. Huntington is recorded here only as history explaining Ontario’s market formation; no current Huntington sales/buyer figure is stated.

Idaho-law consequence for the Ontario buyer. An Idaho resident who lawfully buys in Ontario and then transports marijuana back into Idaho commits an Idaho offence (Idaho marijuana remains illegal for all purposes; trafficking triggers at 1 lb / 25 plants per Idaho secondary summaries — [Verify] against Idaho Code before citing thresholds) and a federal interstate-transport offence, and faces Idaho State Police interdiction emphasis patrols on I-84 (historic and current HIDTA interdiction — see §4.6). Oregon’s lawful sale does not confer Idaho possession rights. The return journey, not the Ontario purchase, is where Idaho law bites.

4.2 Brookings, Oregon — California line (Curry County)

Geography (place discipline). Brookings is in Curry County, Oregon, on US-101 on the southern Oregon coast, a few miles north of the California border. Crescent City is in Del Norte County, California, south of the border. Brookings is not in California, and Crescent City is not in Oregon.

Market structure — no prohibition arbitrage. California legalised adult-use cannabis (Proposition 64, 2016; sales from January 2018) and operates a licensed retail market in Del Norte County / Crescent City. An adult 21+ can therefore buy lawfully on either side of the Brookings line. There is no Ontario-style incentive created by a neighbouring prohibition, and no source in this track reports a Brookings buyer-flow, price-arbitrage, or cross-border purchasing pattern of the Ontario kind.

Retail presence (directory only, not buyer data). Search-directory listings show multiple Brookings retailers (High Tide Wellness Center, West Coast Organics, Bud Bros, La Mota, The Farmers Daughters Dispensary, Stateline Cannabis — the name “Stateline” is a business name, not evidence of cross-border sales — World Famous Top Shelf Cannabis, BudMart, among others). Those listings prove retail presence in Brookings; they prove nothing about California buyers, sales totals, or cross-border flows. - No official Brookings / Curry County sales total, and no official California-buyer share, was located in this track — [Unavailable]. Do not estimate one from dispensary counts. - Tax/price context (general, not a flow finding): Oregon’s 17% state tax (+ up to 3% local) is lower than California’s 15% excise (as adjusted — see California Run 1, not re-litigated here) plus California sales/local taxes, but California retail prices, product mix, and local taxes vary, and no Brookings–Crescent City price comparison was located. Price difference alone must not be presented as proof of cross-border buying.

Interstate rule for Brookings buyers: Identical to §4.1 — lawful purchase in Oregon does not authorise transport into California as a commercial interstate transfer (ORS 475C.229; federal law), even though California adult-use possession is lawful. Personal possession in California after lawful California purchase is a different question from Oregon-to-California transport. The distinction is stated here because Brookings–Crescent City proximity invites conflation.

4.3 Milton-Freewater, Oregon — Washington line (Umatilla County), and Portland / Vancouver

Milton-Freewater — geography. Milton-Freewater is in Umatilla County, Oregon, immediately south of the Washington border. Walla Walla is in Walla Walla County, Washington, about 10 miles north. Milton-Freewater is not Walla Walla, and Walla Walla is not in Oregon.

Market structure — no prohibition arbitrage; tax differential only. Washington legalised adult-use (Initiative 502, 2012; sales from 2014) and operates licensed retailers in Walla Walla (e.g. A Greener Today, Walla Walla Weedery, Walla Walla Cannabis Company — directory listings). Washington’s cannabis excise is 37% (RCW 69.50.535, per Washington Run 1) vs Oregon’s 17% (+ local). That tax gap creates a theoretical price incentive to buy in Oregon rather than Washington, but no official Milton-Freewater sales total, no official Washington-buyer share, and no price-comparison study was located in this track. Directory evidence shows Milton-Freewater dispensary job postings (budtender/manager postings for Milton-Freewater retailers) — proving retail exists there, not who buys there. - Position: [Unavailable] for any Milton-Freewater cross-border flow figure. Do not cite the Washington 37% vs Oregon 17% gap as a measured flow. - CTUIR proximity note: Milton-Freewater is in Umatilla County, the same county as the Umatilla Indian Reservation (though the Reservation itself is centred near Pendleton/Mission, not Milton-Freewater). No source ties Milton-Freewater retail to CTUIR tribal retail (CTUIR retail is held off — see §2.3). Do not conflate the two.

Portland, Oregon — Vancouver, Washington. - Geography: Portland (Multnomah County, Oregon) and Vancouver (Clark County, Washington) sit across the Columbia River from each other, connected by I-5 / I-205 bridges. Portland is not Vancouver, and Vancouver is not in Oregon. - Market structure: Both sides have lawful adult-use retail (Portland is Oregon’s largest cannabis market by county sales — Multnomah $18.3m in December 2023, see §4.1; Vancouver/Clark County is a Washington retail market). The same tax-differential logic as Milton-Freewater applies in theory (Washington 37% vs Oregon 17% + local), and Portland’s scale means any cross-river buying would be submerged in Portland’s large local market. No official Portland–Vancouver cross-border buyer figure was located — [Unavailable]. - Bridge-transport rule: Carrying Oregon-bought marijuana across the I-5/I-205 bridges into Washington is interstate transport (ORS 475C.229; federal law) even though Washington adult-use possession is lawful. The purchase in Portland is lawful; the interstate movement is not authorised outside an SB 582 agreement (none in effect). This is the same rule as Brookings/California, stated here because the Portland–Vancouver commute makes it the most commonly misunderstood crossing.

California and Washington buyers generally. - No official dataset distinguishes California buyers from Washington buyers from Idaho buyers in Oregon retail sales. The only neighbour for which a (non-official) buyer-share estimate recurs is Idaho via Ontario (90% claims above). For California and Washington, the correct statement is: buyers from those states may lawfully buy as 21+ adults in Oregon, and no official count of such buyers was located. Anecdote about “Californians/Washingtonians shopping in Oregon” without a source is not included as fact in this report.

4.4 Medical reciprocity — none

  • Oregon does not recognise out-of-state medical cards. Secondary sources agree: Weedmaps (Oregon law guide) — “While there is no reciprocity for out-of-state medical marijuana patients, non-residents aged 21 and older can purchase cannabis from the adult-use market”; Leafwell reciprocity guide — “Oregon does not recognize out-of-state medical cannabis cards”; OregonStateCannabis medical guide — “Oregon makes no provisions for medical marijuana reciprocity … you cannot purchase medical marijuana if you are a visiting patient.”
  • Sources (secondary): https://weedmaps.com/learn/laws-and-regulations/oregon ; https://leafwell.com/blog/states-medical-marijuana-card-reciprocity ; https://oregonstatecannabis.org/medical — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Official confirmation [Verify]: No OHA/OMMP page stating the no-reciprocity rule in those terms was directly opened in this track. The OMMP FAQ archive (MERCY) states: “At this time, the OMMP is not aware of any ‘reciprocity’ agreements with any other states to honor the Oregon law. This includes even those states that have medical marijuana laws of their own, such as Washington and California.” That is a patient-advocacy FAQ archive, not a current OHA page — official OHA confirmation is [Verify].
  • Source (advocacy archive): http://mercycenters.org/ommp/faqs.html — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Consequences: A Washington or California medical patient visiting Oregon buys (if 21+) as an adult-use buyer, pays the 17% tax, and is subject to adult-use possession limits, not OMMP limits. An Oregon OMMP patient travelling to Washington or California likewise gains no medical purchase right from the OMMP card in those states (Washington/California adult-use purchase at 21+ is the fallback, with their own tax/limits). An OMMP card does not authorise transport of medical marijuana across state lines (ORS 475C.229; federal law).
  • No interstate medical agreement (OMMP reciprocity compact, patient-registry sharing agreement, or tribal medical reciprocity agreement) was located for Oregon with any state or tribe. [Unavailable / none located.]

4.5 Out-of-state buyers — what Oregon retailers must and must not do

  • Retailers must verify age (21+ for adult-use; OMMP card + ID for medical tax-exempt sale) and must not sell above possession/sale limits (ORS 475C.337 maxima — see Parts 0–6, not re-litigated here).
  • Retailers are not required, on any source opened, to ask buyer residence, to refuse non-resident adult-use buyers, or to report buyer residence. A retailer’s voluntary observation (“most cars have Idaho plates”) is not a compliance record.
  • Retailers must not deliver marijuana items out of state, must not facilitate interstate transport (e.g. by packaging for mail/parcel export), and must not sell to a buyer they know intends unlawful interstate export on terms that would make the retailer a party to export — the last point is a general aiding/abetting principle, not a specific OLCC rule quoted here, and is [Verify] against OLCC guidance before compliance use.

4.6 Diversion to other states — official enforcement data only

What counts as diversion evidence here. Only OSP / OLCC / DEA / FBI / HIDTA data that is public is reported, and only with its own limits. Press claims, operator claims, and seizure totals without origin/destination attribution are not presented as diversion rates.

Oregon-Idaho HIDTA initiative seizure totals (OR-ID region, not Oregon-origin diversion). - HIDTA Times, 4th Quarter 2025, Law Enforcement Initiative Activity Report table: - Marijuana: 168,719.7 kg in 2024; 55,135.1 kg year-to-date 2025. - For context in the same table: Cocaine 165.1 kg (2024) / 164.7 kg (YTD 2025); Fentanyl 179.3 kg / 215.4 kg; Heroin 20.5 kg / 28.2 kg; Methamphetamine/Ice 1,568.4 kg / 1,161.6 kg. DTOs/MLOs dismantled/disrupted: 83 in 2024; 83 YTD 2025. Cases opened: 3,523 in 2024; 2,778 YTD 2025. - Source: Oregon-Idaho HIDTA Times, Q4 2025 — http://oridhidta.org/s/HIDTA-Times-4th-Quarter-2025.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 (search-indexed). - Limits (stated, not buried): (1) This is a regional (Oregon + Idaho) initiative total, not an Oregon-only total. (2) It aggregates all marijuana seizures by HIDTA initiatives (illicit grows, interdiction, investigations), not licensed-product diversion. (3) It carries no destination breakdown (how much, if any, was Oregon-grown product seized en route to Idaho, Washington, California, or elsewhere, vs product grown in Idaho, vs product in transit through the region). (4) The sharp 2024→YTD-2025 fall (168,720 kg → 55,135 kg YTD) cannot be read as a fall in diversion without knowing reporting completeness, YTD cut-off date, and whether bulk plant weight vs processed weight is counted consistently — none of which is stated in the excerpt. Do not cite 168,719.7 kg as “Oregon marijuana diverted out of state in 2024.” - Oregon-Idaho HIDTA 2025 Annual Report (calendar year 2025, ISACC): initiatives reported seizing 59,199.2 kg + 1,482,162 dosage units of illicit drugs in total (all drugs); 1,746 arrests; 856 firearms; 2 THC extraction labs / 1 marijuana-extract production lab context in the excerpt (clandestine-lab counts are garbled in search-indexed form and are not relied on here beyond noting their existence). - Source: http://oridhidta.org/s/Oregon-Idaho-HIDTA-2025-Annual-Report-FINAL.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 (search-indexed). - Oregon-Idaho HIDTA 2027 Threat Assessment (June 2026, ISACC): illegal-marijuana grow-operation seizures in Oregon “have generally stabilized since 2023”; “the volume of products and plants seized in 2025 fell by 66 percent from the previous year, [while] enforcement resources were heavily committed to several large, complex [operations]” (sentence truncated in excerpt — the reason for the fall is therefore not stated here as fact beyond resource commitment). The assessment also notes HIDTA interdiction in 2025 seized >289 kg during traffic stops on I-5 and Highway 97 in Oregon and I-15 in Idaho (methamphetamine context in that paragraph — do not attribute that 289 kg to marijuana) and 134 kg in ten passenger encounters (same methamphetamine paragraph). Those figures are not marijuana-diversion figures and are noted here only to prevent misattribution. - Source: https://oridhidta.org/s/2027-Oregon-Idaho-HIDTA-Threat-Assessment-FINAL.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 (search-indexed). - County illustrations (same limits apply): Josephine County HIDTA trend report (April 2026): 20,390 kg in plants seized in 2025 (bulk marijuana, Josephine County task forces; DEA-Medford / OSP DHE statewide seizures not broken out by county). Washington County trend report (April 2026): just over 55 kg of marijuana plants and THC products seized in 2025, down significantly over two years, with Washington County described as “one of the production areas for illicit marijuana in the state.” Washington County 2024 comparison in the March 2025 report: bulk seizures surged from 86 kg (2023) to 3,244 kg (2024). These county swings illustrate enforcement-operation effects, not a stable diversion trend. - Sources: http://oridhidta.org/s/Josephine-County-Trend-Report-2026.pdf ; http://oridhidta.org/s/Washington-County-Trend-Report-2026.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 (search-indexed). - OSP / OLCC / DEA / FBI diversion-specific data [Unavailable in this track]: No OSP annual report diversion table, no OLCC CTS diversion audit, no DEA Oregon-origin seizure-by-destination table, and no FBI Uniform Crime Reporting diversion breakdown was located in the sources searched. If a future audit requires a diversion rate, it must be commissioned from HIDTA ISACC / OSP DHE / DEA with an explicit origin-destination methodology — it cannot be derived from the totals above. - Illicit grows vs licensed diversion — distinction: HIDTA and OSP enforcement in southern Oregon (Josephine, Jackson, Douglas counties) and central Oregon has historically targeted unlicensed / illicit grows, including labour-trafficking and environmental cases, not (on the evidence in this track) systematic diversion of OLCC-tracked licensed product. The HIDTA totals above do not distinguish licensed vs unlicensed origin. Any statement that “licensed Oregon cannabis is diverted at rate X” is unsupported on this track’s sources and must not be made.

5. Federal land in Oregon — possession and use rules

General rule (federal law controls on federal land, regardless of Oregon law). Possession or use of marijuana is prohibited on all federal land in Oregon — National Parks, National Forests, Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land, National Wildlife Refuges, military installations, federal buildings, and federal road systems through those lands — even if the person is 21+, even if the amount is within Oregon’s possession limits, and even (per NPS/Forest Service statements) if the person holds a state medical card. Hemp that qualifies as hemp under federal law is a different product from marijuana for this purpose, but a hemp product that exceeds the federal hemp THC definition, or a marijuana product mislabelled as hemp, is treated as marijuana on federal land. The coming federal hemp redefinition (after 11 Dec 2026) will affect that boundary — [Verify after 11 Dec 2026.]

Crater Lake National Park — verbatim NPS statement (official, search-indexed). Crater Lake is Oregon’s only National Park, in Klamath / Douglas / Jackson county border country (park headquarters in Klamath County). Its NPS Laws & Policies page states:

“Crater Lake National Park is an area of exclusive federal jurisdiction. All law enforcement functions within the park are carried out by commissioned park rangers within the Division of Resource and Visitor Protection who are duly appointed federal law enforcement officers. … Marijuana on Federal Lands — Recreational marijuana was legalized in the state of Oregon on July 1, 2015. That Oregon state law, however, as well as the previous state law that legalized marijuana for medical purposes, has no bearing on federal laws and regulations which continue to identify marijuana as a Schedule I illegal drug and prohibit its use. Possession or use of any amount of marijuana, even for medical purposes with a valid state medical marijuana card, is prohibited in Crater Lake National Park, its facilities, concessions, and campgrounds. Violations are punishable by a fine of not more than $5,000 for an individual or $10,000 for an organization, or imprisonment for not more than six months, or both (18 USC 3559 and 3571).“

  • Source: U.S. National Park Service, Crater Lake National Park, Laws & Policies — https://home.nps.gov/crla/learn/management/lawsandpolicies.htm — accessed 2026-11-01 (search-indexed; direct open not completed in this track — the Schedule I wording on the page pre-dates the given 28 Apr 2026 Schedule III medical baseline, so the page’s “Schedule I” label must not be quoted as current federal scheduling for state-licensed medical without the §2.11 / baseline qualification. The prohibition itself (possession/use of any amount, including medical-card possession, prohibited in the park) is the operative point, and its current enforcement after Schedule III medical rescheduling is [Verify] — no NPS update to the Crater Lake page reflecting Schedule III was located).
  • Jurisdiction note: “Exclusive federal jurisdiction” at Crater Lake means commissioned rangers enforce federal law; the page also notes rangers have authority to enforce applicable Oregon criminal statutes and the vehicle code. That concurrent-enforcement authority does not make Oregon’s marijuana legalisation apply in the park.

National Forests — Forest Service position (official, via Recreation.gov campground pages and Forest Service statements). Mt. Hood National Forest campground pages (e.g. Stone Creek, Hoodview, Lake Harriet — all Timothy Lake / Mt. Hood area) state identically:

“Cannabis: Please remember that Timothy Lake is on federal lands. While cannabis is legal in Oregon, possession and use are illegal on National Forest lands including in campgrounds.”

  • Sources (official Recreation.gov / Forest Service partnership pages): Stone Creek Campground — https://www.recreation.gov/camping/campgrounds/10208831?tab=info ; Hoodview Campground — https://www.recreation.gov/camping/campgrounds/232867?tab=info ; Lake Harriet Campground — https://www.recreation.gov/camping/campgrounds/232856?tab=info — all accessed 2026-11-01 (search-indexed).
  • The Forest Service’s general statement as reported to GearJunkie (secondary reporting of a Forest Service statement) is: “State laws, which allow recreational cannabis use, have no bearing on Federal law, which continues to identify cannabis as a Schedule I illegal drug, and prohibit its use and possession” and “That includes but is not limited to all federally managed lands including National Forests, Bureau of Land Management, National Parks/Monuments, etc. AND their road systems.” The Schedule I label in that statement likewise pre-dates / does not reflect the given Schedule III medical baseline — same qualification as Crater Lake.
  • Source (secondary): https://gearjunkie.com/outdoor/weed-laws-public-land — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Scope in Oregon: Oregon contains 11 National Forests in whole or part (including Mt. Hood, Willamette, Deschutes, Rogue River–Siskiyou, Umpqua, Fremont–Winema, Malheur, Ochoco, Wallowa–Whitman, Siuslaw, Umatilla — list is general knowledge, not a Part 10 finding; the operative point is that National Forest land covers a large share of Oregon, especially in the Cascades and eastern Oregon, so the federal-land prohibition affects a large share of outdoor recreation and a large share of illicit-grow enforcement geography). No forest-by-forest cannabis-enforcement count was located — [Unavailable].

BLM, Wildlife Refuges, military, federal buildings, mail, airports. - BLM land (extensive in eastern Oregon, including Malheur, Harney, Lake counties) is federal land on the same rule: marijuana possession/use prohibited; BLM law-enforcement rangers enforce federal law. No BLM-Oregon cannabis-specific page was opened in this track — the rule is stated from the Forest Service/NPS general federal-land principle, [Verify] against a BLM Oregon page for a BLM-specific citation if needed. - Military installations (e.g. in Oregon, National Guard facilities, Camp Rilea / Camp Withycombe contexts — no installation-specific cannabis page was located): federal law and military orders prohibit marijuana possession/use on installations, independent of Oregon law. [Verify] installation by installation. - Federal buildings and courthouses: 18 U.S.C. § 930 and building rules prohibit marijuana (and firearms) in federal facilities; possession in a federal courthouse/building is a federal matter, not an Oregon possession-limit matter. - Mail / parcel: Placing marijuana in mail/parcel delivery is both an ORS 475C.229 “export” act (if for-hire mode, see §3.1) and a federal offence (21 U.S.C. §§ 841, 843, 844 as applicable; USPS prohibition). Hemp shipped by mail must meet the federal hemp definition and carrier requirements — carrier policies (USPS/UPS/FedEx hemp rules) were not researched in this track — [Verify] with the carrier before shipping hemp. - Airports: Portland International Airport (PDX) is not federal land in the same sense as a National Park, but TSA / federal air-transport rules and destination-state law govern carriage by air; carrying marijuana on a flight, even intrastate or to another legal state, is interstate / federal transport. No PDX-specific cannabis policy page was opened in this track — [Verify] against Port of Portland / TSA guidance before advising travellers. The safe general statement is: do not fly with marijuana bought in Oregon, even to another legal state.

Federal-land cultivation. Cultivation on federal land (National Forest / BLM grows, whether by organised groups or individuals) is a federal offence and a major HIDTA/Forest Service enforcement category (see §4.6 illicit-grow context). Licensed Oregon cultivation must be on non-federal land (or on tribal trust land under tribal licence/compact, which is a different jurisdiction — trust land is not “federal public land” for Forest Service/BLM purposes, though it is held in trust by the United States). Do not conflate tribal trust land with National Forest / BLM public land.

Interaction with Schedule III medical baseline — [Verify]. The given baseline (Schedule III for state-licensed medical eff. 28 Apr 2026) raises, but does not answer on Part 10 sources, whether a state-licensed medical possessor’s possession on federal land is now treated differently from adult-use possession. NPS/Forest Service pages opened/indexed still state the pre-rescheduling Schedule I formulation. No updated NPS/Forest Service/BLM guidance reflecting Schedule III was located. Do not advise that medical possession is now lawful on federal land. Flag as [Verify — NPS/FS/BLM guidance update pending].

6. Interstate agreements — complete inventory on sources opened

What is not an interstate agreement (common confusions avoided): - OLCC membership in the Cannabis Regulators Association (CannRA) is a regulators’ association, not an interstate commerce agreement. - DOR cigarette/other-tobacco refund agreements with all nine tribes (and marijuana rebates with two) are tax agreements, not interstate delivery agreements. - HIDTA task-force participation is enforcement coordination, not market access. - A tribal member’s individual OMMP participation, or a tribal entity’s OLCC licence for an off-reservation facility (if any — none identified here), is state licensing, not an interstate agreement.

Part 11 headlines (operations only)

  • Testing is OHA’s rulebook, OLCC’s licence, ORELAP’s accreditation — three gates, not one. A lab must be ORELAP-accredited (OAR 333 Div. 64, TNI 2016) AND OLCC-licensed (OAR 845-025-5030) before it may sample or test; exercising privileges without accreditation is a Category I violation. No marijuana item may be sold/transferred before passing OAR 333 Div. 7 testing.
  • Sampling is lab-only and batch-representative. Only lab personnel sample; the whole batch must be available; adding kief/concentrate to a sample is a Category I potency-misrepresentation violation — the basis of the 2026 lab/producer enforcement wave.
  • Failed tests have a fixed clock: 7 days to request reanalysis, 30 days for retesting, 24 hours for the lab to report the failure to the overseeing agency. Remediation is available only for the item/test combinations OAR 333-007-0450 allows; otherwise the batch is held for destruction and may not be destroyed without agency direction/permission.
  • Transfers, not new applications, are the market. Under HB 4121 caps, producer/processor/wholesaler/retailer entry is by change of ownership (≥51% = new application in the draft-rule formulation; current-rule threshold Verify — see §11.2.1) or change of location ($1,000). Renewal is annual (licences) / 5-year (worker permits) / 3-year (research certificate) and is gated on tax compliance for retailers and on continued accreditation for labs.
  • No Oregon ownership cap was confirmed on an opened official page. Run 1 Part 4 §4.10 left this Verify; Part 11 leaves it Verify. Do not advise a cap figure without the current OAR 845-025 text.
  • No general insurance or bonding minimum was located in the OLCC rules returned. That absence is reported as a gap (§11.2.8), not filled by analogy to other states. What IS required is a security plan, locked storage, and — for delivery — a lockable container, GPS and alarm (§11.4).
  • Security retention is 90 days on-site (30 days off-site backup in the OLCC premises checklist; the off-site figure is checklist-derived — Verify against OAR 845-025-1450 text). Cameras 24/7, 720p minimum, 10 fps minimum, clear image within 15 ft of every entry/exit — secondary-vendor restatement of OAR 845-025-1440/1450, flagged accordingly; the checklist confirms 24-hour recording, date/time stamp, 90-day on-site retention.
  • Waste, water, pesticides and energy are four different regulators. Waste: OLCC OAR 845-025-7750 + DEQ (DEQ does not regulate marijuana air emissions as such — see §11.5). Water: Water Resources Department (WRD) water-rights enforcement against illegal grows is a real enforcement track, distinct from OLCC licensing. Pesticides: ODA pesticide rules + OAR 333-007 pesticide testing panel. Energy: no statewide cannabis energy code was located — Verify (§11.6.5).
  • Sampling/giveaways/discounts/promotions are tightly bounded: trade samples and trade-show privileges (SB 558, 2025 — Verify chapter/operative date), no marijuana as a prize, no sale below cost as a promotion device in the rule as returned — each proposition in §11.7 is flagged to its rule or marked Verify where the rule text was not opened.
  • Worker permits are the drug-testing story for industry staff, not general employment drug testing. General Oregon employment law has no comprehensive private-employer drug-testing statute and no off-duty protection (Run 1 §1.8); industry staff must hold a $100/5-year OLCC permit, pass a 70% education test, and pass an OLCC background check, with denial grounds in OAR 845-025-5500 series (§11.8).
  • Research is a real but tiny licence class: 1 active research certificate (late Sep 2026). OSU’s Global Hemp Innovation Center is the university anchor for hemp research, but its work runs primarily under ODA hemp licensing and federal/state research authority, not solely under an OLCC research certificate — the two routes are kept distinct in §11.9.

11.1 Testing

11.1.1 Who writes the testing rules, who enforces them

  • OHA writes the testing rules for BOTH markets. OHA Marijuana Testing Requirements page (opened directly 2026-11-01): “The Oregon Health Authority (OHA) is responsible for cannabis testing rules that apply to both the medical and retail market.” — https://www.oregon.gov/OHA/PH/DiseasesConditions/ChronicDisease/MedicalMarijuanaProgram/Pages/testing.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Scope of the OHA testing rules as stated on that page: “All marijuana items and industrial hemp-derived vapor items must be sampled and tested according to OAR 333-007-0300 to 333-007-0600 and OAR 333-064-0100 to 333-064-0130. ORELAP sampling protocols must also be followed.” — same page, accessed 2026-11-01. Note the range to 333-007-0600 on the OHA page vs the older 333-007-0300 to 333-007-0490 range cited inside OAR 845-025-5700/5030 — the OHA page range is the broader, later statement; the difference (rules 0500–0600, covering quality-control/R&D and later additions) is flagged Verify against the current Division 7 table of contents before citing a single range.
  • OLCC enforces through licensing. OAR 845-025-5700 (opened directly 2026-11-01): “(1) Licensees must comply with the Authority’s testing rules in OAR 333-007-0300 to 333-007-0490 and OAR 333, division 64 prior to the sale or transfer of a marijuana item, as specified in those rules” — https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_845-025-5700 — accessed 2026-11-01. “(3) A violation of this rule is a Category I violation.” — same rule.
  • No sale/transfer before passing tests. OHA page (opened): “All marijuana items transferred or sold to a dispensary or retail shop must be accompanied by documentation of passing test results.” — same page. Pre-tested items are quarantined under OAR 845-025-5720 (see §11.1.4).
  • ODA hemp testing mirrors marijuana testing by statute (secondary summary, Morning Ag Clips, undated in return, accessed 2026-11-01): “The Oregon Department of Agriculture (ODA) is required by law to adopt hemp testing rules that mirror the marijuana testing rules.” — https://www.morningagclips.com/microbiological-contaminant-testing-update/ — secondary, accessed 2026-11-01. The underlying ODA hemp-testing rule citation was not opened in this run — Verify (OAR 603 Div. 48 testing provisions, Part 7 territory for full treatment).
