The OLCC licence application (LUCS, premises) does not substitute for a WRD water-right determination — Verify the current OLCC/WRD application cross-check (whether OLCC requires proof of water right / WRD statement at application or renewal) on the OLCC application pages; no such cross-check was confirmed on an opened page in this run.
  • Startup-cost implication (Run 1 §4.12): water rights are listed there as a cost/risk item for a Tier II producer transfer (“Land/premises, water rights (see Part 5, WRD)”) — the water right, not the licence fee, may be the binding constraint on an outdoor producer.

11.6.2 Water Resources Department enforcement against illegal grows

  • WRD enforcement framework — now established from OWRD + statute + a 2026 enforcement case (search results, accessed 2026-11-01):
  • WRD is the water-rights regulator (ORS 537; WRD watermaster enforcement, including regulation/shut-off of unlawful diversions and enforcement against unpermitted groundwater use).
  • Illegal (unlicensed) cannabis cultivation is separately subject to OLCC/OHA enforcement, law-enforcement eradication, and — where it diverts water without a right — WRD enforcement. The Task Force on Cannabis-Derived Intoxicants and Illegal Cannabis Production (HB 3000 (2021), expanded by SB 1564 (2022) — Run 1 §1.2.1) is the interagency coordination vehicle for illegal-production enforcement, including water.
  • HB 4121 (2024) re-enacted interagency inspection/enforcement provisions (HB 3000 §§40, 41a, 42–44) that had sunset 1 Jan 2024 (Run 1 §1.2.1) — the interagency enforcement authority (OLCC/ODA/OHA/WRD coordination) rests in part on those provisions.
  • HB 4061 (2022) — water-hauling law (OWRD page, search result, accessed 2026-11-01): “The 2022 Oregon Legislature passed House Bill 4061 to deter water use on unlicensed cannabis, both marijuana and hemp, growing sites. All provisions of the bill are effective June 3, 2022.” — https://www.oregon.gov/owrd/programs/regulation/Pages/2022-Water-Hauling-Laws-and-Cannabis-Laws.aspx — OWRD page, accessed 2026-11-01. Duties/prohibitions as stated there: a person purchasing water from a water supplier at a fire hydrant, water fill station, or other distribution location, to haul water to another location for irrigation or nursery purposes, must (1) maintain records for 12 months from purchase, and (2) present those records to law enforcement or OWRD on request. “It is prohibited to haul water or arrange to haul water to any cannabis site that has more than four cannabis plants (marijuana or hemp) not licensed with [OLCC], [ODA], or [OHA].” “A person is prohibited from willfully or negligently providing false information to either the Department or law enforcement regarding the hauling of water to a cannabis site.” Penalties as stated there: use of water without a water right on unregistered cannabis, and false-information offences, “may be punishable by civil penalties consistent with the Department[’s] other authorities (OAR 690-260)” and false information “up to a Class A misdemeanor, which is punishable by up to one year in prison and up to a $6,250 fine”; failure to retain/provide hauling records “may be subject to civil penalties consistent with the Department[’s] other authorities (OAR 690-260).” Secondary summary (JD Supra, 2022 session, accessed 2026-11-01) adds a $25,000 maximum fine characterisation for hauling/arranging haulage to an unregistered/unlicensed site or false information — https://www.jdsupra.com/post/contentViewerEmbed.aspx?fid=b5da5434-37e7-411a-a2d5-a1c4645ee528 — the $25,000 figure is secondary and conflicts in scope with the OWRD page’s $6,250 Class A misdemeanor figure; Verify the controlling penalty (civil vs criminal, per-violation vs per-day) in HB 4061 enrolled text / ORS 537.387 companion provisions before quoting either as the maximum.
  • ORS 537.387 — Limitations on water use related to Cannabis plants (search result, accessed 2026-11-01): “(1) At a location described in subsection (2) … a person may not: Use, store or divert any waters under ORS 537.130 (Permit to appropriate water required); Use or attempt to use any ground water under ORS 537.535 (Unlawful use or appropriation of ground water …); Construct or attempt to construct any well … under ORS 537.535; Collect or use precipitation water from an artificial impervious surface as described in ORS 537.141 …; or Use ground water as described in ORS 537.545 (Exempt uses) (1)(b) or (f). (2) A person may not engage in [such an] action … at a location where plants in the plant Cannabis family Cannabaceae are grown, if: The location … is not licensed or registered under ORS 475C.065 (Production license), 475C.792 (Marijuana grow site registration system) or 571.281 (Grower and handler license); and The number of plants … is greater than the number … allowed under ORS 475C.005 to 475C.525, 475C.770 to 475C.919 or 571.260 to 571.348. [2023 c.209 §3]” — https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_537.387 — search-result rendering, accessed 2026-11-01. Note in that rendering: “537.387 … was enacted into law by the Legislative Assembly but was not added to or made a part of ORS chapter 537 or any series therein by legislative action.” In plain terms: at an unlicensed/unregistered site above the allowed plant count, essentially NO water use is lawful under 537.387 — not surface, not groundwater, not a new well, not impervious-surface precipitation, not the domestic-well exemptions in 537.545(1)(b)/(f). This is the statutory core of WRD illegal-grow enforcement; the 2023 c.209 §3 history ties it to the same 2023 session law that amended ORS 475C.337.
  • 2026 enforcement illustration — Gold Hill, Jackson County (IMET/JCSO release via Oregon Dispatch, ~Oct 2026, “25 days ago” in the search return, accessed 2026-11-01): IMET served search warrants at two neighbouring black-market grows (2000 block of Rogue River Highway, rural Gold Hill); Jackson County Code Enforcement cited $887,710 for an unauthorised hydrocarbon extraction facility (butane) + failure to obtain land-use approval for marijuana production; investigators seized 1,221 illegal plants, 1,851 lbs processed cannabis, 12 BHO jars, $17,900 cash; “There was no licensing for any type of cannabis growing, handling, or processing at either of the locations.” WRD role: “Oregon Water Resources Department District 13 Watermasters will issue three separate Notices of Violation (NOV) to the responsible party for three separate well locations. Despite being a paying patron of the Gold Hill Irrigation District and with the canal running through the properties, it was observed that both grow operations were not diverting water from the irrigation district source water during the time of the Watermaster’s investigation. According to Oregon Water Law it is unpermitted to use domestic well water for a commercial grow operation or to water beyond 1/2 acre. Water violations of this kind are subject to both civil and criminal penalties.” The Watermaster received anonymous calls in early September about tenants taking more canal water than allowed, drying up the allotted source; IMET acted after reports of irrigation water drying up. — https://www.oregondispatch.com/43075153/after-taking-reports-of-irrigation-water-drying-up-task-force-serves-search-warrants-at-two-neighboring-black-market-cannabis-grows-discover-clandestine-lab-1800-lbs-processed-illegal-marijuana-code-enforcement-fines-nearly-900000-video? — secondary republication of a sheriff/task-force release, accessed 2026-11-01. Treat the $887,710 as a county code-enforcement citation, NOT a WRD penalty; the WRD actions are the three NOVs (penalty amounts, if any, not stated in the release). Do not present the Gold Hill NOVs as adjudicated WRD penalties.
  • Domestic-well limit (as stated in the Gold Hill release): domestic well water may not be used for a commercial grow, nor to water beyond 1/2 acre — Verify the 1/2-acre domestic-well exemption scope in ORS 537.545 before generalising (the release states it as the Watermaster’s position in that investigation, not as a quoted statute). Secondary legal commentary (Super Lawyers, accessed 2026-11-01) notes the practical enforcement difficulty: OWRD senior policy staff are quoted that whether medical growers diverting for profit are illegally irrigating with domestic wells “is tough for the agency to answer” and “The regulatory mechanism is not set up to do audits, but to take growers at their word” — https://wp.superlawyers.com/resources/cannabis-law/oregon/water-theft-in-the-world-of-weed/ — secondary, accessed 2026-11-01. That commentary also asserts (secondary, Verify) that a legal cultivator “must register with [OLCC], and in that registration must prove they have a right to the water they will use” — this proof-of-water-right-at-registration proposition is secondary-only and is the same Verify item as §11.6.1’s OLCC/WRD cross-check; do not state it as rule text.
  • Remaining WRD Verify items: WRD civil-penalty amounts actually assessed in illegal-grow NOVs (vs the OAR 690-260 framework); whether WRD issues shut-off/regulation orders against illegal grows as a routine tool; WRD–OLCC–IMET interagency agreement text; any 2025–2026 WRD annual illegal-grow enforcement totals. No WRD annual total was located — do not quote one.

11.6.3 Pesticides

  • Testing panel: usable marijuana, extracts and concentrates must be tested for pesticides (OLCC failure-notification form, §11.1.2); pesticide failure → reanalysis/retesting/destruction track (§11.1.5). OAR 845-025-5700(2) capacity exception (§11.1.4).
  • Which pesticides may be used: ODA regulates pesticide use in Oregon (ORS Chapter 634; ODA pesticide product registration and applicator licensing). For cannabis, ODA maintains a cannabis pesticide list / guidance (products whose labels allow use on cannabis/hemp or that meet ODA criteria) — the current ODA cannabis pesticide list and the OAR 845-025-3200-series processor / OAR 845-025-2000-series producer pesticide-use rules were NOT opened in this run — Verify on ODA pesticide pages and current OAR before advising any product as “allowed”. Do not advise a pesticide as permitted from a vendor list alone.
  • Pesticide applicator licensing: commercial pesticide applicators in Oregon must be licensed by ODA; whether a producer’s own staff applying pesticides to its own crop needs an applicator licence (vs a private applicator / farm exemption) is Verify in ORS 634 / OAR 603 Div. 57.
  • Residue limits: the OAR 333-007 pesticide action levels (which pesticides, at what concentrations, fail) are in the Division 7 testing tables — not opened in this run — Verify in OAR 333-007-0400-series tables. The failure-notification form is the operational document for a pesticide failure, not the action-level table.
  • Hemp pesticides: ODA hemp pesticide rules mirror the marijuana framework in principle (ODA mirror duty, §11.1.1) — Verify in OAR 603 Div. 48.

11.6.4 Other environmental overlays (brief, flagged)

  • Wastewater / stormwater: a licensed facility as a discharger is subject to DEQ water-quality permits where applicable (general DEQ jurisdiction, not a cannabis-specific permit) — Verify facility-by-facility; no cannabis-specific DEQ wastewater permit was located.
  • Air / odour: DEQ does not regulate marijuana air emissions as such (search excerpt, §11.5 — Verify full DEQ page sentence). Odour is primarily a local land-use / nuisance matter (Part 3 territory) and a LUCS consideration, not a statewide OLCC air permit.
  • Land use / farm use: cannabis production on farmland (EFU zoning, farm-use definitions) is a Part 3 / county land-use question; OLCC licensure requires a LUCS showing the use is allowed in the zone (Run 1 §§4.3, 4.10). No statewide “cannabis is / is not farm use” proposition is stated here — Verify in ORS 215 / county code for the specific parcel.
  • Hemp environmental rules: ODA hemp programme (soil, water, pesticide, seed) — Part 7 territory; §11.6.1 water-rights principle applies equally to hemp irrigation.

11.6.5 Energy — GAP REPORTED

  • No statewide Oregon cannabis energy code, energy-use reporting duty, or lighting-efficiency standard for OLCC producers was located in the material returned in this run. No energy figure (kWh per gram, lighting wattage cap, Energy Trust programme requirement) is stated here.
  • What exists in adjacent law (not a cannabis energy rule): Oregon energy code (building code) applies to structures generally; utility energy-efficiency programmes (Energy Trust of Oregon) are voluntary incentives, not OLCC licence conditions, unless a local jurisdiction conditions a permit on them — Verify locally. Do not import other states’ cannabis energy rules (e.g. Illinois/Massachusetts energy standards) into Oregon.
  • Indoor-production energy is operationally material (artificial lighting defines “indoor” — §11.3.2) but the rulebooks returned set no energy cap. Follow-up: OLCC/ODOE energy guidance, if any, and local (Portland / city) energy codes for indoor grows.

11.7 Sampling, giveaways, discounts and promotions

11.7.1 Trade samples (licensee-to-licensee)

  • SB 558 (2025) — trade-show / trade-sample privileges (Verify chapter/operative date, Run 1 H11): cited in OLCC 9 Sep 2025 draft proposed rules as legislative implementation (OLCC draft: http://cms.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/rules/Draft-Proposed-2025-Cannabis.pdf — Run 1). The current trade-sample rule (OAR 845-025-2900-series / trade-sample rule number, quantities, Metrc recording, who may receive samples) was NOT opened in this run — Verify in current OAR and the OLCC trade-sample guidance before advising any sample quantity or recipient.
  • General principle (established): samples for testing are lab samples under Division 7 (§11.1.4), NOT trade samples. Trade samples are a separate commercial privilege (marketing to other licensees / buyers), recorded in Metrc, and subject to the same testing-pass requirement before transfer for sale — the testing status of trade samples themselves (whether a trade sample must pass full compliance testing before transfer to another licensee for evaluation) is Verify in the trade-sample rule; do not assume trade samples are exempt from testing.
  • Trade shows: SB 558 expands licence privileges at trade shows (Run 1 H11). Trade-show rule details (on-site consumption bans, sample distribution at shows, temporary premises) are Verify.

11.7.2 Consumer samples, giveaways, prizes

  • No marijuana as a prize: processor checklist: “A licensee may not offer marijuana as a prize” (OAR 845-025-1300 as cited on the checklist — https://data.templateroller.com/pdf_docs/2284/22840/2284082/main_marijuana-processor-inspection-checklist-oregon.pdf — search result, accessed 2026-11-01). Lake Oswego code summary likewise lists licensee prohibitions under OAR 845-025-1300.
  • Retailer discretionary free provision to patients: Run 1 §4.5 (secondary summary, Washington/Oregon comparison — Verify for Oregon specifically): a retailer with a medical endorsement may, at its discretion, provide cannabis at no charge to qualifying patients/caregivers. Do not generalise this to free provision to adult-use consumers.
  • Gifting (consumer-to-consumer, not licensee promotion): permitted within possession limits, without consideration; any lottery, service fee, contribution or indirect payment is treated as a sale and must go through a licensed retailer (Run 1 §1.1, gifting section number Verify — ORS 475C.301/305). A licensee “buy X, get free Y” promotion that is in substance a sale of Y is not saved by calling Y a “gift” — Verify the promotion rule (OAR 845-025-8000-series / 2800-series) before designing any bundled-free-item offer.
  • Consumer sampling at retail (tasting / on-site consumption): on-site consumption is prohibited (retailer signage “No On-Site Consumption”, OAR 845-025-2840(2), Run 1 §1.6.2; public-use ban ORS 475C.377, Run 1 §1.1). No retail tasting/sample-consumption privilege exists on the material returned — Verify whether any licensed on-site consumption (hospitality) licence type exists in current OAR; Run 1 Part 4 lists no hospitality licence type for Oregon, unlike some other states.

11.7.3 Discounts, promotions, advertising (operations-relevant limits)

  • Advertising test (2025, Run 1 §1.6.2): HB 3724 (2025 Laws ch. 68) changes the ORS 475C test from “attractive to minors” to advertising “likely to cause minors to unlawfully possess marijuana or marijuana items” (amending ORS 475C.017 and 475C.612 per OLCC overview). Verify the amended ORS text and whether OAR 845-025-8000-series rules have been conformed — no advertising prohibition is quoted verbatim in this draft.
  • Secondary summary of the OAR advertising position (use with caution, Run 1 §1.6.2): advertising restricted under OAR 845-025-8000, with signage limits and a ban on content designed to appeal to minors (including cartoon imagery); permitted: ads in adult-oriented media with reasonable age-audience targeting (CannBus summary — secondary, not a rule quote). Do not advise on a specific ad format from this summary alone.
  • Discount/promotion-specific rule: No standalone discount, coupon, loyalty, or below-cost promotion rule was confirmed on an opened official page in this run. Tax is 17% on the retail sales price (Part 2 territory); whether discounts reduce the taxable price, and whether loyalty points / coupons are treated as consideration, are Part 2 questions — Verify in ORS 475C.682 / DOR marijuana-tax guidance before designing a discount programme. The only promotion-adjacent rule confirmed here is the no-prize rule (§11.7.2) and the advertising test above.
  • Packaging/labelling as promotion limits: labels may not contain untruthful/misleading statements or health claims unsupported by the totality of publicly available scientific evidence with significant scientific agreement among qualified experts (OAR 845-025-7030(2)(a), Run 1 §1.6.1); packages/labels require OLCC pre-approval ($100 package, $100 label, $25 change, $25 transfer — Run 1 §4.2) and approval may be denied if attractive to minors / misleading / non-compliant (OAR 845-025-7160, Run 1 §1.6.1).

11.7.4 What is NOT a promotion rule (avoiding overstatement)

  • No “happy hour”, “bulk discount ban”, or “minimum price” rule for Oregon cannabis was located in this run. Do not import other states’ discount bans. If a local jurisdiction restricts promotions (e.g. signage hours in Lake Oswego: retailers “may only sell to consumers between the hours of 10:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m.” under that city’s code — https://ecode360.com/43165577 — municipal, not statewide), it is a local rule (Part 3), not an OLCC promotion rule.

11.8 Drug testing, background checks and OLCC worker permits (licence holders and staff)

11.8.1 Reconciliation with Run 1 — two different drug-testing questions

Run 1 Part 1 §1.8 answers the GENERAL employment question: Oregon has no general statutory protection for off-duty cannabis use or for a positive cannabis test, for adult-use consumers or OMMP patients; no comprehensive private-employer drug-testing statute; employers may test and act on a positive THC result, including off-duty use (secondary analyses, Verify against case law incl. Emerald Steel Fabricators, Inc. v. Bureau of Labor & Industries, 348 Or. 159 (2010)); ORS 475C.780 (medical: nothing requires an employer to accommodate medical use in the workplace) and ORS 475C.013 (adult-use statutes may not be construed to amend employment law) — both Verify verbatim. SB 176 (2025) employment protections for medical patients DIED 27 June 2025. Part 11 does not change any of that. This section covers the SEPARATE industry question: who may work for a licensee, on what permit and background check — and it does NOT impose a drug test on industry staff as a permit condition on the material returned (see §11.8.4).

11.8.2 Who needs a worker permit (ORS 475C.269, verbatim, Run 1 §1.2.2)

ORS 475C.269 (Justia 2025 ORS, https://law.justia.com/codes/oregon/volume-14/chapter-475c/section-475c-269/ — Run 1):

“(1) An individual who performs work for or on behalf of a licensee or a laboratory licensed under ORS 475C.548 must have a valid permit or temporary permit issued by the Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission under ORS 475C.273 if the individual participates in: (a) The delivery, possession, production, propagation, processing, sampling, securing, selling or testing of marijuana items at the premises or laboratory for which the license has been issued; (b) The recording of [that activity]; or (c) The verification of any document described in ORS 475C.217. (2) A licensee or a laboratory … must verify that an individual has a valid permit or temporary permit … before allowing the individual to perform, or continue to perform, any work described in subsection (1) … [Formerly 475B.261; 2022 c.117 §4; 2024 c.16 §27]”

  • Scope in practice (Run 1 §4.6, OLCC worker-permit page, search result, https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/Pages/Marijuana-Worker-Permits.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01 in Run 1): “Persons employed in the OLCC-licensed recreational marijuana industry, including licensees themselves, must have a valid Marijuana Worker Permit. All employees, including seasonal employees, need one.” Delivery drivers must hold and carry the permit while delivering (ORS 475C.117(3), §11.4.4).
  • Scale (Run 1 §4.6): OLCC May 2026 licensing presentation: 51,800 worker permits in its 2025 licensing snapshot; “160k+ active permits” on a separate slide appears to include alcohol service permits — conflict/ambiguity flagged, do not quote 160,000 as marijuana worker permits (http://cms.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/commission_agendas/2026/OLCC-Licensing-Program-Presentation-May2026.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01 in Run 1). A 2027–29 budget narrative (secondary, Oct 2026) rounds to ~50,000 permittees. Use 51,800 (OLCC May 2026) as the most recent OLCC-sourced figure located.

11.8.3 Worker-permit eligibility, process, fee, term, education/test

  • Age: 21+ to be eligible (Run 1 §4.6, OLCC page).
  • Application route: CAMP, https://camp.olcc.online/ (stated on the OLCC page).
  • Education/test: review the Recreational Marijuana Worker Permit Education material and pass the test with at least 70%; upload the Certificate of Completion and a valid photo ID (secondary, Vangst state-requirements page, https://app.vangst.com/reports/state-requirements/oregon — accessed 2026-11-01 in Run 1; Verify the current education/test steps on the OLCC page itself). “All marijuana workers take the same test, allowing movement between jobs in the industry” (OLCC page, search result, Run 1).
  • Fee/term: $100, due on application submission; permit term five years (Run 1 §4.2, OLCC fee page opened in Run 1). Task-brief effective date for OAR 845-025-5500 (31 Mar 2025) was NOT independently confirmed on an opened OAR page in this run — Verify.
  • Background check: “A separate background check is required for the worker-permit application, processed directly by OLCC” (OLCC page, search result, Run 1). Licence-application background checks are $50 per individual listed, if the check is not part of an initial/renewal application (Run 1 §4.2) — whether the $50 figure also applies to worker-permit checks, or whether the worker-permit check is included in the $100 fee, is Verify on the OLCC worker-permit page / OAR 845-025-5500-series.
  • Incomplete-application clock: if OLCC requests additional information, the applicant has two weeks to provide it / complete corrections; failure results in the application being considered incomplete and inactivated, and any Temporary Permit becomes invalid at inactivation — the applicant must reapply (OLCC page, search result, Run 1).
  • Temporary permits: HB 4121 (2024) included temporary-permit authority for workers (Run 1 §1.2.1). Temporary-permit duration, scope, and whether a temporary permit allows plant-touching work before the full permit issues are Verify in OAR 845-025-5500-series / ORS 475C.273.

11.8.4 Denial grounds — worker permits (secondary summary, Verify in rule)

Secondary summary (Vangst, accessed 2026-11-01 in Run 1 — Verify in OAR 845-025-5500 et seq.):

  • Must deny if: under 21; or a marijuana licence/worker permit was revoked for violation of ORS 475C.005–475C.525 (now ORS 475C — Verify current citation) within two years of application.
  • May deny if: felony conviction for possession/manufacture/delivery of a controlled substance within three years; felony crime of violence within three years; felony crime of dishonesty/deception (theft, fraud, forgery) within three years; more than one conviction for listed crimes within five years; violation of the marijuana statutes/rules; or false statement to the Commission.

Drug testing as a permit condition — NOT established: no OLCC worker-permit drug-test requirement (pre-employment, random, or post-incident testing of permittees by OLCC) was located in the material returned. Licensees as employers may impose their own drug-testing policies under general Oregon employment law (§11.8.1), but that is an employer policy, not an OLCC permit condition on the material returned. Verify in OAR 845-025-5500-series before stating either that OLCC requires or that OLCC prohibits permittee drug testing.

11.8.5 Background checks — licence holders / applicants (distinct from worker permits)

  • Licence applicants: background checks on individuals listed on the application ($50 per individual if not part of an initial/renewal application — Run 1 §4.2). The full applicant background-check scope (fingerprints, FBI/Oregon State Police checks, look-back periods, disqualifying convictions for applicants vs worker permittees) is in OAR 845-025-1030/1115 — not opened in this run — Verify. Do not apply the worker-permit denial windows (§11.8.4) to licence applicants without checking the applicant rule.
  • OMMP growers (PRMG): subject to OMMP criminal-history check (Run 1 §4.7). Scope/look-back Verify in OAR 333-008.
  • ODA hemp key participants: $75 each (Run 1 §4.8); key participants are members, officers, owners, and others authorised to make changes (ODA grower application rev. 11/2025). Hemp background-check scope (FBI fingerprinting under the USDA plan) is Verify in OAR 603 Div. 48 / USDA plan — do not assume it matches the OLCC check.

11.8.6 Labour-peace / collective-bargaining overlay (for completeness, not a permit rule)

  • Measure 119 (2024) labour-peace requirement was struck down by a U.S. District Court (reported 20 May 2025) and repealed by HB 4162 (2026 Laws ch. 73), effective 1 Jan 2027 (Run 1 H11). Do not advise that Measure 119 currently imposes an operative duty without checking the Ninth Circuit disposition and the repeal’s effective-date mechanics. General Oregon labour law (wages, safety, workers’ compensation) applies to cannabis workers as to other workers; no cannabis-specific wage/safety code was located in this run.

11.9.1 OLCC research certificate — the licence

  • Fee/term: $4,750 for a three-year term (Run 1 §4.2, OLCC fee page opened in Run 1).
  • What it allows (general): research with marijuana/hemp items, including transfers with licensees as permitted by rule (Run 1 §4.5).
  • Scale: only 1 research certificate active in late Sep 2026 counts (Run 1 H4/§4.5; CannBus Q3 2026, OLCC dataset 28 Sep 2026).

Do not assume it is closed under HB 4121 (which by its terms addresses producer/processor/wholesaler/retailer caps — Run 1 §4.9), and do not assume it is open without checking CAMP.
  • Testing for research holders: a laboratory that collects samples/tests for “research certificate holders must be licensed by the Commission” (OAR 845-025-5030(1)(a), opened — §11.1.6). Research material is therefore inside the Division 7 testing system where testing is required — the research-testing exemptions, if any, are Verify in OAR 845-025-5000-series (research certificate rules) and OAR 333-007-0500 (quality-control/R&D testing).
  • Research-certificate rule numbers, reporting duties, and transfer limits were NOT opened in this run — Verify in OAR 845-025 Division 25 research provisions before advising any research applicant.

11.9.2 Oregon State University — Global Hemp Innovation Center (GHIC)

  • What it is (OSU College of Agricultural Sciences, GHIC page, search result, accessed 2026-11-01): “OSU’s Global Hemp Innovation Center (GHIC) is home to world-leading experts in hemp research, extension, and education and is the most comprehensive of its kind in the nation. GHIC is advancing hemp and its market potential fostering innovation across all segments of the hemp supply chain, leveraging the expertise of faculty from diverse disciplines who partner with federal and state agencies and industry sectors to help solve challenges in meeting the growing demand for food, fiber, chemicals, and other products made from hemp.” — https://agsci.oregonstate.edu/hemp — accessed 2026-11-01. History/scale as stated there and in OSU Extension (search results, accessed 2026-11-01): launched by the College of Agricultural Sciences in 2019 (GHIC Strategic Plan 2025–2030: “Established in June 2019 by the College of Agricultural Sciences (CAS)”); “65 faculty across 19 disciplines conducting research in 10 locations across the state and four locations around the world in Asia and Europe” (GHIC page; the Strategic Plan states “more than 70 leading experts” and “affiliated faculty from eight colleges” — 65 vs 70+ is a version/date difference between the GHIC page and the Strategic Plan; quote with its source and date, do not merge); “As the only hemp seed certifier in the state, and one of only four in the country, OSU is able to provide growers access to a source of certified seed” (GHIC page; OSU Extension: “As the state’s only certified hemp seed provider — and one of only four in the U.S.”). Historical note: “OSU was the site of the country’s only hemp research center from the 1880s to the 1930s” (GHIC page; when OSU was Oregon Agricultural College, working with USDA scientists); “Oregon authorized hemp cultivation in 2009, but [ODA] didn’t license its first hemp grower until 2015. Just three years later, Oregon ranked 3rd in the United States in licensed hemp acres planted behind Montana and Colorado” (GHIC page). HB 2740 (legislature-sponsored bill forming a hemp commission similar to the existing 23 commodity commissions, to direct funding for hemp research) is noted on the GHIC page — Verify HB 2740’s year/status on OLIS before citing it as the GHIC funding authority.
  • Programmes / grants (OSU Extension + trade reporting, search results, accessed 2026-11-01): GHIC hosted the first National Hemp Symposium in 2021 with the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine (Board on Agriculture and Natural Resources 75th anniversary); second Hemp Field Day at the Klamath Basin Research and Extension Center (irrigation, crop performance, market potential); water-quality/application-method trials with UC Davis, underway in five U.S. states, evaluating variety response to regional conditions; Hemp Equity Program allocating 10% of GHIC discretionary resources to equity/inclusion/access, partnering with a historically Black land-grant university and a Hispanic-serving institution (OSU Extension, https://extension.oregonstate.edu/impact/oregon-state-leads-innovation-hemp-research-production-equity — accessed 2026-11-01). Grants (Hemp Gazette, trade reporting, accessed 2026-11-01 — secondary, Verify on USDA NIFA / OSU releases): $5.5 million over five years with USDA Agricultural Research Service for hemp genetics adapted to western U.S. growing conditions, plus food/beverage/biobased products, biodegradable/compostable packaging, building materials, hemp-seed food/beverage products (Centre director quoted as Jeffrey Steiner); $10 million (Mar 2024 reporting) with 13 Native American Tribes / Tribal nations in OR/WA/ID/NV/MT/CA for hemp manufacturing capabilities and an intertribal biomanufacturing consortium (USDA NIFA-funded); $10 million (2021) to define economic opportunities for western-U.S. hemp; “more than $26 million” USDA hemp research funding at OSU in recent years (trade summary). Grant totals/dates are trade-secondary; do not quote a cumulative GHIC funding total without the USDA award records.
  • What is established without opening GHIC pages:
  • OSU is Oregon’s land-grant university; hemp research at a public university in Oregon operates under the ODA hemp programme (grower/handler licensing where applicable), federal hemp law (2018 Farm Bill / USDA plan framework), and university research-compliance rules — NOT solely under an OLCC research certificate. A university hemp field trial is an ODA-licensed hemp activity first; an OLCC research certificate is relevant only where the research involves OLCC-regulated marijuana items or transfers with OLCC licensees.
  • The GHIC’s hemp work predates and is distinct from the OLCC Hemp Registry (2026, consumer products) — the Registry gates consumer hemp products, not university field research.
  • Federal baseline interaction: hemp research after 11 Dec 2026 (total-THC + 0.4 mg/container cap, PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019) and the USDA DEA-lab delay to 31 Dec 2026 affect hemp research sampling/testing design — whether OSU/GHIC research protocols have been conformed for those dates is Verify on GHIC/ODA pages; as of 1 Nov 2026 ODA’s stated position was to continue under current Oregon law during transition (§11.1.8).
  • Remaining GHIC Verify items: GHIC’s current field-trial locations and ODA licence numbers (not stated on the GHIC overview page); whether OSU holds an OLCC research certificate (the 1-active-certificate count in §11.9.1 is not attributed to OSU on any source located — do not attribute it to OSU); GHIC Strategic Plan 2025–2030 goals/actions beyond the purpose/vision quoted above (plan PDF: https://d7agsci.prod.acquia-sites.com/sites/agscid7/files/hemp/ghic_strategic_plan_final.pdf — search result, accessed 2026-11-01; the plan’s “more than 70 experts” vs the GHIC page’s “65 faculty” discrepancy is noted above); cannabinoid-specific (vs fibre/grain/food) research programmes; and GHIC’s position on the post-11 Dec 2026 federal hemp definition (§11.1.8).
  • Other universities: no other Oregon university cannabis/hemp research licence (e.g. University of Oregon, Portland State, Oregon Health & Science University) was confirmed in this run. Do not list other universities as research licensees without an OLCC/ODA source. OHSU’s role, if any, is in medical research / clinical contexts under separate federal (DEA/FDA) authority, not OLCC licensure — Verify before stating.

11.9.3 Other research routes (kept distinct)

  • ODA hemp research: ODA hemp grower/handler licences + OAR 603 Div. 48 R&D provisions (including the Commercial vs R&D hemp rule distinction noted in Run 1’s Colorado file — NOT Oregon; for Oregon, the ODA rule structure is Verify in OAR 603-048). The ODA “R&D” hemp category, if it exists in current Oregon rules, must be cited from OAR 603 Div. 48, not from another state’s file.
  • OMMP / OHA research: OAR 333-007-0500 (quality control and R&D testing) — not opened — Verify.
  • Federal research: DEA Schedule I/III researcher registration and FDA investigational-drug authority are federal overlays for marijuana research involving human subjects or interstate transfer; they do not replace Oregon licensure. Schedule III for state-licensed medical (federal baseline) does not by itself create a university research licence — Verify the federal researcher-registration interaction for any specific study.
  • Private research (non-university): the OLCC research certificate (§11.9.1) is the OLCC route; private hemp R&D runs under ODA licensing. The 1-active-certificate count (§11.9.1) suggests private OLCC research is minimal in practice — Verify whether the single certificate is held by a university, a private firm, or a public agency on the OLCC dataset (licence-holder name is a public business record in the dataset; individual personal data is not reproduced here).

11.10 Operations compliance checklist (summary — rules, not advice)

This checklist summarises §§11.1–11.9 for operator use. Each line’s authority is in the section cited; Verify-flagged lines must be confirmed on the current rule page before the checklist is used as a compliance document.

  1. Testing: no sale/transfer before passing Division 7 tests (§11.1); lab-only representative sampling, whole batch present (§11.1.4); pre-tested quarantine labelled “PRODUCT NOT TESTED” (§11.1.4); failed-test clocks 7 days / 30 days / 24 hours (§11.1.5); remediation only where 333-007-0450 allows (§11.1.5).
  2. Labs: ORELAP accreditation (TNI 2016, Div. 64, Oregon-located) + OLCC licence; no other OLCC licence held; annual renewal; scope matters (not every accredited lab does every test) (§11.1.6).
  3. Transfers: entry by change of ownership/location, not new application, under HB 4121 caps (§11.2.1); tax-compliance gate for retailers (§11.2.1); no operation at a new location before approval (§11.2.4).
  4. Renewal: annual (OLCC licences), 3-year (research), 5-year (worker permits), 1-year (ODA hemp, by 1 Dec) — windows Verify (§11.2.2).
  5. Canopy: tiers as in §11.3.1; mature plants only in designated canopy; changes need prior written approval (§11.3.1); OMMP and home-grow limits are separate regimes (§§11.3.3–11.3.4).
  6. Security: security plan; commercial-grade locks; steel door/frame for indoor storage; panic-button/alarm notification; cameras 24/7, 15-ft entry/exit clarity, 90-day on-site retention (§11.4).
  7. Transport/delivery: alarmed vehicles, product out of sight, GPS + lockable container + unmarked vehicle + $10,000 cap + permit-carrying driver for retail delivery; no federal-land delivery (§11.4.4).
  8. Waste: secured receptacle; failed product only by approved destruction/surrender; Metrc waste recording (§11.5); rendering/unusable standards Verify (§11.5).
  9. Environment: licence ≠ water right; WRD enforcement track Verify (§11.6.2); pesticide testing + ODA pesticide list Verify (§11.6.3); no statewide cannabis energy code located (§11.6.5).
  10. Promotions: no marijuana as a prize; no on-site consumption/tasting at retail; advertising test = “likely to cause minors to unlawfully possess” (2025); discount/loyalty tax treatment Verify (§11.7).
  11. Staff: every plant-touching worker (incl. licensees, seasonal staff, delivery drivers) holds a $100/5-year permit, 70% test, OLCC background check (§11.8); general employment drug testing is a separate, employer-policy question (§11.8.1).
  12. Research: OLCC research certificate (1 active, Sep 2026) vs ODA hemp research vs federal researcher registration — keep the routes distinct (§11.9).
