§12.1 Paraphernalia and smoke-shop rules

12.1.1 What counts as “marijuana paraphernalia” — ORS 475C.373

Verbatim definition (search-result rendering; direct open failed with a 429 in this run — Verify against the official ORS page before republication):

“(1) As used in this section, ‘marijuana paraphernalia’ means an object that is marketed to be used for, or that is designed for, planting, propagating, cultivating, growing, harvesting, manufacturing, compounding, converting, producing, processing, preparing, testing, analyzing, packaging, repackaging, storing, containing, concealing, injecting, ingesting, inhaling or otherwise introducing into the human body a marijuana item. ‘Marijuana paraphernalia’ does not include hypodermic syringes or needles.”

Source: ORS 475C.373 as rendered in search results — https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_475c.373 and https://law.justia.com/codes/oregon/2021/volume-14/chapter-475c/section-475c-373/ — accessed 2026-11-01. History note returned: [Formerly 475B.376].

Key points for a consumer/business reader:

  • The test is marketing or design, not the buyer’s actual intent alone: an object “marketed to be used for, or … designed for” one of the listed marijuana-item purposes. That is why the same glass pipe can be paraphernalia in one shop’s display and a tobacco pipe in another’s — the marketing matters. The section directs the trier of fact to consider, in addition to any other relevant factor, a list of factors in subsection (5) (the full factor list was truncated in the search rendering — Verify the complete subsection (5) list on the official ORS page; do not quote a partial factor list as complete).
  • Hypodermic syringes and needles are expressly excluded from “marijuana paraphernalia” in ORS 475C.373(1).
  • The parallel general drug-paraphernalia statute, ORS 475.525, uses a near-identical definition for controlled substances generally, with an illustrative list that includes: metal, wooden, acrylic, glass, stone, plastic or ceramic pipes with or without screens; water pipes; carburetion tubes and devices; smoking and carburetion masks; roach clips; miniature cocaine spoons and cocaine vials; chamber pipes; carburetor pipes; electric pipes; air-driven pipes; chillums; bongs; and ice pipes or chillers. Source: ORS 475.525 as rendered in search results — https://law.justia.com/codes/oregon/2021/volume-14/chapter-475/section-475-525/ — accessed 2026-11-01. That illustrative list is in the 475.525 (general drug paraphernalia) text, not in the 475C.373 text returned — do not attribute the pipe/bong list to 475C.373 itself.
  • The two statutes are coordinated: ORS 475.525(5)(a) provides that ORS 475.525 to 475.565 “do not apply to a person who sells or delivers marijuana paraphernalia as defined in ORS 475C.373 to a person 21 years of age or older.” In other words, a sale of marijuana paraphernalia to a 21+ buyer is carved out of the general drug-paraphernalia prohibition; the same sale to an under-21 buyer is the 475C.373 offence below.

12.1.2 The age rule and penalty — ORS 475C.373(2)–(3)

Verbatim operative text (search-result rendering — Verify as above):

“(2) It is unlawful for a person to sell or deliver, to possess with intent to sell or deliver or to manufacture with intent to sell or deliver marijuana paraphernalia to a person who is under 21 years of age, knowing that the marijuana paraphernalia will be used for the purpose for which it was marketed or designed.” “(3) Violation of this section is a Class B violation.”

Source: same ORS 475C.373 rendering — accessed 2026-11-01.

Practical consequences:

  • Sale/delivery to 21+ is lawful under 475C.373 (subject to the other regimes below — tobacco/inhalant-delivery-system licensing, hemp-registry labelling, and local rules). There is no Oregon statute located in this run that makes mere adult possession of marijuana paraphernalia unlawful as such; the offence is the sale/delivery/manufacture for sale to an under-21 person, knowing the intended use. Do not describe adult paraphernalia possession as a crime in Oregon without locating a separate offence — Verify whether any local ordinance creates a possession offence (none was located in this run).
  • “Knowing” matters: the seller must know the paraphernalia will be used for the marketed/designed purpose. A general-purpose item sold without that knowledge is a different case; the factor test in subsection (5) is how a court/OLCC proceeding decides whether an object is paraphernalia at all.
  • OLCC enforcement overlay: subsection (4) (truncated in the rendering) provides that, subject to ORS chapter 131A and notwithstanding the Class B violation classification, OLCC “may purchase, possess, seize or dispose of marijuana” paraphernalia in the enforcement context quoted — Verify the full subsection (4) text; the truncated rendering does not support quoting its full scope.
  • Class B violation fine ceiling: under ORS 153.018 as summarised in a secondary university compliance summary, Class B violations are punishable by fines of up to $1,000 and Class A violations up to $2,000 — secondary, accessed 2026-11-01 via https://www.uws.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/UWS_2026_Annual_Security_Report.pdf — Verify against ORS 153.018 current text before quoting a dollar figure as the paraphernalia penalty. The same summary confirms the 475C.373 age rule and the ORS 475C.317 under-21 framework, and adds (secondary) that it is a Class C misdemeanor for a person under 21 to misrepresent age to purchase or consume cannabis (citing ORS 165.805, 475C.317, 161.615, 161.635) — Verify that misrepresentation proposition against the cited sections; it is not in the 475C.373 text returned.

12.1.3 Hemp and CBD shops — no OLCC licence needed to sell, but product registration + vendor licence are

This is the most commonly misunderstood smoke-shop point in Oregon, and the OLCC Hemp Registry FAQs page — opened directly 2026-11-01 — settles the licence question:

“You do not need a license from the OLCC to sell hemp products in places like grocery stores, pet stores, gas stations, smoke shops, or online (the ‘general market’). Most Oregon businesses that sell hemp products to consumers, including products intended for animal use or consumption, are required to have a hemp vendor license from the Oregon Department of Agriculture.”

Source: OLCC Hemp Registry FAQs, opened 2026-11-01 — https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/Pages/hemp-registry-faqs.aspx

The full general-market regime, as opened/confirmed in this run:

  • Product registration (OLCC Hemp Registry, OAR 845-026-6000 to 845-026-6120, eff. 1 Jan 2026): a hemp item must be registered with OLCC if (i) it is for sale to a consumer in Oregon, (ii) it is intended for human or animal consumption or use, and (iii) it is not exclusively for topical application to skin or hair. That includes direct-to-consumer online sales and brick-and-mortar sales at grocery/convenience stores and smoke shops. Registration fee $400, renewal $400 annually; amendment fee $25 (OLCC FAQ, opened 2026-11-01). Registration requires at least one label and a certificate of analysis for a batch; label review is part of registration. Enforcement of the registry began 1 June 2026 after a transition period (Run 1 H6; OLCC Bulletin HE2025-01).
  • Exclusions from the registry (OLCC FAQ, opened 2026-11-01): hemp items that do not contain cannabinoids; items intended only for topical use; industrial hemp grain/fiber products without added cannabinoids; commercial feed products for animals registered under ORS 633.006 to 633.089 (regulated exclusively by ODA); and hemp items transported through Oregon en route to another state.
  • Labelling: labels must list THC and CBD content; other cannabinoids may be listed separately or cumulatively (“total cannabinoids”); cannabinoids detected at “<LOQ” (other than THC/CBD) need not be listed; if a label advertises a specific non-THC/CBD cannabinoid (e.g. CBN, CBG), test results for it should be displayed; a target potency on the principal display panel must be within 10% of exact test results or the label may be untruthful/misleading. Adult-use cannabis items bear the ASTM symbol and the warning “For use only by adults 21 and older” (OLCC FAQ, opened 2026-11-01). HB 4121 does not require child-resistant packaging for hemp items (OLCC FAQ, opened 2026-11-01) — contrast OLCC marijuana packaging rules in Run 1 §1.6.
  • ODA vendor-site licence: $100/year, licence cycle 1 July–30 June, required from 1 July 2024 for hemp retailers/wholesalers who store, transfer or sell industrial hemp or hemp items for resale (Run 1 §4.8; OAR 603-048-0175 — Verify current form). The ODA vendor licence (seller registration) and the OLCC Hemp Registry (product registration) are different regimes and must not be conflated.
  • If the shop is an OLCC-licensed marijuana retailer, it needs an OLCC licence (not just the general-market route) — OLCC FAQ, opened 2026-11-01: “If hemp items are sold by an OLCC-licensed marijuana retailer, you must have a license with the OLCC.”
  • Age limits for hemp/CBD in a smoke shop — the 0.5 mg / inhalable rules: secondary summaries of the OLCC General Market Hemp FAQ state the operative line as: a consumable hemp product may be sold to a person under 21 only if it contains less than 0.5 mg total THC, contains no artificially derived cannabinoids, and is not advertised as producing intoxicating effects; at or above 0.5 mg total THC (or any artificially derived cannabinoid) the item is an “adult use cannabis item” and may be sold only to persons 21+. Inhalable hemp items (vape cartridges, smokable hemp flower/pre-rolls) always require the buyer to be 21+, regardless of THC content. Sources: secondary, accessed 2026-11-01 — https://legalclarity.org/how-old-do-you-have-to-be-to-buy-cbd-in-oregon/ and https://sativauniversity.com/cannabis-laws/oregon/ (citing OAR 845-026-0300, eff. 1 Jan 2022, civil penalty up to $10,000 per violation). Verify both the 0.5 mg threshold and the inhalable-always-21+ rule against OAR 845-026-0300 / the OLCC General Market Hemp FAQ itself before advising a retailer — the threshold is stated here as a secondary summary, not as opened rule text. Note also the OLCC FAQ’s own example (opened 2026-11-01): “a hemp beverage that has 1 mg THC in the container would be an adult use cannabis item.”
  • Artificially derived cannabinoids in the general market: “Generally, no” — they may be sold only in very limited circumstances meeting OAR 845-026-0415, and registrations with labels for products containing artificially derived cannabinoids that do not meet those requirements may be denied; as of August 2026 none had received approval under OAR 845-026-0415 (Run 1 H7; OLCC FAQ, opened 2026-11-01).

12.1.4 Tobacco / inhalant-delivery-system licensing for smoke shops — the licence a smoke shop does need

A smoke shop that sells tobacco products or inhalant delivery systems (IDS) needs a Tobacco Retail License — a different licence from anything cannabis-specific:

  • Statewide requirement: ORS 431A.194 (SB 587, 2021 session) requires Oregon retailers selling cigarettes, tobacco, and/or IDS products to obtain a licence. The Department of Revenue (DOR) issues the state licence; the annual state fee is $984 (OHA retailers page, search-indexed — Verify current fee on the DOR page). Source: DOR Tobacco Retail Licensing page (search-indexed) — https://www.oregon.gov/dor/programs/businesses/pages/statewide-tobacco-retail-license.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01; OHA retailers page — https://www.oregon.gov/oha/PH/PREVENTIONWELLNESS/TOBACCOPREVENTION/Pages/retailers.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • What counts: cigarette products including little cigars; tobacco products including cigars, smokeless tobacco, blunt wraps, pipe tobacco, shisha, roll-your-own, oral nicotine products (from 5 June 2026, nicotine pouches/lozenges/strips and other non-food natural/synthetic nicotine products also require the licence); and IDS as defined in ORS 431A.175 (a device used to deliver nicotine or cannabinoids, such as marijuana, in vapor/aerosol form — e-cigarettes, heatsticks, components including e-liquids and cartridges). Source: DOR page + OHA ICAA page (opened 2026-11-01, see §12.4.2) — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Age 21, inspections, signage: all Tobacco Retail License holders must not sell tobacco/IDS products to people under 21; each retailer receives two inspections per year from OHA — one for under-21 sales, one for other tobacco-retail-law compliance; retailers must display signs at each point of sale stating that selling tobacco to under-21s is illegal (ORS 431A.220, secondary summary — Verify sign wording against the statute). Sources: DOR/OHA pages above — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Local licensing carve-outs — the Portland / Multnomah County example: retailers in the unincorporated portions of Benton, Klamath or Multnomah counties, or in listed cities (including Portland, Gresham, Milwaukie, Lake Oswego, Maywood Park, Troutdale, Wood Village — city portions in Multnomah County only where a city spans counties), must apply to the local licensing programme, not DOR. Multnomah County’s programme: one licence per location, non-transferable, annual renewal, displayed where customers/staff can see it, fee $1,184 eff. 1 July 2026, two inspections per year, selling tobacco to someone under 21 is a critical violation. Tobacco sales are never allowed from mobile vendors or vending machines in Multnomah County. Sources: Multnomah County Tobacco Retail License page (search-indexed) — https://multco.us/services/tobacco-retail-license (updated 26 Aug 2026) — accessed 2026-11-01; DOR page above. Other counties/cities: local programmes that pre-dated 1 January 2021 were preserved by ORS 431A.220’s continuity provision (see 21+ Tobacco and Vapor Retail Assn. v. Multnomah County, 339 Or App 554 (2025), secondary court-report summary — Verify citation). A smoke shop outside those local jurisdictions uses the DOR state licence. Do not assume a single statewide smoke-shop licence exists — the licensing authority depends on the shop’s address.
  • Certified smoke shops / cigar bars under the Indoor Clean Air Act are a separate certification (ORS 433.847; OAR 333-015-0030 definitions of “smoke shop A/C” etc.) — see §12.4.2. A Tobacco Retail License is not the same as ICAA smoke-shop certification, and neither, by itself, authorises cannabis consumption on the premises (see §12.4.1).

12.1.5 Local smoke-shop rules — what was and was not located

  • No statewide “smoke shop” zoning, buffer or density rule for cannabis paraphernalia shops was located in this run. State law gives the age rule (475C.373), the tobacco/IDS licence, and the hemp-registry/vendor rules above; siting, business licensing and any additional local restrictions are city/county matters and vary. The Multnomah County tobacco-licensing programme (§12.1.4) is the best-documented local example located; it is a tobacco/nicotine/vaping licensing programme, not a cannabis-paraphernalia-specific programme, and its rules (per-location licence, no mobile/vending sales, inspections) apply to a smoke shop only insofar as the shop sells tobacco/IDS products.
  • Verify / gap: whether Portland, Eugene, Salem, Bend or other Oregon cities impose any cannabis-specific smoke-shop rule (e.g. a local business-licence endorsement, a buffer from schools, or a flavour restriction that reaches hemp vapes) was not located in this run and must be checked city-by-city on the municipal code before advising a specific shop. In particular, Multnomah County’s July 2026 update notes a flavoured tobacco sales ban — its scope (whether it reaches hemp-derived vaping products, and its effective date/ litigation status) was not established in this run and is flagged Verify; do not state that it bans flavoured hemp vapes without opening the county ordinance.
  • What a smoke shop may NOT do: sell marijuana items (usable marijuana, edibles, concentrates, extracts) without an OLCC retailer licence; sell marijuana paraphernalia to under-21s (475C.373); sell adult-use cannabis items (≥0.5 mg THC hemp items / any artificially derived cannabinoid item) to under-21s; sell tobacco/IDS without the applicable Tobacco Retail License; or allow on-premises cannabis consumption in a way that violates ORS 475C.377 / the ICAA (see §12.4).

§12.2 THC driving limits and impairment testing (DUII)

12.2.1 The offence — ORS 813.010 (cannabis expressly included; no per se THC limit)

Verbatim operative text (Justia 2019 rendering; the operative structure is unchanged in the later renderings returned — Verify against the current official ORS page, because one later rendering reflects a 2023–2024 amendment restructuring subsection (1)):

“(1) A person commits the offense of driving while under the influence of intoxicants if the person drives a vehicle while the person: (a) Has 0.08 percent or more by weight of alcohol in the blood of the person as shown by chemical analysis of the breath or blood of the person made under ORS 813.100, 813.140 or 813.150; (b) Is under the influence of intoxicating liquor, cannabis, a controlled substance or an inhalant; or (c) Is under the influence of any combination of intoxicating liquor, cannabis, a controlled substance and an inhalant.”

Source: ORS 813.010 as rendered — https://law.justia.com/codes/oregon/2019/volume-19/chapter-813/section-813-010/ — accessed 2026-11-01. A later rendering (via oregonlaws.org mirror) restructures subsection (1) as “(a) 0.08% alcohol …; (b) under the influence of an intoxicant or a combination of intoxicants; or (c) within two hours after driving … 0.08% …” and retains the pleading rule in subsection (2) for controlled substances/inhalants. Verify which subsection lettering is current — the substance is the same: cannabis impairment is a DUII prong independent of any alcohol number.

The central Part 12 holding — no per se THC limit:

  • Oregon has no per se (number-based) THC blood or urine limit for cannabis DUII. There is no Oregon equivalent of the 0.08% alcohol prong for THC: no nanogram-per-millilitre figure in blood, urine or breath that, by itself, proves DUII. Secondary sources are unanimous on this point in this run, and Run 1 already stated it as secondary (“no per se THC blood limit … impairment is judged by evaluation, not a blood-THC number” — Run 1 §1.3.3, flagged Verify against ORS 813.010; this draft now confirms it against the 813.010 text, which contains no THC number). Sources (secondary, accessed 2026-11-01): https://www.rhettbernstein.com/faqs/duii/ (“There’s no legal ‘limit’ for THC, so officers rely on driving behavior, statements, and field sobriety tests”); https://www.mikearnold.com/eugene-duii-lawyers-oregon-drunk-driving-defense/ (“There is no set legal limit for THC impairment in Oregon”); https://romanolawpc.com/dui/marijuana-cannabis/ (“there is no set amount of THC … in the blood or urine of a driver which is presumed to cause mental or physical impairment”).
  • Why the absence of a number matters evidentially: the State must prove the driver was “under the influence” — in the case-law formulation quoted in secondary sources, that the driver’s physical or mental faculties were “adversely affected to a noticeable or perceptible degree” by cannabis (alone or combined with alcohol/other intoxicants). Mere presence of THC or its metabolite (THC-COOH, detectable in urine for weeks after use) does not by itself prove that degree of impairment, and the secondary sources stress that metabolites can remain long after impairment ends. Conversely, a low or zero breath-alcohol result does not end a cannabis DUII investigation — it is the trigger for a drug evaluation (see §12.2.3).
  • Pleading rule (ORS 813.010(2)): a person may not be convicted of DUII on the basis of being under the influence of a controlled substance or an inhalant unless that fact is pleaded in the accusatory instrument and is either proved at trial or admitted through a guilty plea. Whether cannabis counts as a “controlled substance” for this pleading subsection, or is pleaded under the express “cannabis” prong, is a charging-practice detail — Verify against current charging practice; do not over-read subsection (2) as exempting cannabis DUII from pleading.
  • 2023–2024 amendment note (Verify): one secondary guide states that “House Bill 2316, effective in 2024, expands DUII liability to include any substance that impairs driving — not just alcohol, cannabis, psilocybin, or controlled substances” and that a prescription alone is not a defence. Source: secondary — https://www.christrotterlaw.com/post/oregon-dui-law-guide — accessed 2026-11-01. Verify HB 2316’s enrolled text and its effect on ORS 813.010 before citing an “any impairing substance” prong; the 813.010 text quoted above (liquor / cannabis / controlled substance / inhalant / combination) is the text actually returned, and this draft does not treat the HB 2316 summary as a substitute for it.
  • Where DUII applies: “upon any premises open to the public” (ORS 813.010(4)). A private driveway that is not open to the public is a different question — Verify the “premises open to the public” case law before advising on private-property driving.
  • Bicycles: the later 813.010 rendering includes bicycle-specific alcohol prongs (0.08% / 0.15% within two hours after riding a bicycle). Whether a cannabis-impairment DUII charge can be brought for cycling, and under which subsection, was not established in this run — Verify; do not assume the motor-vehicle analysis transfers to bicycles.

12.2.2 Penalties — Class A misdemeanor baseline; Class C felony on a third in 10 years

From ORS 813.010(4)–(7) as rendered (Justia 2019; fine figures corroborated by secondary guides — Verify current fine/jail figures against current ORS 813.010 / 813.020):

  • Baseline classification: DUII is a Class A misdemeanor (ORS 813.010(4)), punishable by up to 1 year in jail. Minimum fines as rendered: $1,000 for a first conviction; $1,500 for a second; $2,000 for a third or subsequent conviction if the sentence does not include imprisonment; and $2,000 if the offence was committed with 0.15% or more alcohol (the 0.15% prong is alcohol-specific and has no cannabis equivalent). Maximum fine $6,250, or $10,000 if the offence was committed in a motor vehicle with a passenger under 18 who was at least 3 years younger than the driver (ORS 813.010(7) as rendered). Secondary guides summarise first-offence practice as 2 days’ jail minimum (up to 1 year), 18–36 months’ probation, a DUII treatment/education programme, a victims-impact panel, and a 1-year licence suspension — secondary, accessed 2026-11-01 (https://legalbeagle.com/13730386-first-offense-duii-in-oregon-what-you-need-to-know-fines-consequences.html; http://www.themetrolawgroup.com/DUII-Defense-Attorney/). Jail/probation/treatment details are secondary summaries — Verify against ORS 813.010, 813.020 (fee on conviction), 813.021 (screening) and current sentencing practice.
  • Felony DUII: Class C felony if the current offence was committed in a motor vehicle and the person has, at least three times in the 10 years before the current offence, been convicted of (or found within juvenile jurisdiction for) DUII or an equivalent out-of-jurisdiction impaired-driving offence, in any combination (ORS 813.010(5)(a) as rendered). Secondary shorthand: “third DUII within 10 years = Class C felony” — that shorthand is accurate only with the “at least three prior” + 10-year + motor-vehicle conditions; do not shorten it to “third offence, ever.”
  • Fee on conviction: a person convicted under ORS 813.010 is also subject to ORS 813.020 (fee to be paid on conviction) — amount Verify in current ORS 813.020.
  • DUII diversion (ORS 813.200 et seq. — secondary summary, Verify): first-time offenders who meet eligibility conditions (no DUII conviction or diversion in the past 15 years, no commercial driving privileges at the time, no crash injury/death — secondary eligibility list) may petition for diversion, generally within 30 days of first appearance; diversion lasts one year; successful completion results in dismissal of the DUII charge. Diversion requires a DUII screening interview ($150 screening fee, ORS 813.021, secondary), completion of the referred treatment programme, and ignition-interlock installation where required (see §12.2.4). Sources: secondary DUII checklists/guides, accessed 2026-11-01 — https://dui911.org/checklists/dui911-checklist-oregon.pdf; http://www.gilroynapolishort.com/oregon-dui-penalties-chart-2025/. Diversion eligibility for a cannabis-only DUII (as opposed to alcohol DUII) was not separately confirmed — Verify that diversion is available on the same terms for cannabis DUII before advising a cannabis defendant that diversion is available.
  • Two-track consequence (criminal + administrative): every DUII arrest triggers (1) a criminal DUII case and (2) a separate DMV administrative (implied-consent) case. A suspension in one track does not dispose of the other, though DMV credits wait time served on one suspension toward the other for the same offence (ODOT/DMV guide, see §12.2.4).

12.2.3 How impairment is tested — roadside, DRE 12-step protocol, breath/blood/urine, and the warrant line

There is no roadside THC breath test in Oregon practice. A standard breathalyser measures ethanol only and “will never flag marijuana use”; THC-specific breath devices in development have no established breath-THC-to-impairment correspondence and are not relied on as Oregon DUII proof in the sources located (secondary, accessed 2026-11-01 — https://legalclarity.org/does-weed-show-up-on-a-breathalyzer/; https://legalclarity.org/how-do-police-test-for-weed-impairment/). The layered sequence in Oregon practice is:

  1. Roadside observation + field sobriety tests (FSTs). Driving behaviour, statements/admissions, and physical coordination tests (walk-and-turn, one-leg-stand, horizontal-gaze / eye-following). Secondary DUII guides state that in Oregon a driver is not legally required to take FSTs and declining them carries no direct penalty, and that a portable breath test (PBT) at the roadside is voluntary — distinct from the post-arrest official breath test under implied consent (secondary — https://www.rhettbernstein.com/faqs/duii/ — accessed 2026-11-01; Verify the FST/PBT voluntariness propositions against ORS text and current ODOT guidance; they are practice summaries, not quoted statutes).
  2. Arrest + official breath test. After a DUII arrest, police administer a breath test (which detects alcohol only). If the result is below 0.08% but impairment was observed, training treats that as “inconsistent with the level of impairment observed” and the officer calls a Drug Recognition Evaluator / Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) (secondary — https://www.williamfrancis.com/dui/police-seek-to-prove-impairment-from-cannabis — accessed 2026-11-01).
  3. DRE 12-step protocol. The DRE evaluation (International Association of Chiefs of Police protocol, as summarised in secondary Oregon guides) runs: (1) breath-alcohol test; (2) interview of the arresting officer; (3) preliminary examination and first pulse; (4) eye examinations; (5) divided-attention psychophysical tests; (6) vital signs and second pulse; (7) dark-room examinations (pupil size under different lighting); (8) examination for muscle tone; (9) check for injection sites and third pulse; (10) subject’s statements and other observations; (11) analysis and opinions of the evaluator; (12) toxicological examination. For cannabis, the DRE pattern taught is: pupils dilated or normal, pulse and blood pressure usually elevated, lack of convergence typically present, and — critically for distinguishing cannabis from depressants — cannabis generally does not cause nystagmus (involuntary eye jerking). Sources: secondary — https://romanolawpc.com/dui/drug-recognition-evaluations/; https://legalclarity.org/how-do-police-test-for-weed-impairment/ — accessed 2026-11-01. DRE opinion is an officer’s trained opinion, not a medical diagnosis — the secondary defence-side sources stress that DREs are police officers with special police training, not medically trained/certified personnel, and that the protocol’s scientific validity is contested (bias from the arresting-officer interview, non-blinded admissions). Present both sides: DRE evidence is used by the State to prove impairment; its weight is litigated, not settled by statute.
  4. Toxicological sample — blood or urine, analysed by the Oregon State Police Forensic Crime Lab. After the DRE evaluation, police typically request a urine sample (secondary Oregon practice summary) or a blood sample; urine is the sample most often described for drug DUII in the Oregon guides located. A blood/urine result proves presence of THC/metabolites, not — without more — the degree of impairment at driving time. That presence-vs-impairment gap is the central defence and scientific issue in cannabis DUII and is why the absence of a per se limit (§12.2.1) matters.
  5. Admissibility of DRE evidence (Verify): an older bill summary located (HB 2371, undated in the rendering) would have provided that evidence of a test administered or observation made by a police officer as part of a drug-recognition evaluation is admissible if certain conditions are met, with the Department of State Police to set the required tests/observations by rule (secondary blog summary — https://theweedblog.com/ending-marijuana-prohibition/multiple-duii-bills-introduced-in-oregon-aimed-at-marijuana-drivers — accessed 2026-11-01). Whether that bill became law, and the current ORS provision (if any) governing DRE admissibility, was NOT established in this run — Verify on OLIS. Do not cite HB 2371 as law.
  6. Oral-fluid / roadside saliva screening: one secondary guide mentions “oral fluid screening at the roadside” as part of the layered approach, without an Oregon-specific authorising statute or deployment figure. Verify whether Oregon law enforcement uses roadside oral-fluid screening for cannabis, and under what authority, before stating it as Oregon practice.

12.2.4 Implied consent — ORS 813.100, refusal/failure suspensions, hearing deadline, warrant rule for blood

  • The rule: by driving on Oregon roads, a driver impliedly consents to a chemical test (breath, blood, or urine) if a law-enforcement officer has reasonable grounds to believe the driver is driving under the influence (ORS 813.100, as summarised in every secondary guide located — Verify verbatim text on the official ORS page). The test is requested after arrest for DUII; refusal is admissible as evidence in court (secondary) and triggers the administrative suspension below, separate from any criminal penalty.
  • Suspension lengths (ODOT/DMV Suspension/Revocation/Cancellation Guide — official DMV document, search-indexed):
  • Breath/blood/urine test refusal: 1 year (hardship-permit wait 90 days); refusal — increased: 3 years (hardship wait 3 years).
  • BAC failure: 90 days (hardship wait 30 days); BAC failure — increased: 1 year (hardship wait 1 year).
  • Urine test refusal: 1 year, consecutive to any other Motorist Implied Consent suspension (hardship wait 180 days); urine refusal — increased: 3 years, consecutive (hardship wait 3 years).
  • Lengths are increased if, within 5 years before the current arrest (in Oregon or any other jurisdiction), the driver had a DUII conviction, participated in a diversion or similar alcohol/drug programme, or had a suspension under the Implied Consent Law (ORS 813.430).
  • A court may impose a presumptive fine of $650 for refusing a breath or urine test (ORS 813.095, per the DMV guide rendering — Verify; an older guide rendering gives “$500 to $1,000” — conflict flagged; use the DMV guide’s $650 presumptive figure with the Verify flag).
  • Source: ODOT/DMV guide (search-indexed) — https://stage.oregon.gov/ODOT/Forms/DMV/7484.pdf and https://digitalcollections.library.oregon.gov/assets/displaypdf/220185 — accessed 2026-11-01. Corroborated by secondary checklists — https://dui911.org/checklists/dui911-checklist-oregon.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Hearing deadline — 10 days: a driver who failed or refused a test must request an implied-consent hearing from DMV (Hearings Case Management Unit) by 11:59 p.m. on the 10th day after arrest, or the suspension takes effect automatically; the Implied Consent Combined Report given at arrest serves as a 30-day temporary permit, and suspension otherwise takes effect at 12:01 a.m. on the 30th day after arrest (secondary checklists + Combined Report form, accessed 2026-11-01). Verify the 30-day effective date against the current Combined Report / ORS 813.410 — the form rendering cites ORS 813.100, 813.110, 813.120, 813.131, 813.410, 813.420 and 813.300.
  • “Failing” a urine test: secondary Oregon practice notes state there is no suspension for “failing” a urine test as such (urine shows presence, not a per se failure threshold) — the suspension attaches to refusing the urine test. Verify against ORS 813.100 / 813.131; this draft states it as secondary practice, not as quoted statute.
  • Blood draws and warrants — Birchfield / McNeely line: under Birchfield v. North Dakota (2016), a warrantless breath test may be required incident to a DUII arrest, but a blood draw is a more significant intrusion requiring a warrant or valid consent, and a State may not criminalise refusal of a blood draw (though civil licence-suspension consequences for refusal may still apply). Under Missouri v. McNeely (2013), natural dissipation of a substance in the bloodstream does not automatically create exigent circumstances justifying a warrantless blood draw. Secondary Oregon summaries apply this as: in practice, officers who suspect marijuana impairment often seek a warrant for a blood draw; an earlier secondary blog summary states that in Oregon “drawing blood for DUII purposes requires a warrant, unless you were involved in a serious accident and the hospital gives law enforcement a sample of your blood while you are there” — Verify the hospital-sample / serious-accident exception against current ORS 813.140 / 813.150 and Oregon case law; the exception is stated here as a secondary summary, not as verified statute. A proposed bill located in an older summary (HB 3170) would have added blood to the Implied Consent Law so that refusal of a blood draw would itself trigger a 1-year suspension — that bill’s status was not established and it must not be cited as law; Verify on OLIS.
  • Ignition interlock: required after a DUII conviction, and during diversion if BAC was 0.08% or more, the driver refused a test, or drugs were found (secondary checklist — Verify against ORS 813.602 et seq.). Note the practical mismatch the checklist itself implies: an interlock measures alcohol in breath, so its deterrent value for a cannabis-only driver is indirect (it conditions driving privileges, it does not detect THC). Flag that mismatch as a practical observation, not as a statutory exemption — a cannabis DUII offender is not exempt from an interlock requirement merely because the device does not detect cannabis.
  • DUII checkpoints: secondary summary states DUII checkpoints have been illegal in Oregon since the 1980s (citing an Oregon bill debate) — Verify against Oregon constitutional case law (Art. I, §9) before stating this as current law; no checkpoint statute was located in this run.

12.2.5 Medical cardholders and DUII — no exemption, no higher threshold

  • No medical exemption exists in ORS 813.010. The statute’s cannabis prong applies whether the cannabis was used medically (OMMP cardholder) or recreationally. A cardholder who drives while adversely affected to a noticeable/perceptible degree by cannabis commits DUII on the same terms as any other driver. The secondary guides state this expressly: “Whether you enjoy recreational marijuana or use marijuana medicinally, if you use within weeks of driving, you are a target for law enforcement investigation, arrest, and charging of DUI” (secondary — https://romanolawpc.com/dui/marijuana-cannabis/ — accessed 2026-11-01), because metabolites persist long after use and there is no per se threshold to clear.
  • No “medical-use” defence to DUII was located. ORS 475C.883 (medical-use criminal exemption, Run 1 §1.4) exempts compliant medical use from possession/purchase criminal liability within OMMP limits; it does not exempt impaired driving. Verify 475C.883’s text for any driving carve-out — none was returned in this run, and this draft proceeds on the basis that there is none.
  • Schedule III question (Verify — federal baseline does not settle it): the federal baseline moves state-licensed medical marijuana to Schedule III eff. 28 April 2026. Whether that change affects Oregon DUII law at all is Verify and, on the material supplied, almost certainly no: DUII turns on impairment while driving, not on the drug’s federal schedule, and ORS 813.010 lists “cannabis” by name, not by schedule. Do not advise a medical cardholder that Schedule III creates a DUII defence or a higher impairment threshold. The Schedule III question that is live is the firearms question (§12.7), not DUII.
  • Under-21 drivers: under-21 possession while operating a motor vehicle elevates the ORS 475C.317 violation to Class A (Run 1 §1.3.3), with driving-privilege suspension via ORS 809.260/809.280 (Run 1 — Verify current suspension lengths). Separately, secondary DUII guides note an under-21 driver “will fail the [breath] test if [they] have any amount of alcohol in [their] blood” (zero-tolerance alcohol rule, ORS 813.010/813.100 practice summary — https://oregonbreathtest.com/ — accessed 2026-11-01). Whether Oregon has a parallel zero-tolerance cannabis rule for under-21 drivers (any detectable THC = DUII) was NOT established — Verify; do not state a zero-tolerance cannabis DUII rule for minors without a statute.

12.2.6 Consumer transport / open container — the gap, narrowed

Run 1 §1.3.3 recorded: “open-container / transport rule for adults: NOT located in this run — Gap.” This draft narrows it as follows, but does not fully close it:

  • What is settled: use of marijuana items in a vehicle is public use (ORS 475C.377; a vehicle on a highway / in a public place is within the “public place” definition as summarised in Run 1 §1.1.1); delivery drivers “may not … Consume, or be under the influence of, marijuana while making deliveries” (ORS 475C.117(3)(b)(C), Run 1 §1.6); delivery may not be made to a consumer on federal land (ORS 475C.117(5)); and driving while impaired is DUII (§12.2.1). Transport itself, within the 2 oz public possession cap, is lawful — secondary visitor guides state it as “legal for individuals 21+ to travel with cannabis in Oregon within the legal possession limits” (secondary — https://www.stateregstoday.com/health/marijuana-legalization/recreational-marijuana-laws-in-oregon — accessed 2026-11-01).
  • What is NOT settled on the material located: whether Oregon has a specific “closed container,” “trunk,” “not readily accessible,” or “open container” statute for adult consumer transport of marijuana (analogous to ORS 811.170 for alcohol open containers), and if so its section number and penalty. No such marijuana open-container section was located in this run either — the gap persists and is flagged Verify. Practical advice in secondary guides (“keep it sealed / in the trunk / not within reach”) is practice advice, not a quoted statute, and must not be presented as the text of an Oregon marijuana open-container law. The delivery-vehicle rules in ORS 475C.117 are licensee rules, not consumer transport rules, and must not be substituted for them.
  • Interstate transport is a separate, federal prohibition — see §12.5.3.

§12.3 Record setting-aside for marijuana offences (“expungement”)

Oregon does not use the word “expungement” in its statutes as the operative term. The operative term is “setting aside” — an order setting aside a conviction (or a record of arrest) and sealing the record. A set-aside is sealing, not destruction: the record is sealed from public view and the person is deemed not to have been previously convicted for purposes of the law, but courts/law enforcement retain non-public access as provided by statute. Anyone who promises “destruction” or “erasure” of an Oregon marijuana record without that qualification is overstating the remedy.

12.3.1 The three routes — do not conflate them

Route Statute / instrument Who moves it Automatic?
A. General set-aside ORS 137.225 Petition by the person No — petition-based
B. Marijuana-specific expedited set-aside ORS 475C.397 (SB 420, 2019; formerly ORS 475B.401, renumbered 2021) Motion by the person No — petition/motion-based, but expedited, no fee, no 10-year bar, no OSP check (see §12.3.3)
C. Drug-enforcement-misdemeanor sealing (HB 4002 / SB 236) HB 4002 (2024) §§54–56, as amended by SB 236 (2025) Court-driven / automated process (see §12.3.5) Intended to be automatic — but implementation was technically broken at enactment and was the subject of SB 236 fixes + a Presiding Judge Order authorising electronic sealing (see §12.3.5). Whether any individual record has actually been sealed automatically must be checked case-by-case — Verify on the case register.
D. Governor’s pardon (not a set-aside) Governor Kate Brown pardon, Nov 2022 Executive action Yes, as a pardon — but a pardon is not itself a set-aside/sealing order (see §12.3.6)
E. Reclassification / reduction ORS 137.222 Motion by the person No — petition-based

There is no general Oregon “Clean Slate” automatic-expungement statute for marijuana convictions of the Michigan/Minnesota type as of the 1 Nov 2026 cut-off, on the material located. Secondary 2026 briefs describe relief as “petition-based rather than fully automatic” for the SB 420 route, and describe a broader “Oregon Cannabis Equity Act to fund automatic expungement” as discussed, current status unconfirmed (secondary — http://drugpolicywatch.info/states/oregon.html — accessed 2026-11-01). Do not state that Oregon has automatic marijuana expungement as a general rule. The only automatic element located is the HB 4002 drug-enforcement-misdemeanor sealing process (§12.3.5), which covers post-September 2024 drug-possession misdemeanors, not the historic pre-2015 marijuana convictions that SB 420 addresses.

12.3.2 Route A — general set-aside, ORS 137.225 (the baseline every marijuana case must be tested against first)

Verbatim structure (secondary renderings of ORS 137.225 — Verify against current official ORS text; the renderings located are not the current official page):

  • Convictions: “At any time after the lapse of three years from the date of pronouncement of judgment, any defendant who has fully complied with and performed the sentence of the court and whose conviction is described in subsection (5) may apply to the court wherein that conviction was entered for entry of an order setting aside the conviction.”
  • Arrests without charge / acquittal / dismissal: “At any time after the lapse of one year from the date of any arrest, if no accusatory instrument was filed, or at any time after an acquittal or a dismissal of the charge, the arrested person may apply to the court which would have jurisdiction over the crime for which the person was arrested, for entry of an order setting aside the record of such arrest.” Time spent secreting oneself within or without the State is excluded from the one-year calculation.
  • Eligible convictions (subsection (5), as rendered): (a) Class C felonies (except first-degree criminal mistreatment constituting child abuse, or any sex crime); (b) “the crime of possession of the narcotic drug marijuana when that crime was punishable as a felony only”; (c) crimes punishable as either a felony or a misdemeanor at the court’s discretion (except sex crimes and specified child-abuse crimes); (d) misdemeanors, including municipal ordinance violations for which a jail sentence may be imposed (except specified child-abuse/sex crimes); (e) violations under state or local law; (f) pre-1 January 1972 offences that would now fall in (a)–(e).
  • Procedure (secondary summaries — Verify fees and forms): motion + proposed order filed in the court of conviction, notice to the prosecutor, and an OSP (Oregon State Police) fingerprint-based set-aside check. The standard filing fee historically cited for general set-aside is $281 plus an $80 OSP fee (secondary SB 420 comparison — https://oregondefense.com/sb420-expunging-marijuana-convictions-in-oregon/ — accessed 2026-11-01); Verify current ORS 21.135 / OSP fee schedule — fees change and the SB 420 route waives them entirely (see §12.3.3). A person still under supervision or incarcerated “has not fully complied with or performed the sentence of the court” (2015 amendment, ORS 137.225 — see §12.3.4 on post-prison supervision).
  • What general set-aside does NOT do for historic marijuana cases: it imposes a 3-year post-judgment wait for convictions and, in its pre-SB 420 operation, a 10-year clean-record requirement (no other conviction within the preceding 10 years) that SB 420 expressly displaces for qualifying marijuana convictions (see §12.3.3). A person with a recent non-marijuana conviction who cannot yet use ORS 137.225 may still be able to use ORS 475C.397 for the marijuana conviction alone — that displacement is the whole point of SB 420.

12.3.3 Route B — marijuana-specific expedited set-aside, ORS 475C.397 (SB 420, 2019)

Enrolled text (OLIS, SB 420-B, 2019 Regular Session) — quoted from the enrolled bill as rendered in search results:

“(1) Notwithstanding ORS 137.225, a person with a qualifying marijuana conviction may apply to the court in which the judgment of conviction was entered for entry of an order setting aside the conviction as provided in this section.” “(2)(a) The person may file a motion under this section at any time following entry of judgment of conviction for a qualifying marijuana conviction.” “(b) A person filing a motion under this section is not required to pay the filing fee established under ORS 21.135 or any other fee, or file a set of fingerprints.” “(c) No background check or identification by the Department of State Police is required to set aside a conviction under this section.” “(3)(a) At the time of filing the motion, the person shall serve a copy of the motion upon the office of the prosecuting attorney of the jurisdiction in which the judgment of conviction was entered.” “(b) The prosecuting attorney, within 30 days after the filing of the motion under paragraph (a) of this subsection, may file an objection to granting the motion only on the basis that the person’s conviction is not a qualifying marijuana conviction.” “(c) If no objection from the prosecuting attorney is received by the court within 30 days after the filing of the motion, the court shall grant the motion and enter an order as described in subsection (5) of this section.” “(4) If the court receives an objection … the court shall hold a hearing to determine whether the conviction sought to be set aside is a qualifying marijuana conviction. The person has the burden of establishing, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the conviction is a qualifying marijuana conviction.”

Source: SB 420 enrolled — https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2019R1/Downloads/MeasureDocument/SB420 — accessed 2026-11-01. Passed Senate 25 Apr 2019, repassed 11 June 2019; codified as ORS 475B.401 (2019), renumbered ORS 475C.397 (2021).

“Qualifying marijuana conviction” — ORS 475C.397(7)(b) (all three limbs must be met):

“(A) Based on conduct described in ORS 475C.305 or possession of less than one ounce of the dried leaves, stems or flowers of marijuana; (B) Committed prior to July 1, 2015; and (C) For which the person has completed and fully complied with or performed the sentence of the court.”

Source: enrolled SB 420 + State v. Willis (Or. Ct. App. 5 June 2024, No. A177724) summary — https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/or-court-of-appeals/116234118.html and https://wlo.willamette.edu/orappeals/2024/06/state-v-willis.html — accessed 2026-11-01.

Consequences and limits — read carefully, because SB 420 is narrower than its headlines suggest:

  • No waiting period beyond sentence completion: “at any time following entry of judgment” — but only once the sentence is fully complied with/performed (see §12.3.4). There is no separate 3-year or 10-year wait in the SB 420 route, and no fee, no fingerprints, no OSP background check.
  • DA objection is narrow: the prosecutor may object only on the ground that the conviction is not a qualifying marijuana conviction, and only within 30 days. If there is no objection, the court shall grant the motion. If there is an objection, the person bears the burden by a preponderance of the evidence that it is qualifying. The DA may not object on general “best interests of justice” or public-safety grounds under this section (contrast the general ORS 137.225 “best interests” discretion for some offences, secondary summary — Verify the current 137.225 discretion standard).
  • Effect of the order (subsection (5)): “Upon granting a motion … the court shall enter an appropriate order. Upon the entry of the order, the person for purposes of the law shall be deemed not to have been previously convicted and the court shall issue an order sealing the record of conviction and other official records in the case, including the records of arrest, citation or charge.” (Enrolled SB 420, above.) So a successful SB 420 motion seals the conviction record AND the arrest/citation/charge records in that case — broader than a conviction-only order.
  • Date cut-off is hard: conduct committed prior to 1 July 2015 only. A marijuana conviction for conduct on/after 1 July 2015 (when adult-use possession became legal, so post-legalisation convictions are typically for over-limit, unlicensed manufacture/delivery, or delivery to a minor) is not a “qualifying marijuana conviction” under SB 420, however small the amount. Those cases must be tested under ORS 137.225 (Route A) or ORS 137.222 (reduction, §12.3.7) instead. Do not describe SB 420 as covering “all marijuana convictions.”
  • Conduct cut-off is narrow: conduct described in ORS 475C.305 (homegrown/personal-use framework) or possession of less than one ounce of dried leaves/stems/flowers. A pre-2015 conviction for delivery, manufacture for sale, or possession of more than one ounce is outside the definition unless it fits the 475C.305 limb — Verify the 475C.305 limb’s scope (the enrolled text cross-refers to former ORS 475B.301 in the original bill; the renumbered cross-reference is ORS 475C.305 in the Willis summary). A pre-2015 delivery conviction is the paradigm case that fails SB 420 and must use Route A/E instead.
  • No right to appointed counsel at a contested SB 420 hearing: State v. Willis (2024) held the movant was not entitled to court-appointed representation at a contested hearing under Article I, §11, because a set-aside motion is not a criminal prosecution (Willamette summary, above). Practical consequence: a person facing a DA objection should expect to prove qualification without appointed counsel.

12.3.4 “Sentence of the court” includes post-prison supervision — State v. Willis (2024)

  • Holding: in State v. Willis (Or. Ct. App. 5 June 2024, A177724), the appellant had pleaded guilty in 2011 to unlawful delivery of marijuana (former ORS 475.860(2) (2009)) and, while still incarcerated on other charges in 2021, moved to set aside that conviction under ORS 475C.397. The trial court denied the motion because his term of post-prison supervision (PPS) had not yet begun, let alone been completed. The Court of Appeals affirmed: “the legislature intended ‘the sentence of the court’ to include any attendant term of PPS, and consequently, appellant’s conviction is not eligible to be set aside until he completes his term of PPS.” Source: FindLaw opinion summary — https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/or-court-of-appeals/116234118.html — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Why it matters for Part 12 readers: the 2015 amendment to ORS 137.225 had already made explicit that a person still under supervision or incarcerated “has not fully complied with or performed the sentence of the court” (Or. Laws 2015, ch. 820, §32a, as discussed in Willis). The Willis court held the same reading applies to ORS 475C.397 even though SB 420 did not repeat that clarifying language. A person still on PPS (or still incarcerated, or still under supervision) for the qualifying conviction cannot yet use SB 420, however old the conviction is. The legislative-history point in Willis — that SB 420 was meant to be “expedient” (Sen. Lew Frederick, Senate Judiciary, 5 Apr 2019) — did not persuade the court to read PPS out of “sentence.”
  • Interaction with the “at any time” language: “at any time following entry of judgment” in ORS 475C.397(2)(a) means there is no additional waiting period after sentence completion — it does not mean a motion can be granted before sentence completion. Do not quote “at any time” without the sentence-completion qualifier.

12.3.5 Route C — HB 4002 drug-enforcement-misdemeanor sealing, and the SB 236 (2025) fix

This route is not a marijuana route as such — it is the post-Measure 110-recriminalisation route for drug possession misdemeanors generally. It matters for Part 12 because (a) it is the only automatic-sealing mechanism located, (b) secondary sources routinely confuse it with marijuana expungement, and (c) its interaction with cannabis is indirect and must be stated precisely.

  • Measure 110 → HB 4002 arc (Run 1 H9, restated): Measure 110 (Nov 2020, eff. 1 Feb 2021) decriminalised small-amount possession of all drugs to a Class E violation ($100 citation, dismissible by health screening) and funded Behavioral Health Resource Networks substantially from cannabis tax revenue. HB 4002 (2024, ch. 70, eff. on passage / criminal portion 1 Sept 2024) created a drug-enforcement misdemeanor for simple possession of controlled substances, with county deflection programmes (pre-booking deflection → no charge if completed; conditional discharge; probation up to 18 months in secondary summaries — Verify enrolled HB 4002 text for probation/jail parameters). Cannabis possession within ORS 475C limits was never criminalised by Measure 110 and was not recriminalised by HB 4002 — HB 4002’s direct effect on cannabis is via treatment funding/politics and via recriminalisation of other drugs, not via a change to ORS 475C.337 possession limits. Do not describe HB 4002 as “recriminalising cannabis.”
  • Sealing design (HB 4002 §§54–56): the Act “creates a new form of conditional discharge for drug enforcement misdemeanors and establishes processes for sealing records related to the crime” (LegiScan summary of HB 4002 — https://legiscan.com/OR/bill/HB4002/2024 — accessed 2026-11-01). Legislative history quoted in Presiding Judge Order 365 (see below) describes the design as automated: Rep. Kropf (Joint Committee on Addiction and Community Safety Response, 27 Feb 2024): “We have created an automated expungement process so that people who are successful can immediately have their record expunged, that does not exist for any other criminal charge”; Sen. Lieber (Senate floor, 1 Mar 2024): “automatic expungement to prevent the negative impacts of a criminal record.”
  • Why it did not work as designed: SB 236 (2025) staff summaries and committee testimony describe HB 4002 §§54–56 as technically non-functional: Oregon Judicial Department government-relations director Aaron Knott told the Joint Committee (5 Feb 2025) that the automatic set-aside framework “as a technical matter … just didn’t work,” because of multiple distinct record-creation paths (deflection, citation, arrest, conditional discharge, probation) and the difficulty of reconciling data across courts, law enforcement, probation offices and other systems so an automated process can reliably identify eligible records. Sources: SB 236 staff summaries — https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2025r1/Downloads/MeasureAnalysisDocument/92749 and http://apps.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2025r1/Downloads/CommitteeMeetingDocument/306792 — accessed 2026-11-01; committee report — https://citizenportal.ai/articles/6349186/Oregon/Legislative/Committees/Joint/Ways-and-Means/Public-Safety/Committee-hears-technical-corrections-to-HB-4002-including-fentanyl-statute-changes-pharmacy-authority-and-automatic-expungement-fixes — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • SB 236 (2025) — enacted, eff. 17 July 2025 (emergency clause): an omnibus HB 4002 technical-corrections bill (LegiScan: “Passed on July 25 2025 … Effective date, July 17, 2025” — https://legiscan.com/OR/bill/SB236/2025 — accessed 2026-11-01; Verify the chapter number on OLIS). Its sealing provisions: clarifies eligibility and procedures for expungement of records related to (i) participation in a deflection programme or (ii) conviction for unlawful possession constituting a drug-enforcement misdemeanor; establishes a process for expungement when a court issues a warrant in such a case; authorises the court to enter an order sealing all records related to any other charges dismissed or removed from a charging instrument (other than diversion-related arrest/citation records as defined) if no other convictions exist in the case; establishes a process where a case involves two or more drug-enforcement-misdemeanor possession offences; clarifies when and to which court a deflection-programme coordinator must provide notice of completion; and adds dismissal to the available conditional-discharge dispositions. Source: SB 236 A staff summary — https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2025r1/Downloads/MeasureAnalysisDocument/92749 — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Presiding Judge Order 365 — electronic sealing authorised: “In the Matter of Sealing Records [Under HB 4002]” (PJ Order 365, Oregon Judicial Department) orders that the Office of the State Court Administrator may electronically seal circuit court records as required by HB 4002 and SB 236 through automated electronic data processing, may attach a case-specific order to each case through an Automated Processing Integration procedure, and may affix the presiding judge’s electronic signature to individual orders for eligible records. Source: PJ Order 365 — https://www.courts.oregon.gov/rules/Documents/WSH_PJO_365.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01. This order authorises automation; it does not by itself prove that any particular record has been sealed. A reader who needs to know whether a specific record is sealed must check the case register / OJD Records and Calendar Search, not cite PJ Order 365 as proof of sealing.
  • Cannabis-specific caution: a drug-enforcement misdemeanor is a controlled-substance possession offence. Cannabis possessed above ORS 475C.337 limits, or in circumstances that make it a controlled-substance offence rather than a 475C offence, could in principle fall in this route — but no authority located in this run holds that an over-limit cannabis possession conviction is (or is not) a drug-enforcement misdemeanor for HB 4002 sealing purposes. Verify that classification question against the enrolled HB 4002 / SB 236 text and OJD guidance before advising any cannabis defendant that HB 4002 automatic sealing applies to them. The safe statement is: HB 4002/SB 236 automatic sealing is a drug-possession mechanism; its application to any particular cannabis conviction is Verify, and historic pre-2015 marijuana convictions belong under SB 420 (Route B), not HB 4002.
  • Deflection and cannabis: county deflection programmes (e.g. Marion County’s RESTORE — Restitution and Treatment On Route to Expungement, Sept 2024, coordinating MCSO, city police, the District Attorney, LEAD navigators and RESTORE Court for low-level controlled-substance possession after HB 4002 — secondary county summary, accessed 2026-11-01) steer eligible drug-possession cases toward treatment/restitution. Whether a cannabis-only over-limit possession case is deflection-eligible in any given county is a county-programme question — Verify with the county deflection programme; do not assume statewide cannabis deflection eligibility.

12.3.6 Governor’s pardon, November 2022 — numbers, and what a pardon is not

  • Announcement: Governor Kate Brown pardoned an estimated 45,000 people convicted of simple possession of marijuana (announced 21 Nov 2022, a month after President Biden’s federal pardon). The pardon removed 47,144 convictions for possession of a small amount of marijuana from individual records (the 45,000-people / 47,144-convictions difference reflects people with more than one conviction). Sources: secondary reporting of the Governor’s announcement — https://www.gov1.com/legal/articles/ore-gov-pardons-45k-people-with-simple-marijuana-possession-convictions-Bxfb2JkhxCq71UtO/ — accessed 2026-11-01; MPP expungement round-up — https://www.mpp.org/issues/legalization/legalization-states-approaches-to-expungement-and-release/ — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Scope (as reported): convictions for possession of 1 ounce (28 grams) or less of marijuana, where the person was 21 or older, where it was the only charge, and where there were no victims. The Oregon Judicial Department was to ensure that all court records associated with the pardoned offences are sealed. Verify the pardon proclamation’s exact scope (offence, date range, “only charge” condition) against the Governor’s proclamation itself before advising any individual that their conviction was pardoned — the secondary summaries agree on the 1 oz / 21+ / only-charge / no-victim formulation, but this draft has not opened the proclamation.
  • Pardon ≠ set-aside, and pardon ≠ proof of sealing: a pardon forgives the conviction; sealing is the separate record consequence that OJD was directed to effect. A pardoned person whose record was not in fact sealed (e.g. because of a data-matching failure) still needs to check the record. Conversely, the pardon did not cover delivery, manufacture, over-1-oz possession, under-21 possession, or convictions with additional charges — those remain under Routes A/B/E.
  • “Relatively few” SB 420 motions: the same November 2022 reporting notes that, despite SB 420’s 2019 enactment, “to date, relatively few Oregonians have [filed SB 420 motions]” (secondary — Gov1, above). That uptake observation is consistent with the 2026 brief’s point that petition-based relief excludes people who do not file (§12.3.1). No authoritative total count of SB 420 motions granted (or of ORS 137.225 marijuana set-asides granted) was located in this run — that number is Unavailable, not zero. Do not quote an SB 420 grant total without an OJD statistical source.

12.3.7 Reduction / reclassification — ORS 137.222, and arrests vs convictions

  • ORS 137.222 (marijuana conviction reduction): the OJD official motion form (“Motion to Amend or Set Aside Conviction for Marijuana Offense,” July 2023) states: “ORS 137.222 requires the court to grant reclassification of a marijuana conviction if the degree or category of offense has been reduced since the conviction unless the prosecuting attorney files an objection regarding the eligibility of the charge for reduction or completion of/compliance with sentencing requirements within 30 days of the motion filing date.” Source: OJD form (secondary host) — https://data.templateroller.com/pdf_docs/2728/27286/2728653/main_motion-to-amend-or-set-aside-conviction-for-marijuana-offense-and-declaration-in-support-oregon.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01. Verify ORS 137.222’s current text and its relationship to ORS 475C.397 (the form treats them as companion motions on one form: set-aside under 475C.397, reduction under 137.222). Reduction is useful where a conviction does not qualify for full set-aside (e.g. post-2015 conduct, or a delivery conviction) but the offence has since been reduced in degree/category — the judgment is amended to the lower classification rather than sealed as a set-aside. Whether a reduced conviction is then itself set-aside-eligible is a further question — Verify.
  • Convictions vs arrests — different clocks, different sections:
  • Conviction set-aside: ORS 137.225 (3 years post-judgment, sentence fully performed) or ORS 475C.397 (no additional wait after sentence completion, pre-1 July 2015 qualifying convictions only).
  • Arrest-record set-aside (no charge / acquittal / dismissal): ORS 137.225(1)(b) — 1 year after arrest if no accusatory instrument was filed, or at any time after acquittal/dismissal (secretion time excluded). This is the route for a person arrested for marijuana possession but never charged, or acquitted/dismissed — it does not require a “qualifying marijuana conviction” and is not subject to SB 420’s 1 July 2015 cut-off, but it does require a petition, a fingerprint/OSP process (unlike SB 420), and the 1-year clock. Verify current fees/forms for arrest-record set-aside — the SB 420 fee/fingerprint waivers do not apply to a general 137.225 arrest-record motion.
  • Diversion/deflection records: a DUII diversion dismissal (§12.2.2) and a HB 4002 deflection completion (§12.3.5) each have their own record consequences; neither is automatically the same as an ORS 137.225 set-aside. Verify the record consequence of each programme separately for the individual case.
  • Juvenile records: juvenile expunction follows separate rules under ORS chapter 419A (secondary county-guide summary — accessed 2026-11-01). Juvenile marijuana adjudications are not covered by the adult set-aside discussion above — Verify ORS 419A provisions before advising on a juvenile record.
  • Federal records are untouched: an Oregon set-aside, pardon or HB 4002 sealing order does not set aside a federal marijuana conviction or a federal arrest record. Federal relief (including the 2022 federal pardon for simple federal possession) is a separate system — Verify federal pardon/set-aside routes separately; do not imply Oregon relief clears a federal record.

12.3.8 Numbers — what is counted, what is not (honest totals table)

Figure Number What it counts Status
Governor’s pardon, Nov 2022 — people ~45,000 People pardoned for simple possession Secondary reporting of Governor’s announcement — Verify against proclamation
Governor’s pardon, Nov 2022 — convictions removed 47,144 Convictions for possession of ≤1 oz, 21+, only charge, no victims Same — Verify against proclamation / OJD sealing report

Do not add the pardon numbers to any set-aside total. Pardons, SB 420 motions, general set-asides and HB 4002 sealings are different legal acts counted in different systems; summing them double-counts people whose pardoned conviction was also sealed by OJD.

§12.4 Consumption rules and events

12.4.1 The public-consumption ban — ORS 475C.377, and what “public” swallows

  • The ban (Run 1, restated): “It is unlawful for any person to engage in the use of marijuana items in a public place” — Class B violation (ORS 475C.377). “Use of marijuana items” on the statute’s wording covers smoking, vaping and edible/other use in a public place, not only smoking. It applies to everyone, including OMMP patients — there is no medical-use exception to 475C.377 in the text returned. Verify whether any OMMP provision creates a public-use accommodation — none was located, and this draft proceeds on the basis that there is none.
  • Where the ban bites in practice: bars, restaurants, patios, parks, sidewalks, vehicles (see §12.2.6), hotel hallways/lobbies and other parts of apartment houses/hotels not constituting rooms/apartments designed for actual residence, highways, streets, schools, places of amusement, playgrounds, and premises used in connection with public passenger transportation (Run 1 §1.1.1 “public place” summary). Retailer premises must post “No On-Site Consumption” and an exit sign reading “Marijuana or Marijuana Infused Products May Not Be Consumed In Public” (OAR 845-025-2840(2), Run 1 §1.6.2).
  • Licensee overlay — no consumption on licensed premises: OAR 845-025-1160 (as rendered in an OLCC violation-reclassification draft) provides that a licensee, laboratory licensee or permittee “may not permit the use or consumption of marijuana, hemp items, or any other intoxicating substance, anywhere in or on the licensed premises, or in surrounding areas under the control of the licensee,” except for employees as permitted under OAR 845-025-1230(6)(b), with violation as a Category III violation (secondary OLCC draft rendering — https://cms.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/rules/Violation-Reclassification-RAC-Draft-Rules.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01; Verify against current OAR 845-025-1160 text — the rendering is a draft-rules document, not the adopted rule page). The practical point is settled regardless: an OLCC retailer may not operate a consumption room, patio or tasting area on its licensed premises.
  • “Membership required” / private-club workarounds do not cure public-place status by themselves. Secondary visitor guides warn expressly: “Do not assume a lounge, club, event space, or business permits legal cannabis consumption unless it is clearly operating within Oregon and local law. A ‘membership required’ model does not by itself make consumption legal” (secondary — https://herb.co/city-guides/buy-weed-portland-oregon — accessed 2026-11-01). Whether a genuinely private, non-public venue (not open to the general public, no liquor licence, no public access) falls outside “public place” is a fact-specific, local-jurisdiction question — see §12.4.3 on the Metrc/OLCC events guidance, which makes exactly that local-determination point for non-liquor-licensed venues. Do not advise any venue that a membership fee alone makes consumption lawful.
  • Private-residence consumption is the lawful default: consumption in a private residence (room/apartment designed for actual residence), with the property owner’s permission, and not visible from a public place (for homegrown product, ORS 475C.306), is outside the 475C.377 ban. That default is what makes the absence of lounges (§12.4.2) a practical problem for visitors and renters — see §§12.5–12.6.

12.4.2 Consumption lounges — there are none licensed in Oregon as of 1 Nov 2026

There is no Oregon “Marijuana Consumption Lounge Endorsement,” no “cannabis café” licence category, and no licensed social-consumption establishment in Oregon as of the 1 November 2026 cut-off, on the material located.

  • A low-quality secondary source located in this run claims the opposite — that Oregon “allows for licensed businesses … to allow smoking and consumption on their premises,” that the licence “is called the ‘Marijuana Consumption Lounge Endorsement,’” and that OLCC “recently introduced a new license category for ‘cannabis cafes’” (secondary — https://www.stateregstoday.com/health/marijuana-legalization/social-cannabis-consumption-in-oregon — accessed 2026-11-01). That source is rejected as unreliable for this proposition: it contradicts ORS 475C.377, contradicts OAR 845-025-1160’s no-consumption-on-licensed-premises rule, names no OLCC rule or licence type that exists in the OLCC fee schedule (Run 1 §4.2, which lists every OLCC licence/endorsement and contains no consumption-lounge endorsement), and is internally inconsistent (its own §2 states “there are currently no designated areas for social cannabis consumption in Oregon” and “consumption is only permitted on private property with the owner’s permission”). Do not cite that source for a lounge endorsement. If a lounge endorsement is ever created, it will appear in OAR 845-025 and the OLCC fee schedule first — neither contains it as of this cut-off.
  • The live lounge proposal — a withdrawn 2026 ballot initiative (not law): the Oregon Cannabis Cafe Coalition (OCCC) advanced the Oregon Cannabis Social Lounge Act for the November 2026 ballot: OLCC-licensed “social lounges” where adults 21+ could bring their own cannabis for consumption (no on-site cannabis sales; only microbusinesses eligible — retail dispensaries could not operate a lounge under the same name/entity); lounges could sell non-cannabis food/beverages if certified by the local health department and hemp-derived CBD products; alcohol and tobacco (including nicotine vapes) prohibited on the premises; lounges to close by 2 a.m.; venues to post health-warning signs; OLCC + public-health outreach/education; local governments could regulate the number of lounges and impose additional limitations (whether outright local bans were permitted was unclear in the petition summary); violations could lead to fines / licence suspension / revocation, and unlicensed operation to civil/criminal penalties; if passed, eff. 1 January 2027. The Attorney General certified a ballot title in September 2025 (after a draft title in August 2025; 1,400+ voter signatures triggered title drafting; ~117,000 valid signatures would have been needed to qualify). On the Monday reported by Marijuana Moment (article dated in the search rendering as ~345 days before the 1 Nov 2026 crawl, i.e. late 2025), OCCC formally withdrew the measure from consideration for the 2026 ballot — founder/chief petitioner Justyce Seith called the decision “difficult but necessary.” Sources: https://www.marijuanamoment.net/oregon-activists-withdraw-measure-to-legalize-marijuana-social-lounges-from-consideration-for-2026-ballot/; https://oregonstatecannabis.org/news-02sep2025 — accessed 2026-11-01, both secondary. Consequence for Part 12: as of 1 Nov 2026 there is no lounge law, no lounge licence, and no pending 2026 lounge ballot measure. Do not import any post-cut-off revival of the proposal. A future lounge law would require a new initiative or legislation — Verify on the Secretary of State’s initiative list / OLIS before stating that any lounge effort is live.
  • ICAA smoke-shop / cigar-bar exceptions do NOT create cannabis lounges: the Indoor Clean Air Act (ORS 433.835–433.875) exceptions include smoking tobacco products in certified smoke shops, smoking cigars in certified cigar bars, smoking in hotel/motel rooms designated as smoking-allowed (max 25% of sleeping rooms), and smoking non-commercial tobacco for American Indian ceremonial purposes (OHA ICAA page, opened 2026-11-01 — https://www.oregon.gov/oha/ph/PreventionWellness/TobaccoPrevention/SmokefreeWorkplaceLaw/Pages/thelaw.aspx). Those exceptions are for tobacco products / cigars as certified — they do not authorise cannabis smoking, and a certified smoke shop that allowed cannabis smoking would still face ORS 475C.377 (public place) and, for its tobacco certification, the ICAA’s own limits. Do not describe a certified smoke shop as a lawful cannabis-consumption venue.
  • “Designated smoking areas” in workplaces / multi-unit housing are likewise tobacco/ICAA concepts (see §12.4.3 on the ICAA 10-foot rule and §12.6 on housing), not cannabis-consumption permissions.

12.4.3 Indoor Clean Air Act (ICAA) — ORS 433.835–433.875, OAR 333-015-0025 to 333-015-0085

The ICAA is a second, independent ban that layers on top of ORS 475C.377 for smoking/vaping (it does not reach edibles, which 475C.377 does reach). From the OHA ICAA page (opened 2026-11-01) and the OHA ICAA FAQ (April 2025, search-indexed):

  • What it covers: “smoking, vaporizing and aerosolizing of inhalants in and around public places and places of employment.” An inhalant delivery system (IDS) is “a device used [to] deliver nicotine or cannabinoids, such as marijuana, in the form of a vapor or aerosol” (e-cigarettes, heatsticks, components including e-liquids/cartridges). A “smoking instrument” means any cigar, cigarette, pipe or other instrument used to smoke tobacco, cannabis or any other inhalant (OAR 333-015-0030, search-indexed — https://oregon.public.law/rules/oar_333-015-0030 — accessed 2026-11-01).
  • Where it applies: all workplaces and enclosed public places must be smoke/vapor/aerosol free — including work vehicles not operated exclusively by one employee, and hotels/motels. It does not apply to private residences as such, but it does apply to enclosed shared spaces in apartment buildings (shared laundry rooms, enclosed stairwells, other enclosed shared public spaces). Businesses are not required to allow smoking; an owner may designate the entire premises tobacco/smoke-free at any time.
  • The 10-foot rule: smoking/vaping/aerosolising is prohibited within 10 feet of all entrances (including stairs), exits (including stairs), accessibility ramps leading to/from an entrance or exit, windows that open, and air-intake vents serving an enclosed public place or workplace. The OHA FAQ (April 2025) confirms the same 10-foot list and adds that OHA interprets it to include accessibility ramps (secondary OHA FAQ — https://stage.oregon.gov/oha/PH/PREVENTIONWELLNESS/TOBACCOPREVENTION/SMOKEFREEWORKPLACELAW/Documents/ICAA_FAQ_English.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01).
  • Employer duty: under ORS 433.850, every employer must keep the workplace free of smoke/inhalant vapors and post signs notifying people of the requirements (secondary summary — Verify sign wording against ORS 433.850). Enforcement is by OHA, via Local Public Health Authorities’ educational/remediation activity, and is complaint-driven — enforcement only follows a complaint from a member of the public, including employees; reports are public record and confidentiality is not guaranteed; violations may be reported via the OHA online complaint form or 1-866-621-6107 (OHA page, opened 2026-11-01 — agency public contact, reproduced as an official reporting channel, not an individual’s contact).
  • Stricter local laws: some Oregon cities/counties have enacted stricter local smoke-free workplace laws; employers must comply with all local laws, though OHA enforces state law only (OHA page, opened 2026-11-01). Check the city/county smoke-free ordinance for the specific venue — the state 10-foot rule is a floor, not a ceiling.
  • Interaction with 475C.377 — the practical result: outdoor cannabis smoking/vaping is lawful only on private property that is not a public place and is not within 10 feet of a regulated entrance/exit/window/vent — in practice, a private residence’s yard/garden away from neighbouring regulated entrances, with the owner’s permission. Smoking on a sidewalk, in a park, on a bar patio, or within 10 feet of a shop entrance violates at least one of the two bans, and usually both. Edibles consumed outdoors in a public place violate 475C.377 even though the ICAA does not reach them.

12.4.4 Cannabis events — trade shows / promotional events (licensee-only) vs public events (no consumption, no consumer sales)

Oregon has two different event regimes that must not be conflated: (1) OLCC-registered licensee trade/promotional events, where licensees may exhibit and (since 2026) exchange samples, but the public may not buy or consume; and (2) public-facing cannabis events (festivals, markets, competitions with public attendance), where consumption and consumer sales remain governed by 475C.377 and the retailer-licence rules — i.e. generally prohibited on site.

A. Licensee trade shows / promotional events — OAR 845-025-1335 (pre-2026 rule) + SB 558 (2025, operative 1 Jan 2026).

  • Pre-2026 rule (OAR 845-025-1335, “Marijuana Promotional Events”): HB 1057 (2017) allowed licensees to transport marijuana items to and exhibit them at a trade show or similar event.
