The rule required: one participating licensee designated as event organizer (the primary Commission contact, responsible for ensuring all marijuana laws/rules are followed by participants); Commission approval before the event date specifying all approved participating licensees; the organizer to verify that all participants’ manifests accurately reflect items transported to the event, maintain an attendance log, keep a copy of the approved application at the event, and be present (or designate another licensee representative to be present) during the event. Critically, under the pre-2026 rule, participating licensees could exhibit but could NOT exchange products at the event — transfers/samples at promotional events were prohibited (OAR 845-025-1335, as described in the SB 558 staff summary: “no transfers are permitted at marijuana promotional events, per OAR 845-025-1335”). Trade samples generally were governed by OAR 845-025-1330, and quality-control samples to permitted workers by OAR 845-025-1360. Source: SB 558 staff summaries (OLIS) — https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2025R1/Downloads/CommitteeMeetingDocument/299778 and https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2025r1/Downloads/MeasureAnalysisDocument/92749 — accessed 2026-11-01; OLCC draft-rules rendering of OAR 845-025-1335 — https://cms.oregon.gov/olcc/Docs/rules/Violation-Reclassification-RAC-Draft-Rules.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • SB 558 (2025) — enacted, operative 1 January 2026, eff. 91st day after adjournment sine die: permits licensed marijuana producers, processors, wholesalers and retailers to (i) provide samples of marijuana items to other licensees or marijuana workers at trade shows and temporary events registered with OLCC, (ii) allows a licensed wholesaler to sell or transfer items to licensed retailers at those events, (iii) allows producers/processors/wholesalers/retailers to exchange samples with other licensees and provide them to marijuana workers (including outside events, per the House summary), (iv) expands employee-sample limits (including 1 gram of usable marijuana per harvest lot per strain per month in one summary rendering — Verify the final sample-limit rule), (v) removes the requirement that marijuana items sold wholesale or transferred as samples at events be returned to a licensed premises after the event, and (vi) removes the requirement that two or more producers have common ownership to transfer products between them. OLCC was authorised to adopt rules requiring tracking of sample transfers (Metrc) and a registration system for temporary events, with tracking rules not more restrictive than those for samples provided to consumers. Sources: SB 558 -3 and SB 558 A staff summaries (OLIS, above) — accessed 2026-11-01; industry summary — https://themarijuanaherald.com/2025/04/oregon-senate-committee-approves-bill-to-allow-marijuana-businesses-to-give-samples-at-events-and-to-workers/ (7 Apr 2025) — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • What SB 558 does NOT do (stated expressly in committee materials): it does not create consumer sampling or public consumption at events. Proponents emphasised the changes are “limited to licensee-to-licensee transfers and samples, not consumer sampling or public consumption” (secondary committee report — https://citizenportal.ai/articles/6326020/Oregon/Legislative/Committees/Senate/Judiciary/SB-558-would-allow-tradeshow-samples-expanded-employee-samples-and-producertoproducer-transfers-industry-says — accessed 2026-11-01). A trade-show sample given to a consumer, or consumed by a consumer on site, is outside SB 558.
  • 2026 implementation (Verify): OLCC Compliance Education Bulletin CE2025-07 (“Implementation of 2025 Legislative Changes and Technical Rule Amendments”) and “New Rules Adopted January 1, 2026” are cited in the Metrc Oregon Wiki events page as the implementation source for the new event rules (secondary wiki — https://wiki-or.metrc.com/events — accessed 2026-11-01). The final adopted OAR 845-025-1335 / temporary-event registration rule text was not opened in this run — Verify the current rule, the registration process, and the sample limits in CE2025-07 / OAR 845-025 before advising any event organizer. The Metrc wiki’s summary of the resulting position is: event organizer may be a licensee or not (see below); licensees may sell/transfer to one another and provide trade samples to other licensees/employees; if the organizer is not a licensee, samples must be purchased from a retail licensee; producers/processors may transfer items to an OLCC retailer in Metrc, and those items can be purchased at cost by a judge/competition organizer for consumption in the judge’s/organizer’s personal residence (not on site).

B. Public consumption at events — the Metrc/OLCC position.

From the Metrc Oregon Wiki events page (secondary, summarising OLCC rules — accessed 2026-11-01):

“Under Oregon law, no marijuana consumption is allowed in a public place. Any location with an OLCC liquor license would be a public place, even if the venue is specifically reserved for a cannabis event. If the location is not licensed to sell liquor, whether it is considered ‘public’ is determined by the local jurisdiction.”

Practical reading:

  • A venue with an OLCC liquor licence is a public place for 475C.377 purposes even if reserved/private-hire for a cannabis event. Cannabis consumption at a bar, restaurant, brewery, winery or any liquor-licensed venue is unlawful even if the event is ticketed, members-only, or the liquor licence is “not in use” that evening — Verify whether any OLCC guidance creates an exception for a liquor licence surrendered/suspended for the event; none was located, and this draft proceeds on the basis that there is none.
  • A venue without a liquor licence: public-place status is determined by the local jurisdiction. That means a cannabis event at a non-liquor venue (e.g. a private hall, farm, warehouse) is not automatically lawful for consumption — the organiser must confirm with the city/county whether the venue/event counts as a public place, and must also comply with local event, zoning, fire and (if applicable) ICAA rules. Do not advise an organiser that a non-liquor venue is automatically a lawful consumption site.
  • Competitions / judging: the lawful judging model located is the residence model — product purchased (at cost, via a retailer in Metrc) and consumed in the judge’s/organizer’s personal residence, not judged by smoking on the event floor. Any on-site judging consumption at a public event would need to fit the narrow private/non-public analysis above and is Verify on the specific venue/local determination.
  • No “temporary event licence” for consumer cannabis sales/consumption exists in Oregon as of this cut-off, on the material located. The “temporary events” in SB 558 are OLCC-registered licensee trade events, not public temporary retail licences. A member of the public cannot lawfully buy marijuana items at a festival, farmers’ market or concert unless the seller is an OLCC-licensed retailer operating from its licensed premises (or by lawful delivery under ORS 475C.117 / OAR 845-025-2880 — Run 1 §1.6.3) — a pop-up retail stall at an event is not a licensed premises. Verify the delivery-to-event question separately (whether a bona fide delivery order may be delivered to a consumer at an event location, and whether the event location counts as a lawful delivery address) — it was not established in this run.
  • Hemp at public events: hemp items sold at an event to Oregon consumers must still be OLCC-registered and labelled (§12.1.3), and adult-use hemp items only to 21+. Hemp consumption (smoking/vaping) at a public event faces the same 475C.377 / ICAA analysis as marijuana smoking/vaping to the extent the product is a marijuana item or an inhalant — Verify the hemp-smoking-at-events analysis (whether smokable hemp flower smoked in public is “use of a marijuana item” under 475C.377 or is governed only by the ICAA/local rules); this draft does not treat hemp smoking in public as automatically lawful.

§12.5 Cannabis tourism and visitor purchase rules

12.5.1 Visitors may buy — no residency requirement, same limits, 21+ with valid ID

  • No Oregon residency requirement for adult-use purchase. Any person 21+ with valid government-issued photo ID may purchase from an OLCC-licensed retailer, resident or visitor alike, at the same daily sale limits as residents (Run 1 §1.3 sale caps; §12.0 table). Secondary visitor guides state this uniformly: “Out-of-state visitors can purchase the same quantities as Oregon residents; no residency is required” and “Budtenders check government-issued photo ID at entry, with no exceptions” (secondary — https://herb.co/city-guides/buy-weed-portland-oregon — accessed 2026-11-01); a 50-state visitor guide (Oct 2026, secondary — https://markets.financialcontent.com/wral/article/marketersmedia-2026-10-25-alexis-420-publishes-a-50-state-guide-to-where-tourists-can-legally-buy-weed-ahead-of-holiday-travel) lists Oregon among the states that “sell to any visitor 21 or older” with “a valid government photo ID from any state.” Accepted ID types (driver’s licence, passport, state ID, military ID) are stated in secondary tobacco/retailer guidance — Verify the OLCC retailer’s acceptable-ID list in OAR 845-025-2820 / OLCC retailer guidance before publishing an ID list as exhaustive. Expired ID, and ID that does not prove 21+, will be refused; that is retailer practice under OLCC rules, not a visitor-specific rule.
  • Retailer entry rule in practice: secondary guides state visitors must be 21+ to enter a recreational dispensary (ID checked at entry). That entry practice reflects the retailer’s “No Minors Permitted Anywhere on the Premises” signage duty (OAR 845-025-2840(2), Run 1) — a visitor travelling with a minor should expect the minor not to be admitted to the retail sales area at all, even if the minor does not purchase. Verify the entry-vs-purchase distinction for accompanied minors (e.g. a parent with a child) against current OLCC retailer guidance; the signage rule as quoted does not itself state an accompanied-minor exception.
  • Medical purchases by visitors — no reciprocity: “out-of-state medical cards are not recognized for purchases” / “out-of-state medical cards are not valid for purchases” (secondary visitor guides, above). A visitor who holds another state’s medical card but is not an OMMP cardholder may buy only as an adult-use consumer (21+, adult-use limits, 17% state tax applies — the OMMP tax exemption does not travel with an out-of-state card). A visitor who is an OMMP cardholder (e.g. an Oregon resident temporarily away, or a non-resident who qualified for OMMP — Verify whether non-residents may hold OMMP cards and on what terms) buys on OMMP terms (18+ at a medical-endorsed retailer, medical-grade items, tax-exempt). Do not advise any visitor that their home-state medical card entitles them to medical purchase, tax exemption or higher limits in Oregon.
  • Gifting to visitors: gifting between 21+ adults within possession limits without consideration (§12.0) applies to visitors on the same terms as residents (secondary visitor guide: a visitor “can … accept gifts of marijuana from persons 21 or older” — https://cannabisandglassor.com/is-marijuana-legal-in-oregon/ — accessed 2026-11-01). A “gift” that is in fact a sale (admission fee, service fee, contribution, lottery) is a sale and must go through a licensed retailer — the tourism-relevant risk is “cannabis tour / tasting” packages that bundle product with a ticket price (see §12.5.4).

12.5.2 What visitors may NOT do — the same bans, plus the visitor-specific traps

  • No public consumption (§12.4.1) — Portland’s “cannabis-friendly reputation does not extend to public consumption” (secondary visitor guide, above). Parks (including Portland parks, Oregon state parks — Verify state-park-specific smoking rules, which layer additional outdoor restrictions per the secondary ICAA summary), sidewalks, bar/restaurant patios, beaches that are public places, and vehicles are all covered. A visitor’s hotel room is lawful only if the hotel permits it (see §12.5.4).
  • No impaired driving (§12.2) — visitors are subject to DUII on the same terms; rental-car agreements and the visitor’s home-state licence consequences are additional, non-Oregon risks (Verify rental terms separately; not an Oregon-law proposition).
  • No purchase for / delivery to a minor; no use of a false ID. Under-21 purchase/possession and age misrepresentation are addressed in §§12.1.2 / 12.0. A visitor who buys for a minor faces delivery-to-minor criminal liability (secondary summaries describe delivery to a minor as a felony — Verify against ORS 475C.353 / 475C.341 before quoting a felony classification).
  • Opt-out jurisdictions: some Oregon cities/counties have opted out of licensed retail (and, in some cases, of possession/consumption — the secondary guide’s claim that opt-out jurisdictions “don’t allow the legal production, sale, possession, or consumption of cannabis, even in small amounts” overstates the opt-out effect and is flagged here: local opt-out under ORS 475C.600-series governs licensing in the jurisdiction, not the statewide possession legality in ORS 475C.337 — Verify the opt-out scope in Part 3 / ORS 475C.600-series before repeating the guide’s possession claim). The visitor consequence that is settled: a visitor cannot assume a retailer exists in every Oregon town — check the OLCC licensee list / Open Data dataset (Run 1 §5.1, dataset q32u-cmam, updated 28 Sept 2026) for the destination town.

12.5.3 Transport across state lines, by air, and on federal land — the federal warning

This is the single most important visitor warning, and it is federal, not Oregon, law:

  • Crossing a state line with marijuana is a federal offence even between two legal states. Secondary visitor guides state it uniformly: “Taking cannabis out of Oregon is a federal offense, even to neighboring legal states” (Herb guide, above); “it is still illegal under federal law to transport marijuana across state lines” even where both states have legalised (State Regs Today, above); “carrying it across a state line is a federal crime, even between two states that allow it” (50-state guide, above). Oregon law does not authorise interstate transport: ORS 475C.229 prohibits importing/exporting marijuana items (Run 1 §1.2.2 — Verify full text and the HB 3000 1% hemp carve-out), and SB 582 (2019) — the interstate-commerce trigger law — authorises the Governor to enter interstate agreements only if federal law is amended to allow interstate transfer or the U.S. Department of Justice issues an opinion/memorandum allowing/tolerating it; neither trigger has fired as of 1 Nov 2026, and no lawful interstate marijuana commerce has occurred under SB 582 (Run 1 §1.2.1). A visitor driving from Portland, Oregon to Vancouver, Washington (or to California, Nevada, Idaho — Idaho has no legal marijuana at all) with Oregon-purchased marijuana is therefore committing a federal offence and, for Idaho, a state offence in the destination state as well, even if the amount is within Oregon’s possession limits.
  • Flying: “Do not fly with cannabis. TSA says it does not search for illegal drugs, but if cannabis or evidence of illegal activity is discovered during screening, it refers the matter to law enforcement, and cannabis remains illegal under federal law except for narrow exceptions” (Herb guide, above). Airports are federal transportation systems; cannabis in checked or carry-on baggage, and cannabis in a vehicle at an airport, must be treated as a federal-law exposure, not as “Oregon-legal because I bought it legally.” Verify current TSA policy wording before quoting TSA’s position verbatim — the guide’s paraphrase is secondary.
  • Federal land and federal buildings in Oregon: state authorisation does not apply on federal land (national parks, national forests, federal buildings, military installations, and land owned/leased by the federal government). Delivery may not be made to a consumer on federal land (ORS 475C.117(5), Run 1). A visitor consuming or possessing marijuana in Crater Lake National Park, on a national-forest trail, or in a federal building in Portland is subject to federal enforcement, not Oregon’s possession limits. The same applies to mailing marijuana: mailing cannabis via USPS (or any interstate carrier) is interstate transport and a federal offence — secondary guides state it as “illegal to transport or mail marijuana across state lines due to federal laws” (State Regs Today, above).
  • Hemp nuance (Verify — federal baseline transition): hemp that meets the federal hemp definition may be transported interstate under federal hemp law, but Oregon-purchased marijuana may not be recharacterised as hemp by the buyer, and after 11 December 2026 the federal hemp definition tightens to total-THC + 0.4 mg/container (federal baseline). A visitor carrying a hemp product across a state line should carry its certificate of analysis and OLCC registration/label information and should Verify the destination state’s hemp rules and the post-11-December-2026 federal definition before travelling — this draft does not advise that any particular hemp product is lawful to carry interstate after that date.
  • No “visitor consumption” exception, no “tourist” defence: ignorance of Oregon law, visitor status, and a home state where cannabis is also legal are none of them defences to an Oregon public-use, DUII or over-limit charge, nor to a federal interstate-transport charge.

12.5.4 Hotels, tours, and where a visitor may lawfully consume

  • Hotels: the ICAA applies to hotels/motels as enclosed public places / places of employment, with an exception for hotel/motel rooms designated as smoking-allowed (max 25% of sleeping rooms) (OHA page, opened 2026-11-01). A hotel may designate its entire premises smoke-free at any time, and a hotel’s smoking policy is a contract/policy matter on top of the ICAA. Secondary visitor guides state the rule as: “Hotel rooms — only if the hotel expressly permits cannabis use; smoking or vaping is subject to the hotel’s policy and Oregon’s Indoor Clean Air Act” (Herb guide, above). Practical visitor rule: (i) smoking/vaping cannabis in a hotel room is lawful only if that room is a designated smoking-allowed room AND the hotel permits cannabis (not merely tobacco) smoking there; (ii) non-smoked consumption (edibles, tinctures) in a private hotel room designed for actual residence is outside the “public place” definition, but remains subject to the hotel’s policy (a hotel may prohibit cannabis use by contract and charge cleaning fees / terminate the stay for breach — Verify any specific hotel’s terms); (iii) smoking/vaping in hotel hallways, lobbies, stairwells, shared balconies that are public places, or within 10 feet of a regulated entrance, violates 475C.377 and/or the ICAA regardless of the room policy.
  • Short-term rentals (Airbnb/Vrbo-type): a rented house/apartment room designed for actual residence is, for 475C.377 purposes, a private residence room, not a public place — but the rental agreement / house rules may prohibit smoking and/or cannabis use entirely, and the landlord/host may enforce that by contract (see §12.6). A visitor must check the listing’s smoking/cannabis policy; “the host didn’t say anything” is not permission to smoke. Verify whether any Oregon short-term-rental ordinance (Portland, Bend, etc.) adds a cannabis-specific rule — none was located in this run.
  • Cannabis tours / “cannabis cafés” / tasting rooms marketed to tourists: as of this cut-off there is no licensed cannabis-café or tasting-room category (§12.4.2), and a tour that includes on-site consumption at a public venue, or that bundles marijuana items into the ticket price, risks both the 475C.377 public-use ban and the unlicensed-sale rules (gifting-with-consideration = sale, §12.0). A lawful Oregon cannabis tour, on the material located, is a tour that visits licensed retailers / farms (where lawful) and transports visitors between private lawful consumption locations, without itself selling or furnishing marijuana items for on-site public consumption. Verify any specific tour operator’s OLCC licence / event-registration status before recommending it — this draft does not endorse any operator.
  • Payment: secondary visitor guides note credit cards rarely work at dispensaries because card networks avoid cannabis while it is federally illegal, and advise cash or debit (50-state guide, above). That is a banking-network practice point under the federal baseline (“no federal cannabis banking law”), not an Oregon statute — Verify at the specific retailer; do not state that any particular payment method is guaranteed.

§12.6 Landlord and tenant rules

12.6.1 The starting point — private use is not a crime, but the lease governs

Run 1 §1.1 already corrected the common overstatement: “Landlords may restrict use and growing by lease. Secondary summaries stating ‘cannot use in a rented house’ overstate the rule: the statute restricts public use and visibility; a private lease ban is a contract matter, not a criminal ban on private-home use as such.” Part 12 develops that correction into the full housing picture:

  • Criminal law does not ban private-home use in a rental as such. ORS 475C.377 bans use in a public place. A tenant’s private room/apartment designed for actual residence is not a public place (Run 1 §1.1.1). Smoking/vaping in that room is, however, subject to (a) the ICAA for shared enclosed spaces (not the private room itself — see §12.4.3), (b) the lease, and (c) any smoke-free housing policy the landlord has lawfully adopted (see §12.6.2).
  • A lease ban is enforceable as a contract / rental-agreement violation, not as a 475C offence. Oregon statutes permit landlords to enforce tenant violations of their rental agreements, rules, and general laws (secondary Oregon real-estate-law analysis — https://q-law.com/tenant-medical-marijuana-oregon-toke-landlords-line/ — accessed 2026-11-01). A tenant who breaches a no-smoking / no-cannabis lease clause faces the ordinary rental-agreement enforcement remedies (cure-or-quit notices, termination for cause, FED — forcible entry and detainer — proceedings under ORS 105.105–105.168), not a 475C.377 prosecution for the private-room use itself — unless the use also occurred in a public place (hallway, shared balcony, yard visible/accessible to the public) or violated another law (e.g. DUII, over-limit possession).
  • Secondhand-smoke / nuisance angle (secondary, Verify): one secondary Q&A summary argues that marijuana smoked “in and around a building with multiple tenants” affecting other residents “would be considered public” and, combined with a landlord’s advertised no-smoking policy, could justify the affected tenant terminating the lease on 30 days’ notice (secondary — https://www.askalawyeroncall.com/landlord-tenant/ee8al-need-know-break-lease-without-penalty.html — accessed 2026-11-01). That “smoke affecting neighbours = public place” argument is a secondary advocate’s argument, not a quoted ORS definition, and is flagged Verify. The safer statement is: smoke migrating into shared enclosed spaces or other units engages the ICAA (shared spaces), the lease’s smoke-free terms, and general habitability/nuisance principles (ORS 90.320 landlord habitability duties — Verify the habitability application to secondhand smoke), and the affected tenant’s remedy depends on the lease, the landlord’s enforcement, and the specific facts, not on a blanket “public place” reclassification of a private room.
  • Growing in a rental: a tenant’s home grow (4 plants per household, ORS 475C.305) in a rental is subject to (i) the lease (a landlord may prohibit growing by lease — sample Oregon month-to-month agreements located include “NO MEDICAL MARIJUANA MAY BE GROWN OR CONSUMED ON THE PREMISES WITHOUT THE PRIOR WRITTEN CONSENT OF LANDLORD” — secondary form, accessed 2026-11-01; that form language is a private form, not a statute, and is cited only as evidence of common lease practice), (ii) the visibility rule (ORS 475C.306 — not visible from a public place by normal unaided vision), (iii) OMMP grow-site rules where applicable (from 1 Jan 2026, a notarised property-owner consent form is required where the patient/grower does not own the property — Run 1 §4.7, SB 907 (2025) per secondary summary — Verify bill and OAR text), and (iv) any local / fire / electrical / mould / water-damage lease or code consequences of an indoor grow. A landlord who has not prohibited growing in the lease cannot retroactively prohibit it for an existing tenancy without a lawful lease change / notice — the secondary real-estate analysis stresses a no-medical-marijuana policy “should not be retroactive to tenants holding legal medical marijuana cards who have already signed their rental agreements or leases” and “should so state” that it applies going forward (Q-Law, above). Verify the retroactivity / lease-change notice rules in ORS chapter 90 (ORS 90.427 / 90.432 as applicable) before advising on a mid-tenancy policy change.

12.6.2 Smoke-free housing — landlord adoption, disclosure, and enforcement

  • Landlords may designate a property smoke-free. The OHA ICAA FAQ states: “Nothing in ICAA prevents organizations and businesses from having stronger policies. This includes smoke-free properties. If your building has a smoke and vapor-free policy, check with your management company for its policy. The Oregon Health Authority enforces the state law, not the policies of companies. Landlords and management companies must enforce their own smoke and vapor-free policies” (OHA FAQ, April 2025, search-indexed — accessed 2026-11-01). The OHA smoke-free-housing resources page (https://smokefreeoregon.com/resources/smoke-free-housing-tools/, cited in the FAQ) is the official tenant/landlord resource — Verify its current contents; it was not opened in this run.
  • Disclosure (Verify — gap): whether Oregon law requires a landlord to disclose a smoking policy (or a change to it) to a prospective/existing tenant, and in what form / with what notice period, was not established by a located ORS section in this run and is flagged Verify. Secondary landlord-tenant summaries list “smoking policy” among Oregon required disclosures, but without a cited section in the material returned. Do not quote a disclosure statute number until ORS chapter 90 is checked for a smoking-policy disclosure section. What is settled is the practical advice: a tenant should obtain the smoking/cannabis policy in writing in the rental agreement before signing, and a landlord should state it in the agreement rather than relying on oral policy.
  • Enforcement of a smoke-free policy: breach of a smoke-free lease term is enforced as a rental-agreement violation (cure notice / termination for cause under ORS chapter 90 — see §12.6.3 for the drug-free-housing fast track, which is a different mechanism and must not be confused with an ordinary smoke-free-policy breach). Cleaning / deodorising charges at move-out for smoking in violation of the lease are a deposit-deduction / lease-damages question (ORS 90.300, 31-day deposit return — secondary summary — Verify current deposit rules), not a cannabis-specific penalty. A landlord may not use self-help eviction; possession must be recovered through ORS 105.105–105.168 proceedings.

12.6.3 Drug- and alcohol-free housing — ORS 90.398 (the 48-hour / 24-hour fast track)

Verbatim text (Justia 2017 rendering; Springfield-Eugene Tenant Association rendering updates the cross-reference to ORS 475C.009 — Verify against the current official ORS page):

“(1) If a tenant living for less than two years in drug and alcohol free housing uses, possesses or shares alcohol, marijuana items as defined in ORS 475C.009, illegal drugs, controlled substances or prescription drugs without a medical prescription, the landlord may deliver a written notice to the tenant terminating the tenancy for cause and take possession as provided in ORS 105.105 to 105.168. The notice must specify the acts constituting the drug or alcohol violation and state that the rental agreement will terminate in not less than 48 hours after delivery of the notice, at a specified date and time. The notice must also state that the tenant can cure the drug or alcohol violation by a change in conduct or otherwise within 24 hours after delivery of the notice.” “(2) If the tenant cures the violation within the 24-hour period, the rental agreement does not terminate. If the tenant does not cure the violation within the 24-hour period, the rental agreement terminates as provided in the notice.” “If substantially the same act that constituted a prior drug or alcohol violation of which notice was given reoccurs within six months, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement upon at least 24 hours’ written notice specifying the violation and the date and time of termination of the rental agreement.”

Sources: ORS 90.398 as rendered — https://law.justia.com/codes/oregon/2017/volume-03/chapter-090/section-90.398/ and https://www.springfieldeugenetenantassociation.com/90_398_termination_of_tenancy_for_drug_or_alcohol_violations (verified 29 Oct 2024) — accessed 2026-11-01. History: [2005 c.391 §10; 2017 c.21 §34].

Limits that prevent over-reading ORS 90.398:

  • Only “drug and alcohol free housing,” only tenancies under two years. The fast track does not apply to ordinary housing that is not designated drug/alcohol-free, nor to a tenant who has lived there for two years or more. A landlord of ordinary housing who wants to terminate for a cannabis-lease breach must use the ordinary cure/termination notices in ORS chapter 90 (see §12.6.4).
  • “Marijuana items” as defined in ORS 475C.009 — the section reaches use/possession/sharing of marijuana items in designated drug/alcohol-free housing, even if the use/possession would be lawful under ORS 475C.337 in ordinary housing. Designation as drug/alcohol-free housing is what makes otherwise-lawful cannabis use a terminable violation there. Whether a designated drug/alcohol-free housing provider must meet any registration, funding or programme criteria to qualify for ORS 90.398 (e.g. recovery housing, subsidised housing) was not established in this run — Verify the “drug and alcohol free housing” definition in ORS 90.100 and any qualifying criteria before advising that any landlord may self-designate.
  • Cure by “change in conduct or otherwise” within 24 hours — the tenant who stops the violating conduct within 24 hours of delivery does not lose the tenancy on that notice. The notice must specify the acts, the termination date/time (≥48 hours after delivery), and the 24-hour cure right; a notice missing any element is defective — Verify service rules (mailing adds 3 calendar days in secondary summaries; electronic delivery requires a special written addendum to the rental agreement — secondary form guidance, accessed 2026-11-01).
  • Repeat violation within 6 months: substantially the same act reoccurring within 6 months of a noticed violation may be terminated on ≥24 hours’ written notice, without a cure right (subsection (3) as rendered above).
  • “Without a medical prescription” qualifier: the section lists “prescription drugs without a medical prescription” as a separate category from “marijuana items.” Whether a tenant’s OMMP medical use of marijuana items in drug/alcohol-free housing is protected, or is still a terminable violation because marijuana items are listed without a medical-use qualifier, is Verify and genuinely ambiguous on the text returned — the “without a medical prescription” phrase grammatically attaches to prescription drugs, not clearly to marijuana items. Do not advise either way without checking ORS 90.100 definitions, ORS 90.398 case law, and the housing provider’s programme rules. This ambiguity is a live Part 12 gap, not a drafting oversight.

12.6.4 Ordinary termination for cannabis-lease breaches (non-drug-free housing) — Verify

  • For housing that is not designated drug/alcohol-free, and for tenancies of two years or more, cannabis-related termination follows the ordinary ORS chapter 90 termination framework: written notice specifying the violation, a cure period, and FED proceedings if uncured. The specific ordinary cure periods, notice forms, and first-year vs post-first-year termination rules (ORS 90.392, 90.394, 90.427, 90.630 et seq. for manufactured dwellings) were not quoted in this run and are flagged Verify — this draft does not state a cure period for ordinary housing, because stating the 48-hour/24-hour drug-free-housing periods as if they were the general rule would be wrong. Secondary summaries also note a separate 24-hour unconditional quit notice for specified serious violations (e.g. intentionally causing substantial property damage, Class A felony on the premises including manufacture of a cannabinoid extract, unlawful manufacture/delivery/possession of a controlled substance — secondary landlord-notice pack, accessed 2026-11-01). Whether “manufacture of a cannabinoid extract” on the premises triggers a 24-hour unconditional notice, and how that interacts with a lawful home grow / OMMP grow site, is Verify against current ORS 90.396 / 90.398 and the FED notice forms — do not advise a tenant or landlord on a 24-hour notice for a grow without that check.
  • Retaliation / discrimination protections: ORS chapter 90 prohibits retaliatory termination and discrimination on protected grounds, but OMMP status is not listed as a protected class in the material located — see §12.6.5 on reasonable accommodation. A landlord may not terminate for a discriminatory reason, but may terminate for a lawful lease violation even if the tenant is a cardholder, subject to the §12.6.3 ambiguity and §12.6.5.

12.6.5 Medical-use protections in housing — essentially none as a cannabis-specific right; reasonable-accommodation law does not compel cannabis use

  • No Oregon statute located creates a right to use or grow medical marijuana in rental housing over a landlord’s lawful lease ban. ORS 475C.780 (medical code construction) provides that nothing in ORS 475C.770–475C.919 requires an employer to accommodate medical use in the workplace (see §12.9.3); there is no parallel housing-accommodation section located, and the absence of a housing section cuts against implying one — but the absence of a section is not itself a prohibition. The secondary real-estate analysis (Q-Law, above) concludes landlords may, going forward, enact rules prohibiting on-premises medical-marijuana use, with “little fear of a fair housing / reasonable accommodation claim” to compel smoking on the premises, because (a) marijuana remains federally illegal (adult-use Schedule I; medical Schedule III only within the federal baseline’s state-licensed scope — §12.7), and (b) federal fair-housing reasonable-accommodation law does not require accommodation of federally illegal drug use. That analysis is secondary and pre-dates the 2026 Schedule III change — Verify whether the Schedule III change alters the federal fair-housing analysis for state-licensed medical use (see §12.7.4). Do not advise a cardholder-tenant that they have, or do not have, a federal reasonable-accommodation right to smoke medical marijuana in a rental without that Verify check.
  • What a cardholder-tenant CAN rely on: (i) the lease as written (if it does not prohibit medical use/growing, the landlord cannot invent a prohibition mid-tenancy without a lawful lease change); (ii) the ORS 90.398 ambiguity (§12.6.3) — if the housing is drug/alcohol-free, the medical-use question is unresolved, not decided against the tenant; (iii) non-smoked medical use (edibles, tinctures, topicals) does not implicate smoke-free / ICAA rules and is harder for a landlord to characterise as a nuisance, though a blanket “no marijuana items” lease clause would still reach it as a contract matter; (iv) disability law for the underlying condition (as opposed to the marijuana use itself) — an employer/landlord must not discriminate on the basis of disability, but that does not compel permitting marijuana use (see the Washburn employment analogy in §12.9.3).
  • Federally assisted / public housing — federal law controls (see §12.6.6).

12.6.6 Public housing and federally assisted housing — federal prohibition overrides Oregon legality

  • HUD smoke-free public housing rule: the federal smoke-free rule for public housing (24 CFR Part 965, Subpart G — secondary summary via NIEHS/HUD materials, accessed 2026-11-01) prohibits smoking inside all public housing units and common areas and outdoors within 25 feet of any public housing or administrative building. That 25-foot federal buffer is stricter than Oregon’s 10-foot ICAA buffer and applies “regardless of what Oregon’s state rules say about the surrounding area” (secondary ICAA summary — https://legalclarity.org/oregon-outdoor-smoking-laws-where-can-you-smoke/ — accessed 2026-11-01). Verify the current 24 CFR 965.653 text and its Oregon PHA implementation — the 25-foot figure is stated here as a secondary summary of the federal rule.
  • Marijuana in federally assisted housing is prohibited as a matter of federal law, even if Oregon-legal. Public housing authorities (PHAs) operate under federal law that treats marijuana as a controlled substance (adult-use Schedule I; and, for housing purposes, the Schedule III medical change’s effect is Verify — see §12.7.4). Federal law permits (and, for drug-related criminal activity, in some circumstances requires) PHAs to deny admission, terminate assistance, or evict for drug-related activity, including marijuana use/possession, and to apply “one strike” policies. No Oregon PHA’s specific admissions/termination policy was opened in this run — Verify the policy of the specific PHA (e.g. Home Forward (Portland), Housing Authority of the City of Salem, etc.) before advising any applicant/tenant. The safe general statement is: do not assume Oregon legality protects a tenant in public housing, Section 8 / Housing Choice Voucher housing, or any other federally subsidised housing; the federal rules, the PHA’s Admissions and Continued Occupancy Policy (ACOP) / Section 8 Administrative Plan, and the lease’s federal drug provisions control, and they may prohibit marijuana entirely.
  • State-funded / non-federal affordable housing: housing funded only by Oregon/local sources, without federal assistance, is governed by Oregon law + the lease ( §§12.6.1–12.6.5). Whether a particular affordable-housing development is federally assisted is a development-specific funding question — Verify funding source before advising.
  • Homeless shelters / transitional housing / recovery housing: many such programmes are designated drug/alcohol-free housing for ORS 90.398 purposes and/or operate under federal grant drug-free requirements. A resident’s cannabis use in such housing is governed by the programme rules + ORS 90.398 (§12.6.3), not by the general private-rental analysis. Verify the specific programme’s rules.

§12.7 Gun ownership conflicts

This section is the most litigation-sensitive in Part 12, and the federal baseline’s Schedule III change makes it more unsettled, not less, as of 1 Nov 2026. The rule to carry into any advice is: Oregon state law and federal law point in opposite directions, and the federal direction is in active flux (draft Form 4473 + pending Supreme Court case). No advice that “a medical cardholder can safely buy/possess a firearm” or that “a medical cardholder can never possess a firearm” is safe without the Verify flags below.

12.7.1 Federal baseline — 18 U.S.C. §922(g)(3) (“unlawful user”), Form 4473, and the 2011 ATF open letter

  • The statute (unchanged by the Schedule III order as given): 18 U.S.C. §922(g)(3) makes it unlawful for any person “who is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance (as defined in section 102 of the Controlled Substances Act)” to ship, transport, possess, or receive any firearm or ammunition. Congress has not amended §922(g)(3) (secondary analysis, accessed 2026-11-01 — https://educate.uslawshield.com/what-rescheduling-marijuana-to-schedule-iii-means-for-gun-owners/). The penalty for violating §922(g)(3) is stated in secondary sources as up to 15 years’ imprisonment and up to a $250,000 fine in one analysis, and up to 10 years for a false statement on Form 4473 in another — Verify current penalty provisions (18 U.S.C. §§922(g)(3), 924(a)(8), 924(c) as applicable) before quoting a maximum; the secondary sources conflict on the headline number and this draft does not resolve it.
  • Form 4473 (current, still-in-force form as of this cut-off): every purchase through a federal firearms licensee (FFL) requires ATF Form 4473 (Firearms Transaction Record). Current Question 21.f (numbering varies by form revision — older summaries cite Question 11.e) asks whether the buyer is “an unlawful user of, or addicted to, marijuana or any depressant, stimulant, narcotic drug, or any other controlled substance,” with a bolded warning: “The use or possession of marijuana remains unlawful under Federal law regardless of whether it has been legalized or decriminalized for medicinal or recreational purposes in the state where you reside.” Answering “yes” means the dealer cannot complete the sale; answering “no” while actively using marijuana is a false statement on a federal form (felony, up to 10 years per secondary summaries — Verify). Sources: secondary — https://legalclarity.org/do-you-lose-your-gun-rights-if-you-have-a-medical-card/; https://educate.uslawshield.com/what-rescheduling-marijuana-to-schedule-iii-means-for-gun-owners/ — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • 2011 ATF open letter: in September 2011, ATF directed all FFLs that, regardless of whether a State has authorised marijuana for medical purposes, a person is an “unlawful user” and is prohibited by federal law from possessing firearms or ammunition — and that if an FFL has reasonable cause to believe a buyer holds a medical marijuana card, the FFL must deny the sale. That letter is the origin of the “cardholder = prohibited person at the point of sale” practice. Source: secondary summaries of the letter — https://www.rabbylaw.com/how-legalized-marijuana-affects-gun-rights/; https://flbusiness.law/mmj/ — accessed 2026-11-01. Whether the 2011 letter has been withdrawn, superseded or narrowed by the 2026 draft Form 4473 (below) was NOT established — Verify with ATF’s current FFL guidance; do not assume withdrawal.
  • Background checks in Oregon (SB 941, 2015): Oregon requires background checks for private/unlicensed firearm transfers as well as FFL sales (ORS 166.438 / 166.434, secondary summaries — Verify section numbers). A private seller who transfers a firearm to a person they know or have reasonable cause to believe is a prohibited person faces the same federal prohibition analysis as an FFL. The secondary legislative-testimony summary located (2015, Lane County Sheriff’s CHL unit, via OLIS committee document) states the pre-2026 practical paradox bluntly: “a marijuana user can own, use & even conceal carry a firearm, but cannot legally buy one” — and that a close relative who is a marijuana user could not lawfully be gifted a firearm because they would be a prohibited person unable to pass a background check under SB 941 (secondary testimony — https://apps.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2015R1/Downloads/CommitteeMeetingDocument/67701 — accessed 2026-11-01). That testimony is a lay summary, not law, and its “can own” limb is contradicted by the federal possession prohibition in §922(g)(3) — see §12.7.2. Do not quote the paradox as a legal rule.

12.7.2 The two cases that frame Oregon — Willis v. Winters (Or. 2011) and Wilson v. Lynch (9th Cir. 2016)

These cases answer different questions and must not be merged:

A. Willis v. Winters, 253 P.3d 1058 (Or. 2011) — Oregon concealed handgun licences (CHL): YES, a cardholder may not be denied a CHL solely for medical-marijuana status, under Oregon law.

  • Facts (secondary summaries): sheriffs in two Oregon counties (Jackson County Sheriff Mike Winters is the named respondent) denied concealed handgun licences to medical-marijuana users who admitted use during the CHL process, reasoning that because the applicants could not possess firearms under federal law, they were prohibited from obtaining a CHL. The Oregon Supreme Court unanimously (19 May 2011, secondary date) held the sheriffs were wrong under Oregon law: the applicants satisfied Oregon’s “shall issue” CHL statutory requirements (ORS 166.291 et seq.), medical-marijuana status is not a state-law disqualifier, and the federal Gun Control Act does not preempt Oregon’s CHL licensing statutes. The U.S. Supreme Court denied certiorari (132 S.Ct. 199 (2012), secondary citation — Verify), leaving the Oregon ruling in place.
  • Critical limit stated by the Oregon court itself (quoted in secondary analysis): the CHL “may exempt [the holder] from prosecution or arrest under ORS 166.250(1)(a) and (b), but it does not in any way preclude full enforcement of the federal law by federal law enforcement officials.” In other words: Willis guarantees a state licence; it does not guarantee federal-law immunity for possession. A Willis CHL holder who possesses a firearm remains exposed to federal prosecution under §922(g)(3) as the federal law stood pre-Schedule III. Sources: secondary — https://oregonstatecannabis.org/mmj-gun-ownership; https://flbusiness.law/mmj/; https://www.calguns.net/forum/politics-litigation-and-activism/california-2nd-amend-political-discussion-activism/1213853-prop-64-ca-gun-owners/page2 — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Oregon-law consequence today: county sheriffs, as state law-enforcement officials, must abide by state law and issue CHLs to persons who qualify under Oregon law, even if they do not qualify under federal law (secondary summary, above). Measure 67 (Oregon’s medical law) contains no provision banning a CHL holder from obtaining an OMMP card, and vice versa. Open carry: Oregon does not issue licences for open carry to residents (secondary summary — Verify ORS 166.250 / local open-carry ordinances, which vary by city/county and are outside this section’s scope).

B. Wilson v. Lynch, 835 F.3d 1083 (9th Cir. 2016), cert. denied 137 S.Ct. 1396 (2017) — federal FFL sales: NO, an FFL must deny a sale to a known medical-marijuana cardholder, and that denial does not violate the Second Amendment (on the pre-Schedule III law).

  • Facts: a Nevada medical-marijuana cardholder (Wilson) sued after an FFL refused to sell her a firearm, consistent with the 2011 ATF letter. The Ninth Circuit held the ATF interpretation was valid, the Second Amendment was infringed but the government had a right to infringe it on the evidence (empirical data / legislative determinations supporting “a strong link between drug use and violence”), and an FFL with reasonable cause to believe a buyer holds a medical card must deny the sale. The U.S. Supreme Court declined review. Because Oregon is in the Ninth Circuit, Wilson is binding circuit law for federal FFL sales in Oregon on the law as it stood — subject to the Schedule III / Hemani developments below.
  • What Wilson did NOT decide: Wilson did not hold that a cardholder who already possesses a firearm must surrender it, nor did it address possession (as opposed to purchase) as a standalone question on its facts (there was no showing Wilson actually possessed a firearm — secondary analysis, above). Do not cite Wilson as a “possession” holding without that qualification.
  • Tension, stated plainly: after Willis + Wilson, an Oregon medical cardholder could (under Oregon law) hold a CHL and (under federal law, pre-2026) be a prohibited person who could not lawfully buy from an FFL and could be federally prosecuted for possessing a firearm. That tension is the pre-2026 status quo. The 2026 developments below may resolve it for medical users — or may not, depending on final ATF action and the Supreme Court.

12.7.3 The 2026 inflection — draft Form 4473 (May 2026, NOT final) and United States v. Hemani (argued 2 Mar 2026, decision pending at cut-off)

Both developments are pending, not law, as of 1 November 2026. Do not present either as a decided change.

  • Draft Form 4473 (ATF, published 8 May 2026 — secondary date; NORML report 12 May 2026): ATF posted a draft revision of Form 4473 revising the definition of an “unlawful” drug user. The draft removes references to medical marijuana as a basis for disqualification and focuses instead on recreational marijuana use: the draft question asks whether the buyer is an unlawful user of / addicted to marijuana or any other controlled substance, with the warning recast as “Federal law does not permit the use or possession of marijuana for recreational purposes” — omitting any reference to medical marijuana as a disqualifier. NORML’s summary states the draft “acknowledges that this prohibition no longer applies to those who exclusively consume state-authorized medical cannabis products, which the Justice Department recently reclassified from Schedule I to Schedule III.” Sources: secondary — https://norml.org/blog/2026/05/12/atf-posts-draft-document-acknowledging-medical-cannabis-scheduling-change/ (12 May 2026); https://educate.uslawshield.com/what-rescheduling-marijuana-to-schedule-iii-means-for-gun-owners/ — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • Draft ≠ operative form: “The ATF’s revisions are not yet official, as several other proposed changes to the form require public comments” (NORML, above); “The draft form is not yet legally operative. Until the ATF completes rulemaking and publishes a final revised form, the current Form 4473 remains in effect. FFLs must continue using the current form” (U.S. LawShield, above). A medical cardholder who answers the current form’s question on the basis of the draft form’s logic risks a false-statement prosecution under the form actually in force. Do not advise any buyer to rely on the draft.
  • What the draft would and would not do if finalised (Verify — analysis, not ATF text): if finalised in the draft’s form, a person who exclusively consumes state-authorised medical cannabis would no longer be an “unlawful user” for Form 4473 purposes, while a recreational user would remain prohibited. Open questions the draft does not settle on the material located: (i) what counts as “exclusively” medical (a cardholder who also uses recreationally? a cardholder whose card lapses?); (ii) whether the draft changes the possession prohibition in §922(g)(3) itself, or only the purchase-form question (the statute is unchanged — §12.7.1 — so possession exposure may persist even if the purchase question changes); (iii) whether “state-authorized” means OLCC-licensed retail medical-grade sales, OHA-registered OMMP grow-site use, or both — the same “state-licensed” ambiguity as the §280E question in Run 1 Part 1, now in firearms form, and marked Verify; (iv) whether ATF will finalise the draft at all, and in what form, after public comment.
  • United States v. Hemani — Supreme Court, argued 2 March 2026: the Court heard oral argument on whether §922(g)(3) can constitutionally bar drug users from possessing firearms. Secondary reporting (pre-decision, accessed 2026-11-01) states a decision was “expected by the end of the Court’s current term in summer 2026” and that NORML filed an amicus brief arguing the blanket ban lacks historical precedent and is unconstitutional. Sources: secondary — https://legalclarity.org/do-you-lose-your-gun-rights-if-you-have-a-medical-card/; https://norml.org/blog/2026/05/12/atf-posts-draft-document-acknowledging-medical-cannabis-scheduling-change/ — accessed 2026-11-01. No Hemani decision was located in this run as of the 1 Nov 2026 cut-off, and none is imported here. Whether Hemani was decided, and what it held, after the cut-off is outside this draft — Verify on the Supreme Court docket before advising on §922(g)(3)’s constitutionality. (The task’s cut-off discipline applies: a summer-2026 expected decision that was not located in the 1 Nov 2026 research is Unavailable in this draft, not assumed.)
  • Interaction of Hemani + draft Form 4473 + Schedule III (Verify — the core Part 12 firearms question): even if Hemani narrows §922(g)(3) and even if ATF finalises a medical-carve-out Form 4473, the three mechanisms operate on different planes (constitutional validity of the possession ban; the purchase-form question; the drug’s schedule). A medical cardholder’s position after all three could be: (a) fully clear to buy and possess; (b) clear to buy but still exposed on possession; (c) clear on possession (if Hemani strikes the ban) but still blocked at purchase by an unrevised form; or (d) unchanged. This draft does not choose among (a)–(d). The correct Part 12 statement as of 1 Nov 2026 is: federal firearms law for Oregon medical cardholders is in transition; the current Form 4473 and §922(g)(3) remain in force; the draft form and Hemani are pending; and the Schedule III question — whether Oregon OMMP registration, OLCC medical-grade retail sales, or both count as “state-licensed medical” for firearms purposes — is marked Verify.

12.7.4 Oregon-specific firearms rules that do NOT depend on the federal flux

  • Oregon CHL law (ORS 166.291 et seq.): a CHL is required to carry concealed in Oregon; medical-marijuana status alone is not a state-law disqualifier (Willis, §12.7.2). Other CHL disqualifiers (felony convictions, certain misdemeanors, mental-health adjudications, etc.) apply on their own terms — Verify the current ORS 166.291 disqualifier list; a marijuana conviction (as opposed to cardholder status) may itself disqualify on a ground independent of use.
  • Oregon has no state statute located that prohibits a medical cardholder from owning a firearm under state law. The prohibition a cardholder faces is federal (§922(g)(3) + Form 4473), not an Oregon ownership ban. Conversely, Oregon has no state statute located that protects a cardholder’s federal firearms rights or that directs Oregon law enforcement not to cooperate with federal firearms enforcement against cardholders — Verify whether any Oregon “sanctuary” / non-cooperation firearms statute exists; none was located.
  • Hunting / employment / federal-land carry: a cardholder who hunts, works in a firearms-sensitive job, or carries on federal land faces additional federal and employer rules (federal-land firearms rules, employer drug policies, DOT/safety-sensitive rules — see §12.9.3) that are not resolved by Willis. Verify each context separately.
  • Practical advice that IS safe as of this cut-off (not legal advice, but the only safe general statement): (1) do not lie on Form 4473 — a false statement is a separate federal felony regardless of the underlying prohibition; (2) do not assume a CHL, an OMMP card, or the draft Form 4473 protects a purchase or possession under current federal law; (3) check the current Form 4473 and ATF FFL guidance on the date of any proposed purchase, and check the Hemani docket, before acting; (4) a person who has stopped using marijuana is in a different position from a current user for “unlawful user” purposes — but how long after last use a person ceases to be an “unlawful user” under federal law was not established in this run and is Verify (ATF’s “reasonable cause / inference of current use” guidance, including any time-based inference from a card’s currency, must be checked, not guessed).

§12.8 Pet and veterinary products

12.8.1 What is sold for pets in Oregon — hemp/CBD pet products are general-market hemp items (with animal-specific overlays)

  • OLCC Hemp Registry applies to pet products. From the OLCC Hemp Registry FAQs (opened 2026-11-01): “If the product is intended for animal consumption or use and meets the other requirements for registering, it must be registered with the OLCC and labeled according [to] OLCC rules.” And, specifically: “As of January 1, 2026, most hemp pet products are required to be registered with OLCC and labeled according to OLCC rules prior to being offered for sale. The requirements apply to most hemp products that contain cannabinoids, whether intended for human or animal use or consumption. THC and CBD are the most common cannabinoids. … Hemp derived pet products like tinctures, chews, and treats are required to be registered with OLCC and labeled according to OLCC rules prior to being offered for sale, even if they are marketed as only containing CBD.” Topically applied hemp products (lotions, balms, salves, shampoos) are excluded from the registry. Source: OLCC Hemp Registry FAQs, opened 2026-11-01 — https://www.oregon.gov/olcc/marijuana/Pages/hemp-registry-faqs.aspx.
  • No OLCC licence needed to sell pet hemp products in the general market; ODA vendor licence generally required. “You do not need a license from the OLCC to sell hemp products in places like grocery stores, pet stores, gas stations, smoke shops, or online (the ‘general market’). Most Oregon businesses that sell hemp products to consumers, including products intended for animal use or consumption, are required to have a hemp vendor license from the Oregon Department of Agriculture” (OLCC FAQ, opened 2026-11-01). See §12.1.3 for the vendor-licence / registry distinction. A pet store selling CBD chews therefore needs (i) the product to be OLCC-registered + labelled, and (ii) (generally) an ODA vendor licence — but not an OLCC retailer licence, unless it is selling OLCC marijuana items.
  • Commercial feed vs supplement/remedy line — ODA exclusively regulates commercial feed: “commercial feed products are not subject to the OLCC hemp item registry; commercial feed products are registered under ORS 633.006 to 633.089 and regulated exclusively by ODA” (OLCC FAQ, opened 2026-11-01). A hemp product marketed as animal feed (registered under ORS 633) follows the feed route; a hemp product marketed as a pet treat / tincture / chew for consumption/use follows the OLCC registry route. Whether a given product is “feed” or a “hemp item” is a labelling/marketing determination — Verify the product’s registration route before advising a manufacturer; marketing a feed-registered product with remedy/supplement claims risks reclassification.
  • Labelling for pet hemp items: labels must list THC and CBD content (see §12.1.3 for the full labelling rules, including the <LOQ rule, the advertised-cannabinoid rule, and the 10% target-potency rule). No pet-specific THC/CBD potency cap was located in this run — the general hemp-item THC/cannabinoid limits in OAR 845-026-0400/0410 apply, and the adult-use threshold (≥0.5 mg THC = adult-use item, 21+ only — secondary summary, Verify per §12.1.3) would, on its terms, make a high-THC pet product an adult-use item saleable only to a 21+ buyer. Whether Oregon imposes a pet-specific THC cap, a pet-specific serving limit, or a prohibition on THC in pet products was NOT established — Verify in OAR 845-026 and ODA animal-product rules before formulating a pet product. Do not state that pet CBD products must be THC-free, or that they may contain any THC level, without that check.
  • Marijuana-derived pet products (from OLCC marijuana, not hemp) are NOT general-market pet products. A cannabinoid product derived from marijuana (not industrial hemp) may be sold only through the OLCC licensed system to 21+ consumers / OMMP patients, not as an over-the-counter pet product in a pet store. There is no Oregon “pet medical marijuana card” or veterinary marijuana authorisation — see §12.8.2. A pet owner who gives an OLCC marijuana edible to a pet is using a human marijuana item off-label for an animal, with the toxicity risks in §12.8.3, and without any veterinary authorisation framework.
  • Federal overlay (Verify — transition): no CBD product (human or animal) is FDA-approved as a veterinary drug, and FDA has warned firms marketing CBD pet products with disease claims. After 11 December 2026, the federal hemp definition + 0.4 mg/container cap (federal baseline) will affect hemp pet products that are “intended for consumption … by humans or animals” on the federal definition’s terms (secondary summary of PL 119-37 §781 — https://www.atlrx.com/blogs/cbd/is-cbd-legal-in-oregon/ — accessed 2026-11-01). Oregon’s response to the federal hemp dates for pet products specifically was not located — Verify after 11 Dec 2026. Do not advise a pet-product manufacturer that their product will remain federally lawful after that date without that check.

12.8.2 What veterinarians may and may not do in Oregon — discuss yes, prescribe/recommend medical marijuana no (2016 OVMEB guidance, currency Verify)

  • Oregon Veterinary Medical Examining Board (OVMEB) guidance (August 2016, mass e-mail, as reported in contemporaneous news): “Veterinarians may discuss veterinary use of cannabis with clients, and are advised to inform clients about published data on toxicity in animals, as well as lack of scientific data on benefits. Please be aware that a client’s written consent is needed for any unorthodox treatment.” Source: secondary news report of the OVMEB memo — https://www.knkx.org/news/2016-12-20/legal-haze-clouds-cannabis-for-pets (20 Dec 2016) and https://www.nwnewsnetwork.org/health-and-medicine/2016-12-21/legal-haze-clouds-cannabis-for-pets — accessed 2026-11-01. Secondary summaries restate the position as: “the Oregon Veterinary Medical Examining Board allows that ‘veterinarians can discuss the use of cannabis with clients’” (secondary — https://www.pawcbd.com/blogs/posts/what-you-need-to-know-about-veterinarians-and-cbd-for-pets — accessed 2026-11-01).
  • What “discuss” does not include: the OVMEB position as reported in veterinary-press summaries is that “Marijuana is not approved for veterinary use” and a veterinarian may not write a prescription for “pet marijuana” (secondary veterinary-press summary — https://www.veterinarypracticenews.ca/the-latest-on-cannabis-and-hemp-for-pets/ — accessed 2026-11-01, citing OVMEB’s website as accessed 2015). The AVMA position as reported is that it is illegal for veterinarians to recommend medical marijuana (same summary). A Portland veterinarian quoted in 2016 put the practice position as: “even though recreational marijuana use is legal in Oregon now, as veterinarians we are not allowed to prescribe it. So we have to be careful about giving recommendations” — with rare, client-initiated, low-dose advice for cancer patients where all other treatments had failed, under a signed consent form stating the vet cannot prescribe the substance, the owner must obtain it themselves, and use must stop and the vet be consulted if negative effects (disorientation, drooling, inability to move) arise (KNKX/NW News, above).
  • Currency warning — Verify: the OVMEB guidance located is from 2016. Whether OVMEB has issued updated guidance (e.g. addressing hemp-derived CBD specifically, as distinct from marijuana; addressing the 2018 Farm Bill hemp framework; or adopting a California-style discuss-but-not-recommend statute) was NOT established in this run. Do not present the 2016 memo as current OVMEB guidance without checking OVMEB’s current website / rules. In particular, the discuss-vs-recommend line for hemp-derived CBD (as opposed to marijuana) may differ from the marijuana line, and no Oregon statute located in this run draws that line for veterinarians — Verify whether any Oregon statute or OVMEB rule now addresses veterinary CBD discussion/recommendation specifically. (California’s AB 221 (2018) / AB 1885 framework — vets may discuss cannabis but not recommend/dispense — is California law, not Oregon law, and must not be cited as Oregon law.)
  • No Oregon veterinary cannabis authorisation system: there is no OMMP-equivalent for animals, no veterinary cannabis card, and no “designated caregiver” for a pet. An owner who obtains marijuana for a pet does so as a 21+ consumer (or OMMP patient for their own use) and administers it without veterinary authorisation — at their own risk and with the toxicity profile in §12.8.3.
  • ODA veterinary product registration — the animal-remedy overlay: Oregon law requires that all animal remedy products sold in Oregon must be registered with ODA (OAR 603-012-0210 programme). “Animal remedies means any product used to prevent, inhibit or cure or enhance or protect the health or well-being of animals, but does not include food, surgical instruments or accessories.” Exemptions include: animal remedies compounded by Oregon-licensed veterinarians for use in their practice; animal food registered under ORS 633.015; dog/cat food licensed under ORS 619.031; and pesticides with an EPA number on retail packaging. Source: ODA Veterinary Product Registration page (search-indexed) — https://www.oregon.gov/oda/animal-health-feeds-livestock-id/ahlicensing/pages/veterinary-product-registration.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01. Whether a hemp CBD pet product marketed with health/well-being claims is an “animal remedy” requiring ODA veterinary-product registration IN ADDITION TO OLCC Hemp Registry registration (and ODA vendor licensing) is a product-claims determination — Verify with ODA for the specific product/claims. A product marketed merely as a treat, without remedy claims, and a product marketed as “for joint health / anxiety / pain” may fall on different sides of that line, and the registration consequences differ. Do not advise a manufacturer that OLCC registration alone suffices for a remedy-claimed pet product without that ODA check.

12.8.3 THC toxicity in pets — Oregon Veterinary Medical Association guidance (opened 2026-11-01)

From the Oregon Veterinary Medical Association (OVMA) “Marijuana & Pets” page (opened directly 2026-11-01 — https://www.oregonvma.org/care-health/companion-animals/health-safety/marijuana-pets):

  • Risk statement: “Pet owners should be aware of the potential risks to their dogs or cats if they ingest marijuana. THC is the component of marijuana that can cause illness in pets, particularly dogs. Please keep all cannabis plants, as well as products and foods containing marijuana, in secure locations such as pet-proof containers and in locked cabinets.”
  • Routes of poisoning: inhalation of smoke; ingestion of the plant; ingestion of products containing marijuana or hashish; ingestion of foods containing marijuana (“edibles”) such as brownies, cookies, candies, oils, and butter. “When foods also contain chocolate, the risk of poisoning is increased. Never leave a plate of marijuana-laced brownies or packages of marijuana edibles out where your dog can reach them.”
  • Symptoms (usually within 30–60 minutes of inhalation or ingestion): glassy eyes; stumbling / lack of coordination; disorientation; dilated pupils; drowsiness or agitation / excitement (dogs); urinary incontinence / dribbling (dogs); vomiting; tremors and seizures; coma.
  • Action: “Seek veterinary care promptly. While it’s rare for pets to ingest enough marijuana to be fatal, it can happen. Inform your veterinarian what the pet has ingested, as proper treatment can be administered only if the veterinarian is aware of the toxin. Treatment for cannabis toxicity can include decontamination of the GI tract, IV fluids, and anti-vomiting medication. In severe cases, it may include oxygen support, monitoring blood pressure, regulating the pet’s temperature, and ventilator/respiratory support.”
  • CBD for a sick pet (OVMA): “Please consult with your veterinarian before giving your pet any medication, herb or supplement, as there may be contraindications.” OVMA does not, on the page opened, endorse any CBD product, dose or condition — and neither does this draft.
  • Corroborating clinical detail (secondary, for the veterinarian/owner reader — not a substitute for veterinary advice): dogs and cats are significantly more sensitive to THC than humans (higher density of cannabinoid receptors); clinical signs often appear within 30 minutes to a few hours and may last 24–72 hours; small dogs/cats are at greatest risk per dose; most cases resolve with supportive care within 24–72 hours, but death, while rare, has occurred, particularly with very high-dose edibles; edibles may compound toxicity with chocolate or xylitol; ASPCA Animal Poison Control (888-426-4435) and Pet Poison Helpline (855-764-7661) are the 24/7 toxicology resources cited in secondary guides (agency/public helpline numbers, reproduced as official emergency resources). Sources: secondary — https://isitpoisonous.com/marijuana/ (reviewed 27 Apr 2026); https://www.vetgeni.com/guides/emergency-veterinary-toxicology-reference; https://herb.co/learn/420-pet-safety — accessed 2026-11-01. Doses, lethal-dose figures and specific treatment protocols (e.g. intralipid emulsion dosing in secondary toxicology references) are clinical matters for the treating veterinarian — this draft does not state a “safe” THC dose for any pet, and no such dose is established in the Oregon sources located.
  • No Oregon “THC toxicity” offence / reporting rule was located. There is no Oregon statute located that makes pet THC exposure a reportable offence or that imposes a specific penalty on an owner whose pet ingests marijuana, beyond general animal-cruelty / neglect law (ORS chapter 167 — Verify whether any animal-cruelty prosecution for cannabis exposure has been brought in Oregon; none was located). The OVMA guidance is animal-health guidance, not a criminal rule. A veterinarian treating a THC-exposed pet is not, on the material located, required to report the owner to law enforcement — Verify any OVMEB / mandatory-reporting rule before stating a reporting duty.

§12.9 Medical marijuana in schools

12.9.1 The headline — Oregon has NO enacted school-administration statute for medical marijuana as of 1 Nov 2026

This is the single most important correction in §12.9, because other states’ school-cannabis laws are routinely misattributed to Oregon:

  • SB 871 (2019) — the bill that would have created a school-administration regime — FAILED. Its OLIS staff summary states it would have allowed “school nurse, school nurse designee or designated primary caregiver of registry identification cardholder who is student enrolled in primary or secondary school to administer noncombustible medical cannabinoid product to student on premises of school or during school-sponsored event” and would have allowed “school to adopt policy prohibiting administration of noncombustible medical cannabinoid product to student” (OLIS summary — https://apps.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2019R1/Downloads/MeasureAnalysisDocument/45587 — accessed 2026-11-01). LegiScan records SB 871 as “Fail — In committee upon adjournment, 30 June 2019” (https://legiscan.com/OR/legislation/2019?sort=desc&order=Status&page=6&chamber=senate — accessed 2026-11-01). SB 871 is NOT law. Do not cite it as Oregon’s school-marijuana law, and do not describe its nurse/designee/caregiver administration model as current Oregon law.
  • No successor school-administration bill was located as enacted through the 1 Nov 2026 cut-off. The laws that do exist for other states — Maine, Colorado, New Jersey (parent/guardian/caregiver administration on school grounds, typically non-smokeable forms only), California’s Jojo’s Act (SB 223, 2019) — are not Oregon law and must not be presented as such. The Florida / Delaware / Maine district policies that dominate web search results for “medical marijuana school policy” (e.g. Sarasota / Bradford County, Florida policies; Delaware designated-caregiver rules) are not Oregon policies and were excluded from this section’s Oregon holdings for that reason.
  • What Oregon law DOES say about students and marijuana (the provisions that actually govern):
  • Public-use / possession framework: schools are expressly within the “public place” concept (Run 1 §1.1.1), and use of marijuana items in a public place is unlawful for any person (ORS 475C.377). A student who uses or possesses marijuana on school grounds, in a school vehicle, or at a school activity is therefore within the general prohibition, subject to the student-discipline and juvenile-justice systems (see §12.9.2), not within a school-administration exception.
  • Under-21 framework: ORS 475C.317 prohibits a person under 21 from possessing, attempting to purchase or purchasing a marijuana item (with the OMMP cardholder / caregiver framework as the medical exception for possession/use outside school — see §12.9.2). A minor OMMP patient may lawfully possess/use medical marijuana through a designated primary caregiver (custodial parent/guardian) outside school (Run 1 §1.1); that caregiver framework does not by itself authorise possession/use on school grounds or administration by school staff.
  • School medication-administration law (ORS 339.866–339.871) does NOT include medical marijuana. ORS 339.869 requires the State Board of Education (with OHA, the Board of Nursing and the Board of Pharmacy) to adopt rules for administration of prescription/nonprescription medication to students, including premeasured epinephrine, adrenal-insufficiency medication, and naloxone; ORS 339.871 shields a school administrator/nurse/teacher/designated employee from criminal/civil liability for good-faith assistance with a student’s self-administration of medication (as described in ORS 339.866, with written parental / licensed-professional permission/instructions) and for good-faith epinephrine administration. Medical marijuana is not a “medication” within ORS 339.866–339.871 on any text located — it is not prescribed by an Oregon-licensed health-care professional as a prescription drug (OMMP uses an “attending provider statement” that medical use “may mitigate” symptoms, not a prescription), and no ORS 339.869 rule located authorises school administration of a cannabinoid product. Verify the current ORS 339.866 definition of “medication” and any State Board rule before advising that school medication law covers cannabinoids — this draft proceeds on the basis that it does not.
  • HB 4142 (2026) (“Ryan’s Law”) is NOT a K-12 school law. HB 4142 (enacted 2026) expands the OMMP “debilitating medical condition” definition to include hospice/palliative/comfort-care need and imposes duties on organisations/residential facilities designated as additional caregivers (ORS 475C.791) to allow a qualifying patient/resident to engage in medical use on their premises, maintain a written policy, and provide staff education, with hospital/hospital-affiliated-clinic exemptions (Run 1 §1.2.1). It does not impose duties on K-12 schools, does not authorise school nurses to administer cannabinoids, and does not create a student school-administration right. Do not cite HB 4142 as a school law.

12.9.2 Student use, possession and discipline on school grounds — district policy + state discipline law

  • District practice (Oregon examples located): Oregon school handbooks located state the prohibition without a medical exception. Examples (secondary district documents, accessed 2026-11-01):
  • Walter L. Kraxberger Middle School (North Clackamas / Oregon district — handbook 2025–2026, via 5il.co): “Students being under the influence of, using, being in possession of and/or intending to possess, distribute, share or selling in any form will not be allowed on school property, in School District vehicles, or at school events or activities and violates Oregon Law and District policy” — with a 1st-offence consequence list including 5 days’ out-of-school suspension, referral to law enforcement, referral to drug/tobacco counselling, possible expulsion, and a safety plan. Source: https://5il.co/2yt97 — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • North Douglas High School (North Douglas School District, Oregon — handbook 2024–2025, revised 15 Aug 2024): “A student shall not possess, use, transmit, or be under the influence of alcohol or any illegal substance on school grounds, while traveling to and from school, or at a school activity, function, or event. Illegal substance includes, but is not limited to, any narcotic drug, hallucinogenic drug, amphetamine, barbiturate, marijuana, alcoholic beverages, any type of vapes, inhalant or intoxicant of any kind, including apparatus or paraphernalia.” Suspension up to 10 school days pending further process. Source: https://core-docs.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/documents/asset/uploaded_file/1762/NDSD/4913399/2024-25_NDHS_Student-Parent_Handbook_Revised_6-19-24.pdf — accessed 2026-11-01.
  • These are district policies, not state statutes. They illustrate the prevailing Oregon district position (no on-campus medical-use exception in the handbook text located), but each district’s policy must be checked individually — a district could, in principle, adopt a more accommodating practice for a specific student (e.g. allowing a parent to administer off-campus, or a 504/IEP accommodation discussion — see §12.9.4) without that practice appearing in a general handbook prohibition. Do not state that every Oregon district prohibits all medical-marijuana accommodation — state that no district policy located creates a general on-campus administration right, and that the handbooks located prohibit possession/use/influence on school property/vehicles/events.
  • State discipline framework: ORS 339.250 (duty of student to comply with rules; district discipline, suspension and expulsion requirements) is the state framework within which district drug policies operate (cited on the Oregon Department of Education substance-use page — https://www.oregon.gov/ode/educator-resources/standards/health/Pages/Substance-Use-Prevention-and-Intervention.aspx — accessed 2026-11-01). ODE’s substance-use page requires districts to have comprehensive prevention/intervention plans, including school policies/procedures on substance use, resources/referral processes, and staff training/procedures; to prohibit tobacco use/possession on school grounds; and to meet medication-administration requirements (including naloxone). ODE’s page as indexed does not state a medical-marijuana school-administration policy — Verify ODE’s current guidance; the absence of a medical-cannabis item on that page is consistent with §12.9.1 (no state school-administration regime), but absence on an indexed page is not proof of absence in ODE guidance generally.
  • The North Bend illustration (why districts are cautious): a 2017-era report on the federal/state school conflict quotes Brad Bixler, communications specialist with the North Bend School District (Oregon), stating students who are registered medical-marijuana patients “could have an identified need to access some of the cannabis plant during the school day,” but “because it’s not a prescription from a doctor, we can’t handle it through our prescription medication policy and it isn’t something we can sign off on because it’s not an over-the-counter medication. We’re really restricted on what we can do” (secondary — https://merryjane.com/news/state-and-federal-laws-at-odds-over-allowing-medical-marijuana-on-school-grounds/ — accessed 2026-11-01). That quotation, while old, captures the structural reason Oregon districts do not administer: without a prescription, the school medication system has no hook for cannabinoids, and without a school-administration statute, the district has no authorisation to create one.
