  • Off-campus / parent-administration workaround (practice, not a right): in the absence of a statute, the practical route families use in other states — and the route a district may accommodate as a matter of discretion — is for a parent/guardian/caregiver to administer the student’s medical product off school grounds (e.g. at home before/after school, or by the student leaving campus with parental permission for administration off grounds and returning). No Oregon statute located guarantees a student the right to leave campus for that purpose, guarantees re-admission after off-campus administration, or protects a student who returns to campus under the influence from discipline under the district’s “under the influence” policy. Each of those is a district-policy / 504 / IEP question (see §12.9.4) — Verify with the specific district. A student who is “under the influence” on campus after off-campus administration may still face discipline under the handbook prohibitions quoted above, even if the administration itself was lawful off-campus.
  • Smoking/vaping on school grounds is doubly barred: ORS 475C.377 (public place — schools are listed) + ICAA (schools as public places / places of employment; state-park/school-grounds outdoor restrictions noted in secondary ICAA summaries) + district tobacco/vape prohibitions. Non-smokeable forms do not cure the school-grounds problem — the bar is on possession/use/administration on school grounds as a matter of district policy + 475C.377, not only on smoking. SB 871’s “noncombustible” limitation (had it passed) would have addressed only the smoking aspect, not the possession/administration authorisation — and it did not pass.

12.9.3 School employees — no accommodation duty, drug-free workplace, and the Washburn rule

  • No duty to accommodate medical use in the workplace (ORS 475C.780, verbatim): “Nothing in ORS 475C.770 to 475C.919 requires: (1) A government medical assistance program or private health insurer to reimburse a person for costs associated with the medical use of marijuana; or (2) An employer to accommodate the medical use of marijuana in the workplace. [Formerly 475B.794]” Source: ORS 475C.780 (Justia 2025) — https://law.justia.com/codes/oregon/volume-14/chapter-475c/section-475c-780/ — accessed 2026-11-01. Schools, as employers, are within that rule: a school district is not required to accommodate a teacher’s, nurse’s or other employee’s medical marijuana use in the workplace — including use on school premises, being under the influence at work, or a positive drug test.
  • Adult-use construction (ORS 475C.013): the adult-use statutes “may not be construed to amend or affect state or federal law pertaining to employment matters” (Run 1 §1.2.2, secondary summary — Verify verbatim text). Together, 475C.780 + 475C.013 mean Oregon cannabis legalisation did not create a right to use at work, to be impaired at work, or to force an employer to tolerate either (secondary employment-law summary — https://www.americanscreeningcorp.com/blogs/news/drug-testing-laws-oregon — accessed 2026-11-01).
  • Washburn v. Columbia Forest Products (Or. 2010, secondary summary): the Oregon Supreme Court held an employer had no duty to accommodate an employee’s medical-marijuana use, and that an employee whose condition is mitigated by medical marijuana is not thereby protected as “disabled” for the marijuana use itself in the manner the employee claimed (secondary summaries — https://www.nationaldrugscreening.com/marijuana-considerations/oregon/; https://www.bigreport.com/resource-center/occupational-health-screening/the-evolving-world-of-medical-marijuana-and-employment-drug-screening/ — accessed 2026-11-01). Verify the Washburn citation and holding against the opinion — the secondary summaries agree on the no-accommodation holding but differ in their disability-law glosses, and this draft states only the no-accommodation holding as settled.
  • School-employee drug policies in practice: Salem-Keizer Public Schools’ practicum/student-teacher policy agreement (revised 17 May 2024, secondary district document — accessed 2026-11-01) illustrates the district-employer position: “No employee shall unlawfully manufacture, distribute, dispense, possess (including possession by ingestion), or use at the workplace, on school premises, or as part of any District activity, alcohol, tobacco, tobacco look-a-likes, electronic cigarettes, or any narcotic, hallucinogenic drug, amphetamine, barbiturate, marijuana, or any other controlled substance as defined in Schedules I through V of the Controlled Substances Act … or any substance that is illegal under federal or state law.” That policy’s reference to Schedules I–V (federal schedules) means the Schedule III medical change does not, on that policy’s wording, remove medical marijuana from the prohibition — but whether a district updates such a policy after Schedule III, and whether “illegal under federal … law” still captures state-licensed medical use after 28 April 2026, is Verify (see §12.9.4). School employees in safety-sensitive / federally regulated roles (e.g. school-bus drivers under DOT rules) face additional federal drug-testing and prohibition rules that Oregon law does not displace.
  • SB 176 (2025) — the died bill that would have changed employment law (not law): SB 176 (2025) would, in MPP’s summary, have prohibited employers from hiring/firing solely on medical-patient status or a positive metabolite test, among other OMMP reforms. It died in Joint Ways and Means on adjournment, 27 June 2025 (Run 1 §1.2.1). Do not cite SB 176 as an employment protection — Oregon has no such protection as of this cut-off. The 2026 session produced no successor employment-protection bill located in this run — Verify on OLIS if a 2026 employment bill is asserted.
  • Nurses and the Board of Nursing (Verify): HB 4142 (2026) summaries state it “prohibits the Oregon State Board of Nursing from disciplining a nurse for discussing medical cannabis” (Run 1 §1.2.1 — Verify enrolled text). That is a discussion protection for nurses generally, not a school-nurse administration authorisation, and not a school-employee use protection. Do not conflate “may discuss” with “may administer” or “may use at work.”

12.9.4 Federal funding tension — why a school cannot simply “allow it” (and why Schedule III does not resolve it) — Verify

  • The federal tension, as it stood pre-Schedule III and as reported: (i) the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) requires districts to provide a free appropriate public education in the least restrictive environment, including accommodations for children with disabilities; (ii) federal drug law bans possession/use of controlled substances (including state-legal medical cannabis, when Schedule I) within 1,000 feet of a school (21 U.S.C. §860, drug-free school zone — secondary summary, Verify section and penalty); (iii) federal education funding (including Drug-Free Schools / Elementary and Secondary Education Act drug-free requirements, and the federal Drug-Free Workplace Act for federal grantees/contractors) conditions funding on drug-free school/workplace policies. A district that allowed medical marijuana on campus risked, on the secondary analysis, violating federal law and potentially jeopardising federal funding. Source: secondary — https://merryjane.com/news/state-and-federal-laws-at-odds-over-allowing-medical-marijuana-on-school-grounds/ — accessed 2026-11-01. The “funding cuts” consequence is stated in secondary sources as a risk (“could potentially lead to federal funding cuts”), not as a documented instance of Oregon funding actually being cut for a medical-marijuana school policy — no such Oregon funding-cut instance was located, and none is asserted here.
  • Schedule III question (Verify — federal text does not settle Oregon school application): the federal baseline moves state-licensed medical marijuana to Schedule III eff. 28 April 2026. Whether that change (a) removes state-licensed medical marijuana from the federal drug-free school-zone prohibition, (b) removes it from federal drug-free workplace / grantee requirements, (c) changes the “controlled substance” analysis for school discipline, or (d) does none of those things because the school-zone / funding statutes use their own definitions or because Oregon school use is not “state-licensed medical” in the federal order’s sense (OMMP registration vs OLCC licence — Run 1 Part 1 Verify point), was NOT established in this run and is marked Verify in full. Do not advise a district, family or employee that Schedule III “solves” the school problem, or that it “does nothing” — both statements require the federal order’s text + the funding statutes’ text, neither of which was opened for this section.
  • 504 / IEP / disability-accommodation route (Verify — the only live individual route located, and it is not a cannabis right): a student with a disability that qualifies for a Section 504 plan or an Individualized Education Program (IEP) may seek accommodations for the underlying condition (e.g. seizure disorder, chronic pain, nausea) through the 504/IEP process. Whether a 504/IEP team may, or must, accommodate medical marijuana administration on campus as the means of accommodating the condition is Verify and, on the material located, unresolved in Oregon — no Oregon 504/IEP medical-marijuana determination was located, and the federal drug-free / Schedule III questions above would need to be resolved first. A family pursuing this route should do so through the district’s 504/IEP process with legal advice, not by relying on a general “medical marijuana in schools” right that Oregon has not enacted.
  • Higher education (brief note — Verify scope): this section addresses K-12 primary/secondary schools, as the task specifies (“student use, school employee rules, SB/HB law, administration on school property”). Oregon colleges/universities have their own drug-free campus policies (federal Drug-Free Schools and Communities Act, 20 U.S.C. §1011i, + campus policies) and are not covered by the K-12 analysis above. Verify any college/university’s cannabis policy separately — a university’s federal funding exposure differs from a K-12 district’s, and campus housing is also subject to §12.6.6’s federal-housing analysis.
